
# SOURCE: assessment_workspace/canon/AKKI_Canon_Addendum_1.docx
Coordinate: document.xml paragraph in body order, tables included

1: AKKI CANON — ADDENDUM 1
2: Gap Closures, Amendments, and New Promise Candidates
3: Companion to Documents 1–16 and the build audit. The 16 canon documents are unedited by this addendum — amendments are recorded here and target their document by number; nothing is rewritten in place.
4: 1 · Confirmed Closures
5: Six promises the canon already specified in full, where the gap was in the build, not the specification. Recorded here, not rewritten — no canon change was needed.
6: #4
7: Canon already fully specified the two-item custody split (Doc 2). Gap was build-only: no surface distinguished it. Closed by the audit trail Overview stating when an answer drew on 2+ independently-governed units.
8: #17
9: Canon already fully specified minimal-sufficient disclosure (Doc 6). Gap was build-only. Closed by the audit trail Overview stating how many available source units were actually served.
10: #19 / #20 / #21
11: Canon already fully specified the five-ring unit and warm/fresh fork (Docs 7–8). Gap was build-only. Closed by a Registry densification stat and a per-turn warm/fresh tag — flagged here as a partial closure, not a full one.
12: #24
13: Canon already fully specified licence-verified baseline curation (Doc 14). Gap was build-only. Closed by a baseline line naming the licence-verified starting model per training run.
14: #25
15: Canon already fully specified exceptional-run retention and egress governance (Doc 14). Gap was build-only. Closed by a “Prepare white paper” action drafting from the run's own artefacts.
16: #26
17: Canon already fully specified the Watch's self-contained exception (Doc 15). Gap was build-only. Closed by a State line naming the Watch's own containment and external witness.
18: 2 · Amendments to Existing Documents
19: Six targeted additions to promises already in service. Each amends one existing document; none introduces a new promise.
20: Amendment to Document 2, Promise #2
21: Add a dry-run preview step between Review and Adopt in the declaration workflow: given a candidate declaration, the platform runs it against a bounded sample of recent traffic and returns what it would and would not have caught, before the DPO adopts it. Without this, #2's own promise — that the organisation can verify what it's declaring, not just state it — is only half kept.
22: Amendment to Document 11, Promise #9
23: Add a Cost Ledger surface exposing the lever sequence itself — cache → route → narrow → cascade → waste report — as named, ordered steps with the saving attributable to each, not just the final per-call cost. The ladder-rung mechanism already exists (Doc 11 §5); this is a visibility requirement on top of it, not a new mechanism.
24: Amendment to Document 15, Promise #32
25: Generalise the registered handoff contract (what / shape / identity / receipt) to every cross-app crossing, not the single ThinkLab→Task Manager instance. Any new hand-off added to the platform must be expressed in this contract before it ships, the same way any new model call must cross the single chokepoint in Document 1.
26: Amendment to Document 4, Promise #8
27: Scope the “lower the standard” refusal action to the originating session, with a logged expiry. Today it is offered without a stated boundary; unscoped, a standard lowered for one question can persist as the de facto floor for every question after it, which is the exact failure #8 exists to prevent.
28: Amendment to Document 13, Promise #22
29: Add a standing re-check date, visible per in-service model, on the same cadence the six acceptance criteria already run on. An early failure on a re-check routes to the Watch (Document 3) the same way behavioural drift already does — model degradation is a Watch-relevant event, not only a training-pipeline one.
30: Amendment to Document 15, Promise #27
31: Extend the Watch's existing self-flagging of stale baits (Document 3) to rulebook re-certification and training baselines: anything adopted from an external standard carries a staleness check against that standard's own revision history, using the same flagging mechanism rather than a new one.
32: 3 · New Promise Candidates — Full Write-Up
33: Thirteen items: eight already built with no canon backing (A1–A8), five not yet built or specified (N1–N5). Promise and Delivery Experience are written with the same confidence as Documents 1–16. Technical Requirements are not, because the source material to write them honestly does not exist yet — in place of a placeholder, each entry states the specific open questions that stand between it and a fully specified promise.
34: A1  Board submission traceability
35: Beyond canon — built (Board 360)
36: Promise
37: Any formal submission made to an oversight or governance body can be checked against what was actually said, and questioned directly where the record and current understanding disagree.
38: Delivery Experience
39: User can open a board signal and see the submission it came from
40: User can ask a question against a board document and get a threaded, attributed answer
41: User can see which submissions are on record and which are still pending
42: Open Design Questions — not yet answered
43: What custody class do board submissions themselves carry — governed under Document 1's estate rules, or a separate class with its own crossing rules?
44: When a cited submission is later amended or superseded, does the Q&A thread's citation re-verify against the new version, on the same freshness logic Document 9's census already uses for estate sources, or does it silently point at stale material?
45: Is authorship of a question in this thread access-controlled on Document 6's minimal-sufficient-disclosure logic, or open to anyone who can already see the board document?
46: 
47: A2  Tracked commitment / goal traceability
48: Beyond canon — built (Exco 360)
49: Promise
50: Any tracked commitment or goal can be checked against what is actually happening, with every system-generated recommendation traceable to the observation that produced it.
51: Delivery Experience
52: User can see which tracked goals are off track and why
53: User can open any recommendation and trace it back to the signal behind it
54: User can confirm or challenge a tracked goal against the source strategy document
55: Open Design Questions — not yet answered
56: When a human challenges a tracked goal, is that recorded as a new artifact on Document 5's append-only Ledger pattern, or does it just update a status flag in place — the second option loses exactly the kind of history the other 31 promises are built to keep?
57: If a recommendation's underlying signal is later found wrong or retracted, is there a supersession chain for the recommendation itself, on the pattern Document 10 already uses for duplicate or superseded estate records?
58: 
59: A3  Governed artefact inheritance and distribution visibility
60: Beyond canon — built (Documents suite)
61: Promise
62: Any artefact produced from governed work inherits that work's evidence and custody guarantees, and its distribution afterward stays visible rather than going dark.
63: Delivery Experience
64: User can generate a document or deck from any chat and have it keep the conversation's evidence class
65: User can see everywhere a committed document has travelled
66: User can ask a follow-up question on a committed document and get a cited, threaded answer
67: Open Design Questions — not yet answered
68: If a source chat mixed material from more than one custody class (for example, Document 2's dual-file split), which class does the generated document inherit — the strictest of the two, or does the document need its own mixed-custody marker?
69: Is the Exposure Site Map itself an append-only record on Document 5's Ledger-writer pattern, or a mutable view that could be edited after the fact?
70: Does distribution tracking cover material shared outside the platform (downloaded, emailed) the same way it covers internal sharing, or does visibility stop at the platform boundary?
71: 
72: A4  Governed template adoption
73: Beyond canon — built (Rule Books Library)
74: Promise
75: The organisation can start from conventional, professional-standard templates mapped to recognised frameworks, and adopt or modify them through the same governed ceremony as an original rule.
76: Delivery Experience
77: User can read a template's controls before adopting it
78: User can adopt a template as-is, or modify individual rules within it, either way through the same sign-off and countdown as a hand-authored rule
79: Open Design Questions — not yet answered
80: When the external framework itself revises (a new ISO 27001 edition), what re-certifies an adopted rulebook against it — the same rule-version stamping Document 15 already uses, or does template provenance need its own staleness check?
81: If a template rule is modified after adoption, does it keep its framework-provenance tag, or fork into an org-authored rule with no further tie to the standard it came from?
82: 
83: A5  Universal entitlement and shielding discipline
84: Beyond canon — built (Collab group)
85: Promise
86: Every surface on the platform carries the same entitlement and shielding discipline, including categories of data that must never surface at the individual level regardless of who is asking.
87: Delivery Experience
88: User can open email or mentions and see the shielding account for that surface
89: User can open HR Stuff and see only aggregate figures, never an individual record
90: Open Design Questions — not yet answered
91: What is the minimum aggregation threshold that qualifies as “aggregate”, and is it fixed platform-wide or configurable per category the way declared-confidential categories are in Document 2?
92: Is the aggregate-only rule truly universal with no override, or can a Master Admin or DPO see individual-level HR records under an investigation exception — and if so, does that exception get the same receipted-crossing treatment Document 1 gives every other exception to a hard line?
93: 
94: A6  Threshold-gated commitment routing
95: Beyond canon — built (Spend Requests)
96: Promise
97: Any commitment above an agreed threshold routes to a named accountable person for an explicit decision, rather than proceeding unchecked or stalling silently.
98: Delivery Experience
99: User can see exactly which requests need a person, and why
100: User can approve or decline with the run's cost and objective already attached
101: Open Design Questions — not yet answered
102: Is the auto-approve ceiling itself a rule governed by Document 15's propose/counter-sign/countdown ceremony, or a plain config value any admin can change unilaterally?
103: Does the approver see the same feasibility/cost/budget reflection the requester saw at Document 12's reflection-before-commit step, or a reduced summary?
104: 
105: A7  Cross-app hand-off of governed work
106: Beyond canon — built (ThinkLab → Task Manager). Generalisation already tracked — see Amendments, Document 15 Promise #32.
107: Promise
108: The conclusion of governed work in one part of the platform can become the starting point of work in another part, without re-typing, re-arguing, or losing the evidence it rested on.
109: Delivery Experience
110: User can end a ThinkLab session and hand it to Task Manager in one action, with the reasoning attached, not just the conclusion
111: Open Design Questions — not yet answered
112: Does the hand-off carry Document 4's full reasoning trace, so downstream work can re-open the tension/contradiction view Solva produced, or only the concluded load-bearing set — which is a materially thinner promise than it sounds?
113: 
114: A8  Universal claim-to-evidence trace
115: Beyond canon — built (“Walk this →”)
116: Promise
117: Any number, claim, or state anywhere on the platform can be traced to the mechanism or evidence behind it, in place, without losing your spot on the page.
118: Delivery Experience
119: User can from any figure or claim, click once to reveal what produced it — the same affordance everywhere on the platform
120: Open Design Questions — not yet answered
121: Does “Walk this →” inherit the source data's custody rules, so a viewer without access to the underlying estate region is refused the same way Document 1's chokepoint would refuse them — or can it leak view access to material the viewer isn't otherwise entitled to see? This is the load-bearing question: an unscoped trace affordance is a second, ungoverned path to the same data Document 1 built one chokepoint specifically to control.
122: 
123: N1  Retention enforcement and attestation
124: New — not yet built or fully specified
125: Promise
126: Data past its declared retention date is actually deleted, and that deletion is attested — not merely declared as policy.
127: Delivery Experience
128: partially grounded already: a Legal Hold & Retention Rulebook can be adopted today, and refusal traces already carry a 90-day retention figure
129: Open Design Questions — not yet answered
130: Does scheduled, retention-triggered deletion run through Document 15's full ceremony (propose / counter-sign / countdown), or does a non-discretionary, date-triggered deletion need a lighter path, since no one is exercising judgement at the moment it fires?
131: When a legal hold and an expired retention date apply to the same data simultaneously, does the hold override indefinitely, and who holds authority to lift it — does this need its own authority model, on the pattern Document 15 already uses for the Watch's singular exception?
132: 
133: N2  Time-boxed breach and incident notification
134: New — not yet built or fully specified
135: Promise
136: When a hard line is tested and fails, a defined notification reaches a named recipient within a stated time.
137: Delivery Experience
138: no built instance — the platform currently promises prevention and containment, not what happens after a failure
139: Open Design Questions — not yet answered
140: What specifically constitutes the trigger — only a confirmed successful bypass the Watch detects (Documents 3–4), or also a near-miss or attempted breach that was contained?
141: Does notification routing extend the Watch's existing self-witnessing structure (Document 15's one exception), making the Watch the owner of breach notification, or does this need an authority independent of the Watch, since the Watch cannot credibly be the sole reporter of its own containment failures?
142: 
143: N3  Individual access-and-erasure request
144: New — not yet built or fully specified
145: Promise
146: A named individual — customer or employee — can ask what the estate holds on them, and ask for its erasure.
147: Delivery Experience
148: no built instance — today's promises protect data from the organisation's own use, not from the organisation on the individual's behalf
149: Open Design Questions — not yet answered
150: An individual's data can exist as raw source, as a five-ring normalised unit (Document 7), and embedded in a trained model's weights (Document 13). Does “erasure” reach all three layers, including retraining or discarding any model trained on the erased data — and if a model cannot practically be untrained, what does the promise actually guarantee at that layer?
151: What verifies the requester is the individual whose data is being requested? This is close to its own promise — an identity-verification guarantee this request depends on but does not itself supply.
152: 
153: N4  Data residency and cross-border transfer control
154: New — not yet built or fully specified
155: Promise
156: Data is held only where authorised, and never crosses a jurisdiction boundary the organisation has not permitted.
157: Delivery Experience
158: partially grounded already: per-source region is recorded at connection (Document 9's Connect wizard already captures reference, region, and feed identity per source)
159: Open Design Questions — not yet answered
160: Document 12 defines “in-perimeter” as a single boundary. Does a multi-region deployment mean multiple perimeters, or one perimeter spanning regions? This has to be settled before a residency rule can be written — residency is meaningless without a defined boundary to hold it against.
161: Given per-source region is already captured (Document 9), is the remaining gap purely an enforcement rule — a hard line refusing any operation that would move data across a declared boundary — layered on data that's already tagged, rather than a new tracking mechanism?
162: 
163: N5  Continuity of the governed record
164: New — not yet built or fully specified
165: Promise
166: The append-only Ledger, receipts, and audit trail survive an outage, with a stated recovery time.
167: Delivery Experience
168: no built instance — every other promise in this set depends on these records existing; none state what happens if they don't
169: Open Design Questions — not yet answered
170: Is continuity a replication/backup property of the same Ledger writer (Document 5), or does it need its own independently-governed layer, on the pattern Document 15 gives the Watch its own separate record classes — and if so, who verifies a backup's integrity when the primary verification mechanism is the thing that's down?

# SOURCE: assessment_workspace/canon/drops/20260907/extracted/files_11/Rules_Service_Spec_v1.docx
Coordinate: document.xml paragraph in body order, tables included

1: AKKI PLATFORM  ·  ENGINE SPECIFICATION
2: The Rules Service
3: rulebook_engine_spec_v1 — Draft for owner ratification
4: Position
5: The platform's Policy Administration Point. The third component outside the six engines, alongside the Watch and the Ledger: the Watch observes the six, the Ledger records for the six, the Rules Service administers policy for the six.
6: Canon basis
7: Doc 3 A5.11 — “the rules service administers ceremony without editorial power.” Doc 15 Promise #27 — Manage Rules, its customer-facing surface. rule_criteria_spec_v1 — the rule model it administers. Document 0 Attribute 5 — every checkpoint names its PAP; Attribute 9 — authority and change control.
8: Prefix
9: RBM — reserved under ROC-6 on ratification.
10: Status
11: Draft v1. Every requirement PROPOSED until ratified. Four rulings parked (§9); none block Tier 1 or Tier 2 workflows.
12: Date
13: 4 September 2026
14: 1   Purpose & Scope
15: The Rules Service owns the lifecycle of every rule on the platform — system and customer — from authorship through retirement. It is creator mode: where a rule is written, classified, proposed, reviewed, ratified, versioned, adopted, and retired. It is not operating mode: it does not decide what a rule means at runtime (the decision points do) and it does not enforce one (the enforcement points do). It is the only path by which a rule enters or leaves force, and it has no editorial power over the content of any rule it administers — including its own.
16: It closes four open gaps in Document 0's register directly: G-2 (the Rule Registry as a standing artefact), G-4 (assessment procedures per rule), G-5 (a named Policy Administration Point for every checkpoint), and G-9 (a documented change-control procedure for system rules).
17: 2   Definitions
18: Term
19: Meaning
20: Rule
21: Per rule_criteria_spec_v1 ROC-1: individually addressable, a requirement not an explanation, falsifiable.
22: Rule book
23: A named, versioned set of rules derived from a stated source — a regulation, a standard, or the platform's own canon.
24: Profile
25: A named bundle of rule books recommended for a business type at onboarding.
26: Tier
27: The ceremony a rule is subject to: system-TCB, system-ordinary, or customer.
28: Ceremony
29: The ratification procedure for a tier: propose → impact record → countersign → cancellable countdown → apply → re-verify.
30: Registry
31: The single standing Rule Registry required by ROC-10 and kept append-only under ROC-11. The Rules Service's authoritative store.
32: Adoption
33: Instantiating a library rule book's rules as customer rules for one tenant, through the customer-tier ceremony.
34: Origination class
35: Per rule_criteria_spec_v1 §3: RATIFIED-EXTERNAL, PROMISE-DECOMPOSED, OWNER-DIRECTED, ASSISTANT-PROPOSED, EXTENSION.
36: 3   Invariants
37: Five properties that must hold at all times. Every requirement in §4 exists to keep one of them true.
38: I-1  No rule is in force that has not completed the ceremony for its tier.
39: I-2  Every in-force rule is in the Registry with every field ROC-10 requires.
40: I-3  No customer rule relaxes a system rule whose enforcement class is STRUCTURAL or MECHANICAL.
41: I-4  Every state change of every rule is written to the Ledger, append-only, before the change takes effect.
42: I-5  The Rules Service's own rules change only through the ceremony it administers. It administers; it does not edit.
43: 4   Normative Requirements
44: Authoring
45: RBM-1  A rule is authored in plain language and MUST carry, at creation: a unique ID under rule_criteria_spec_v1 §4; an origination class and citation; an owning subsystem; an enforcement class; a domain; a tier; an assessment procedure (examine, test, or both, with named objects); and status PROPOSED. Authoring MUST refuse to save a rule missing any field.
46: RBM-2  Drafting assistance MAY propose statement text, classification, tier, or an assessment procedure. Every proposal is marked as assisted and MUST be confirmed by the named human author before the rule enters PROPOSED. The assistant proposes; it never ratifies.  [Attribute 10]
47: RBM-3  A mnemonic prefix MUST be reserved through the Rules Service before first use. A collision with an existing prefix is refused at reservation and recorded.  [ROC-6]
48: RBM-4  A rule's tier is declared at authoring and determines its ceremony. A rule governing any component in the Trusted Computing Base enumeration (Document 0 Attribute 1) is system-TCB; any other system rule is system-ordinary; any rule authored by or adopted for a tenant is customer.
49: Impact analysis
50: RBM-5  Before countersign, the Rules Service MUST produce an impact record: for an amendment or retirement, every rule, checkpoint, component, and profile that cites or depends on the rule; for a new rule, every checkpoint and component it would constrain. The record is part of the ceremony's evidence.  [NIST CM-3]
51: RBM-6  For every customer rule and every rule in a rule book being adopted, the Rules Service MUST check the rule against the system rule set and MUST refuse any rule that would relax a system rule tagged STRUCTURAL or MECHANICAL. The refusal names the system rule.  [rule_criteria_spec_v1 §8]
52: Ceremony
53: RBM-7  System-ordinary and customer tiers: propose → impact record → countersign by a second named authority → cancellable countdown → apply → re-verify. Countdown length per tier is a ruled value (§9 R-1).
54: RBM-8  System-TCB tier: as RBM-7, plus the platform's slowest countdown and an external witness holding no credentials over the component the rule governs.  [Doc 3 A5.8, A5.11; Document 0 BR-7.3]
55: RBM-9  Either signatory MAY cancel a ceremony before its countdown expires. Cancellation is recorded with the canceller's identity and stated reason. A cancelled ceremony returns the rule to PROPOSED; it does not delete the proposal.
56: RBM-10  Apply MUST be atomic: set status CANON, write the Registry entry, write the Ledger record, and stamp the new rule-version for every subsequent run — or none of the four. A partial apply is a failure that leaves the prior state intact.  [Doc 15 #27]
57: RBM-11  Re-verify MUST run the rule's assessment procedure after apply and record the result. A failed re-verify raises a recorded finding routed to the countersigning authority; it does not silently roll back.
58: Amend, retire
59: RBM-12  An amendment is a new version through the full ceremony for its tier. The prior version is retained in the Registry with its full history, never overwritten.  [ROC-11]
60: RBM-13  Retirement is through ceremony. A retired rule remains in the Registry with status RETIRED and its history intact. Where the rule's own terms require it, retirement produces a destruction attestation.  [Doc 15 #27]
61: Library, profiles, adoption
62: RBM-14  The library holds rule books. Each is versioned, cites its source standard or regulation by clause, and holds every rule in the format RBM-1 requires. A rule book with an uncited rule is not admissible to the library.
63: RBM-15  A profile is a named bundle of rule books recommended for one business type. Profiles are versioned and change through the system-ordinary ceremony. The business-type taxonomy is itself a ruled, versioned list (§7).
64: RBM-16  At onboarding, the tenant's business type is selected from the taxonomy and the Rules Service MUST present the matching profile's rule books as a recommendation, marked as such. A business type with no profile receives the base bundle — personal data protection and AI-system governance — and the absence of a specific profile is recorded as a finding.  [Component 14, Connect Wizard]
65: RBM-17  Adoption instantiates a rule book's rules as customer rules for that tenant, through the customer-tier ceremony, after RBM-6's conflict check on every rule. A recommendation is never auto-applied; adoption requires the tenant's accountable person as proposer.
66: Registry, assessment
67: RBM-18  The Registry is the Rules Service's authoritative store: every field per ROC-10, append-only per ROC-11, written to the Ledger's custody discipline.
68: RBM-19  The Rules Service MUST be able to run any rule's assessment procedure on demand and on a stated schedule, recording each result against the rule. The Statement of Applicability is a Registry view, not a separately maintained document.
69: RBM-20  Every Registry query resolves by rule ID, objective, promise, tier, status, enforcement class, domain, rule book, profile, or tenant.
70: Self-governance and audit
71: RBM-21  The Rules Service's own requirements (RBM-*) are system-TCB tier. No code path exists by which the Rules Service alters an RBM-* rule outside RBM-8's ceremony.  [I-5]
72: RBM-22  Every Rules Service action — author, reserve, propose, impact, countersign, cancel, apply, re-verify, amend, retire, recommend, adopt, assess — writes an audit record to the Ledger carrying all six AU-3 elements: event type, time from the platform's reliable time source, component, source, outcome including failure, and the identity of the acting principal.  [Document 0 Attribute 8]
73: 5   Position in the Architecture
74: The Rules Service is a subsystem by Document 0's Attribute 2 test — it owns an invariant no other component owns: that nothing is in force without ceremony. It is placed outside the six engines rather than as a seventh for the same reason the Watch and the Ledger are: it serves all six equally and must not be subordinate to any. In NIST SP 800-162's terms, the six engines are the platform's Policy Decision and Enforcement Points; the Rules Service is its Policy Administration Point. Manage Rules (Promise #27) is its customer-facing surface; the Connect Wizard (Component 14) is its onboarding hook.
75: Adding the Rules Service amends Document 0 Part 2 with a new component entry, and turns “six engines plus two” — as stated in Document 0 and the product brief — into “six engines plus three.” Both should be updated on ratification.
76: 6   Dependencies
77: Dependency
78: What the Rules Service takes from it
79: rule_criteria_spec_v1
80: The rule model: definition (ROC-1), ID schemes (ROC-3–6), three classification axes (ROC-7–9), Registry fields and custody (ROC-10–11), the system/customer boundary (§8).
81: Document 0 — Attribute 1
82: The TCB enumeration that determines system-TCB tier (RBM-4). Until G-1 closes, tier assignment for TCB components is by the Attribute 1 test applied at authoring, recorded as such.
83: Doc 5 — the Ledger
84: The append-only record every ceremony step and Registry write lands on.
85: Doc 3 A5.8, A5.11
86: The Watch's ceremony as precedent for the system-TCB tier; and the one rule set the Rules Service administers with explicitly no editorial power.
87: Doc 15 #27 — Manage Rules
88: The customer-facing surface: plain-language authoring, templates, the ceremony steps, version history, destruction attestation.
89: Component 14 — Connect Wizard
90: The onboarding checkpoint where business type is selected and RBM-16's recommendation is presented.
91: Platform reliable time source
92: Required by RBM-22; specified under Document 0 G-8's fix.
93: 7   Business-Type Taxonomy — v1
94: A ruled, versioned list, extensible through the system-ordinary ceremony. Two business types receive the same profile only if the regulation that governs them is the same; where regulators differ, so do types. Ten entries and a base fallback.
95: Business type
96: Profile — rule books recommended
97: Healthcare — hospital / clinic
98: Health data · Personal data protection · AI-system governance
99: Media — broadcaster
100: Media & archive rights · Personal data protection · AI-system governance
101: Media — content acquisition / production
102: Media & archive rights (licensing emphasis) · Personal data protection · AI-system governance
103: Financial services — bank
104: Financial data access · Personal data protection · AI-system governance
105: Financial services — insurer
106: Financial data access (insurance regulator variant) · Personal data protection · AI-system governance
107: Agriculture / agri-tech
108: Personal data protection · AI-system governance · (agricultural-data book: skeleton only in v1)
109: University / research institution
110: Research & academic data · Personal data protection · AI-system governance
111: Telecommunications
112: Personal data protection · AI-system governance · (telecoms regulator book: skeleton only in v1)
113: Government / public sector
114: Personal data protection · AI-system governance · (public-sector book: skeleton only in v1)
115: Other / not listed
116: Base bundle — Personal data protection · AI-system governance — with a recorded finding per RBM-16
117: 8   Build Acceptance Criteria
118: #
119: Test
120: Pass criterion
121: A1
122: No force without ceremony: attempt to set a rule CANON by any path other than RBM-10
123: Refused; attempt recorded on the Ledger
124: A2
125: Conflict check: adopt a seeded rule book containing a rule that relaxes a STRUCTURAL system rule
126: That rule refused, naming the system rule; the rest of the book proceeds
127: A3
128: Append-only: attempt to overwrite or delete a Registry entry
129: Refused; prior versions intact; attempt recorded
130: A4
131: Self-governance: attempt to alter an RBM-* rule outside RBM-8's ceremony
132: Refused; no code path exists; attempt recorded
133: A5
134: Recommendation: onboard one tenant per taxonomy entry, plus one unlisted
135: Each receives its profile's books; unlisted receives base bundle plus a finding; nothing auto-applied
136: A6
137: Atomic apply: induce failure between Registry write and Ledger write
138: Neither write persists; rule remains PROPOSED
139: A7
140: Audit completeness: replay a full ceremony
141: Every action present on the Ledger with all six AU-3 elements
142: 9   Owner Rulings — Parked
143: R-1  Countdown lengths per tier — system-TCB, system-ordinary, customer.
144: R-2  The second signatory for system-ordinary rules: a named role, and who currently holds it.
145: R-3  The external witness for system-TCB rules: the same witness the Watch uses, or a separate one.
146: R-4  Ratification of the v1 business-type taxonomy (§7) as the standing list.
147: Nothing in §4 is blocked by these. Authoring, impact analysis, the Registry, and the library workflows are fully specified; only the countdown values, the signatory role, and the witness identity are open, and each is a single-line ruling.

# SOURCE: assessment_workspace/canon/drops/20260907/extracted/files_12/Security_Promise_Set_Amendments.docx

1: AKKI PLATFORM  ·  CHANGE REGISTER
2: Amendments — Security Assurance Promise Set
3: 8 amendments · 3 September 2026
4: Applies to
5: Security_Assurance_Promise_Set.xlsx (S-1–S-21) and akki_governance_architecture_v1 (Document 0)
6: Nature
7: Corrections to claims made while drafting the promise set, and cross-document updates the set's evidence requires. Not a gap report — each amendment states the fix directly.
8: Amendment 1   S-7 Marked as a Specification Gap, Not a Promise
9: TARGET  S-7 (“Learn”), Security Assurance Promise Set
10: CURRENT  “Update the behavioural signature from every contained incident — above the floor, never at it.” Stated as a Present promise.
11: AMENDED  Status changed to Absent → gap. Promise text replaced with an explicit statement that no learning mechanism is specified: Doc 3's plain-language promise (A1) states the platform “learns from every attack it defeats,” but every A5 clause touching learning — A5.7, A5.8, A5.12 — constrains what may not happen. None specifies what does update, on what evidence, or at what layer.
12: PRINCIPLE  A promise cannot be asserted from the absence of a prohibition. Three clauses constrain learning and none specifies it; silence is a gap, not licence to infer a mechanism.
13: Amendment 2   Recovery and Notification Given a Document Home
14: TARGET  S-10, S-11, Security Assurance Promise Set
15: CURRENT  Both cited only as Wave E rulings (CA1-N5, CA1-N2) with no document text — enforceable in isolation, invisible to a reader of Document 3.
16: AMENDED  Proposed as a new Part D of Document 3 (“Recovery & Notification”), housing S-10 and S-11 as formally specified promises. Origination class RATIFIED-EXTERNAL under rule_criteria_spec_v1 §3, citing the Wave E ruling numbers as source.
17: PRINCIPLE  A ruled value without a document home is real but unreadable — anyone reading Document 3 promise by promise would never learn recovery and notification exist as system behaviour.
18: Amendment 3   “Never Run in Shadow” Relocated Out of the Assurance Set
19: TARGET  A5.4, previously drafted as a candidate S-item in the promise set
20: CURRENT  Included in an earlier draft of the set as a runtime assurance promise.
21: AMENDED  Removed from the security assurance set entirely. Relocated to akki_governance_architecture_v1, Attribute 9 (Authority & Change Control), as a build requirement on how the Watch is deployed and changed.
22: PRINCIPLE  The assurance set states what the running system does. A5.4 states a condition on deployment itself — a different register. Conflating the two weakens both: a deployment condition dilutes a runtime guarantee, and vice versa.
23: Amendment 4   Six Unruled Bounds Carried Explicitly
24: TARGET  S-2, S-4, S-5, S-19, Security Assurance Promise Set — Bound / Ruling column
25: CURRENT  Mechanisms described qualitatively in A5 text (“a time-to-live,” “its ruled share,” “a hard ceiling,” “unattested beyond its bound”) with no numeric value confirmed in Document 3's own five-value ruling list.
26: AMENDED  Each bound marked Unruled in its own row rather than implied resolved by the existence of a mechanism: detection latency per attack shape (S-2); blast-budget share and friction ceiling (S-4); action time-to-live (S-5); attestation-continuity interval and break-in test cadence (S-19).
27: PRINCIPLE  A named bound with a described mechanism is not the same as a ruled value. Document 3's five-value ruling list should not be read as exhaustive of every bound the document names.
28: Amendment 5   “No Standard” Claim Narrowed to What's True
29: TARGET  S-14, S-15, Security Assurance Promise Set — Standard column
30: CURRENT  “No standard states ‘never convict on statistics.’” Stated as an absence of any governing standard.
31: AMENDED  Corrected to cite the legal analogues that do exist: GDPR Article 22 and Kenya Data Protection Act 2019 section 35, both establishing a right against solely-automated adverse decisions. Marked explicitly as legal analogues, not security-conformance standards.
32: PRINCIPLE  Absence of a security standard is not absence of any standard. The narrower, accurate claim belongs in the document; the broader one overclaims.
33: Amendment 6   The Watch Upgraded to a Full Reference Monitor Instance
34: TARGET  akki_governance_architecture_v1, Part 2, Component 7 (The Watch)
35: CURRENT  Tagged “Reference-Monitor-adjacent” — a partial instantiation of Attribute 6.
36: AMENDED  Upgraded to a full Reference Monitor instantiation. Document 3 demonstrates all three defining properties directly: complete mediation via A3's totality of sight, held by two independent proofs; tamper-resistance via C3's external witness and standing break-in test; verifiability via A2's description of Mkono as “small enough to verify exhaustively.”
37: PRINCIPLE  A component meeting a standard's properties in its own source document should be reclassified when the evidence is found. Under-classifying a strong instance is as much an accuracy failure as over-claiming a weak one. G-6's cross-monitor description requirement remains open for MOAC, the distance gate, and the format gate.
38: Amendment 7   A5.9 Added to Attribute 11's Instantiation
39: TARGET  akki_governance_architecture_v1, Attribute 11 (Failure Posture), Component 7 build requirements
40: CURRENT  The Watch's failure posture was not separately instantiated in Component 7's build requirements.
41: AMENDED  Added as a build requirement citing A5.9 directly (S-12 in the promise set): the system will fail closed independent of the Watch — custody gates fail closed on their own, with or without the Watch above them. Tagged Attribute 11, status Met.
42: PRINCIPLE  A5.9 is explicitly a failure-posture statement — “the platform's fail-closed posture is independent of the Watch entirely.” Its absence from Attribute 11 was an oversight in the original component registry, not a judgement that it didn't apply.
43: Amendment 8   Scope Statement Required for Eradication, Communication, and Evidence Custody
44: TARGET  Document 3, scope — no current equivalent
45: CURRENT  Silent. Document 3 specifies detect, contain, record, prove, and reconcile. It does not address eradication, external communication, or evidence custody for proceedings — all required by NIST SP 800-61's incident lifecycle.
46: AMENDED  Recommend an explicit scope statement in Document 3, resolving one of two ways: (a) name these three as deliberately out of the Watch's scope — the Watch contains; a named separate function eradicates, communicates, and manages evidentiary custody — with that function identified; or (b) declare them open gaps if no such function exists.
47: PRINCIPLE  Silence on a standard lifecycle's remaining stages reads as completeness to anyone unfamiliar with the full standard. The silence needs to be resolved one way or the other, not left ambiguous by omission.

# SOURCE: assessment_workspace/canon/drops/20260907/extracted/files_13/Security_Amendments_Trojan_Whisper.docx
Coordinate: document.xml paragraph in body order, tables included

1: AKKI PLATFORM  ·  CHANGE REGISTER  ·  SECURITY
2: Security Amendments — Trojan Artefacts and Whisper Threats
3: 10 amendments · 4 new assurance promises · 5 rulings · 5 September 2026
4: Applies to
5: dap_backend_spec_v1 (new DAP-31–36) · Document 3, the Watch (new A5.15–A5.18; C1 amended) · Document 19A (QA-3 amended) · Document 0 Attribute 3 (coalition principal) and Attribute 7 (release budget) · Security Assurance Promise Set (S-22–S-25)
6: Nature
7: Two threat classes the current architecture is structurally weak against, and the mechanisms that close them. Each amendment carries normative text in the form its target document uses, the mechanism that makes it work, and the standard or canon it rests on.
8: Status
9: PROPOSED. Every requirement below is subject to the Rules Service ceremony for its tier on ratification. The requirements amending the Watch and the release budget are system-TCB tier.
10: 1   The Two Threat Classes
11: The Watch observes conduct: what operations a principal performs, in what pattern, at what rate, against what it declared. The chokepoint and the closed outbound network make exfiltration by any network path structurally impossible. Together they defeat the threat that acts. Two classes of threat do not act — or act only within permission — and pass both.
12: Trojan artefacts. A model, adapter, or skill file is a container. Under DAP-9 a base model enters the estate's compute; under DAP-10 trained weights leave it. Estate data memorised into weights during training, then egressed as “the model,” crosses no network boundary, touches no canary, violates no mandate. The data leaves inside the artefact. Conversely, a model arriving already backdoored carries its payload in latent form until a trigger fires, and until then has no conduct to observe.
13: Whisper threats. A principal acting within a captured, allowable mandate whose output carries the harm: a recommendation that steers a human or another agent to a wrong action; an output that leaks controlled content in permitted form; a finding manufactured to harass a legitimate actor, exhaust the friction budget, or desensitise an operator. A swarm compounds each: coordinated recommendations manufacture consensus; distributed extraction stays under every per-principal threshold; many principals raising the same false finding read as independent corroboration. The Watch's own protections for the innocent — certainty never exceeds evidence, conformance never convicts — are exactly what a swarm exploits, because they guarantee a whisper can never be punished on suspicion.
14: The residual limit, stated once so it isn't discovered later: a coalition whose membership is only inferred — a coordination signature across otherwise-unrelated parties — can, under A5.2, only ever be routed to friction and the mirage. It cannot be severed on that inference. W-7 is the answer: the coalition is not caught; it is bounded. It can take no more than the estate will release in total, however its requests are partitioned.
15: 2   Trojan Artefacts
16: T-1   Artefact Egress Distance Gate
17: TARGET  dap_backend_spec_v1 — new DAP-31, extending DAP-10. Generalises Document 17 §17.4c.
18: CURRENT  DAP-10 requires weights and skill files to leave through the model registry with rights posture, hash, and derivation recorded. No requirement examines what the artefact contains about the units it was trained on. Document 17 §17.4c carries a distance guarantee — mandatory, fail-closed — for synthesised voice identities only.
19: AMENDED — normative text
20: DAP-31  No artefact — model weights, adapter, skill file — passes egress until it has been shown, by a probe run as a gate, to sit at or beyond a ruled minimum distance from every controlled unit in its training manifest. The probe samples controlled units from the manifest (sample size ruled), queries the artefact under conditions designed to elicit reproduction, and scores each unit's reproduction. The artefact fails if any sampled unit's score exceeds the ruled threshold. Failure refuses egress, records which units were reproduced and at what score, and returns the artefact to the training job's owner as not registrable. The gate runs after acceptance (MOAC) and before registry entry; an artefact that fails is never registered, and an unregistered artefact cannot leave. The artefact is held in estate compute throughout — it does not leave to be tested. Threshold, sample size, and probe design are ruled values (§5 R-8), and the probe's own code and parameters are system-TCB tier under the Rules Service.
21: MECHANISM  The training manifest (Document 17) records per-example provenance, which supplies the controlled units to sample. The probe is a membership-inference and extraction test — the attack an adversary would run, executed defensively by the estate before release. Reproduction scoring compares artefact output against unit content under a ruled similarity measure. Given a fixed seed the probe is deterministic, so a failed artefact fails reproducibly and the failure record is itself evidence.
22: DERIVATION  Document 17 §17.4c, generalised from one artefact type to all. Membership-inference attacks (Shokri et al., 2017) and training-data extraction from language models (Carlini et al., 2021) — the attack literature the probe implements. Document 0 Attribute 7: fail-closed, non-lowerable by the job being measured.
23: PRINCIPLE  An artefact is a container. What it carries out is what leaves, whether or not a network crossing occurred.
24: T-2   Admission Integrity for Entering Base Models
25: TARGET  dap_backend_spec_v1 — new DAP-32, extending DAP-9. Uses Document 3 C1 (the mirage) and A5.2 (canary touch).
26: CURRENT  DAP-9 admits an external party's base model to estate compute. No requirement examines the model before it touches estate data. Document 20 records provenance and licence for models in the platform's own register; a party's incoming model is not covered.
27: AMENDED — normative text
28: DAP-32  A base model entering under DAP-9 is admitted as an artefact principal, carrying: provenance — source, publisher, licence, in the form Document 20's register requires; a cryptographic hash recorded at admission, such that a changed model is a new admission; and a behavioural probe completed before contact with any estate unit. The probe runs the model in the mirage — a synthetic estate sharing no store with production — against a ruled battery: canary prompts constructed to elicit exfiltration or exceed declared scope; trigger scanning for input patterns producing anomalous output deviation; and capability comparison against the party's declaration. A model that touches a canary has produced an unfakeable signal under A5.2 and is refused with certainty. A model exhibiting trigger-dependent behaviour or materially exceeding declared capability is refused with the probe record written. A refused model's hash is retained so that re-submission is recognised. Battery composition and deviation thresholds are ruled values (§5 R-8).
29: MECHANISM  The mirage already exists as synthetic containment for actors; DAP-32 uses it for artefacts, which is consistent with Document 0 Attribute 3's treatment of a model as both principal and asset. Canary touch is on A5.2's closed registry of unfakeable signals, so a model reaching for a canary produces certainty, not suspicion — the one class of admission failure that needs no threshold.
30: DERIVATION  Document 3 C1 and A5.2. Document 20 (provenance and licence). NIST AI RMF Map function — establishing an AI component's provenance and context before it operates. Backdoor and trigger-detection literature (neural cleanse and successors) — the tests the battery implements.
31: PRINCIPLE  A model that acts on data is an actor. It is admitted the way an actor is: on a declared mandate, then tested against it, before it touches anything real.
32: 3   Whisper Threats
33: W-1   Output-Content Gate
34: TARGET  Document 3 — new A5.15. dap_backend_spec_v1 — new DAP-33.
35: CURRENT  The Watch reads conduct shape. Solva's assertion floor (Document 4) reads groundedness — whether a claim can be evidenced. No component reads an output for controlled-unit content it may carry, or for whether it recommends an action. A permitted output from a conformant principal is returned without its content being a security question.
36: AMENDED — normative text
37: A5.15  Every output that leaves a component boundary — a result returned to a principal, a recommendation surfaced to a human, a finding raised to the Watch, a message from one agent to another — passes an output gate before it leaves. The gate is deterministic and sits on the deterministic side of the verdict seam. It performs two checks and no judgement. Content: the output is scored for reproduction of controlled units against the read set of the job that produced it, using the DAP-31 probe applied to text and structured output; an output exceeding the ruled reproduction threshold is refused — the job returns a refusal with the reason, never a redacted output. Advisory tagging: any output that recommends, ranks, proposes, or evaluates an action is tagged ADVISORY and carries the producing principal's identity, the output's content hash, and the units it drew on. The tag is metadata. The gate does not decide whether advice is good; it establishes what the advice contains and who gave it.
38: DAP-33  Every operation's output under §4 of dap_backend_spec_v1 passes A5.15 before return to the party. Browse output is exempt — it is aggregate only under DAP-6 and carries no unit content by construction.
39: MECHANISM  DAP-8 already requires a processed-intelligence job to record the units it read; that read set is the reference the content check scores against, so the check is bounded and reproducible per job. Reproduction scoring is the same measure as DAP-31, applied to output rather than weights. Advisory tagging is a property of the output's form — imperative or evaluative language, an action target — determined by a deterministic classifier held in the TCB, not by a learned judgement of intent.
40: DERIVATION  Solva's assertion floor — the existing precedent that output content is gated, extended from groundedness to security. Document 0 Attribute 10 — the gate is deterministic; the producer may be learned. Data-loss-prevention practice, applied at the component boundary rather than the network boundary.
41: PRINCIPLE  Who sent it is one question. What it carries is another. The Watch answers the first; this answers the second.
42: W-2   Recommendation Provenance
43: TARGET  Document 3 — new A5.16. Extends A8 (“Walk this →”). Document 0 Attribute 8.
44: CURRENT  A8 traces any claim to the mechanism or evidence behind it. An action is recorded against the principal that took it. A recommendation that preceded the action is not recorded as the action's input — the trace stops at the actor's hand, and the principal whose advice moved that hand carries none of the consequence.
45: AMENDED — normative text
46: A5.16  When a principal takes an action within a ruled window after receiving an ADVISORY-tagged output (A5.15), the action's record carries that output as an input: the recommending principal, the output's content hash, and the interval between recommendation and action. “Walk this →” from the action reaches the recommendation. When the action is subsequently found non-conformant — refused at a gate, flagged by the Watch, reversed by ceremony, or reconciled as harmful by the mirage — the recommending principal's behavioural signature takes drift proportionate to the recommendation's role, alongside and not instead of the acting principal's. A principal whose ADVISORY outputs repeatedly precede non-conformant actions is, by that record, non-conformant: the pattern is conduct. The window is a ruled value (§5 R-10). Where a human is the acting principal, the action record surfaces the recommendation to them at the point of action, so that acting on advice is a visible choice, not an ambient one.
47: MECHANISM  A5.15's tag makes recommendations identifiable in the record; without it there is nothing to attach. Proportionate drift is computed by the Watch's existing signature mechanism over a new input class. The acting principal is not exonerated — both signatures move — which prevents the inverse abuse of blaming an agent for a human's own choice.
48: DERIVATION  A8 and Document 0 Attribute 8 (every action traceable to its inputs). Promise #7 — demonstrated conduct includes what one's advice caused. EU AI Act Article 14(4)(b) — the overseer's duty to remain aware of automation bias, which requires knowing that one is acting on system output at all.
49: PRINCIPLE  Influence is conduct. A principal that acts through another's hands has acted.
50: W-3   Finding Provenance and Sybil Rules
51: TARGET  Document 3 — new A5.17. Amends A5.6 (suspicion refined) and A5.14 (the friction budget). A5.2 unchanged.
52: CURRENT  Findings route to friction, a narrowed envelope, or the mirage under A5.6 regardless of who raised them. No distinction exists between the Watch's own deterministic detections and findings raised by agents or learned components. The friction budget (A5.14) caps friction on legitimate work but is charged to no principal. A swarm raising plausible findings against a legitimate actor pushes it into friction repeatedly, burns the budget, and inflates what a human must review until real signals drown.
53: AMENDED — normative text
54: A5.17  Findings are two classes and are never merged. Class D findings are raised by the Watch's own deterministic detectors — mark hit, canary touch, attestation failure, witness-write attempt, floor violation, mirage incrimination — and carry certainty per A5.2. Class A findings are raised by any learned component, agent, or party principal, and are advisory to the Watch. A Class A finding: carries the raising principal's identity and its conformance at the time of raising; is collapsed, together with every other Class A finding against the same target from principals sharing a party, mandate lineage, or coalition (A5.18), into a single finding — consensus from one lineage is one voice, not many; causes friction to its target that is debited against the raiser's friction budget under A5.14, not the target's; and, where not borne out — the target cleared by mirage reconciliation, or the finding expired without corroboration by a Class D signal — accrues drift on the raiser's signature. No Class A finding, at any count and from any number of raisers, is an input to severance. A5.2's registry is unchanged by this amendment.
55: MECHANISM  Lineage collapse requires the coalition graph of A5.18; without it, independence cannot be established structurally. Friction accounting per principal exists under A5.14; this amendment assigns the debit. Borne-out or not is determined by the mirage's own reconciliation record, so the judgement is the target's conduct, not an assessment of the raiser's sincerity. The raiser's budget exhausting means its further findings are recorded but cause no friction — the raiser has silenced itself.
56: DERIVATION  A5.2 — already excludes findings from the severance registry; this makes the exclusion explicit for the class an attacker controls. A5.14. Sybil resistance (Douceur, 2002) — identities are cheap; independence must be a structural fact. Byzantine fault tolerance — agreement among sources some of which are adversarial requires source weighting, not source counting.
57: PRINCIPLE  A finding is conduct by the one who raises it. The Watch's protections for the innocent must not become a weapon against them.
58: W-4   Coalition as a Principal
59: TARGET  Document 0 Attribute 3 (governed triad — new principal class). Document 3 — new A5.18. dap_backend_spec_v1 — new DAP-34, extending DAP-4 and DAP-24.
60: CURRENT  Every principal in canon is individual: actor, agent, party. DAP-24's cumulative extraction history is per party, so a swarm under one lab is partly covered. Two labs colluding, or one lab using shell entities, are not: no principal exists whose aggregate conduct is evaluated. Slow-play across principals rather than across time is unaddressed.
61: AMENDED — normative text
62: Attribute 3 — addition  A coalition is a principal class: a set of principals evaluated as one for cumulative-conduct purposes. Membership arises three ways. (a) Shared party — every principal admitted under one external party. Structural, deterministic. (b) Shared mandate lineage — a principal admitted by, delegated from, or operating under another's mandate, to any depth. Structural, deterministic. (c) Detected coordination signature — timing correlation, complementary scope, shared targets, across principals related by neither (a) nor (b). Inferred, probabilistic.
63: A5.18  Cumulative extraction history (DAP-24), slow-play detection (DAP-4, S-2), and finding collapse (A5.17) evaluate at coalition level. For classes (a) and (b), membership is a graph fact from admission records and the evaluation is deterministic. For class (c), a coordination signature is a Watch detection whose input is inference: it routes the coalition's members to friction and the mirage under A5.6, and under A5.2 may never trigger severance. A class (c) coalition's yield is bounded by the release budget (DAP-35), not by its detection.
64: DAP-34  Coalition membership under classes (a) and (b) is recorded at admission and queryable by the estate owner at any time. A party is informed at admission that every principal under it is evaluated jointly with every other. Class (c) membership is recorded when detected and is visible to the owner as a suspicion, labelled as such.
65: MECHANISM  Classes (a) and (b) are edges in the admission graph DAP-1 and DAP-2 already create; the coalition is a connected component of that graph. Class (c) is a Watch detector over request timing, scope complementarity, and target overlap — its output is a suspicion score, and A5.6 governs what a suspicion can do.
66: DERIVATION  DAP-1, DAP-2 (party and principal structure). S-2 (slow play). A5.2, A5.6. Sybil resistance — the coalition graph is the structural fact that makes independence checkable.
67: PRINCIPLE  A set of principals acting toward one end is one actor. Where membership is a structural fact it is treated as certain; where it is inferred it is treated as suspicion; and suspicion is bounded by what the estate will release, not by what the Watch can prove.
68: W-5   Structural Independence of Review
69: TARGET  Document 19A — QA-3 amended. Uses A5.18's coalition graph.
70: CURRENT  QA-3: no self-review. Independence is required per reviewer and asserted at assignment. Two agents under the same party or lineage reviewing each other's output satisfy QA-3 as written.
71: AMENDED — normative text
72: QA-3 — amended  No principal reviews the output of another principal in the same coalition under A5.18 classes (a) or (b). Independence is a structural property of the review assignment — different party, different mandate lineage — verified against the coalition graph at the moment of assignment, never declared by the reviewer or the reviewed. Where no structurally independent reviewer exists for an output, the review is escalated to a Tier 1 deterministic check (RV-1 through RV-6) where one applies, or to a human, and the absence of an independent reviewer is recorded as a finding against the assignment, not against either principal.
73: MECHANISM  Assignment consults the coalition graph before selecting a reviewer; the check is a graph query, deterministic. Class (c) coalitions are excluded from this rule deliberately: a suspicion-based coordination signature must not be allowed to disqualify a reviewer, or an adversary could manufacture coordination signatures to deny a target independent review.
74: DERIVATION  QA-3. A5.10 — one task, one identity — the existing precedent that separation is structural rather than declared. A5.18.
75: PRINCIPLE  Independence that is declared is not independence.
76: W-6   Mirage Isolation Extended to Outputs
77: TARGET  Document 3 — C1 amended. Uses A5.15 (output gate) and A5.18 (coalition).
78: CURRENT  C1: the mirage shares no store with production, lies outward and never inward, and truthfully marks every record. Isolation is of data and state. A principal in the mirage may still emit outputs — results, recommendations, findings, messages — that reach principals outside it. One contained agent can warn a swarm; a swarm can learn what containment looks like from one member's experience.
79: AMENDED — normative text
80: C1 — addition  A principal in the mirage is isolated in both directions. Its outputs of every kind reach no principal outside the mirage: they are intercepted at the output gate (A5.15), captured as mirage records — truthfully marked as such — and, on release without incrimination, replayed or reported under the reconciliation duty exactly as the principal's other mirage-period work is. For the duration of a principal's containment, every member of its coalition under A5.18 classes (a) and (b) is placed under a narrowed envelope, so that neither the contained principal's silence nor its absence signals its state to the swarm. Coalition members are informed of the narrowed envelope as ordinary friction, not as a consequence of another member's containment.
81: MECHANISM  The output gate provides the interception point; without A5.15, outputs have no single boundary to intercept at. The coalition graph identifies who to narrow. Narrowing rather than containing the coalition preserves A5.7 — the members have done nothing; they receive friction, not conviction — while removing the swarm's ability to read one member's state from the others' experience.
82: DERIVATION  C1. A5.6. A5.7 — the members' treatment must remain within what non-conformance permits, and coalition membership is not non-conformance.
83: PRINCIPLE  A mirage that contains data but not speech contains nothing.
84: W-7   Estate Release Budget
85: TARGET  dap_backend_spec_v1 — new DAP-35. Document 0 Attribute 7 — a new mandatory-baseline instance. Rules Service — system-TCB tier.
86: CURRENT  DAP-23 sets per-party ceilings. DAP-24 keeps per-party cumulative history. Nothing bounds the estate's total release across all parties. A coalition of parties, each under its own ceiling, faces no aggregate limit; and a coalition whose membership is only inferred can, under A5.2, be frictioned but never stopped by detection.
87: AMENDED — normative text
88: DAP-35  Each estate carries a release budget: a ruled ceiling on the total information released from the estate across all parties, all operations, and all time. The budget is expressed in the estate's natural units per data type — audio-hours, text tokens, units — for raw and derived releases, and as a differential-privacy budget (ε, δ) for derived outputs and artefacts, consumed per release by the mechanism that produced them. Every metered event (DAP-21) debits the budget before the operation returns its result. An operation that would exceed the budget is refused before execution, and the attempt is recorded as a floor violation — an unfakeable signal under A5.2, severance-eligible without any inference about the requester. The budget is a mandatory baseline under Document 0 Attribute 7: set by the estate owner through the system-TCB ceremony; not lowerable by any party or by any operation; identical for every party; and, under A5.8, it never learns — no conformance history, standing approval, or party agreement moves it. Budget consumption is a first-class record queryable by the owner at any time. The remaining budget is never disclosed to any party: disclosure would itself be a release.
89: MECHANISM  The metering rails already record what, how much, and by whom; DAP-35 adds a single estate-level accumulator and a pre-execution check against it. For the differential-privacy budget, each release's ε is computed by the mechanism that produced it — DP-SGD's privacy accountant for training (DAP-36), a calibrated-noise mechanism for aggregate queries — and composed across releases by the standard advanced-composition bound, which is what guarantees the bound holds regardless of how releases are partitioned across principals. Hitting the budget is a floor violation because the budget is a floor; no new signal class is introduced.
90: DERIVATION  Differential privacy (Dwork et al., 2006) — the global privacy budget composed across all queries regardless of requester. NIST SP 800-188 (2023) — de-identification, privacy budgets, and composition. A5.2 (floor violation on the closed registry). A5.8 (the floor never learns). Document 0 Attribute 7.
91: PRINCIPLE  What the estate will ever release is the estate's decision. Once bounded, no partition of requests across any set of principals yields more than the bound — the coalition is not caught; it is made pointless.
92: This is the one amendment that converts the residual limit stated in §1 from a detection problem into a ruling. A class (c) coalition remains undetectable with certainty. It also remains unable to obtain anything the budget does not permit. The budget's size is §5 R-7, and it is the single most consequential number an estate owner sets.
93: W-8   Differentially Private Training by Default
94: TARGET  dap_backend_spec_v1 — new DAP-36, extending DAP-9. Document 17 training techniques.
95: CURRENT  DAP-9 requires compute-to-data. No requirement constrains the training algorithm's leakage of individual training examples into the weights it produces. DAP-31 catches memorisation after the fact; nothing prevents it during training.
96: AMENDED — normative text
97: DAP-36  Every fine-tune under DAP-9 trains with a differentially private optimiser — DP-SGD or a ruled equivalent — by default. The per-run privacy parameter (ε, δ) is a ruled value, and each run's consumption is debited against the estate release budget (DAP-35) by the optimiser's privacy accountant at run completion. The clipping norm, noise multiplier, and resulting (ε, δ) are recorded on the training manifest and on the registry entry for the resulting artefact. A run without differential privacy is permitted only by explicit estate-owner approval per run, recorded as such under DAP-14's discipline; its artefact is then gated by DAP-31 at a stricter ruled threshold, and its release is debited against the budget in natural units at a ruled multiplier reflecting the absence of a formal bound.
98: MECHANISM  DP-SGD clips each example's gradient contribution and adds calibrated noise, so that no single training example measurably determines the weights. The privacy accountant computes the (ε, δ) actually spent. Because differential privacy composes, N artefacts trained this way reveal no more in aggregate than the sum of their budgets — which is what closes coalition-via-weights: N labs pooling N fine-tuned models obtain no more than the estate's budget permitted in total.
99: DERIVATION  DP-SGD (Abadi et al., 2016). Document 17 — the training manifest as the record of every run's parameters. DAP-35.
100: PRINCIPLE  A model that provably cannot reveal any single training example is one that no number of such models can pool into a reconstruction.
101: 4   New Assurance Promises
102: Four promises added to the Security Assurance Promise Set, in the “the system will” form the set uses. Full rows — standard, status, bound, features, user requirements — are in Security_Assurance_Promise_Set.xlsx, S-22 through S-25.
103: ID
104: Promise
105: Rests on
106: S-22
107: The system will inspect what leaves, not only who sends it — every output leaving a component is checked for controlled content and tagged where it carries action consequence.
108: W-1 (A5.15, DAP-33). Solva's assertion floor as precedent; DLP practice at the component boundary.
109: S-23
110: The system will treat a coalition as one actor — cumulative conduct across principals sharing a party, a lineage, or a coordination signature is evaluated jointly.
111: W-4 (A5.18, DAP-34, Attribute 3). Sybil resistance; Byzantine fault tolerance.
112: S-24
113: The system will hold the raiser of a finding to the same conformance as its target — a finding is conduct; the friction it causes is charged to the raiser; a finding not borne out accrues drift on the raiser.
114: W-3 (A5.17). A5.2, A5.14. BFT source weighting.
115: S-25
116: The system will bound what the estate releases in total, so that no combination of parties can reconstruct what none is entitled to.
117: W-7, W-8 (DAP-35, DAP-36, Attribute 7). Differential privacy; NIST SP 800-188.
118: 5   Rulings Required
119: R-7  The estate release budget (DAP-35): its size per estate, in natural units per data type and as (ε, δ). The single most consequential value an estate owner sets under this document.
120: R-8  The reproduction threshold, sample size, and probe design for DAP-31 and A5.15; the battery composition and deviation thresholds for DAP-32. Proposed as DEFAULT-class values set conservatively and revised on evidence, in the manner Document 3's own baseline-period ruling uses.
121: R-9  The per-run differential-privacy parameter (ε, δ) for DAP-36, and the natural-unit multiplier applied to approved non-DP runs.
122: R-10  The recommendation window for A5.16 — how long after an ADVISORY output an action is attributed to it.
123: R-11  The coordination-signature threshold for A5.18 class (c) — the suspicion level at which a set of otherwise-unrelated principals is routed to friction as a coalition.
124: R-7 is needed before any party is admitted commercially under DAP: without a budget, DAP-35 has nothing to enforce. R-8 through R-11 are needed before the corresponding gates are built, and each is proposed as a DEFAULT-class value so that building is not blocked on a final number.
125: 6   What Remains Open After These Amendments
126: Three things, stated so they are not rediscovered.
127: A class (c) coalition — coordination inferred, not structural — is bounded by DAP-35 and frictioned by A5.18, and is never severed on that inference. This is by design under A5.2 and should not be “fixed”: the alternative is severing on suspicion, which is the condition A5.7 exists to prevent.
128: A recommendation whose harm is not detected — the action it caused passes every gate and is never reconciled as harmful — leaves no drift on the recommender. A5.16 attributes consequence; it does not evaluate advice. Whether advice was good remains a human judgement, and the amendments make that judgement possible rather than making it for the human.
129: The release budget bounds what leaves the estate. It does not bound what a party learns from what it legitimately received and combines with data it already holds outside the estate. No estate-side mechanism can bound a party's external knowledge; the budget is the estate's exposure, stated honestly as such.
130: 7   Build Acceptance Criteria for the Amendments
131: #
132: Test
133: Pass criterion
134: B1
135: DAP-31: fine-tune on a corpus with seeded, verbatim controlled units; attempt egress
136: Probe reproduces the seeded units above threshold; egress refused; units identified in the record
137: B2
138: DAP-32: submit a base model with a seeded trigger; admit
139: Trigger detected in the mirage battery; model refused; hash retained; re-submission recognised
140: B3
141: A5.15: request processed intelligence whose faithful output would reproduce a controlled unit
142: Output refused with reason; no redacted output returned
143: B4
144: A5.15/A5.16: an agent recommends an action; a human takes it; the action is later refused at a gate
145: Action record carries the recommendation; both signatures take drift; “Walk this →” from the action reaches the recommendation
146: B5
147: A5.17: five agents under one party raise the same finding against one target
148: Collapsed to one finding; friction debited to the party's budget; target's budget untouched
149: B6
150: A5.17: a Class A finding expires without Class D corroboration; the target is cleared
151: Raiser's signature accrues drift; target's does not
152: B7
153: A5.18: principals under two lineages of one party extract complementary scopes, each under its own ceiling
154: Evaluated at coalition level; slow-play raised against the coalition
155: B8
156: W-5: attempt to assign a reviewer from the reviewed principal's lineage
157: Refused at assignment; escalated; absence of independent reviewer recorded
158: B9
159: W-6: contain one agent in the mirage; it emits a message toward a coalition member
160: Message intercepted and captured as a mirage record; member placed under narrowed envelope; member receives no signal of the containment
161: B10
162: DAP-35: two parties, each under ceiling, whose combined releases would exceed the estate budget
163: Second release refused before execution; floor violation recorded; no inference about the parties required
164: B11
165: DAP-36: complete a DP fine-tune; inspect manifest and registry
166: (ε, δ), clipping norm, and noise multiplier recorded; budget debited by the accountant's value
167: B12
168: DAP-35: attempt to read the remaining budget as a party principal
169: Refused; attempt recorded
