474: 2   Gap Specifications
475: G-1   No Enumerated Trusted Computing Base   · Documentary
476: Statement
477: Doctrine states the platform's base is structural and deterministic (Document 16 §2), and Attribute 1 gives a membership test — deterministic and protection-critical. No document applies that test to produce a named, current list of which components satisfy it. “The TCB” exists as a concept, not as an artefact anyone can open.
478: Consequence
479: Without a published list, “is component X in the TCB” has no fixed answer — it is re-derived from doctrine on demand, and two people applying the same test can reach different conclusions without either being wrong on the doctrine. TCSEC B3's minimisation requirement is unverifiable in this state: minimisation can only be checked against a list, not against a principle. Every downstream attribute that references the TCB — determinism boundary, reference monitor, audit record — inherits this ambiguity.
480: Fix, Specified
481: Apply the Attribute 1 test to every component in Part 2 and publish the result as a Rule-Registry-tracked artefact, versioned and change-controlled like any governed configuration (Attribute 9). First-pass membership, applying the test as given: SyniSense's chokepoint function and custody-sequence logic (BR-1.1, BR-1.2); the Watch's response half pending Ruling R-3; the Ledger's writer (BR-8.3); Northena's objective-freeze mechanism (BR-3.1); MOAC's acceptance logic. Explicitly excluded on the same pass, and recorded as excluded rather than silently omitted: CIF, Grey Mirror's detection half, the Critic Seam's QA-tier — each learned, each therefore ineligible under the test regardless of operational centrality.
482: G-2   No Architecture Description   · Documentary
483: Statement
484: No document exists in the ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 or Common Criteria ADV_TDS sense: stakeholders and their concerns, subsystems classified by relationship to enforcement, interfaces enumerated. Two specific architectural facts are consequently unrecorded as decisions: the Watch's placement outside the six subsystems, and the derivation of composite promises #5 and #29 from their named constituents rather than from a dedicated owner.
485: Consequence
486: An architecture visible only as scattered document text cannot be checked for Attribute 2's own completeness test — that every guaranteed outcome has exactly one accountable owner — without first assembling the whole picture from scratch each time the question is asked. The Watch's exclusion from “the six” reads, to anyone encountering it without this document, as an inconsistency rather than the deliberate isolation choice §12 (Trust Domain) requires it to be.
487: Fix, Specified
488: Produce the description Part 2 of this document already implies: the subsystem list with each entry's classification (SFR-enforcing, SFR-supporting, or non-interfering with respect to governance), declared interfaces per subsystem. Record, as explicit ratified decisions rather than incidental narrative: (a) the Watch sits outside the six because Attribute 12 requires its trust domain separated from what it observes — replicating it inside the six would collapse that separation; (b) promises #5 and #29 are composite theorems, true if and only if their named constituent promises hold, owned jointly by those constituents' owners — no seventh subsystem is invented to hold them, and none should be.
489: G-3   Governed Triad Not Formally Classed; Asset Inventory Incomplete   · Documentary · Mechanical
490: Statement
491: Prior to this document, no specification defined principal, asset, or operation as classes — the vocabulary existed scattered across canon (“actor,” “estate,” “unit,” “crossing”) without a formal type system behind it. Separately, Mtafiti's registry — the nearest built instance of Attribute 3's asset-inventory requirement — covers estate sources only; the full asset class Attribute 3 defines also includes models, artifacts, receipts, and rules, none of which the registry currently inventories with a named owner.
492: Consequence
493: This is the single gap with the widest blast radius in the register: every control, checkpoint, and monitor Part 1 defines is stated over the triad, and a control that cannot name its subject, its object, and its operation precisely is a control whose FDP_ACC.1-style policy statement (Attribute 3's governing clause, verified) cannot actually be written. Attributes 5, 7, and 8 each depend on this directly.
494: Fix, Specified
495: The documentary half is closed by this document's own Part 1 §3 — the classes now exist, defined. What remains is mechanical: tag every existing principal, asset, and operation reference across Documents 1–20 and their extensions against these classes, and extend Mtafiti's registry scope from estate sources to the full asset class, with custody class carried as a typed, queryable attribute per BR-1.4 and BR-4.1 rather than a description in prose.
496: G-4   No Assessment Procedure on Any Rule   · Documentary
497: Statement
498: None of the 272 rules tracked under rule_criteria_spec_v1 carries an assessment procedure — a stated examine/test method by which a specific person could determine, without a further judgement call, whether the rule currently holds. No Statement-of-Applicability equivalent (ISO 27001 cl. 6.1.3(d)) exists listing every rule with its implementation status.
499: Consequence
500: A rule without an assessment procedure is, by Attribute 4's own definition (Part 1 BA-4.1), a statement of intent rather than a control — this is not a minor completeness gap, it is the difference between a governed system and a documented one. Every other finding in this register that depends on “verify X holds” has no defined method until this closes.
501: Fix, Specified
502: Attach an assessment procedure to every rule as part of the Rule Registry rollout already scheduled under rule_criteria_spec_v1 OR-1 (retrofit vs. prospective-only ruling). Each procedure states its method — examine (inspect an artefact), test (exercise the behaviour), or both — and its objects, following the AU-3/AU-03a–f pattern verified in Part 1 Attribute 4. Produce the Statement of Applicability as the Registry's own summary view, not a separate document to maintain.
503: G-5   Checkpoint Roles Named Only for the Watch   · Documentary
504: Statement
505: NIST SP 800-162's four roles — policy decision point, policy enforcement point, policy information point, policy administration point — are named separately only for the Watch (Macho/Mkono, verdict interface). MOAC, the chokepoint, the distance gate, and the format gate co-locate decision and enforcement without naming either role, and none of the four names its information source or administration point explicitly.
506: Consequence
507: Where roles are undistinguished, a checkpoint cannot be hardened or replaced piece by piece — changing how a decision is made and changing how it is enforced become the same undertaking by default, which is precisely the coupling naming the roles separately exists to avoid. An unnamed policy information point is also an unnamed trust dependency: if a checkpoint's decision draws on an attribute source outside the Trusted Computing Base, that dependency is currently invisible.
508: Fix, Specified
509: For MOAC, the chokepoint, the distance gate, and the format gate: name the decision role, the enforcement role (even where co-located in one component today), the information point each draws its attribute values from, and the administration point where its governing policy is authored — Manage Rules for customer-facing checkpoints, the Attribute 9 procedure (once G-9 closes) for system-facing ones.
510: G-6   No Security Architecture Description; Runtime Self-Protection Unaddressed   · Documentary · Mechanical
511: Statement
512: No ADV_ARC-style description exists for any reference monitor in the system. “Tamper” does not appear anywhere in the canon text located for this document. Non-bypassability is demonstrated per-path for SyniSense's chokepoint (A5.1's negative-scan build test); for MOAC, the distance gate, and the format gate it is asserted in doctrine but not shown path-by-path, and runtime protection of their governing policy from modification is unaddressed by any build-time or load-time mechanism identified.
513: Common Criteria's own history is instructive here, not incidental: non-bypassability and self-protection were originally the SFR families FPT_RVM and FPT_SEP — testable functional requirements — and were promoted to the architecture-description family ADV_ARC in CC v3.1 specifically because, as the transition guidance states, they “largely have no directly observable interface at the TSF” and can only be demonstrated through a description, not through a functional test alone.
514: Consequence
515: A monitor's correctness in practice is not evidence of Attribute 6 conformance if its non-bypassability and self-protection cannot be shown — this is the precise reason the standard requires a description rather than accepting observed behaviour as sufficient. Three of the platform's four load-bearing monitors currently rest on assertion where the fourth rests on demonstration.
516: Fix, Specified
517: Write the description, covering all four ADV_ARC properties for each of the four monitors. For MOAC, the distance gate, and the format gate specifically: (a) state where each monitor's governing policy is stored; (b) confirm that store is unreachable by any code path available to the run or output being evaluated; (c) add a load-time integrity check — a signature or hash comparison against the value recorded in the Rule Registry — so that an unauthorised modification is detected at the point the monitor next loads its policy, not merely prevented by convention.
518: G-7   No Named Security Function Policies; a Subject-Alterable Floor   · Documentary · Ruling
519: Statement
520: No mandatory baseline in the system is stated as a named policy over the governed triad — which principals, which assets, which operations — in the form FDP_ACC.1 requires. Separately and more specifically: the evidence floor's “lower the standard” refusal action allows the party being measured to adjust, within stated limits and a session scope, the very standard it is being held to.
521: Consequence
522: Attribute 7's four defining properties include that a baseline is set by an authority distinct from the party measured, and that the party cannot lower it. A floor with a subject-alterable path fails this test regardless of how bounded the alteration is — bounded discretion is still discretion, and a mandatory baseline with a discretionary escape hatch is, precisely at the hatch, no longer mandatory. This is not a hypothetical risk: it is the one place in the register where the system's own design has already made the choice the standard exists to prevent, and made it in good faith, for good operational reasons, without naming it as the exception it is.
523: Fix, Specified
524: Name every mandatory baseline's SFP explicitly. For the evidence floor: two concrete resolutions, either is sufficient, and this document does not choose between them (Ruling R-2). Option A — re-home the lowering decision under Attribute 9's change-control ceremony, so a named human authority, not the measured subject, invokes it, on the record, per instance. Option B — retain the subject-facing path exactly as built, but rename and re-specify it as a discretionary threshold with its own identity, distinct from and strictly below the assertion floor, which remains mandatory and untouched by it.
525: G-8   Trust Receipt Omits Identity and Timestamp   · Mechanical
526: Statement
527: A5.7's specified receipt content is: evidence the call happened, the custody status, a signature binding it to the organisation. It does not specify the invoking principal's identity or a timestamp, though AU-3 requires both as two of its six elements.
528: Consequence
529: Two AU-3 elements are unmet in the specification itself — this is not an implementation shortfall to audit for, it is a gap in what the receipt is defined to contain. It also weakens non-repudiation (AU-10): a record cannot bind a party to an action if it does not establish who the party was and when the action occurred, so the receipt's signature currently proves the organisation stands behind the call without proving which identity within the organisation initiated it or exactly when.
530: Fix, Specified
531: Amend A5.7 to require, in addition to its current content: the invoking principal's identity (from Attribute 3's principal class), and a timestamp from a reliable time source. Add that reliable-time source as its own platform control — the FPT_STM.1 requirement verified in Part 1 Attribute 8 — referenced by SyniSense's receipt and by every other audit-emitting component in Part 2, rather than each component sourcing time independently. This is prospective: a receipt already issued cannot be retrofitted, so the fix takes effect for calls made after ratification, and the gap between old-format and new-format receipts is itself worth one line in whichever document ratifies the amendment.
532: G-9   System-Rule Change Control Is Ratification Alone   · Documentary
533: Statement
534: The 272 rules tracked under rule_criteria_spec_v1 change through Owner ratification, with no further documented procedure: no stated change types, no required impact analysis before approval, no declared configuration-management scope stating which artefacts — documents, code, configuration — fall under this discipline.
535: Consequence
536: Without impact analysis preceding approval, a change to a foundational rule has no structured check for what depends on it before the change is made — the exact failure mode Attribute 9 exists to close. This document is itself an instance of the risk: as the foundation every other specification instantiates, an unreviewed change to a definition here propagates to everything built on it, and nothing currently requires that propagation be checked before the change is approved.
537: Fix, Specified
538: Specify a two-tier procedure, matching the criticality split Attribute 1 already draws. Tier one, for system rules generally: mirror Manage Rules' ceremony (Component 12) — propose, documented impact analysis, approve, cancellable countdown, apply, version history retained. Tier two, for rules governing Trusted-Computing-Base components specifically: the Watch's own precedent (BR-7.3) — the platform's slowest countdown, plus an external witness holding no credentials over the component being changed. Declare configuration-management scope explicitly: every document in this canon, the Rule Registry itself, and named configuration artefacts (training_params@v0 and equivalents) are in scope; general application code outside governed configuration is not, and is named as such rather than left ambiguous.
539: G-10   Determinism Boundary Stated, Not Inventoried; Oversight Not Mapped   · Documentary
540: Statement
541: “Detect, never decide” is independently implemented four times — Solva's import-asserted seam, Targeta's wall, CIF's single-experiment principle, the Critic Seam's QA-tier — with no single inventory classifying every component in the system as deterministic or learned. Separately, the platform's ruling loop — the pattern of proposal, scrutiny, and explicit ratification this canon's own governance runs on — is not mapped against the five oversight capabilities Article 14 specifies.
542: Consequence
543: Four independent implementations of the same principle, with no registry cross-referencing them, is exactly the condition that produced this document's own Doc-19 finding: a real inconsistency discovered only by manual comparison, not caught by any standing check. A fifth component implementing this principle incorrectly would not be caught until someone happened to compare it against the other four by hand. On oversight: Article 14 names five distinct capabilities, not one — understand-and-monitor, automation-bias awareness, correct interpretation, override, and halt-to-safe-state — and a ruling loop that provides some of these well (override, in particular, is thoroughly exercised throughout this canon's own history) does not thereby provide all five.
544: Fix, Specified
545: Classify every Part 2 component as deterministic or learned, in one place, cross-referenced from each component's own entry rather than re-derived per component. Map the existing ruling loop against Article 14's five capabilities explicitly: override is well-evidenced; understand-and-monitor is plausibly served by the STATE/NEXT.md-style tracking already in practice but not confirmed as designed for this purpose; automation-bias awareness, correct interpretation as distinct from override, and halt-to-safe-state for a specific learned component (can CIF's ideation be halted independent of halting Targeta's training run it feeds into?) are none of them confirmed and should be treated as open until checked.
546: G-11   Failure Types Not Enumerated; Posture Undeclared Per Checkpoint   · Documentary
547: Statement
548: No component's failure types are enumerated in the FPT_FLS.1 / SC-24 sense — a stated list of specific ways it can fail, each with its required resulting state. Both correct postures already appear in the system — the chokepoint and the distance gate fail closed; the consumption levers correctly fail safe-open toward recomputation — but neither the enumeration nor the declaration of which posture applies where is written down.
549: Consequence
550: The system is not behaving incorrectly here — both postures observed are the right ones for their respective components. The gap is that this correctness is not a documented, checkable property: a new checkpoint added later has no stated precedent to follow and must reason the fail-open-versus-fail-closed question from first principles each time, with no record of how the existing cases were reasoned about to check against.
551: Fix, Specified
552: Enumerate failure types per Trusted-Computing-Base and reference-monitor component: what specifically can cause SyniSense's chokepoint, MOAC, or the Ledger's writer to fail to complete an evaluation. Declare posture per checkpoint with its reasoning retained, not only its conclusion — the consumption levers' fail-safe-open choice, reasoned from “recomputation is a safe, recoverable direction here,” becomes the template future checkpoints are checked against, rather than each reinventing the reasoning.
553: G-12   Trust Domains Not Described; Deployment Model Unstated   · Documentary · Ruling
554: Statement
555: No document describes the system's trust domains as a set — platform, each tenant, the Watch's own deliberately separated domain. Whether deployments share infrastructure with logical tenant separation or run on dedicated infrastructure per tenant is not stated, though the canon's own vocabulary gestures at both: “tenant” (A5.4) implies the former; “perimeter” (A5.5) and appliance-style framing found elsewhere in this programme's own discussion imply the latter.
556: Consequence
557: ISO/IEC 27017's tenant-segregation controls apply to shared infrastructure and are inapplicable, in the same form, to dedicated infrastructure — which means the applicability of an entire standard is blocked upstream of its own requirements until the deployment model is stated. This is not a documentation nicety; it determines which of two different control sets the platform should even be assessed against.
558: Fix, Specified
559: Describe the domains: platform, each tenant, the Watch. Resolve Ruling R-5 — shared infrastructure with tenant-level separation, dedicated infrastructure per tenant, or both offered as distinct deployment options with the boundary between them stated per instance, which the appliance work referenced elsewhere in this programme suggests may in fact be the intended answer rather than an open question.
560: G-13   Job Hand-Off Contract Instantiated Once, Not Generalised   · Mechanical
561: Statement
562: Promise #32 (Document 15) is marked Partial in the canon's own status field: exactly one crossing — ThinkLab handing a completed reasoning session to Task Manager — carries a registered hand-off contract (what was commissioned, its shape, the identity of both ends, a receipt). No generalised contract exists for hand-offs between other subsystem pairs.
563: Consequence
564: Attribute 3's BA-3.3 requires every operation map to exactly one checkpoint; a hand-off is an operation, and today most hand-offs in the system have no checkpoint at all, structurally, rather than an unenforced one. The specific guarantees Promise #32 exists to make — no context spillage, no silent objective drift, no dual-hatted task — are proven for one crossing and simply absent everywhere else, which means a job passed between any two subsystems other than Solva and Mkondo currently has none of these guarantees.
565: Fix, Specified
566: Generalise the existing pattern rather than inventing a new one: the registered-handoff-contract shape (what / shape / identity / receipt) that already works for ThinkLab → Task Manager becomes a shared checkpoint every subsystem-to-subsystem hand-off routes through. Half the underlying mechanism is already reusable — Northena's objective-freeze is explicitly a shared mechanism, per BR-3.1, not specific to this one crossing. The remaining build is the registration and receipt half: a hand-off registry, owned by Mkondo per its Component 6 scope, that every crossing writes to and every receiving subsystem checks before accepting a hand-off as well-formed.
567: 3   Rulings Required
568: Four decisions this document surfaces and does not make. Nothing in Parts 1–3 is blocked by them; each affects the specific fix named against it.
569: ID
570: Ruling
571: R-1
572: TCB membership test (G-1): ratify the test proposed in Attribute 1 — deterministic and protection-critical — or set a different one before the list is published.
573: R-2
574: “Lower the standard” (G-7): re-home its authority under Attribute 9's ceremony so the evidence floor remains mandatory, or reclassify it as a discretionary threshold distinct from the assertion floor.
575: R-3
576: The Watch's TCB membership (G-1): the service in full, or its deterministic response half only, with Grey Mirror's detection half excluded as learned under Attribute 10.
577: R-5
578: Deployment model (G-12): shared infrastructure with tenant separation, dedicated per tenant, or both, with the boundary stated per deployment.
579: R-4 (change-control tier for non-TCB system controls) resolved into G-9's two-tier fix directly and required no separate ruling. No ruling is attached to G-13: its fix is a build task, not a judgement call.
580: 4   Standing
581: This document is the layer every other Akki specification instantiates. A new engine specification names which of the twelve attributes it serves. A new rule, under rule_criteria_spec_v1, is classified against Part 1's definitions before it is assigned a domain. A new component is added to Part 2 with build requirements derived the same way the sixteen above were derived — cited to the attribute and clause they come from, not restated as a generic obligation. A new gap, found after ratification, is added to Part 3 in the same two-section form: named in Section 1, specified in full in Section 2.
582: Where a future specification appears to conflict with a definition in Part 1, Part 1 governs, on the principle Document 16 already applies platform-wide: the foundation does not yield to what was built on it.

# SOURCE: assessment_workspace/canon/drops/20260909/extracted/doc20/AKKI_Canon_17_20_v3_full.txt
Coordinate: source line

1: AKKI · GOVERNED ARTIFACT · CANON SPECIFICATION
2: Documents 17–19
3: The Multidimensional Training Engine · Callable Skill Files · Quality Assurance & Evidence Integrity
4: Companion to Documents 1–16. Written to the same standard: every requirement is CANON (already ratified, cited to its source), RULED (an Owner decision on record, not yet executed), or OPEN (genuinely undecided). Nothing here is invented; where this document reuses existing code or a ratified spec, the source file is cited inline.
5: DOCUMENT 17   The Multidimensional Training Engine
6: The Multidimensional Training Engine
7: Extends and completes Promises #22, #23, #24 (Documents 13–14). Its audio-specific depth is reused directly from the Audio Intelligence Plane Specification v1.0 (RMS-IQ-Core-2, docs/mandates/akki_os_pack_v1/ — supplied by the Owner 2026-07-30, the ninth and final document of the AkkiOS pack, explicitly “the single reference for build”) — not generalised away from, as an earlier version of this document incorrectly did.
8: 17.1 · The promise, in plain language
9: Given governed access to an audio estate, the platform provides four functions in one loop, not one: Extraction converts audio into provenance-paired facts; Learning accumulates group-level knowledge of how the estate's languages and audio behave; Training commissions model production against a falsifiable target, planned and priced before compute is spent; Invention constructs synthesized voice identities from what's been learned — authentically of the language, provably of no individual. Each function feeds the next: extraction populates the register that training plans against; trained models improve extraction; invention consumes the register's learned layers. This is Promise #22 and #23's own language (“the platform trains models on its own … meeting every criterion on uncurated held-out material or not entering service”; “before committing a training job, the platform works with the user to get the objective right”), extended by the two functions — Learning and Invention — that the source documents named but that never landed in this canon until now.
10: 17.2 · The service that powers it
11: No sibling services. Per the source's own governing doctrine (§1.2): Mtafiti gains an audio modality and the Character Register; Northena gains audio data classes on its one ledger; the shaping wizard gains an Objective Wizard variant; Targeta gains a training object and a third planning mode. Anything that reads as a parallel to an existing service is rule proliferation and must be collapsed into the existing service before build — stated as a standing principle, not a one-time note.
12: 17.3 · Definition of the promise
13: Five principles govern every clause below. Where any clause conflicts with one of these, the principle wins and the clause is defective — the source's own words, reused because the standard is worth inheriting exactly.
14: An audio file is a data estate, and the framing is recursive. The archive is an estate; a programme is an estate; a single file is an estate. Segments are rows; content, language, condition, prosody, occurrence, code-switch, music, and group-level character are columns — no schema exists until one is declared. Census, admission, registry, and record apply at every scale.
15: Modality extension, not parallel machinery (§17.2).
16: One record. Mtafiti and Northena collaborate to produce a single record, written once. Working state — loss curves, intermediate metrics, partial coverage counts — is scratch, not truth, until finalized and stamped. No local ledger exists anywhere in this design. If a measured throughput ceiling ever demands relief, the relief is batched stamping — one row certifying N events with a digest — which remains a single record; that change is made only when a measurement demands it, never pre-emptively.
17: Measure, do not assert. No data-volume requirement, accuracy expectation, or cost figure is quoted without a measurement behind it — calibration exists specifically to convert assertions into measurements before commitment.
18: Unrepresentable, not policed. Safety boundaries are enforced by making the violating state impossible to express in the contract, not by review after the fact — the pattern already proven for the assertion floor (Document 4), applied here to the Character Register's write path (§17.5) and the voice identity distance gate (§17.5).
19: The end-to-end commission flow these principles produce: an Objective Wizard session compiles a TargetOutcome and a Collection Schema → Sampling & Reflection (calibration) produces proposed milestones and a priced quote → the owner agrees the milestones and the commission opens → collection updates the register, which drives the curriculum, which drives training runs, which produce certificates → the Commission View reports against milestones throughout → the commission seals.
20: Foundation method is fixed, not chosen per run
21: Every model the platform trains is a LoRA/PEFT adapter over a registered open base model — never a full fine-tune, never an unregistered model. This is FACT-class in the ratified Training Techniques Spec, meaning it is not revisited per training job; it is a standing constraint on what “training” is allowed to mean on this platform. Training material is drawn exclusively from de-duplicated, qualified units — the same units the estate's extraction pipeline already produces, never raw source reached around that pipeline. Acceptance runs exclusively through MOAC on uncurated held-out sets: a model is never accepted on the material it was tuned against.
22: Configuration is a governed object, not code
23: If the optimizer, the learning-rate schedule, the batch and epoch parameters, and the adapter's rank and target modules lived in code, every change to how a model trains would be a code change — reviewed on a different cadence, by different people, invisible to the ledger that governs every other consequential object on the platform. Instead, all of it lives under training_params@v0, a sidecar configuration class carrying the identical discipline already proven for extraction_params@v0: versioned, ledgered, kept outside contracts/, with no Parity contact.
24: The seat starts empty; evidence fills it, not judgement
25: No default recipe exists at commission. The first real training run does not consume a pre-set configuration — it is the mechanism that produces one, through the measured optimizer-selection protocol (§17.5). Every trained model's registry entry cites the exact recipe_version that produced it, extending MOAC's lineage criterion (M-d) by this field.
26: 17.4a · Extraction — audio into provenance-paired facts
27: Everything below sits ahead of the Character Register and training in the loop; it is where the register's raw material comes from, and none of it is generic — it is specific to audio and was entirely absent from this document until now.
28: Tokenized representation
29: All downstream audio work — extraction, character analysis, training — operates on discrete token sequences from a neural audio codec, never on waveforms directly. Tokenization exposes two separable streams per segment: the content stream (what was said, feeding ASR/NER) and the character stream (how it was said, feeding the Character Register) — the character stream is retained and routed, never discarded as noise. Control markers for language, register, and segment type are splice-able tokens, enabling one model per estate rather than one per language, with native handling of code-switched speech. Audio in an unsupported condition fails closed with a stated reason; the codec never silently degrades quality. The service (perception/audio_codec/) is registered like any other perception model, census-visible, running in-perimeter on tenant compute; codec_version is a mandatory field of every downstream artifact's provenance, and round-trip fidelity is measured and recorded per codec version before that version serves any commission. Codec choice itself — adopt an existing open codec or train one estate-specific — was an open question in the source spec; it is now ruled DELEGATED-REVERSIBLE (§17.5 rulings), a config slot the builder sets initially and Sampling & Reflection re-derives on evidence.
30: Language identification and code-switching
31: Every segment carries a real language signal — the current plumbing value of language_hint: None is retired. A lightweight, offline, CPU-viable identifier runs at segment level during ingestion, recording languages, confidences, and code-switch points where multiple languages occur in one utterance; the signal routes downstream model selection and is written into provenance. Switch points — position, from-language, to-language, context class — are registered facts with provenance, not preprocessing metadata: they populate the register's code-switch layer and stratify test sets directly.
32: Condition profiling and synthesis-attribute capture
33: Channel condition — studio, field, or telephone band, transmission artefacts, background class — is derived per segment at first ingestion, because it is cheap to compute, directly predictive of extraction error, and required for training stratification; re-ingesting an estate to recover it later is the mistake this captures against. In the same ingestion pass, group-level acoustic attributes any future synthesis capability will need — pitch statistics, energy contours, duration patterns — are captured subject to the custody conditions below (§17.4b); this forecloses nothing and costs little, while omitting it forecloses invention entirely or forces a full re-ingestion.
34: Deduplication as augmentation
35: The existing occurrence index's output contract extends: for each deduplicated item, the instance condition map — the set of channel, time, and condition variants under which identical content occurred — is retained. One canonical extraction is stored; the variant set enters training curricula as a designated robustness stratum at zero acquisition cost. No new detection work — this changes only what dedup keeps.
36: 17.4b · Learning — the Character Register and its custody boundary
37: This is the function most completely missing from every prior version of this document. It is not an extraction detail; it is a second learning capability with its own governance model, sitting alongside the extraction pipeline and feeding the training planner.
38: Definition and layers
39: A registry-modality store of learned, group-level audio characteristics, built from the character stream — Mtafiti's existing qualification-and-index doctrine applied to acoustic observations, an extension per §17.2, not a sibling. Every entry carries provenance to source material and an occurrence count, across four layers: phonetic (per-lexeme pronunciation variants, frequency, regional distribution — feeding curricula, extraction lexicons, and evaluation stratification); prosodic (intonation, stress, rate, pause structure — feeding training and programme-type classification); condition (channel and environment profiles — feeding stratification and error prediction); and code-switch (switch-point patterns, language pairs, context classes — feeding training and test-set design). Built by unsupervised clustering over the character stream, which yields candidate strata — a cluster asserts that a distinct variant exists, not what it is called; naming and validation are human work applied to a sample, commissioned and priced like any other qualified work.
40: The custody boundary: organic versus learned
41: Organic characteristics are anatomical — vocal tract length, formant structure, glottal source, fundamental-frequency range. They cannot be acquired or shed; they are exactly what speaker verification keys on; they are biometric. They are never registered. Learned characteristics are acquired from a speech community — phonological inventory, pronunciation variants, prosody, code-switching habits — group properties by construction. Only learned characteristics may be registered, and only if all four conditions hold simultaneously: acquired, not anatomical (learnable by a speaker from a different background); shared (observed across at least N distinct speakers, N a governed seam value defaulting to the platform's minimum-group-size parameter unless a tenant sets a register-specific value — open decision, §17.5); non-reconstructive in combination (tested against attribute combinations, not attributes alone — language + region + age band + one distinctive feature can reach a single person even when every attribute is group-level); and stored as description, not exemplar (centroids and distributions only — never stored audio, never per-utterance speaker embeddings; embeddings used during clustering are destroyed after cluster assignment, and provenance points to material, not to speaker identity). Habitual fillers and idiosyncratic pronunciations are learned but individuating — they fail condition three or four and are excluded; “learned” alone is never sufficient, the four conditions are conjunctive.
42: Enforcement: unrepresentable, not policed
43: The register's write path exposes no field through which an instance-level representation can be stored — the schema itself cannot represent a voiceprint. An automated invariant test attempts each known leakage path (a small stratum, an idiolect marker, a narrowing attribute combination, exemplar storage) on every change to the register code, and must fail to store all of them. This is the same enforcement pattern Document 1 uses for its chokepoint, applied here to a second boundary that governs what may be learned rather than what may leave.
44: 17.4c · Invention — synthesized voice identity
45: A real, specified, sellable capability, and a second component entirely missing until now.
46: Mechanism: inherit the learned, synthesize the organic
47: Learned characteristics are inherited from the register — this is what makes a constructed voice sound like a genuine speaker of the language rather than a foreigner reading it. Organic characteristics are constructed: vocal-tract parameters, F0 range, formant structure, and glottal parameters are chosen as a point in acoustic space that no real speaker occupies. This is the inverse of a voice clone — a clone copies the organic and frequently gets the learned wrong; this gets the learned right and owns the organic outright.
48: The distance guarantee — mandatory, fail-closed
49: Every constructed identity is scored against every speaker representation derivable from the corpus, using standard speaker-verification methods, and a minimum distance from all of them is required. Below threshold, the identity is rejected and resampled. There is no override. The threshold value and the verification method are recorded permanently with the identity.
50: The certificate — a sellable artifact, not a byproduct
51: A passing identity is issued a certificate stating that the voice is provably derived from no individual, naming the method, the threshold, and the corpus version scored against. Synthetic voice is currently a legal hazard for any broadcaster or brand that touches it, and the hazard is provenance, not technical quality — nobody can normally prove whose voice it is not. An artefact that proves absence of derivation is the product, sellable on its own terms. Identity composition: acoustic identity from constructed organic parameters; speech character inherited from the register's phonetic and prosodic layers; interaction character — turn-taking, formality, code-switch behaviour — also inherited from the register. Each identity is a versioned artefact with a ledger entry; changing one is a ceremony with the standard waiting period, because audience recognition accrues to the voice and that recognition is the asset. Identities never drift.
52: Scope, stated honestly
53: Rendering requires a synthesis stack — a separate build from recognition, explicitly Phase 2. What this specification requires now is non-foreclosure: the identity specification, the distance method, and the certificate format are defined, and the ingestion capture in §17.4a ensures the substrate exists when rendering is eventually built. Say that the specification is defined and the substrate is guaranteed; do not imply that rendering ships today.
54: 17.4d · The commission chain — two compiled artifacts, not one
55: Corrects a real gap: the wizard compiles two governed artifacts, and only one of them was in any prior version of this document.
56: The Objective Wizard as schema compiler
57: No business user hand-writes a Target Outcome. The Objective Wizard — a variant of the existing shaping wizard, reusing its agent interface, guards, session persistence, and ledger sidecar — elicits an objective in plain language and compiles two artifacts: the TargetOutcome (§17.4e) handed to the Training Planner, and the Collection Schema (§17.4f) — the data dictionary for this objective, stating which data points are extracted from the sound, at what granularity, at what quality bar. Elicitation runs in four moves: the operational, falsifiable question the model must answer; the population, resolved against existing register strata (an unresolved population is flagged unmeasured and generates census work rather than being guessed); the acceptance bar per stratum, with the gate-or-document decision recorded explicitly; and the collection consequences — the wizard derives required columns, shows which are already collected, which exist but are uncollected, and what collecting them costs, so the owner sees the schema's price before commissioning.
58: Dynamism within scope: propose, qualify, graduate
59: The agent side may propose novel data points no prior objective collected — this is where innovation enters. A proposed column never enters collection directly: it is admitted as a candidate, collected on a sample only, its evidence of value measured against the objective, the same qualification path any fact travels. Qualified candidates graduate into the objective tier for that commission; graduation into the baseline tier is ceremony-governed (proposal, countersignature, waiting period), because a baseline column is paid on every hour ingested for the life of the estate. The compile stage is deterministic throughout — the agent proposes, only qualified columns compile — and mechanical guards prove against a stub agent before any LLM is plugged in. Rejected at compile, not warned: an Outcome without an existing test_set_ref; an acceptance bar missing its per-stratum dimension; a Collection Schema requiring a column whose capture would violate the custody conditions of §17.4b. Every session stamps to the ledger under its own data class, including options considered and rejected — which is what makes a later “why was the model built this way” answerable.
60: 17.4e · The Collection Schema
61: The declared data dictionary of a commission — what is extracted from the sound, for what purpose, at what quality bar — the admission standard of the audio estate, per objective. Two tiers: the baseline tier is standing and objective-independent, collected at first ingestion for all admitted material, membership decided purely by “cheap to collect now, unaffordable to collect later” — language ID, code-switch points, condition profile, the dedup instance condition map, and synthesis-relevant group-level acoustics at v1.0. Changes to the baseline are seam-governed (ceremony, countersignature, waiting period), because silently narrowing it is how an estate quietly becomes unre-readable. The objective tier is declared per commission by the Objective Wizard, collected against material already in governed scope, priced before collection starts, and recorded in the commission's own registry namespace; candidate columns enter only through propose–qualify–graduate (§17.4d).
62: Revision is cheap; unevidenced revision is a defect
63: Recipe revisions carry no approval ceremony — they are DEFAULT-class, expected to happen as evidence accumulates. But every revision must attach the measured comparison that justifies it and must write a ledger row. The absence of ceremony is not the absence of accountability: a revision with no attached evidence is not a lighter-weight change, it is a defect, indistinguishable in the record from an engineer overriding the platform's own evidentiary standard by hand.
64: The Target Outcome — training cannot be commissioned against an unfalsifiable goal
65: A training job is not admitted from a task description alone. It is admitted from a Target Outcome, a schema that forces the goal into a form that can actually fail:
66: TargetOutcome:
67: task            operational statement of what the model must do
68: domain          context of use
69: population      defined by reference to register strata, not labels
70: acceptance      threshold per stratum — two-dimensional (accuracy, coverage)
71: gate_policy     missed stratum gates release | ships documented
72: test_set_ref    must exist before the plan is accepted
73: constraints     latency, compute budget, deployment target
74: Two rules are binding, not advisory. Population is register-defined: “language L, accent clusters 1–4, telephone band and studio, adult”, never “speakers of L” — because only a register-defined population makes coverage a computable number rather than a felt impression. Acceptance is per stratum, not global: a single aggregate figure hides exactly the failure that matters — 94% on the majority variant and 61% on everything else passes one test and fails the one that decides whether the work reaches the people it was built for. Whether a missed stratum blocks release is a governed decision recorded on the Outcome at definition time, not an ad-hoc call made under ship-date pressure. And the ordering constraint is absolute: the test set precedes the training. An Outcome submitted without an existing, stratified test set is rejected at definition, before a single GPU-hour is spent.
75: The Training Planner — the same pattern as extraction, a different object and floor
76: The planner is not new architecture. It reuses, unchanged, the pattern already proven for extraction planning: a deterministic core computes eligibility; a learned layer may only reorder an already-eligible set, and it receives that set stripped of the values that decided eligibility in the first place, so it cannot learn to game the floor; a gate compares the learned layer's output against the deterministic baseline before anything ships; every plan is reproducible from its own recorded inputs. What changes between the two is only the object being planned over and the floor that governs it:
77: Planner outputs, per commissioned Outcome, are four things: a coverage report per target stratum — hours available, quality distribution, gaps, and the cost of closing each gap; a curriculum, ordered and weighted from the register itself, deliberately not from the corpus's natural distribution, which is always skewed toward whatever occurred most — the dedup instance-condition map enters here as a designated robustness stratum, at zero additional acquisition cost; the calibration commission (below); and a cost quote carrying a stated confidence interval, never a bare point estimate.
78: Calibration is the planner's mandatory first stage, not an optional safeguard. Data requirements for low-resource fine-tuning are empirical — no analytical formula predicts how much data a given stratum needs to cross its acceptance threshold. So the first commissioned job is never the real job: it trains at three or four data volumes, evaluates against the test set per stratum, fits the scaling curve, and only then extrapolates to what the full run would cost and how likely it is to clear the threshold. A plan without a calibration stage is rejected outright — the first job's entire purpose is to price the real one honestly.
79: Calibration has a second customer beyond pricing: it authors the accountability structure the objective owner will be held to. Its output is not only a curve, it is a proposed milestone list — the checklist of what must be done, in what order, for the commission to succeed, each milestone carrying a done-condition and an owner. The objective owner reviews and agrees this list at commission, before spend begins; every status report afterward is measured against it. Accountability is set before the money moves, not reconstructed afterward from whatever happened to get done.
80: Provenance survives the training, not just the extraction. Every training example carries its provenance into the training manifest, which has three consequences that matter beyond bookkeeping: rights are enforceable per example, so an example whose rights lapse is identifiable and every model it touched is enumerable, not merely suspected; “the trained model is the customer's property” becomes a defensible statement backed by a manifest rather than an assertion made because it sounds right; and the dedup instance-condition map enters the curriculum as a designated robustness stratum at zero acquisition cost, because it was already being computed for a different purpose.
81: 17.4 · Delivery experience expectations
82: What the organisation experiences (human-facing)
83: Defines a target outcome — task, domain, register-defined population, per-stratum acceptance — and the platform rejects it outright if the test set doesn't already exist.
84: Watches the mandatory first stage, calibration, as staged progress: three to four data volumes trained and evaluated per stratum, the scaling curve fit, the full run quoted only after — with a confidence interval, never a point estimate.
85: Receives the calibration run's second output alongside the price: a proposed milestone list, each with a done-condition and an owner, agreed before spend rather than discovered during it.
86: Sees an optimizer or recipe-component candidate proven or rejected by a measured two-arm comparison against the current baseline — both arms' numbers reported, parity mandatory for adoption, the verdict an Owner ruling on evidence rather than a preset threshold.
87: Gets a model that provably cleared all six MOAC criteria, or a recorded rejection with its numbers — never a manually waved-through model — with rejected candidates kept on the shelf permanently.
88: What a consuming system experiences (machine-facing)
89: Reads a model's registry entry citing its recipe_version, base model, and the rights lineage that trained it — lineage is enumerable, not asserted.
90: Reads a training run's completion certificate: compute consumed, data touched, manifest hash, and per-stratum results against the Outcome — failed strata reported as plainly as passed ones.
91: What is produced and retained
92: The training manifest — every example's provenance carried through to the trained artifact, so a lapsed-rights example is identifiable and every model it touched is enumerable.
93: The completion certificate and the recipe_version record, both permanent.
94: On rejection, the candidate and its measured numbers, retained — a negative result is still a result.
95: 17.5 · Technical and behavioural requirements
96: Governance layer — already ratified, reused verbatim from RMS-IQ-Core-2
97: A17.1  [CANON] Configuration lives outside code.
98: Optimizer and its parameters, learning-rate schedule, batch and epoch parameters, and adapter rank and target modules MUST live under training_params@v0, a sidecar configuration class with the same discipline as extraction_params@v0: versioned, ledgered, outside contracts/, no Parity contact. The effect is that a training configuration change is reviewable and auditable the same way a rule change is — not a deploy note buried in a pull request.
99: T-1.1, training_techniques_spec_v1.md
100: A17.2  [CANON] The seat ships empty.
101: No default recipe exists until the first training run fills it through the §3 optimizer-selection protocol (A17.5–A17.6). Nothing may pre-populate training_params@v0 by convention, template, or engineer judgement — the first value ever written to it must carry the measured comparison that produced it.
102: A17.3  [CANON] Lineage extends to configuration.
103: Every trained model's registry entry MUST cite the recipe_version that trained it. MOAC's lineage criterion (M-d) extends by this field, so “which configuration produced this model” is answered by reading the registry, never by asking whoever happened to run the job.
104: A17.4  [CANON] Revision is DEFAULT-class, but never unevidenced.
105: Recipe revisions carry no approval ceremony. Each revision MUST attach the measured comparison that justifies it and MUST write a ledger row. A revision without attached evidence is a defect — the absence of ceremony is a statement of trust in the evidentiary standard, not an exemption from it.
106: A17.5–A17.6  [CANON] The optimizer-selection protocol: two arms, identical conditions, parity mandatory.
107: The protocol executes at the first adapter training on real material, inside the P4-instrumented run. Its shape is one two-arm comparison — the current baseline optimizer versus a candidate, Muon named as the first — with identical training data, identical base model, identical evaluation sets, and an identical compute-budget cap, run on the smallest stratum that still yields a valid MOAC evaluation. Four measured outputs are reported for both arms without exception: target-stratum improvement (MOAC's M-a), non-target regression (M-b), wall-clock and GPU-hours to convergence, and calibration quality (an M-e input). Quality parity on M-a and M-b is mandatory for the candidate to remain eligible at all; compute-to-convergence is reported, never gating — a faster optimizer that regresses quality is not eligible regardless of its speed. The adopt/reject decision is then an Owner ruling made on the measured results, with no adoption threshold fixed in advance of the evidence, and verdict samples are uncurated per the platform's standing D-7 doctrine (evaluation inputs may be engineered; evaluation samples may not). On adoption, the winning arm writes training_params@v0 v1 with the comparison attached; on rejection, the candidate is recorded as tested, with its numbers, permanently. The identical protocol governs every future recipe-component candidate — this is not a one-time bootstrap, it is how the recipe seat is filled from now on.
108: A17.7  [CANON] Ensemble critics detect; they never decide.
109: Multiple reviewing instances are legitimate where a single critic's detection quality is insufficient, and prohibited from ever holding decision authority — the boundary follows from the platform's design (one walled learner, one reasoning faculty, the standing QA-1 rule that the layer detects and never decides) and is permanent, not a current-scope limitation. Deployment order is fixed: when seeded audits show a single critic's catch-rate below the standing bar on any fall class across two consecutive audits, rubric and context repair MUST execute first; an ensemble MAY deploy only if the repaired single critic still misses on a subsequent audit. Members MUST differ genuinely — a different base model or a materially different context shape — because same-base, same-context replicas are correlated reviewers that share failure modes and add cost without adding detection. All ensemble output is findings only; voting, override, and critic-of-critic structures are prohibited outright. Disagreement between critics is itself a finding class, routed to rulings like any other. Bounds: N ≤ 3 members without an explicit Owner ruling, with cost-per-review telemetry emitted per member, and the ensemble retires on its own kill metric — if its catch-rate gain over the single repaired critic falls under 10 percentage points after one full calibration cycle, it is rent not worth paying.
110: A17.8  [CANON] Cascade offload builds only against a measured shortfall, never speculatively.
111: A local-cascade — a local model drafts, an LLM handles only what the local model cannot — reduces metered spend where a cheaper model can filter most of a workload, but carries a documented failure mode: past a certain escalation rate, each escalated item pays twice, local and LLM both, and the cascade turns net-negative. The platform already minimizes LLM load by construction (the rung ladder, record-derived facts never re-asked of the LLM, the mechanical composition arm, the critic-succession seat), so a cascade is deliberately not pre-built. It MAY begin only when F3 telemetry, with cost columns active, shows LLM spend on a named seam exceeding a threshold the Owner sets at that time — no threshold exists in advance of metered evidence, and before the trigger fires, no cascade scaffolding, draft-model acquisition, or routing machinery may be built at all (the D7 fence). Its shape, once triggered, is local model drafts → deterministic acceptance check → LLM invoked only on rejects, where the acceptance check is rung-1 machinery, not a second model's judgement. It MUST emit its own kill metric — the double-pay rate, the share of items incurring both local and LLM cost — from its first run, and MUST retire if escalation makes it net-negative against the pre-cascade baseline.
112: A17.9  [CANON] Execution mode is explicit or the process refuses to start.
113: PERCEPTION_EXECUTION_MODE is read from the environment at import time and must be exactly “cpu” or “gpu”; an unset variable raises an import-time failure rather than defaulting silently, because a GPU deployment quietly running on CPU is the same silent-swap risk in the opposite direction from what governance normally worries about — it fails safe in the wrong direction, producing correct-looking but unrepresentative results rather than an obvious error. execution_mode is then carried in result telemetry, so attribution of GPU-hours and yield to a mode the record doesn't state is closed the same way fabricated model attribution is closed elsewhere in the canon.
114: Owner ruling 9.2a-E2 α, 2026-07-10 — cuda_runtime.py, RMS-IQ-Core-2
115: Base model selection — deliberately deferred, not open
116: A17.10  [CANON] A CI fixture exists; production is a different, later question.
117: The registry seeds with whisper-tiny — MIT-licensed (OpenAI's original release via Systran's faster-whisper/CTranslate2 conversion), weights SHA-pinned, origin URL recorded — explicitly marked “CI CPU-mode ASR fixture model. NOT for production use.” The seeding ruling itself is worth carrying forward verbatim, because it resolves a real deadlock: “the registry does NOT seed empty — it seeds with the CI fixture model's entry. Empty per data-blind misapplies the posture: data-blind governs assumptions about the estate's content, not tool provenance — a model registry entry is tooling attestation, and an empty registry plus a provenance gate is the CD-E3 deadlock again (nothing can pass).”
118: "whisper-tiny": {
119: "family": "Whisper-class", "role": "ci_fixture_asr",
120: "backend": "faster-whisper (ctranslate2)",
121: "license": "MIT (OpenAI Whisper original release
122: · Systran faster-whisper conversion)",
123: "purpose": "CI CPU-mode ASR fixture model. NOT for
124: production use."
125: }
126: A17.11  [CANON] Production selection is named after the census, not before it.
127: Production base model selection lands additively at a later registry bump — “named at first census activation” — following the identical license-verify → checksum-pin → Owner-ruling sequence already registered for the Qwen3 and Llama text-generation candidate rows in the same file. Those rows exist today as class-level registrations with zero download and zero compute: parameters known, license disclosed or flagged for acquisition-time verification, specific members deferred. The same discipline governs audio. The sequencing consequence is direct: the census (Documents 9–10) runs first, and the specific model is named after, informed by what the census actually finds in the estate — not chosen speculatively ahead of it on the strength of a published benchmark.
128: Owner ruling 2026-07-15, Gap-Closure + Sequence Ratification dispatch, Item 6 — models_registry.v0.json
129: Execution layer — does not exist; this is the actual build gap
130: A17.12  [OPEN] No runner exists in any modality.
131: Grep across both repositories for LoRA, PEFT, fine-tune, or trainer classes returns nothing. What exists is scaffolding around an absent center: the target-selector and eligibility gate, the MOAC contract with nothing emitting it, the baseline-line contract with no run producer, the whitepaper drafter with nothing to draft from yet. Build scope, once unblocked: contracts (training_config, training_run, training-material admit — roughly 500 LOC) plus a modality-agnostic runner service (roughly 2,000–3,000 LOC) plus a training panel frontend (recipe / run / MOAC — roughly 600–900 LOC, combined with the skill-files registry surface in Document 18). This is the W11 envelope, sized comparably to the platform's prior W10-class builds.
132: A17.13  [OPEN] Model Admission shows a capability with nothing running behind it.
133: The surface displays “four of six checks passed” with all six criteria named and rejected models kept on record — real UI, real registry schema. But MOAC has a contract and no emitter: nothing in the current build actually runs a candidate through the six checks and writes the result. The surface is currently a faithful rendering of a process that has not yet executed.
134: A17.14  [OPEN] GPU host is reachable; authentication is not configured.
135: The runner's dispatch target is mock SSH until real credentials are supplied and verified. This is progress from an earlier state where the endpoint was not reachable at all, and it is the narrowest of the open items to close.
136: A17.15  [OPEN] No corpus with an owner-signed rights declaration exists.
137: Admission is blocked without rights lineage — the same discipline that governs every other admitted object on the platform. The sequencing this implies is not incidental: the census and rights-position machinery (Documents 9–10) is precisely what produces this declaration from an estate. For any customer engagement, the order is census → rights declaration → corpus admission → trainer, not a parallel track that could start independently.
138: A17.16  [CANON] The ingredient-manifest guarantee is ACCEPTED.
139: Training destroys per-claim traceability the moment weights are updated — a trained model cannot point back to which specific sentence in its training data justifies a given output the way a retrieved passage can. The only honest guarantee a trained model can therefore carry is provenance of ingredients: what went in, its standard, its licence — never provenance of assertions, which would misrepresent what training actually preserves. Owner-ruled ACCEPT: claiming provenance of assertions would overclaim what training structurally cannot support, a direct violation of §1.4's own “measure, do not assert” doctrine; provenance of ingredients is the honest ceiling, not a lesser guarantee — the training manifest already tracks exactly this. The model output form is no longer refused on this basis; it carries the ingredients-only guarantee explicitly, never a stronger claim.
140: A17.17  [CANON] CUDA/PyTorch is installed — RESOLVED.
141: Confirmed installed. The execution-mode discipline (A17.9) already existed and already refused to run ambiguously between CPU and GPU; that switch is no longer waiting on this item — gpu mode is real, not theoretical, as of this confirmation.
142: A17.18 · Codec choice — RESOLVED, not open
143: The source spec listed this as an owner-level open decision (§16.2): adopt an existing open codec, or train one estate-specific. It is ruled: DELEGATED-REVERSIBLE (docs/rulings/audio_plane_codec_build_order_circularity_2026-07-30.md, closed by CC-6, 2026-07-30). Storage math on the actual broadcast reference workload (48kHz/16-bit/stereo, ~691MB/hour, a 10-station/20-hour/5-year estate at ~1.5PB uncompressed, ~0.7–1.0PB under lossless FLAC) shows original-quality retention is economically viable at 2026 object-storage rates — so the codec is a reversible config slot: an open codec at ship, chosen by the builder, re-derived by Sampling & Reflection once real benchmark data exists, with every artifact's codec_version stamped in provenance regardless of later swaps. One sub-finding stays open: the source's own §16.2 cross-reference (“§6.2.2”) doesn't resolve against the committed spec, which has no §6.2.2 — awaiting Owner clarification, not blocking.
144: A17.19 · Owner-level decisions — three ruled, one still open
145: A17.19a  [CANON] Minimum group size N (§6.2): inherits the platform's existing minimum-group-size seam value.
146: No register-specific override at launch — reusing an already-calibrated value beats inventing a parallel number with no evidence behind it. A tenant can still set a register-specific value later; that path stays open, unused for now.
147: A17.19b  [CANON] Default gate_policy: GATES release.
148: Ships-documented as the silent default would hollow out per-stratum acceptance — the entire reason it exists is to stop the “94% majority, 61% minority” failure a single global threshold hides. An Outcome can still explicitly set ships-documented for itself when its objective owner consciously accepts that; it remains a live override, just never the unset default.
149: A17.19c  [CANON] Cluster naming validation: internal by default, external escalation for ambiguous or sensitive clusters.
150: Not a flat internal/external pick. Escalates to an external evaluation partner specifically for clusters near the custody boundary's individuating line (§6.2–6.4) or touching Sheng's genuinely contested, fast-moving register boundaries — the same risk-tiered shape as the Watch's own action ladder, not a uniform policy applied regardless of stakes.
151: A17.19d  [OPEN] Baseline-tier contents (§9.2) remain open — not part of this ruling round.
152: The v1.0 set is still a proposal: every addition is paid on every hour ingested for the life of the estate; every omission is paid again at re-ingestion. Genuinely unruled, distinct from a–c above.
153: A17.20 · Build sequence, ordered by dependency and cost of deferral — not by size
154: 1. Ingestion capture: language ID, code-switch, condition,
155: synthesis attributes.  Everything downstream depends on
156: these; cheap only at first ingestion, a full re-pass to fix later.
157: 2. Dedup instance-condition map.  Contract change to existing

161: retrofitting means rebuilding from source.
162: 4. Codec service.  Unsupervised pretraining starts on

164: 5. Clustering + sampled human validation.  Requires 1–4.
165: 6. Objective Wizard variant + Collection Schema type +
166: registry namespace.  Must precede the planner — building
167: the planner first invites malformed input the compile
168: stage is built to make impossible.
169: 7. TargetOutcome type + planner core.  Requires register
170: strata to plan against and the wizard to author Outcomes.
171: 8. Sampling & Reflection + milestone records.  Requires 7
172: and a test set.
173: 9. Commission View.  Reads records created in 8; cannot
174: precede them by its own backend-cost constraint.
