179: 17.6 · What must be true for the service to deliver as intended
180: No training run commits without an existing, stratified test set — a target outcome without one is rejected at definition, not at run time.
181: No model enters service without clearing all six MOAC criteria on uncurated held-out material, with no human in the acceptance path.
182: The recipe seat is never filled speculatively — only by measured evidence from a real run against real material.
183: Base model selection never precedes the census it depends on.
184: No ensemble critic holds decision authority; ensembles surface findings, never verdicts.
185: Cascade offload never builds ahead of a measured cost pressure that names its own trigger.
186: A GPU deployment never silently runs on CPU, and a CPU deployment never silently claims GPU throughput.
187: DOCUMENT 18   Callable Skill Files
188: Callable Skill Files
189: A new promise — Promise #33. Owner-confirmed architecture (July 2026, RMS-IQ-Core-2); complete donor code exists but is not in the current build.
190: 18.1 · The promise, in plain language
191: A skill is a stay-running, key-scoped query capability over a defined corpus slice — an application calls it and receives governed answers, repeatedly, on the platform's own infrastructure. It is not model weights, and it is not a file handed over: governance does not end at delivery, because there is no delivery. It travels into every call, for the life of the skill.
192: 18.2 · The service that powers it
193: The existing inner-gate crossing infrastructure (Document 1), extended by the callable-skill donor package — complete implementation, ~356 LOC, present in both RMS-IQ-Core-2 and Akki-OS-V1: a frozen provisioning contract, a per-call governance gate, and write-once persistence. Not in the current build; sized by the builder at a clean ~40% LIFT into the W11 envelope alongside Document 17's runner.
194: 18.3 · Definition of the promise
195: The reasoning below is reused close to verbatim from the July 2026 architecture ruling, because the reasoning is the part worth keeping intact — a conclusion without it invites re-litigating the same ground later.
196: Why this needed its own ruling, not an extension of the export model
197: Every output the platform can produce looks, at first, like a variation on “produce something, then define who can access it.” Treating all outputs that way is a trap: it architects the live ones as static deliverables, and the mistake surfaces only once a skill gets queried a thousand times and turns out to need per-call governance the export model was never built to carry. The real distinction is not output-then-access. It is whether the system finishes and hands over, or stays running and answers.
198: Two classes, one dividing line
199: Hand-over: qualified data, a knowledge artifact, a trained model file. The system produces, packages, and delivers a finished thing; governance is enforced once, at export. Stay-running: a callable skill, an API feed. The system stays up and a consumer queries it repeatedly; governance has to travel into every one of those calls, live. Skills are stay-running by definition — an application queries them, they are not model weights, and the “trained behaviour” reading of “skill” belongs to the model-output form (§17), not here. This is not new architecture: it is the identical governance-travels-inline requirement the platform's integration surface already carries for API responses, now extended to a standing service rather than a single call.
200: What this fixes about the delivery model, concretely
201: Hand-over outputs continue to fit the existing two-perimeter export model without change. Stay-running outputs need per-call inline governance, which is the reason this document exists as its own promise rather than a line item under an existing one — the liability model, the access architecture, and the governance surface for “a file the consumer runs themselves” and “a service they call on the platform's own infrastructure, forever” are genuinely different products, and conflating them is what produces the failure mode described above.
202: Grain is per_claim and synthesized_whole, per query — deliberately distinct from a knowledge artifact's per_claim/aggregated grain, because a skill composes a fresh answer to each specific question rather than exporting one fixed graph once.
203: 18.4 · Delivery experience expectations
204: What the organisation experiences (human-facing)
205: Provisions a skill over a frozen, named corpus slice and hands a consumer a scoped key and an endpoint — nothing else about the underlying data.
206: Revokes a skill and has every subsequent call refuse immediately — enforcement is server-side, not a client convention that can be ignored.
207: Reads the provisioning record for any skill: who was granted what scope, over which slice, from when to when.
208: What a consuming system experiences (machine-facing)
209: Calls the skill repeatedly and receives an answer with its class carried inline on every response — never a response the inner gate hasn't governed.
210: Queries below the skill's floor and receives the refusal envelope, not a degraded or partial answer.
211: Cannot reach a slice wider than the one bound at provisioning — a changed slice is a new skill, never a silent edit of the old one.
212: What is produced and retained
213: The provisioning record itself: skill_id, corpus_slice_ref, key_grant_id, floor, scope, endpoint_path, provisioned_at, and revoked_at once set.
214: Every call's governance class, carried on the response, per the inner gate's existing per-call record discipline.
215: 18.5 · Technical and behavioural requirements
216: A18.1  [CANON] The provisioning record, reused verbatim.
217: This is the frozen contract every skill is created against — not a draft to redesign, a specification already anchored to owner rulings TF-E2/TF-E4 and reused as-is:
218: Callable-skill provisioning record
219: { skill_id, corpus_slice_ref: artifact-store key,
220: key_grant_id, floor, scope, endpoint_path,
221: provisioned_at, revoked_at?: str }
222: §3.7 annex, RMS Intelligence spec, 2026-07
223: A18.2  [CANON] The slice freezes; it never edits.
224: Corpus slice binds at freeze, an endpoint is provisioned against it, and a key is scoped to that endpoint. The slice persists via the artifact store, write-once. If the underlying material needs to change, the platform provisions a new skill against a new slice — it does not mutate the old one, because a mutating slice would mean the governance decision made at provisioning (“this key may see this material”) silently stops describing what the key can actually reach.
225: A18.3  [CANON] Governance rides every response, not just the first one.
226: Every response carries its class inline through the inner gate's per-call governance — the platform's existing live-response contract, applied here to a standing service instead of a single crossing. Nothing about the mechanism is new; what changes is that it now runs once per query for the life of the skill, rather than once per delivery.
227: A18.4  [CANON] Below the floor is a refusal, never a degraded answer.
228: The standard is enforced per call. A query that falls below the skill's floor returns the refusal envelope — the same governed refusal shape used everywhere else on the platform — rather than a thinner or hedged version of an answer.
229: A18.5  [CANON] Scope is enforced server-side, not by client discipline.
230: Access rides the engineer key-grant records. A consuming application's own good behaviour is never the control — scope is checked at the gate on every call, so a compromised or careless client can narrow what it asks for but cannot widen what it's able to get.
231: A18.6  [PROPOSED] Async delivery, if fresh extraction ever backs a skill's answer.
232: Not yet confirmed as part of skill files specifically, but already a ratified contract shape elsewhere in the same source, and the natural fit if a skill's query ever requires extraction rather than a warm read: fork at admission — warm returns a synchronous full response; fresh returns 202 with { objective_id, status: accepted, delivery_estimate, quote? }. States move accepted → running → delivered | refused, with a late refusal a normal terminal state carrying the same refusal envelope, never rendered as a failure. Delivery is a thin webhook plus a governed fetch: the webhook payload is { event, objective_id, trace_id, status } — never claim content — and the actual result is pulled over the caller's authenticated key, scope enforced there, not pushed to an app-configured URL, because pushing claims to arbitrary endpoints would be an egress path the gates don't control. No partial egress, including on cancellation — a cancelled run is still ledgered. An idempotency key is required on submission so a retried call cannot double-commission or double-charge.
233: §7, RMS Intelligence spec, 2026-07 — proposed here for skill files by extension, not yet owner-confirmed for this specific case
234: A18.7  [RULED] The concept is owner-confirmed; its adoption into this canon is not inherited.
235: “Skill files” as a named artifact appear nowhere in the 16-document canon. The architecture above is owner-confirmed [STAKED] in the July specification — that ruling is real and reused here verbatim — but formally landing it as Promise #33, with its own number in this codebase's canon, is this document's own act. It should be read as adoption, not as a restatement of a decision already made at this level.
236: A18.8  [OPEN] Complete donor code exists; it is not in this build.
237: Roughly 356 lines across RMS-IQ-Core-2 and Akki-OS-V1 implement the frozen provisioning contract, the per-call governance gate, and write-once persistence — a clean ~40% of it liftable directly. Build scope: the remaining contracts, the corpus-slice custody seam (shared with Document 17's execution layer), and a skill-files registry surface on the frontend, delivered inside the same W11 envelope as the trainer runner.
238: 18.6 · What must be true for the service to deliver as intended
239: A corpus slice is bound and frozen before an endpoint is ever provisioned — no skill is provisioned against a moving target.
240: No response leaves the inner gate without its governance class carried inline.
241: Revocation is enforced at the gate, not at the client — a revoked key produces a refusal even if a consumer never checks its own state.
242: A widened or changed slice is never expressed as an edit to a live skill — only as a new one, with its own provisioning record.
243: DOCUMENT 19   Quality Assurance & Evidence Integrity
244: Quality Assurance & Evidence Integrity
245: Two parts. Part A, the Critic Seam, is CANON — Owner-ratified 2026-07-15, reused here in full. Part B, the Evidence Protocol, is PROPOSED — my own prior synthesis from an August chat, explicitly offered there for ratification and never confirmed adopted; checked directly against both repositories, with no trace of a build or a ruling. It is written here to the same standard as everything ratified, with its status stated plainly rather than smoothed over.
246: 19A.1 · The promise, in plain language
247: Every intelligent worker in this build — the builder agent executing phases, any LLM worker the platform harnesses at runtime, and the ruling authority's own drafts and rulings — has its output checked against the on-disk record before it can mislead, not corrected by hand after it already has. The layer mechanizes exactly the half of quality assurance that is mechanizable: verification against canon. It deliberately does not attempt the other half — reframing the problem, changing the product's direction — which remains the Owner's seat, permanently.
248: 19A.2 · The service that powers it
249: No single named engine; a layer integrated into the standing build loop itself — the Registry (every function's mandate, promise, service trace, enforcement, cost, owner), the Registry Doctrine's binding rules, and the existing ruling loop (dispatch → Stage A proposal → escalation → ruling → execution → close report). It extends two precedents already standing in the build rather than introducing new machinery: the standing queries' findings-not-actions pattern, and Targeta's wall — the constitutional precedent that a subordinate intelligence detects and optimizes but never decides, which the critic inherits verbatim.
250: 19A.3 · Definition of the promise
251: Origin: every check mechanizes a catch the Owner actually made, by hand
252: This is not a speculative layer designed against a hypothetical failure mode. Five documented fall classes from this build's own correction history fix its boundary: memory-ruling (asserting something false against the on-disk record — the origin of doctrine rule D-11); re-derivation (proposing something as fresh advice that the Owner's own specification already states, caught once at the cost of a full audit cycle); invented scope or schedule (work categories or sequencing authored without instruction, against an explicit fence); false status (a register claiming a close was never returned while it sat on disk, a day old); and unclassed assertion (values and claims stated without their evidence class). The line that fixes the layer's boundary: every catch above is a verification — the truth existed on disk and the worker diverged from it. The Owner's other interventions in this build's history were frame changes — rewriting canon rather than diverging from it — and no layer that verifies against canon can catch a correction to canon. Frame authority is permanently outside this layer's reach.
253: Five design principles, each tied to a standing precedent
254: Detect, never decide — the layer emits findings; every consequence is a ruling. A QA layer with veto power would be a governor nobody mandated.
255: Canon is the oracle — all deterministic verification resolves against the on-disk record, never a summary, a context window, or another model's recollection.
256: Zero loop drag — the layer adds no turns to the dispatch loop; deterministic checks run as cells at submission boundaries, the critic runs asynchronously between turns, findings arrive with the artifacts they review, never before them.
257: Halving, not zeroing, stated honestly — a critic sharing a worker's blind spot misses what both cannot see; the claim is a measurable shrinkage of the residual, not its elimination, which is why the layer measures itself rather than trusting itself.
258: The layer pays rent — its own catch and false-alarm ledger is standing; if it stops catching and starts noising, it shrinks or retires by ruling, the same discipline every other function on the platform is held to.
259: 19A.4 · Delivery experience expectations
260: What the organisation experiences (human-facing)
261: The Owner's reviewing role compresses; it does not disappear. Instead of reading every artifact, a measured fraction of critic findings and all-clears is sampled for review — the sampling rate itself shrinks as the critic's measured reliability accumulates.
262: Sees findings, never a blocked workflow — the one exception is a hard format gate on missing required sections, form only, never substance.
263: Reads a standing calibration ledger: the critic's catch-rate and false-alarm rate per worker class, versioned like model calibration, so “how much can I trust this layer” is a citable number rather than a felt impression.
264: What a consuming system experiences (machine-facing)
265: A Stage A proposal or close report submitted without its required sections — including the self-audit table — is rejected at the format gate before it enters the loop at all.
266: Every other check returns a finding row, never a block: citation mismatches, untraceable scope, unclassed assertions, schema gaps, status contradicted by the repository, and lexical collisions with existing Registry entries all surface as findings, not failures.
267: What is produced and retained
268: Findings reports, evidence-classed and cited like every other producer's output on this platform — an unclassed finding is itself a finding.
269: The calibration ledger, carrying a staleness field; a critic whose calibration falls outside its window renders its findings UNCALIBRATED rather than silently stale.
270: The checks themselves register in the Registry with their own rows — they are functions, and functions pay rent like every other function on the platform.
271: 19A.5 · Technical and behavioural requirements
272: Tier 1 — deterministic record-verification (rung 1)
273: Six check families, all mechanical, all resolving against the repository, running on Stage A proposals and close reports at submission:
274: Tier 1's conceded limit, stated by the source rather than discovered later: it verifies form and existence, not pertinence — an artifact can cite real SHAs for irrelevant objects and pass. Pertinence is exactly what Tier 2 is for; the two tiers are designed as a pair, and adopting Tier 1 alone buys the cheap half while advertising the whole.
275: Tier 2 — the critic pass (rung 3/4), independent by construction
276: An independent model instance reviews each Stage A and close asynchronously, after landing, against a fixed six-item rubric drawn directly from the Owner's own catch history: anti-re-derivation (does this already exist in the record under any name), anti-fabrication (is any claim stronger than its evidence class permits), the conflation test (does every proposed function trace to a real named service), scope semantics (does the work's substance stay inside the dispatch's intent, beyond what the mechanical trace alone catches), enforcement honesty (is any rule proposed whose only enforcement is prose), and self-audit audit (does the artifact's own self-audit table's reasoning hold, or is it reflexive pass-stamping). The critic never shares the worker's conversation — its context is exactly the artifact under review, the canon set, and the rubric, never the worker's reasoning or drafts, because a critic reading the worker's own justification inherits the worker's frame, which is precisely the blind-spot-sharing failure the design exists to avoid. No worker ever critics its own output; where critic and worker share a base model, independence is by context isolation alone, and Tier 3's seeded audits exist specifically to measure whether that isolation is sufficient rather than assume it. The critic runs at the cheapest sufficient rung, and its findings carry the same evidence-classing and citation discipline as every other producer on the platform.
277: Tier 3 — human calibration sampling: the Owner's role compresses, it does not vanish
278: Verdict sampling: a fraction of critic findings and all-clears (default 20% of findings, 10% of all-clears, decaying as measured reliability accumulates) is human-scored as a true catch, a false alarm, or a miss.
279: Seeded-defect audits: on a standing cadence, a known defect from a documented fall class is deliberately planted in a review copy — never a landing artifact — and the critic's catch or miss is recorded. This is the only honest measurement of a reviewer that mostly reports clean: detection proven on known positives, drawn across fall classes, never curated toward the critic's own strengths.
280: The calibration ledger: catch-rate and false-alarm rate per worker class and rubric item, versioned like model calibration, with a staleness field — a critic whose calibration is stale past its window renders its findings UNCALIBRATED at the point of use, the same honesty rule the platform applies to model confidence generally.
281: Behavioural rules, binding on adoption
282: QA-1  [CANON] Detect, never decide. No finding blocks execution, edits an artifact, or gates a phase — every consequence is a ruling. One scoped exception: QA-2.
283: QA-2  [CANON] The format gate. Schema-completeness (RV-4) is the single hard gate — a submission missing its required sections is returned for completion before it enters the loop. Form, never substance.
284: QA-3  [CANON] No self-review. No worker critics its own output; independence is by context isolation, itself measured by seeded audits.
285: QA-4  [CANON] Findings carry the honesty grammar — every finding is evidence-classed and cited; an unclassed finding is itself a finding.
286: QA-5  [CANON] The layer pays rent. The catch/false-alarm ledger is standing; a layer that stops catching shrinks by ruling. A second QA layer above this one is a meta-spiral defect on sight.
287: QA-6  [CANON] Frame authority is untouchable. No check, rubric item, or finding may dispute an Owner ruling, a service sentence, or a frame decision — the layer verifies divergence from canon; it has no standing on changes to canon.
288: 19A.6 · What must be true for the service to deliver as intended
289: It is not a governor — it holds no mandate, asserts nothing about the estate, and gates nothing but submission format.
290: It is not the Owner's replacement — the build's largest course-corrections were frame changes, which this layer would catch none of, by design; claiming otherwise is exactly the overclaim its own anti-fabrication rubric item exists to flag.
291: It is not inline — nothing here adds a synchronous step to any serving path or a turn to the dispatch loop.
292: It makes no zero-residual claim — it halves the residual, measurably and repeatedly, and its own dashboard is built to show its misses, not hide them.
293: PART B — STATUS: PROPOSED, NOT RATIFIED
294: 19B.1 · The promise, in plain language
295: No number earns the right to be quoted outside the platform until it resolves to a register row — its method, its judges, their measured agreement, the rubric version, and the source rows behind it. A judgement call becomes a published figure only through this door, never around it. This is my own synthesis, proposed for ratification in an August 2026 chat and never confirmed adopted; the source specification it responded to (sections A-1 through A-4) was not found as a standalone document in either repository, and neither the evidence register nor the dual-judge protocol appears anywhere in the current build. It is written here at full weight because the reasoning holds regardless of its ratification status — not to imply that status is settled.
296: 19B.2 · The service that powers it
297: No existing named engine. Proposed as one capability with two parts: an evidence register (a ledger-backed record, structurally similar to the Registry's own pattern) and the dual-judge protocol (A-2) as its scoring mechanism, applied wherever a judgement call is about to become a published number.
298: 19B.3 · Definition of the promise
299: The register's proposed schema: one row per figure, carrying the figure itself, the method that produced it, the judges and their versions, the rubric version applied, the inter-annotator agreement (kappa), the date, and the source rows it derives from. The standing rule proposed alongside it: no figure is quoted externally without resolving to a register row — mechanizing a discipline the platform already practises informally (the source chat cites an existing re-measurement practice, 1,523 revised to 1,559, as evidence the norm already exists in spirit; the register would make it structural rather than a matter of remembering to do it).
300: 19B.4 · Delivery experience expectations
301: Named application sites — proposed, not built
302: The terminal test itself: the platform's human-qualified benchmark slice, scored dual-judge with a published kappa — named as the highest-priority site, since the single verdict everything else rests on is currently single-judge.
303: Per-language custody recall: the claim most exposed under diligence, currently single-scored by design.
304: Model Acceptance (Document 17, MOAC): the canon already mandates human quality judgement over the six checks — that judgement is exactly the artifact dual-judging exists to make defensible.
305: Refusal correctness (Document 8): the refusal-health surface counts refusals today but scores whether the named rule actually justified each one; a sampled dual-judge audit would give the refusal grammar a measured integrity figure.
306: The existing verification loop: builder verification versus independent tester is already de facto dual-judge; recording their disagreement rate per cycle turns an existing process into a measured instrument at close to zero additional cost.
307: What is produced and retained, if adopted
308: The evidence register itself — the single place any externally-quoted figure must resolve to.
309: A-4, proposed as a companion mechanism, never a build gate: claims validation functioning as the re-entry path for previously killed backlog (a parked idea returns only with a three-arm result behind it) and as the bake-off court for competing implementation choices.
310: 19B.5 · Technical and behavioural requirements
311: Evidence register row (proposed)
312: { figure, method, judges: [..], judge_versions: [..],
313: rubric_version, kappa, date, source_rows: [..] }
314: Standing rule: no figure quoted externally without
315: resolving to a register row.
316: EP-1  [PROPOSED] Build the register first — cheapest piece, and it immediately hardens the custody-recall and Model Acceptance sites above.
317: EP-2  [PROPOSED] Dual-judge scoring (A-2) applies at every named site in §19B.4, plus any future site where a judgement call becomes a published number.
318: EP-3  [PROPOSED] A-4 (claims validation) rides inside this capability, scoped explicitly as validation, never a build gate — its real experiments require real material and naturally sequence after the terminal test.
319: EP-4  [OPEN] Hard ordering constraint, stated by the original proposal: the evidence register and dual-judge protocol must exist before the terminal test runs, or that test's verdict is single-judge permanently — there is no retroactive fix once the terminal test has already run single-judge.
320: EP-5  [PROPOSED] Explicitly not adopted, per the same proposal: the source spec's “insurance telemetry” aside (serves a goal never named) and its internal reduction-skill mandate (process tooling the Quality Rule Book already covers in doctrine — building enforcement machinery for it fails the platform's own reduction test).
321: 19B.6 · What must be true for the service to deliver as intended
322: No figure reaches an external document without a resolvable register row — stated as absolute in the proposal, not aspirational.
323: The register and protocol exist before the terminal test runs — the one constraint the proposal calls genuinely ordering rather than merely preferred.
324: A-4 never becomes a gate by drift — its scope is validation and re-entry, and staying there is a condition of adoption, not a detail.
325: This entire part remains PROPOSED, not CANON, until an explicit Owner ruling says otherwise — nothing above should be cited elsewhere as settled.
326: DOCUMENT 20   The Model Capability Register
327: The Model Capability Register
328: Closes Promise #24 (Document 14), which Document 17 (A17.10–A17.11) named but only partly landed. Extends the existing models_registry.v0.json mechanism — the same registry, not a new one — with real candidate population and a formal resolution rule. Owner-ruled: the PROPOSED rows below (A20.3–A20.10) are adopted now as live PROPOSED-class config, not held for individual per-model ratification — license verification is already complete for each, and A20.13's calibration-decides mechanism is itself the ratification step.
329: 20.1 · The promise, in plain language
330: Every training or extraction objective is served by the strongest license-verified base model for its actual task — never a default reached for out of habit, and never a model the business user has to know exists, name, or choose. This is Promise #24's own language: “the platform holds a curated set of the strongest openly-available pretrained models, organised by task each is good at, so that … the platform trains its own model for a task starting from the best available baseline.”
331: 20.2 · The service that powers it
332: The existing model registry (backend/services/perception/models_registry.v0.json, Owner-ruled 2026-07-10 and extended 2026-07-15) — today four C1 candidate classes (text, document, vision, audio), two with named comparison-arm members (Qwen3/3.5, Llama) and two registered empty (document, vision), plus audio's own CI-fixture-only entry. This document populates the two empty classes with license-verified real candidates and formalises how the Objective Wizard resolves a stated task to a dimension and a candidate — the registry's structure does not change; what it holds, and how it gets read, does.
333: 20.3 · Definition of the promise
334: Listing and availing, not ranking and asserting
335: The register's job is to make license-verified candidates available per dimension — it does not itself declare a single global “best” model, because best is a function of the task, the population, and the constraints stated in a specific TargetOutcome, not a property a model carries on its own. A candidate strong on one axis (vocal realism, document layout, long-context reasoning) is not automatically the right pick for a different task in the same dimension. This is why the register supplies eligible candidates and calibration (§17.3, mandatory first stage of every training plan) proves fit on real data — the register narrows, calibration decides.
336: Four dimensions, license-verification only at registration
337: Per the existing C1-candidate discipline: registering a class or a candidate is license verification and parameter disclosure only — zero download, zero compute. A specific member's weights are pulled and checksummed only at acquisition, when a real objective actually needs it. This document adds real, current candidates to the document and vision classes, which existed only as empty placeholders before it.
338: Resolution is compiled, not chosen
339: A business user states an objective in plain language. The Objective Wizard's existing compile step (§17.4d) resolves the stated task to a dimension the same deterministic way it resolves population to register strata — the model pick is a third compiled artifact alongside TargetOutcome and Collection Schema, never a menu rendered for the user to browse. This extends, rather than duplicates, the wizard's existing discipline that no business user hand-writes a technical parameter directly.
340: 20.4 · Delivery experience expectations
341: What the organisation experiences (human-facing)
342: States the objective in plain language and never sees a model name during that conversation — the same discipline the wizard already applies to every other technical parameter.
343: Sees the resolved candidate only as part of the commission's record afterward, with the reasoning — which candidates were eligible, which was picked, and why — available on request, never pushed into the front-of-conversation flow.
344: Where a dimension has more than one strong eligible candidate, sees calibration's measured comparison between them before a full run commits — the same Sampling & Reflection stage already mandatory for every training plan, now also settling model choice, not only recipe choice.
345: What a consuming system experiences (machine-facing)
346: TargetOutcome's task and domain fields resolve deterministically to a dimension; an objective that doesn't resolve cleanly is flagged for the same census-style clarification an unresolved population already triggers.
347: The resolved candidate's license, checksum, and origin data flow automatically into training_params@v0 and the training manifest — no separate step re-enters this information by hand.
348: What is produced and retained
349: The resolution record itself: which candidates were eligible for the dimension, which was selected, and the calibration evidence (where more than one candidate was tested) the selection rests on — permanent, part of the same provenance chain the training manifest already carries.
350: 20.5 · Technical and behavioural requirements
351: Text — CANON, already named
352: A20.1  [CANON] Qwen3 / Qwen3.5 (Alibaba) — Apache 2.0, text generation candidate.  — Owner ruling 2026-07-15 Item 6, models_registry.v0.json
353: A20.2  [CANON] Llama (Meta) — comparison arm; commercial-use gated, license verified and checksummed at acquisition, not at registration.  — models_registry.v0.json
354: Document / OCR — class registered, real candidates added here
355: A20.3  [PROPOSED] Qwen2.5-VL / Qwen3-VL (Alibaba) — Apache 2.0 at 7B/32B. Mixed OCR and document understanding in one model — text, tables, charts, formulas, handwriting — at roughly GPT-4o-comparable DocVQA accuracy. Same publisher and licence pattern already trusted for A20.1, extended natively to this dimension.  — current web research, 2026-08
356: A20.4  [PROPOSED] GOT-OCR2 (StepFun) — Apache 2.0, 580M parameters. The leading dedicated pure-OCR model — plain text, formatted text, tables, and math formulas — where a lighter, cheaper model suffices and full document understanding is not the task.  — current web research, 2026-08
357: A20.5  [PROPOSED] PaddleOCR-VL — Apache 2.0. Strongest multilingual coverage found (100+ languages), mature table and layout recognition, the most production-battle-tested open OCR pipeline.  — current web research, 2026-08
358: A20.6  [PROPOSED] ColPali v1.3 — MIT. Not OCR at all: embeds document pages directly for retrieval, bypassing text extraction entirely. Named as a candidate for the document dimension's retrieval task specifically, not its transcription task — the two are different jobs the same dimension covers.  — current web research, 2026-08
359: Vision — class registered, real candidates added here
360: A20.7  [PROPOSED] Qwen2.5-VL-72B — Apache 2.0. Leads open-weight vision benchmarks generally (≈888 OCRBench); the largest-scale option in the family already trusted for A20.1 and A20.3.  — current web research, 2026-08
361: A20.8  [PROPOSED] InternVL3-78B (Shanghai AI Lab) — MIT. The strongest permissively-licensed alternative where Qwen's Apache terms are for any reason insufficient — ≈72% MMMU, no commercial gate at any scale.  — current web research, 2026-08
362: A20.9  [PROPOSED] Llama 4 multimodal, Maverick and Scout (Meta) — Llama Community License, commercial-use gated same as A20.2. Leads MMMU outright (≈73.4%) among the candidates found; the comparison-arm role A20.2 already plays for text extends here.  — current web research, 2026-08
363: A20.10  [PROPOSED] Pixtral 12B (Mistral) — Apache 2.0. Smaller and cheaper to serve than the 70B-class options above; the right candidate where the task's constraints (§10.1) cap latency or compute below what the larger models need.  — current web research, 2026-08
364: Audio — governed entirely by Document 17, referenced here, not restated
365: A20.11  [CANON] Audio's resolution rule is not this document's to set. Document 17 A17.10–A17.11 already rules it: whisper-tiny is CI-fixture-only; production selection lands additively at a later registry bump, named at first census activation, following the identical license-verify → checksum-pin → Owner-ruling sequence this document uses for every other dimension. That sequencing is inherited here unchanged — audio's census-first rule is the general rule's origin, not an exception to it.
366: The resolution rule — binding across all four dimensions
367: A20.12  [PROPOSED] A stated objective resolves to exactly one dimension at wizard compile time, on the same deterministic basis TargetOutcome's population resolves to register strata. An objective that resolves ambiguously is refused at compile, the same way an Outcome without a test_set_ref is refused — not silently defaulted to a guess.
368: A20.13  [PROPOSED] Where a dimension holds one eligible license-verified candidate, it is used. Where it holds more than one (as document and vision now do), calibration's mandatory first stage (§17.3) tests the eligible set on the objective's own material and the measured result decides — never a static leaderboard rank substituting for evidence on the platform's own data.
369: A20.14  [PROPOSED] No candidate is ever surfaced as a user-facing choice, at any point in the wizard flow. This is a compile-time discipline, structurally identical to §17.4d's rule that a business user never hand-writes a TargetOutcome field — model selection is a fourth field of the same kind, not a different kind of decision.
370: 20.6 · What must be true for the service to deliver as intended
371: No dimension's candidate list is ever rendered as a menu — resolution is compiled, the same way every other technical parameter in a commission is compiled.
372: No candidate is selected before its licence is verified — registration and acquisition stay two distinct steps, as they already are for every existing class.
373: Where more than one eligible candidate exists, the pick rests on calibration's measured result on the objective's own material, never on benchmark reputation alone.
374: Audio's census-first sequencing is inherited, not duplicated or overridden — this document adds three dimensions' worth of real candidates and one shared resolution rule; it does not re-open what Document 17 already settled.

# SOURCE: assessment_workspace/canon/drops/20260909/extracted/files_14/Akki_Governance_Architecture_v1.docx
Coordinate: document.xml paragraph in body order, tables included

1: AKKI PLATFORM  ·  FOUNDATIONAL SPECIFICATION  ·  DOCUMENT 0
2: The Akki Governance Architecture
3: Akki Defined as a Governance Operating System, Against the Standards That Define the Category
4: akki_governance_architecture_v1
5: Position in canon
6: Foundational. This document defines the categories every other Akki specification instantiates. It precedes Document 1 in dependency, not in number — referenced as Document 0.
7: Governs
8: What Akki is, attribute by attribute: the definition of each attribute at the standard that defines its category, independent of Akki; the Akki component that instantiates it; and the current gap between the two.
9: Does not govern
10: Individual engine behaviour — specified in Documents 1–20 and their extensions. Rule identity and classification — specified in rule_criteria_spec_v1. This document is what those specifications instantiate, not a replacement for them.
11: Status
12: Draft v1, for owner ratification. Every attribute below is defined independent of Akki; Part 2's mapping and Part 3's gap register are the current state of the instantiation, dated to this document's date.
13: Citation discipline
14: Every governing clause is marked [V] verified against published text during preparation of this document, [K] cited from established knowledge of a freely published standard with a stable clause reference, or [P] a paywalled standard cited by clause number and title, requirement paraphrased. No clause is asserted beyond what its marking supports.
15: Date
16: 1 September 2026
17: 
18: Part 1 — Definition
19: Akki is a governance operating system: software that lets an organisation's AI act on its data and models while making the constraints on that action structurally enforced, evidenced, and answerable to a named authority — rather than policed by review after the fact.
20: A governance operating system is built from twelve attributes. Each is defined here independent of Akki, against the standard that already governs its category in established security and AI-governance practice. Akki's own name for each attribute is given as an alias, because the product's vocabulary is not being replaced — it is being measured. Where a mature standard does not yet exist for an attribute, the closest established practice is named as such, and the absence of a standard is stated plainly rather than filled with an invented one.
21: The twelve are ordered as a dependency stack, not a list. Each attribute after the first presupposes the ones before it:

24: Depends on

28: 2
