36: Not confirmed as existing in canon. If built, it proposes a classification; a deterministic confirmation step (undefined — flagged) would need to decide.
37: Targeta — yield wall / MOAC
38: Deterministic
39: — holds acceptance authority directly
40: Targeta — the model being trained
41: Learned
42: Cannot accept or refuse its own output. MOAC, downstream and deterministic, decides.
43: Mkondo — hand-off registry
44: Deterministic
45: —
46: The Watch — Mkono (response)
47: Deterministic
48: — holds containment authority directly
49: The Watch — Grey Mirror (detection)
50: Learned
51: Mkono acts only on a signed verdict Grey Mirror cannot itself produce authority over — Grey Mirror asserts facts; Mkono decides (A2, verified verbatim).
52: The Ledger — writer
53: Deterministic
54: —
55: CIF — ideation faculty
56: Learned
57: Single-experiment principle: existence unconditional, but every adopted idea passes a deterministic acceptance point before affecting a run (BR-9.2, already on record).
58: Critic Seam — RV-tier
59: Deterministic
60: —
61: Critic Seam — QA-tier
62: Learned
63: QA-1's own rule: findings route to RV-tier or a human; a QA finding cannot block execution on its own.
64: Rules Service — ceremony engine
65: Deterministic
66: —
67: Rules Service — AI-assisted drafting
68: Learned
69: RBM-2: proposes; the named human author confirms before a rule enters PROPOSED. The confirmation is the deterministic decision point.
70: Whitepaper Wizard — eligibility gate
71: Deterministic
72: —
73: Whitepaper Wizard — prose assembly
74: Learned
75: Draws only on Tier 1/2 artefacts (WPW-13); the eligibility gate, not the prose engine, decides whether a paper may publish.
76: DAP — release budget, distance gate, output-content gate
77: Deterministic
78: — each holds its own admit/refuse authority directly
79: DAP — admission-probe trigger scan (backdoor detection half)
80: Mixed — flagged
81: Where the technique is statistical, it informs; the canary-touch half of the same probe (on A5.2's closed registry) is what actually decides admission.
82: Deck Rendering Engine
83: Deterministic
84: — not a decision authority in the governance sense; included for completeness
85: 2   Human Oversight Against Article 14
86: Where a human, not a deterministic component, is the check on a learned component's output, Article 14 names five distinct capabilities. The platform's own ruling loop — every decision recorded across this programme, from the four owner rulings at the start through every parked ruling since — is mapped against each separately, because a loop that serves one well does not thereby serve all five.
87: Capability
88: State
89: Evidence
90: (a) Understand & monitor
91: Partially evidenced
92: STATE/NEXT.md-style tracking and the Rules Registry (once built) give an overseer a current, queryable view. Not confirmed as designed for this specific purpose — it was built for change-control, and happens to serve oversight.
93: (b) Aware of automation bias
94: Directly addressed
95: A5.16 (recommendation provenance) exists specifically because a human acting on an agent's advice without knowing it was advice is the automation-bias failure mode. The action record surfaces the recommendation at the point of action — not after.
96: (c) Correctly interpret output
97: Evidenced by design, not tested
98: Every claim traces to evidence in one step (A8, “Walk this →”). Whether a given overseer actually interprets correctly, given that trace, has never been tested with a real reviewer.
99: (d) Override, disregard, reverse
100: Strongly evidenced
101: The best-evidenced capability on this list. Every ruling in this canon's own history is an instance of exactly this — including several that reversed or corrected a prior proposal, this document's own predecessors among them.
102: (e) Halt to a safe state
103: Partially evidenced, one confirmed gap
104: The Watch can stop anything (A5.3, “destroy does not exist in the Watch”). Whether CIF's ideation can be halted independently of halting the Targeta run it feeds — named as unconfirmed when W-3 through W-8 were drafted — remains unconfirmed here too.
105: 3   Findings
106: Sixteen components classified without ambiguity. One genuinely mixed case — the DAP-32 trigger scan — carried forward from the amendment that created it rather than forced to a single verdict here. Of Article 14's five capabilities, one (override) is strongly evidenced by this canon's own working method; one (automation bias) is directly and deliberately addressed by a named requirement; two (understand-and-monitor, correct interpretation) are plausible but unconfirmed by design intent or by test; and one (halt-to-safe-state) has a specific, named, still-open question — whether CIF can be stopped independent of the run it feeds.
107: DET-1  Confirm or build a halt mechanism for CIF independent of halting the Targeta run it feeds — closing capability (e) fully rather than leaving it partially evidenced.
108: DET-2  Where an AI-assisted classification capability is built into Mtafiti, name the deterministic confirmation step before it ships — not after, per this inventory's own method for every other learned component.
109: This inventory itself should be re-run, not assumed permanent, whenever a new component is added to the platform — consistent with tcb_enumeration_v1's own standing clause. The two share a maintenance obligation because they share almost all their evidence.

# SOURCE: assessment_workspace/canon/drops/20260909/extracted/files_14/Failure_Posture_Enumeration_v1.docx
Coordinate: document.xml paragraph in body order, tables included

1: AKKI PLATFORM  ·  ENGINE SPECIFICATION  ·  5 OF 9
2: Failure Posture Enumeration
3: failure_posture_v1 — Draft for owner ratification · Closes Document 0 G-11
4: Requirement answered
5: CC FPT_FLS.1: preserve a secure state for an enumerated list of failure types — the enumeration is the requirement, not a general commitment. NIST SC-24: fail to a known state, preserving defined state information.
6: Scope
7: Every component in tcb_enumeration_v1's IN column, plus DAP's already-specified posture (DAP-28–30), carried here rather than re-derived, and the three unconfigured-gate defaults flagged in security_architecture_v1 (SEC-4, SEC-6, SEC-7), absorbed as one platform-wide rule rather than three separate clauses.
8: Finding, stated up front
9: The platform already gets this right in the cases that have been examined closely — the chokepoint fails closed, the consumption levers correctly fail safe-open toward recomputation. What was missing was the enumeration, not the behaviour.
10: Date
11: 9 September 2026
12: 1   The Platform Default
13: FP-1  Every component in the Trusted Computing Base fails closed by default. An evaluation that cannot complete — configuration unset, a dependency unreachable, a check erroring — refuses the operation it governs. This is the default; §3 lists the components that correctly depart from it, and why.
14: FP-2  A gate whose governing configuration is unset or fails integrity verification at load refuses by default rather than passing by default. This absorbs security_architecture_v1's SEC-4 (MOAC), SEC-6 (the distance gate), and SEC-7 (the admission probe) as one rule rather than three restatements of it — an unconfigured gate is a closed gate, platform-wide, not per-component.
15: 2   Per-Component Enumeration
16: Component
17: Failure types
18: Posture
19: Preserved state
20: SyniSense — chokepoint
21: Custody policy unreadable; de-identification step errors; re-identification key unavailable
22: Fail-closed
23: The crossing attempt itself — who, what, when — written before the attempt, so a failed crossing is still evidenced
24: SyniSense — closed network
25: Allowlist configuration unreachable
26: Fail-closed
27: No outbound connection attempted; the refusal reason
28: Solva — assertion-boundary seam
29: Anchor map cannot be computed; source material unreachable
30: Fail-closed
31: The unanchored draft is discarded, not served; the refusal with structured reason (A5.5)
32: Northena — objective-freeze
33: Freeze record unreadable at a hand-off point
34: Fail-closed
35: The job halts rather than proceeding on an unverifiable scope
36: Mtafiti — registry
37: Write path unavailable
38: Fail-closed for writes; fail-safe-open for reads of already-committed data
39: Last successfully committed state remains queryable even while writes are refused
40: Targeta — yield wall / MOAC
41: Criteria configuration unset or unverifiable
42: Fail-closed
43: The run's own artefacts remain intact; nothing is marked accepted
44: Mkondo — hand-off registry
45: Registry write fails mid-handoff
46: Fail-closed
47: Neither side treats the hand-off as complete; the attempt is recorded as failed, not silently retried as success
48: The Watch — Mkono
49: Verdict cannot be read; policy table unreachable
50: Fail-closed on new actions; already-active containments persist
51: Every action already in force stays in force — a Watch outage does not release a contained actor
52: The Ledger — writer
53: Storage unreachable; hash-chain verification fails on write
54: Fail-closed — and everything that depends on writing to it (§1 FP-1) fails closed in consequence
55: The chain up to the last verified entry; no entry is ever appended out of order to “catch up”
56: MOAC
57: As Targeta's wall — same component, listed once above
58: —
59: —
60: Critic Seam — RV-tier
61: A deterministic check cannot execute
62: Fail-closed — escalates to a human rather than passing unchecked
63: The submission awaiting review; nothing is marked reviewed
64: Rules Service — ceremony engine
65: Countdown timer or countersign verification unreachable
66: Fail-closed — no rule reaches CANON on an unverifiable ceremony
67: The rule remains PROPOSED; the ceremony's partial progress, so it can resume rather than restart
68: DAP — release budget, distance gate, output-content gate
69: As specified in dap_backend_spec_v1 DAP-28–30 and this set's own SEC-6/security_architecture_v1
70: Fail-closed
71: Carried by reference — not restated
72: 3   The Departures — Where Fail-Safe-Open Is Correct
73: Two departures from §1's default, both already correct in the system as built, now stated as deliberate rather than left to be discovered.
74: FP-3  Mtafiti's read path fails safe-open: a write failure never blocks a query against already-committed estate composition. The alternative — refusing to answer “what exists” because “what changed most recently” cannot be confirmed — would make an outage indistinguishable from data loss to everyone reading the registry, which is a worse failure than serving slightly stale data marked as such.
75: FP-4  The Watch's already-active containments persist through a Watch outage rather than lapsing. This is fail-closed for new decisions and explicitly not fail-open for standing ones — the two are evaluated separately, and conflating them would silently release every contained actor the moment the Watch itself failed, which is precisely when containment matters most.
76: Recovery time objective and recovery point objective for the Ledger writer specifically are covered in the Business Continuity Annex (document 8 of this set), not restated here — this document specifies posture per component; that one specifies how long a failure may last and how much may be lost before it is a breach in its own right.
77: 4   Standing
78: A component added to the Trusted Computing Base under tcb_enumeration_v1's own standing clause is added here in the same turn — posture, failure types, and preserved state, not deferred to a later pass. §1's default applies until stated otherwise; a new TCB member that departs from it states so explicitly, the way §3 does for Mtafiti and the Watch.

# SOURCE: assessment_workspace/canon/drops/20260909/extracted/files_14/Handoff_Generalisation_v1.docx
Coordinate: document.xml paragraph in body order, tables included

1: AKKI PLATFORM  ·  ENGINE SPECIFICATION  ·  7 OF 9
2: Hand-Off Generalisation
3: handoff_registry_v1 — Draft for owner ratification · Closes Document 0 G-13
4: Problem
5: Promise #32's guarantee — clean hand-offs, no dropped context, no silently recalibrated objective — is instantiated exactly once: ThinkLab handing a completed reasoning session to Task Manager. Every other subsystem-to-subsystem hand-off has no registered contract at all, per BR-6.1 and the Security Amendments' G-13 finding.
6: What already exists to build on
7: Two ingredients, both already shared mechanisms: Northena's objective-freeze (BR-3.1, “a single, shared implementation invoked identically by every subsystem that hands off a job”) and the registered-handoff-contract shape the one working instance already uses — what was commissioned, its shape, the identity of both ends, a receipt.
8: What this document adds
9: The missing half: a hand-off registry every crossing writes to and every receiving subsystem checks, owned by Mkondo, generalising the one instance to all of them.
10: Date
11: 9 September 2026
12: 1   The Registry
13: HR-1  Mkondo owns a hand-off registry. Every job passed from one subsystem to another — not only ThinkLab to Task Manager — writes an entry before the receiving subsystem may act on it.
14: HR-2  A hand-off entry carries: the commissioning subsystem's identity; the receiving subsystem's identity; the job's frozen objective, from Northena's existing mechanism (BR-3.1); the shape of what is being handed off (a reasoning session, a training commission, an extraction request, a rule proposal — whatever the job class); a timestamp from the platform's reliable time source; and a receipt once the receiving subsystem acknowledges.
15: HR-3  A receiving subsystem MUST refuse to act on a hand-off that has no registry entry. This is the generalisation of the one existing guarantee (Promise #32: a malformed hand-off surfaces as a finding at the point of hand-off) to every crossing, not only the instantiated one.
16: HR-4  The no-dual-hatted-task rule (Promise #32) is enforced at registration: a hand-off entry naming a job already open under a different receiving subsystem is refused, not merely discouraged. This moves the rule from convention (as BR-6.3 found it) to a registry-level check.
17: HR-5  Objective freeze applies at the point of registration, not at the point of eventual action — a receiving subsystem inherits the frozen scope Northena set at hand-off, and cannot itself widen it. This is the same discipline DAP-18 already applies to commissioned jobs, generalised to every internal hand-off, not only DAP's external-facing ones.
18: HR-6  The registry is queryable by either end of a hand-off, by job, by subsystem pair, or by time range — so “what did we hand this subsystem, and when” has an answer without reconstructing it from each engine's own logs.
19: 2   Failure Posture
20: HR-7  A hand-off registry write that fails leaves the job un-commissioned on the receiving side — fail-closed, consistent with failure_posture_v1's platform default and its own treatment of Mkondo's registry (“neither side treats the hand-off as complete; the attempt is recorded as failed, not silently retried as success”).
21: 3   What This Does Not Change
22: ThinkLab's hand-off to Task Manager is not re-specified — it already meets HR-1 through HR-6 by construction, having been the pattern this document generalises from. No existing behaviour changes for that one crossing; every other crossing now has to meet the same bar it already does.
23: 4   Standing
24: A new subsystem, or a new job class passed between existing ones, registers its hand-off shape here at the point it is built — not discovered later as a second uninstantiated guarantee the way this one was.

# SOURCE: assessment_workspace/canon/drops/20260909/extracted/files_14/Pruning_Unlearning_Amendment_v1.docx
Coordinate: document.xml paragraph in body order, tables included

1: AKKI PLATFORM  ·  CHANGE REGISTER  ·  SECURITY  ·  9 OF 9
2: Pruning & Unlearning Amendment
3: 2 amendments · 1 new promise · 1 ruling · 9 September 2026
4: Applies to
5: dap_backend_spec_v1 (new DAP-37, DAP-38) · Security Assurance Promise Set (S-26)
6: What this closes
7: Two questions raised while defining artefact egress that DAP-31/DAP-36 did not answer: can a fine-tuned model be made smaller and cleaner before it leaves, and what happens to an artefact already registered or egressed when the right to a unit it trained on is later withdrawn.
8: Honesty condition stated up front
9: Pruning reduces memorisation empirically; it does not prove its absence. DP-SGD (DAP-36) is the guarantee; pruning is a second reduction on top of it. This amendment does not present pruning as a substitute for differential privacy, and DAP-37 says so explicitly.
10: T-3   Artefact Pruning Before Egress
11: TARGET  dap_backend_spec_v1 — new DAP-37, extending DAP-31 and DAP-36.
12: CURRENT  DAP-31 gates egress on a reproduction probe. DAP-36 trains with differential privacy by default. Neither addresses reducing an artefact's size or memorisation surface between acceptance and egress — an artefact either passes DAP-31 as trained, or it doesn't.
13: AMENDED — normative text
14: DAP-37  A fine-tuned artefact MAY be pruned — magnitude pruning or an equivalent structural reduction — between MOAC acceptance and DAP-31's distance gate, as a ruled optional step. Pruning is a second, empirical reduction in memorisation surface on top of DAP-36's differentially private training; it is never a substitute for it, and this document does not present it as one. A pruned artefact MUST re-pass MOAC's acceptance criteria — pruning can degrade performance below the accepted bar, and acceptance is re-evaluated, not assumed to survive the change. A pruned artefact's hash differs from its pre-pruning hash; it is a new artefact for every purpose DAP-10 and DAP-31 govern, including a fresh pass through the distance gate at the ruled threshold. Pruning ratio and method are ruled values, ratified alongside DAP-31's own probe parameters.
15: MECHANISM  Magnitude pruning removes the weights contributing least to model output, which empirically also reduces the model's capacity to have memorised specific training examples — a smaller, sparser artefact has less room to encode any one unit's content precisely. This is a capacity reduction, not a guarantee; DAP-31's probe, re-run on the pruned artefact, is what actually confirms the result.
16: DERIVATION  Han, Mao, and Dally, “Deep Compression” (2015) — magnitude pruning and its empirical effect on memorisation capacity. DAP-31 (the gate this feeds back through). DAP-36 (the guarantee this does not replace).
17: PRINCIPLE  A smaller artefact is not a safer artefact by assertion. It is a candidate for re-testing, and DAP-31 is what turns the candidacy into a fact.
18: T-4   Unlearning on Rights Withdrawal
19: TARGET  dap_backend_spec_v1 — new DAP-38. Rules Service (registry query, RBM-20) as the mechanism that makes affected artefacts findable.
20: CURRENT  No requirement addresses what happens when a contributor withdraws consent, or a unit's licence expires, after an artefact trained on that unit has already been registered or has already egressed under DAP-10. DAP-31 gates what leaves; nothing governs what happens to what already left.
21: AMENDED — normative text
22: DAP-38  When a unit's rights status changes to withdrawn — consent revoked, licence expired, or an equivalent event — every artefact whose training manifest cites that unit is identified via the registry (a query, per RBM-20's design, not a search) and is either re-derived without the unit or recalled. Re-derivation trains a replacement artefact excluding the withdrawn unit, using the same run configuration recorded in the original training manifest, and passes it through DAP-31 and MOAC as a new artefact before it replaces the original in the registry. Recall withdraws the original artefact's registry entry and, where the artefact was already delivered under DAP-10, notifies the receiving party that the artefact's rights basis has changed. A unit's contribution to the estate release budget (DAP-35) is NOT refunded on unlearning — the privacy loss from the original release already occurred; unlearning restores the artefact's cleanliness going forward, not the budget already spent.
23: MECHANISM  Sharded, isolated training (SISA — Sharded, Isolated, Sliced, Aggregated) makes re-derivation tractable by limiting retraining to the shard containing the withdrawn unit rather than the whole model; DAP-36's DP-SGD defaults make the retrained shard's own privacy accounting straightforward, since the accountant already runs per training job. Where SISA-style sharding was not used for the original run, re-derivation means a full retrain, and §5 R-12 rules whether that is mandatory or whether recall alone suffices in that case.
24: DERIVATION  Bourtoule et al., “Machine Unlearning” — SISA (2021). Guo et al., “Certified Data Removal from Machine Learning Models” (2020) — the formal standard re-derivation approximates. Kenya Data Protection Act 2019 s.40 (erasure). GDPR Art. 17 (right to erasure). CA1-N3, already ruled: raw source and five-ring units get real erasure; a trained model is flagged via A17.15's rights-lapse mechanism rather than untrained on demand — DAP-38 is that same discipline's extension to artefacts DAP now governs.
25: PRINCIPLE  The erasure right does not stop at the database. A model that carries a unit's influence is still carrying it, whatever the registry says about the source record.
26: This generalises CA1-N3's model-flagging answer, already ruled for the platform's own trained models, to every artefact DAP-9/DAP-10 admits an external party's model into or egresses — not a new principle, an extension of one already decided.
27: 3   New Promise
28: ID
29: Promise
30: Rests on
31: S-26
32: The system will remove a unit's influence from every artefact that carried it when the right to that unit ends — by re-derivation or recall, findable by registry query, with the release budget's prior consumption left unrefunded.
33: T-3, T-4 (DAP-37, DAP-38). CA1-N3. SISA; certified removal; DPA s.40; GDPR Art. 17.
34: 4   Ruling
35: R-12  When the original training run was not sharded for isolated retraining, is re-derivation mandatory regardless of cost, or does recall alone satisfy DAP-38 where re-derivation is uneconomic? Neither this document nor CA1-N3 answers this; it is a genuine owner decision, not a technical one.
36: Nothing above is blocked by R-12. Where sharding was used, re-derivation is the norm and inexpensive enough that the question doesn't arise. R-12 matters only for the harder case, and DAP-38's recall path is fully specified either way — it is available now, pending only the ruling on when it's sufficient versus when re-derivation is required.

# SOURCE: assessment_workspace/canon/drops/20260909/extracted/files_14/Security_Architecture_Description_v1.docx
Coordinate: document.xml paragraph in body order, tables included

1: AKKI PLATFORM  ·  ENGINE SPECIFICATION  ·  2 OF 9
2: Security Architecture Description
3: security_architecture_v1 — Draft for owner ratification · Closes Document 0 G-6
4: Requirement answered
5: Common Criteria ADV_ARC.1: for every reference monitor, demonstrate non-bypassability, self-protection, domain separation, and secure initialisation — as a description, since these properties “largely have no directly observable interface” (the CC v2→v3.1 transition rationale, verified earlier this programme).
6: Scope
7: Every candidate reference monitor named in tcb_enumeration_v1: SyniSense's chokepoint, the Watch's Mkono, MOAC, the DAP-31 distance gate, the DAP-32 admission probe, and QA-2's format gate. Each treated separately — meeting the properties for one does not transfer to another.
8: Method
9: Each property is demonstrated by citation where canon text already establishes it, and specified fresh where it does not. Fresh specification is marked as such — this document does not claim as existing what it is proposing for the first time.
10: Date
11: 9 September 2026
12: 1   SyniSense — The Chokepoint
13: 1.1. The Chokepoint
14: Property
15: Demonstrated as
16: Non-bypassability
17: Exactly one function may invoke the external model client; a negative-scan build test fails the build if any second path is introduced. Demonstrated at build time, on every build, not asserted once.
18: Self-protection
19: Custody-sequence logic and the closed-network allowlist are held in configuration outside the reach of any subject the crossing mediates. Runtime integrity verification of the loaded policy is not yet specified — the one property this monitor does not yet fully meet.
20: Domain separation
21: The chokepoint operates entirely within SyniSense's own boundary; it does not reach into Solva, Targeta, or Mtafiti to make its decision.
22: Secure initialisation
23: The closed outbound network and allowlist are build-time invariants, present before the component accepts its first request — there is no partially-initialised state in which the chokepoint runs without them.
24: Verdict: Three of four fully met. Self-protection is partial — build-time gates exist; runtime tamper-resistance for the loaded policy is proposed below, not yet built.
25: SEC-1  SyniSense's custody-sequence policy and network allowlist MUST be integrity-verified at load — a signature or hash comparison against the value recorded in the Rule Registry — so that a runtime modification is detected, not merely prevented by the absence of an edit path.  [Closes the remaining gap in 1.1]
26: 2   The Watch — Mkono (Response)
27: 2.1. Mkono, the deterministic response half
28: Property
29: Demonstrated as
30: Non-bypassability
31: “Totality of sight” (A3, verified verbatim): no path reaches the estate or a model outside the Watch's observed surface, held by two independent proofs, static and runtime. This is Mkono's mediation guarantee — it acts on everything Macho can see, and Macho sees everything.
32: Self-protection
33: Mkono “contains no model, no content parsing, no reasoning — a deterministic mapping from verdict properties to actions, small enough to verify exhaustively” (A2, verified verbatim). It reaches behind the verdict seam for nothing; there is no surface for a mediated party to tamper with beyond the seam itself.
34: Domain separation
35: Mkono and Macho “meet at exactly one interface: a signed, replayable verdict” (A2). The hand never inspects raw behaviour. This is domain separation stated in the source text, not inferred.
36: Secure initialisation
37: The Watch's own ceremony — slowest countdown, external witness — governs any change to Mkono's policy tables (A5.8, A5.11), which is the initialisation discipline for a component whose “policy” is closer to configuration than code.
38: Verdict: All four met, directly from canon text. The strongest-evidenced monitor on the platform after the chokepoint.
39: 3   The Watch — Grey Mirror (Macho)
40: Grey Mirror is not itself evaluated as a reference monitor. Per tcb_enumeration_v1, Macho is learned and holds no decision authority — “it cannot block, throttle, mark, reroute, or notify. Its sole output is a verdict” (A2, verified verbatim). ADV_ARC.1 applies to components that mediate and decide; Macho detects and proposes. Its self-protection is covered separately, under C3 below, as the subject the witness watches — not as a monitor in its own right.
41: 4   The External Witness (C3)
42: 4.1. The witness — the mechanism that makes 2.1's self-protection checkable
43: Property
44: Demonstrated as
45: Non-bypassability
46: Not applicable in the usual sense — the witness doesn't mediate operations. Its role is to make the Watch's own self-protection an ongoing measurement rather than a one-time claim.
47: Self-protection
48: “A watchdog that alarms on Watch silence holds no Watch credentials and lives in neither authority's deployment; a standing break-in test attempts, on schedule, to modify the Watch's own records with the Watch's own production credentials — and must fail” (C3, verified verbatim). This is self-protection demonstrated as a repeated test, not asserted once at design time.
49: Domain separation
50: Explicitly “belongs to neither authority” — domain separation is the witness's entire purpose.
51: Secure initialisation
52: The break-in test runs “on schedule” — its own cadence is a ruled value (Security Amendments §5 R-8 family; not yet set).
53: Verdict: Structurally sound and directly evidenced. The one open item is the schedule's actual cadence — a ruling, not a design gap.
54: 5   MOAC
55: 5.1. The acceptance gate
56: Property
57: Demonstrated as
58: Non-bypassability
59: “Every criterion or no service” (Promise #22), no human in the acceptance path. Every path to a trained result accepted as usable is required to pass through it — asserted in doctrine; not yet demonstrated path-by-path the way the chokepoint's negative-scan test demonstrates SyniSense's.
60: Self-protection
61: Not specified anywhere in canon before this document. This is the gap Document 0 named and this document now closes with a proposal, not a citation.
62: Domain separation
63: Not specified. Proposed below alongside self-protection, since the two are naturally answered together for this monitor.
64: Secure initialisation
65: Not specified. Proposed below.
66: Verdict: Non-bypassability asserted, not demonstrated. The other three properties do not exist in canon and are specified fresh immediately below.
67: SEC-2  MOAC's acceptance criteria MUST be held in versioned, Rules-Service-governed configuration — the same discipline as SyniSense's custody policy — with integrity verified at load. No criterion is editable by the run it measures, by construction rather than by convention.  [Self-protection]
68: SEC-3  MOAC operates entirely within Targeta's boundary and reads only the run artefacts Targeta produces. It does not query Solva, Mtafiti, or any other engine to reach its decision.  [Domain separation]
69: SEC-4  MOAC MUST refuse to evaluate — not default-accept, not skip — if its criteria configuration is unset or fails integrity verification at load, on the same pattern as A17.9's execution-mode raise.  [Secure initialisation]
70: SEC-5  Every path by which a run's result could be treated as accepted MUST be enumerated and shown to pass through MOAC's evaluation, in a build-time test comparable to SyniSense's negative-scan gate.  [Non-bypassability, demonstrated not asserted]
71: 6   DAP-31 — The Artefact Egress Distance Gate
72: 6.1. The distance gate
73: Property
74: Demonstrated as
75: Non-bypassability
76: Specified in DAP-31 itself: the gate runs after MOAC's acceptance and before registry entry; an artefact that fails is never registered, and an unregistered artefact cannot leave. Every egress path terminates at registration — there is no second door.

78: “The probe's own code and parameters are system-TCB tier under the Rules Service” (DAP-31, as written). Self-protection is specified in the source amendment, not newly proposed here.
79: Domain separation
80: The probe operates on the artefact inside estate compute; “the artefact is held in estate compute throughout — it does not leave to be tested” (DAP-31). It does not reach into the party's domain to run.
81: Secure initialisation
82: Not explicitly specified. The gate's precondition — a valid, ruled threshold and sample size — is implied but not stated as a refuse-if-unset rule.
83: Verdict: Three of four met by the amendment that created it. Secure initialisation is the one gap.
84: SEC-6  DAP-31's probe MUST refuse to run — and MUST refuse egress by default in that state — if the reproduction threshold, sample size, or probe design values are unset. Absence of configuration is a refusal condition, not a bypass.  [Secure initialisation]
85: 7   DAP-32 — Admission-Integrity Probe

88: Demonstrated as

91: Self-protection
92: The mirage shares no store with production (C1); a model under test cannot reach real estate data regardless of what it does inside the battery.
93: Domain separation
94: The battery runs inside the mirage's own isolated domain — by construction, per C1.
95: Secure initialisation
96: Not specified. As with DAP-31, the precondition of a valid battery configuration is implied, not stated as a refuse-if-unset rule.
97: Verdict: Three of four met, inherited directly from the mirage's own established properties. Secure initialisation is the gap, same shape as 6.1's.
98: SEC-7  DAP-32's battery MUST refuse to admit a model — default to refusal, not default to pass — if battery composition or deviation thresholds are unset.  [Secure initialisation]
99: SEC-4, SEC-6, and SEC-7 are the same rule applied three times: an unconfigured gate refuses. Worth ratifying once, as a platform-wide default under Attribute 11 (Failure Posture), rather than as three separate clauses that happen to say the same thing — flagged for the Failure Posture Enumeration (document 5 of this set) to absorb.
100: 8   QA-2 — The Format Gate

104: Non-bypassability
105: “The single hard gate — a submission missing its required sections is returned for completion before it enters the loop” (QA-2, verified verbatim). Every submission passes through it before any further review.
106: Self-protection
107: Not specified in canon. QA-2 is form-only by its own text (“form, never substance”) — its lowest-stakes monitor on this list, and correspondingly the least specified.
108: Domain separation
109: Operates within the Critic Seam's own boundary, ahead of RV/QA tiers.
110: Secure initialisation
111: Not specified.
112: Verdict: Non-bypassability and domain separation reasonably inferred from its position in the loop; self-protection and initialisation are unspecified. Lowest priority to close — QA-2 gates form, not access or disclosure.

# SOURCE: assessment_workspace/canon/drops/20260909/extracted/files_14/Security_Function_Policies_v1.docx
Coordinate: document.xml paragraph in body order, tables included

1: AKKI PLATFORM  ·  ENGINE SPECIFICATION  ·  4 OF 9
2: Named Security Function Policies
3: security_function_policies_v1 — Draft for owner ratification · Closes Document 0 G-7
4: 1   A Correction Before the Substance
5: G-7, as originally stated in akki_governance_architecture_v1, characterised “the evidence floor's lower-the-standard path” as subject-alterable — a party being measured able to weaken the bar it is held to — and R-2 offered two options to fix it. Re-checking the source text this document was supposed to fix shows that characterisation is wrong.
6: “Lower the standard” is Document 4 A5.5, Solva's refusal mechanism, verified verbatim: when a conclusion cannot be supported at the class an objective asked for, the platform refuses visibly and offers the person asking three actions — accept the result as recorded at the class it did achieve, narrow the objective, or lower the standard being asked for. This is a query-recalibration option for the party asking a question. It is not a mechanism by which a party under evaluation weakens the evaluation it is subject to.
7: The mechanism this was conflated with — the Watch's own binding of certainty to evidence — is A5.2 (Doc 3), verified verbatim: severance may be unlocked only by signals “an outsider cannot fabricate,” computed by “a function with no parameter through which a detector's confidence can enter,” explicitly built by transplanting “the same assertion-boundary discipline Solva uses.” A5.2 is not alterable by the party it measures. It is the opposite of the gap G-7 described.
8: R-2 is therefore closed with a different finding than either option it originally offered: no violation exists. What remains genuinely open — and is the actual substance of G-7 — is that no mandatory baseline in the system, A5.2 included, has ever been written as a named security function policy in the form Attribute 7 and FDP_ACC.1 require. That work was never blocked by the lower-the-standard question. It proceeds below.
9: Standing correction to R-2's entry in akki_governance_architecture_v1 §3 and to the Security Amendments' G-7 row: both should read “RESOLVED — no violation found on re-examination of Doc 4 A5.5 and Doc 3 A5.2” rather than carrying two unresolved options. Update 11 of this batch applies this correction to the governance architecture directly.
10: 2   Method
11: FDP_ACC.1's form, applied to every mandatory baseline found across the canon: the TSF enforces a named policy on a stated set of subjects, objects, and operations. Each entry below states that triple explicitly — the thing G-7 actually found missing — and cites the floor's own source text.
12: 3   The Policies
13: ID
14: Name
15: Policy
16: SFP-1
17: Assertion Floor
18: Subjects: any principal requesting a composed answer. Objects: the claim being composed. Operations: assert, compose, refuse. Rule: no sentence enters a composed answer without a per-sentence anchor to material; an unanchorable sentence is refused, not weakened (Doc 4 A2, A5.5).
19: SFP-2
20: Certainty-to-Evidence Binding
21: Subjects: the Watch's response function (Mkono). Objects: severance authority. Operations: unlock, withhold. Rule: severance unlocks only from the closed six-signal registry; no confidence score, however high, is an eligible input (Doc 3 A5.2).
22: SFP-3
23: Acceptance Floor
24: Subjects: any training run. Objects: model output. Operations: accept, refuse. Rule: every stated criterion satisfied or the run is refused in full; no partial acceptance (Promise #22, MOAC).
25: SFP-4
26: Custody Floor
27: Subjects: any data crossing the chokepoint. Objects: the crossing itself. Operations: cross, de-identify, re-identify. Rule: no asset crosses without de-identification appropriate to its custody class (Promise #1, A5.1–A5.3).
28: SFP-5
29: Non-Conformance Ceiling
30: Subjects: any actor whose behavioural signature drifts from its declared conduct. Objects: the actor's trust discount. Operations: reduce, revoke. Rule: loss of conformance alone returns an actor to baseline verification; it is never, by itself, grounds for conviction (Doc 3 A5.7).
31: SFP-6
32: Release Budget
33: Subjects: all external parties, jointly and severally. Objects: the estate's total information release. Operations: release, refuse. Rule: total release across all parties, operations, and time is bounded; exceeding it is a floor violation, not a negotiable ceiling (DAP-35).
34: SFP-7
35: Reproduction Ceiling
36: Subjects: any artefact or output leaving a component boundary. Objects: controlled-unit content. Operations: egress, refuse. Rule: no artefact or output passes carrying reproduction of a controlled unit above the ruled threshold (DAP-31, A5.15).
37: 4   What Was Deliberately Not Named as a Policy
38: Solva's “lower the standard” option (A5.5) is not listed above, on the finding in §1: it is not a policy constraining a subject, because nothing is being measured against it in the Attribute 7 sense. It remains exactly as specified in Document 4, unchanged by this document.
39: 5   Standing
40: These seven are the platform's complete set of mandatory baselines as currently identified. A future floor — any new “no X without Y” rule — is added here in the same form, with its own subject/object/operation triple, at the point it is ratified, rather than left implicit in whichever document first states it.

# SOURCE: assessment_workspace/canon/drops/20260909/extracted/files_14/TCB_Enumeration_v1.docx
Coordinate: document.xml paragraph in body order, tables included

1: AKKI PLATFORM  ·  ENGINE SPECIFICATION  ·  1 OF 9
2: The Trusted Computing Base — Enumeration
3: tcb_enumeration_v1 — Draft for owner ratification · Closes Document 0 G-1
4: Applies BA-1.1
5: “A component is in the TCB if and only if it is deterministic and its failure would falsify a guarantee this document or a document it governs makes.” Two conditions, both required. Neither alone qualifies.
6: Method
7: Every component named in akki_governance_architecture_v1 Part 2, plus every mechanism added since by dap_backend_spec_v1 and the Security Amendments, evaluated against both conditions separately. Where a component is internally mixed — part deterministic, part learned — it is split rather than given one verdict for the whole.
8: Resolves
9: Document 0 Ruling R-3 (the Watch's TCB membership) — not by new policy, but as the mechanical output of applying BA-1.1 consistently. Confirmed compatible with BR-9.1 (CIF) and BR-7.4 (Grey Mirror), both already on record.
10: Status
11: Draft v1. This list is itself TCB-tier content per BA-1.2 — its own future changes go through the Rules Service's system-TCB ceremony (RBM-8) once ratified.
12: Date
13: 9 September 2026
14: 1   The Test, Applied Literally
15: BA-1.1 sets a conjunction, not a list of examples: deterministic, and protection-critical. A component can be highly consequential and still fail the test if it is learned — CIF is the standing example, excluded under BR-9.1 regardless of how central its ideation is. A component can be perfectly deterministic and still fail the test if nothing depends on it — deterministic housekeeping code that no guarantee cites is not TCB by virtue of being predictable.
16: “Deterministic” is evaluated at the level of the mechanism actually making a decision, not the subsystem that hosts it. Several entries below split a subsystem in two for exactly this reason: the decision point inside it is deterministic even where the subsystem's broader function is not.
17: “Protection-critical” is evaluated by BA-1.1's own clause: would this component's failure falsify a stated guarantee. Each row below names the guarantee.
18: 2   The Enumeration
19: Component / mechanism
20: Guarantee at risk if it fails
21: Deterministic?
22: Verdict
23: Reasoning
24: SyniSense — chokepoint (custody sequence)
25: No leakage of confidential information (#1)
26: Yes
27: IN
28: Sole invoking function, negative-scan build test. Deterministic and directly protection-critical — the platform's founding guarantee.
29: SyniSense — closed outbound network
30: No leakage; no path around the crossing
31: Yes
32: IN
33: Allowlist and static-analysis gate. Removing it doesn't change behaviour probabilistically — it removes the boundary.
34: Solva — assertion-boundary seam (import assertion)
35: Assertion floor (Doc 4)
36: Yes
37: IN
38: The enforcement mechanism is deterministic even though what it constrains — Solva's generated reasoning — is not. Split below.
39: Solva — reasoning / generation itself
40: —
41: No
42: OUT
43: Learned. Informs; the seam decides what may be asserted. Excluded by the same logic as CIF.
44: Northena — objective-freeze mechanism
45: No silent scope recalibration (#32)
46: Yes
47: IN
48: A shared, deterministic lock on a job's declared scope.
49: Mtafiti — registry write/query path
50: Estate composition is what it's recorded to be
51: Yes
52: IN
53: Storage and retrieval logic. Any AI-assisted classification suggestion feeding it is a separate, learned input — not itself TCB.
54: Targeta — yield wall / acceptance gate (MOAC)
55: No result accepted without every criterion (#22)
56: Yes
57: IN
58: Fixed criteria evaluated mechanically. No human, and no model, decides acceptance.
59: Targeta — the training process itself
60: —
61: Partial
62: OUT
63: Reproducible under a fixed seed, but not a decision point — nothing is admitted or refused by training running. The wall, not the run, is TCB.
64: Mkondo — hand-off registry
65: Clean hand-offs, no dropped context (#32)
66: Yes
67: IN (pending build)
68: Deterministic by design once built (BR-6.1). Included now so the enumeration doesn't need revisiting the day it ships.
69: The Watch — Mkono (response: annotate/shape/contain/sever)
70: Nothing is misused (#6/#7), acted on before a human wakes
71: Yes
72: IN
73: Executes signed policy against the certainty registry (A5.2). Resolves R-3: the response half qualifies on its own terms.
74: The Watch — Grey Mirror (Macho: detection)
75: —
76: No
77: OUT
78: Learned pattern-matching, per BR-7.4 already on record. Detects; does not decide. Resolves R-3's other half.
79: The Ledger — writer
80: Every claim traceable to evidence (A8)
81: Yes
82: IN
83: Append-only, hash-chained, single writer. If this fails, nothing else on this list is verifiable either — the platform's evidentiary floor.
84: CIF — ideation faculty
85: —
86: No
87: OUT
88: Confirms BR-9.1, already on record. Included here for completeness, not as a new finding.
89: Critic Seam — RV-tier (deterministic record checks)
90: Evidence integrity (Doc 19A)
91: Yes
92: IN
93: Six mechanical verification checks against the record itself.
94: Critic Seam — QA-tier (model-based judgement)
95: —
96: No
97: OUT
98: QA-1's own rule: detect, never decide. Findings route to RV-tier or a human.
99: MOAC — acceptance-criteria evaluation
100: No result accepted without every criterion (#22)
101: Yes
102: IN
103: Same guarantee as Targeta's wall; MOAC is the mechanism that evaluates it.
104: Rules Service — ceremony engine (RBM-7–RBM-13)
105: No rule in force without ceremony (I-1)
106: Yes
107: IN
108: Countdown, countersign verification, atomic apply. Procedural logic, not judgement.
109: Rules Service — AI-assisted drafting (RBM-2)
110: —
111: No
112: OUT
113: Proposes rule text; a named human confirms. The confirmation step is TCB; the proposal isn't.
114: Whitepaper Wizard — Tier 3 eligibility gate (WPW-11)
115: No human may confer eligibility outside stated conditions
116: Yes
117: IN
118: Two-path mechanical check against a run's own results.
119: Whitepaper Wizard — prose assembly
120: —
121: No
122: OUT

124: Connect Wizard — rights-recording at admission
125: Downstream checkpoints have a trustworthy PIP (BR-14.1)

127: IN
