1: AKKI PLATFORM  ·  ENGINE SPECIFICATION  ·  8 OF 9
2: Business Continuity Annex
3: business_continuity_v1 — Draft for owner ratification · Document 3, Part D · Houses S-10, S-11
4: 1   Recovery — S-10
5: S-10  The system will restore Ledger continuity within 3,600 seconds, under independent countersign, following any continuity-affecting incident.  [Ruled — CA1-N5]
6: Recovery Time Objective: 3,600 seconds (one hour). DEFAULT-class — revisable on incident evidence, not a number derived from a formal risk assessment. Applies to the Ledger writer specifically; other components' recovery times are addressed in failure_posture_v1, which this annex does not duplicate.
7: BC-1  Restoration MUST be countersigned by someone independent of the primary Ledger writer's own infrastructure — the same logic as the Watch's external witness: the verifier cannot be the thing that might be down. A countersigner whose own access depends on the failed infrastructure does not satisfy this.
8: BC-2  Ledger continuity is itself attested on a standing cadence, independent of any incident — proposed quarterly, DEFAULT-class, revisable on evidence. This is a routine health check, not a response to failure; its purpose is confirming the RTO would hold if tested, before it has to be.
9: 2   Notification — S-11
10: S-11  The system will issue breach notification within 72 hours of a qualifying incident, to the parties and authorities the incident requires.  [Ruled — CA1-N2]
11: 3   What Remains Open
12: BC-3  Recovery Point Objective — how much committed activity may be lost, not merely how long recovery may take — is not ruled anywhere in this canon. RTO (§1) bounds downtime; it does not bound data loss during that downtime. This is a genuine gap, not a restatement of S-10.
13: RPO cannot be answered responsibly without first knowing whether a replica Ledger writer exists or is planned — an RPO of zero requires synchronous replication; a non-zero RPO requires stating exactly how much is acceptable to lose, in what unit (time, or number of unwritten entries). Neither is specified in canon. This document does not invent an answer; it names the precondition the answer depends on.
14: BC-4  Disaster scenarios beyond single-component failure — total site loss, where the appliance itself (Akki_Appliance_Assembly_Spec_RevA) is destroyed or inaccessible — are not addressed by S-10 or S-11, both of which assume the Ledger writer is recoverable in place. Given the appliance's own dedicated, per-site deployment model (trust_domains_v1 §1), a total site loss scenario has no ruled answer: whether there is an off-site backup, and if so its own RPO/RTO, is unaddressed.
15: 4   Standing
16: This annex is Document 3, Part D. S-10 and S-11 move from “ruled, no document” to “ruled, homed” on ratification. BC-3 and BC-4 are not blocking — the platform functions without an RPO ruling or a disaster-recovery plan for total site loss — but both should be resolved before the appliance programme scales past a small number of deployed units, since the cost of resolving them after an actual incident is considerably higher than the cost of ruling them now.
17: [TABLE 0]
18: What this closes | The document flagged as missing outright when the builder's requirements audit was reconciled. Formally homes S-10 (recover) and S-11 (notify), which existed as Wave E rulings with no document — the gap named explicitly when the security assurance set was built.
19: Ruled already, restated here as canon rather than scattered ruling log entries | CA1-N5 (Ledger continuity) and CA1-N2 (breach notification), both from Wave E. Nothing in §1–§2 is newly decided; it is gathered and given a home.
20: What's genuinely new here | The Recovery Point Objective is not ruled anywhere in this canon. §3 names this rather than inventing a number to fill the gap.
21: Date | 9 September 2026
22: [/TABLE]
23: [TABLE 1]
24: Element | Ruling
25: Recipients | The DPO (Document 2's owner role) and the Watch's external witness — specifically because that witness is already independent of the Watch by design, which is what makes it the right party to also check the Watch's own containment failures.
26: Window | 72 hours, matching Kenya's Data Protection Act 2019 and the GDPR standard it is modelled on. Not an arbitrary figure chosen for this annex.
27: Channel | The existing enforcement-view record, plus a real-time alert to both recipients. A Ledger row alone does not guarantee visibility inside 72 hours — the alert is what makes the window meetable, not merely recordable.
28: Threshold | A hard line actually crossed — not a contained or shaped event. The Watch successfully catching and containing an attempt is the system working as designed; treating every caught attempt as a reportable breach would drown the incidents that are genuinely reportable in noise from the ones that weren't.
29: [/TABLE]

# SOURCE: assessment_workspace/canon/drops/20260909/extracted/text/DAP_Backend_Spec_v1.txt
Coordinate: source line

1: AKKI PLATFORM  ·  APPLICATION SPECIFICATION  ·  BACK END
2: RMS Data Access Portal
3: dap_backend_spec_v1 — Draft for owner ratification
4: 1   Purpose & Scope
5: DAP is how an estate owner monetises a governed estate without surrendering control of it, and how an external party — an AI lab, a research institution, a commercial buyer — acquires what it needs from that estate under terms the owner sets and the platform enforces.
6: Six operations are in scope: browse an estate's composition; connect an external workspace by API key; extract processed intelligence; fine-tune a model on estate data; develop skills against estate data; and download raw data. These are not six variants of one action. They are six distinct crossings with six different governance profiles, and §4 states each one separately because collapsing them would defeat every guarantee the platform makes.
7: Two sides are in scope: the external-party side (a party acquiring) and the estate-owner side (an owner configuring what is available, on what terms, and approving what requires approval). The external-party side is built first; the owner side reuses Manage Rules and Spend Requests where they already exist.
8: 2   Definitions
9: 3   The External-Party Principal
10: The governed triad (Document 0, Attribute 3) has no class for a party outside the estate owner's own organisation. DAP adds one, because every requirement below is stated over it.
11: DAP-1  An external party is admitted as an organisation-level principal carrying: legal identity; a declared governance posture; the terms it is admitted under; its trust domain identifier; and an admission-time mandate stating what it came to do. Individuals and agents act under it, never beside it.
12: DAP-2  Every request carries a party principal — a named individual or a registered agent — with its own mandate, mark state, and behavioural signature under the Watch. An agent's mandate is separate from its operator's and is admitted separately.  [Doc 3 #7]
13: DAP-3  Connecting an external agent admits an autonomous non-human principal. It MUST be admitted as its own principal under DAP-2, MUST carry a stated scope of autonomy, and is subject to the Watch's machine-speed attack shape from its first request.
14: DAP-4  Slow-play extraction — a sequence of individually-permitted requests whose aggregate would reconstruct material the party is not entitled to — MUST be detected as a distinct attack shape against the party's cumulative extraction history, not evaluated per request.  [S-2]
15: DAP-4 is the reason cumulative extraction history is a first-class record (DAP-24) rather than a reporting convenience. Every individual request in a slow-play sequence is legitimate; only the aggregate is not.
16: DAP-5  DAP is a trust-domain boundary. The external party's domain and the estate's domain share no identifier resolution, no store, and no credential. A unit identifier meaningful inside the estate MUST NOT resolve to anything in the party's domain except through an operation §4 permits.  [Attribute 12]
17: 4   The Six Crossing Profiles
18: Each operation is governed differently. This table is the spine of the specification: every requirement in §5 and §6 implements a row of it, and no operation may be added to DAP without a row stating its profile.
19: What the profiles mean in practice
20: DAP-6  Browse MUST return aggregate composition only — volume, type, language, period, counts per type — and MUST NOT return, sample, or preview unit contents. Browsing an estate is not a crossing and MUST NOT be recorded as one.  [Mtafiti]
21: DAP-7  A connected workspace's queries execute inside the estate's perimeter. The party's query enters; de-identified results leave. Estate data MUST NOT leave under this operation, and no code path may make it do so.  [Promise #10, the pull seam]
22: DAP-8  Processed intelligence egresses derived output only. The source units read to produce it MUST be recorded in the receipt and MUST NOT be reconstructable from the output. Where an objective cannot be served without exposing source, the operation is refused, not degraded.  [Attribute 7]
23: DAP-9  Fine-tuning is compute-to-data only. The party's base model is admitted to estate compute; estate data MUST NOT be transferred to compute outside the estate's perimeter under any configuration. There is no permitted inverse of this operation.  [Owner ruling, 5 Sep 2026]
24: DAP-10  Trained weights and skill files leave as artefact egress: through the model registry, with a rights posture stamped, a hash recorded, and the terms in force cited. Weights derived from controlled units carry the derivation on the registry entry.  [#24, #30]
25: DAP-11  Raw download is the outer-gate crossing of Promise #25, not the ordinary chokepoint crossing. Disclosure depth is bounded by rights and custody; the redaction pass runs as a gate, not a prompt; and the operation writes an evidence record. Every unit released is individually recorded.  [#25]
26: DAP-9 states a prohibition with no exception clause because the compute-to-data direction is the platform's sovereignty guarantee. A configuration flag permitting the inverse would make the guarantee a preference.
27: 5   Back-End Services
28: Admission & keys
29: DAP-12  Admission of an external party is a governed act producing: the organisation principal (DAP-1), its trust domain, its terms, and its mandate. Admission MUST be recorded and MUST require the estate owner's named authority. A party is never self-admitting.
30: DAP-13  API keys are issued per party principal, never per organisation, and carry the principal's mandate. A key MUST be revocable in a single act with immediate effect, MUST expire on a stated lifetime (§10 R-4), and MUST NOT be transferable between principals. Key material is never written to any record, including receipts.  [A5.7]
31: Approval
32: DAP-14  A request containing at least one controlled unit MUST route to the estate owner's named approving authority before execution, carrying: the requesting principal, the objective, the units or scope in question, why each is controlled, and the terms that would apply. The request does not execute while pending.
33: DAP-15  Approval decisions are recorded with the deciding authority's identity, the decision, and its stated reason. A refusal states why. Neither approval nor refusal may be inferred from silence — an unanswered request expires unexecuted rather than proceeding by default.  [fail-closed]
34: DAP-16  Fine-tune and skill-development requests always require approval, controlled or not, because both produce artefact egress (DAP-10). Raw download always requires approval where the request is controlled; the estate owner configures whether uncontrolled raw download requires it (DAP-22).
35: DAP-17  An estate owner MAY grant a standing approval for a named party, a named scope, and a stated window — replacing per-request approval within it. A standing approval is itself an approved act under DAP-14's discipline, is revocable in one act, and MUST NOT cover controlled units unless it names them explicitly.
36: Extraction
37: DAP-18  Every extraction is a commissioned job with a frozen objective. Objective freeze applies at commission: after commission, no path — including the portal's own assistance chat — may widen the job's scope. A wider scope is a new job.  [#32, Northena]
38: DAP-19  Every job routes to the engine that governs its operation per §4 and MUST NOT execute through any other path. DAP holds no extraction logic of its own; it composes.
39: DAP-20  The portal's assistance chat MAY help a party shape an objective, identify relevant scope, or understand terms, before commission. It MUST NOT approve, widen scope after commission, or decide any gate. It proposes; the gates decide.  [Attribute 10]
40: Metering & receipts
41: DAP-21  Every operation in §4 emits a metered event carrying: operation type; what was accessed (unit identifiers, or the aggregate scope where units are not individually released); quantity in the unit natural to the operation — audio-hours, tokens, compute-seconds, units, queries; the terms identifier in force; the party principal; and the timestamp from the platform's reliable time source. Metered events are written to the Ledger before the operation's result is returned.  [AU-3]
42: DAP-22  Terms attach at three levels, resolved most-specific-first: per party agreement, then per custody class, then estate default. Every receipt cites the terms identifier actually applied, not the level it came from.
43: DAP-23  Spend against a party's ceiling is evaluated before execution. An operation that would exceed the ceiling routes to a person as a spend request rather than failing silently or executing over-budget.  [#11]
44: DAP-24  Cumulative extraction history per party is a first-class, queryable record — what has been taken, in what quantity, under which terms, over what period — retained for the party's full admission, and readable by the estate owner at any time.  [supports DAP-4]
45: DAP-21 through DAP-24 are the pricing rails, not a pricing model. Whatever tariff is later ruled — per audio-hour, per token, per compute-hour, subscription, or revenue share — every event required to compute it is already on the Ledger, attributed and timestamped. §10 R-6 carries the tariff as a named dependency.
46: Estate-owner configuration
47: DAP-25  An estate owner configures, per custody class and per operation, whether that operation is available at all, available on approval, or available under standing terms. The default for every combination is unavailable — availability is granted, never assumed.  [fail-closed]
48: DAP-26  An estate owner sets default terms per custody class, per-party overrides, and per-party ceilings. Changes take effect through the Rules Service ceremony for the estate's own rules and MUST NOT retroactively alter the terms cited on receipts already issued.
49: DAP-27  An estate owner MUST be able to suspend a party — halting every in-flight and future operation for that party in one act — and to revoke its admission. Suspension is immediate; in-flight jobs stop and are recorded as stopped, not silently completed.  [Doc 3 A5.3 — stop, never delete]
50: 6   Failure Posture
51: DAP-28  Every gate in DAP fails closed. An approval service that cannot be reached, a metering write that cannot complete, a terms resolution that returns nothing, a ceiling check that errors — each refuses the operation. No path returns estate data, an artefact, or a query result when a governing check could not complete.  [FPT_FLS.1]
52: DAP-29  A metered event that cannot be written to the Ledger refuses the operation it meters. An unrecorded extraction is not permitted to have happened.  [I-4 pattern]
53: DAP-30  Browse degrades rather than refuses: where the census is stale or partially unavailable, DAP returns what it has, marked as stale with its as-of time, and never silently presents an incomplete estate as complete.  [honesty grammar]
54: 7   Composition Map
55: DAP owns no invariant of its own. Every guarantee it makes is a guarantee of a component it composes, exercised through this surface. This map is what makes the claim checkable.
56: 8   Dependencies & Their Status
57: 9   Build Acceptance Criteria
58: 10   Owner Rulings — Parked
59: R-1  The controlled-unit definition (§2): ratify as proposed — personal data, declared-confidential, rights-encumbered for the requested use, or sensitive category — or set a different line.
60: R-2  The approving authority at RMS for controlled requests and artefact egress: the named role, and who currently holds it.
61: R-3  Per-party extraction ceilings per window — whether a platform default exists, or every ceiling is set per party agreement.
62: R-4  API key lifetime and rotation cadence.
63: R-5  Whether external parties acquiring data receive a business-type entry in the Rules Service taxonomy, or are governed entirely under the estate's own rule books.
64: R-6  The licensing and pricing model. DAP specifies the metering rails; the tariff is a separate document and a separate decision.
65: R-1 and R-2 are needed before the approval path can be built. R-3 through R-6 are needed before a party can be admitted commercially, not before the platform is built.
66: 11   Standing
67: DAP is the first instance of a generic Data & Intelligence Acquisition Platform. Nothing in §1–§9 is specific to RMS except the named estate; a second estate owner adopting this platform inherits every requirement here and configures §5's owner-side settings for its own estate.
68: The front-end specification — the three-panel layout, navigation, per-screen content, and the assistance chat's interaction design — depends on this document and follows it. Where the two conflict, this document governs: the front end may not offer an operation §4 does not profile.
69: [TABLE 0]
70: What this is | The back-end specification for the RMS Data Access Portal (DAP) — the surface through which an external party acquires data, intelligence, trained models, or skills from a governed estate. DAP is the first instance of a generic Data & Intelligence Acquisition Platform; nothing in this document is RMS-specific except where stated.
71: Position | A composition, not an engine. DAP owns no invariant of its own: it composes SyniSense, Mtafiti, Targeta, Solva, Mkondo, the Watch, the Ledger, and the Rules Service, and adds one thing none of them has — an external-party principal and the trust boundary around it.
72: Not in this document | The three-panel layout, navigation tree, per-screen content, and the right-panel chat's interaction design. Those are the front-end specification, which depends on this one.
73: Prefix | DAP — reserved under rule_criteria_spec_v1 ROC-6 on ratification.
74: Status | Draft v1. Every requirement PROPOSED until ratified. Six rulings parked (§10); none block §5–§6.
75: Date | 5 September 2026
76: [/TABLE]
77: [TABLE 1]
78: Term | Meaning
79: External party | An organisation admitted to DAP to acquire from an estate it does not own. The highest-risk principal class the platform admits.
80: Party principal | A named individual or autonomous agent acting under an external party's mandate. Every request has one.
81: Estate owner | The organisation that owns the estate and sets what is available, to whom, on what terms. RMS, for this instance.
82: Controlled unit | A unit whose custody class is personal data, declared-confidential (Promise #2's list), rights-encumbered for the requested use (Doc 17 A17.15), or a sensitive category. §10 R-1 ratifies this definition.
83: Controlled request | Any request containing at least one controlled unit. Requires per-request approval (DAP-14).
84: Crossing profile | The governance treatment of one operation: what enters, what leaves, which gate governs, whether approval is required, what is receipted.
85: Terms | The commercial and rights conditions in force for an operation — attached at estate, custody-class, or party level. DAP specifies how terms attach and meter; it does not set prices (§10 R-6).
86: Metered event | The record of a chargeable or countable operation: what, how much, under which terms, by which principal, when.
87: Artefact egress | The governed departure of a derived artefact — model weights, a skill file — as distinct from the departure of estate data.
88: [/TABLE]
89: [TABLE 2]

93: Processed intelligence | The party's objective | Derived output only — never source units | SyniSense chokepoint; Solva's assertion floor | None for uncontrolled; per-request if controlled | Objective, output, units read
94: Fine-tune model | The party's base model, into estate compute | Model weights, via the registry with rights posture stamped | Targeta; artefact egress (#24, #30) | Always — artefact egress | Training manifest, weights hash, terms
95: Develop skills | The party's skill objective | Skill file, via artefact egress | Doc 18 callable skill files; artefact egress | Always — artefact egress | Skill file hash, units read, terms
96: Download raw data | Nothing | Estate data itself | Outer gate (#25) — not the ordinary crossing | Always for controlled; owner-configurable otherwise | Every unit, redaction log, sign-off
97: [/TABLE]
98: [TABLE 3]
99: Component | What DAP composes it for
100: Mtafiti — the Registry | Estate composition for browse (DAP-6): volume, types, languages, period, per-type counts. The landing surface is a census view.

Coordinate: source line

1: AKKI PLATFORM  ·  ENGINE SPECIFICATION  ·  3 OF 9
2: The Determinism Inventory
3: determinism_inventory_v1 — Draft for owner ratification · Closes Document 0 G-10
4: 1   Classification
5: Deterministic: given the same input and state, the same output, reasoned about exhaustively. Learned: statistically characterised, not exhaustively reasoned about, whatever its accuracy. A component is one or the other; where a named subsystem contains both, it is split, consistent with tcb_enumeration_v1's treatment of Solva, Targeta, and the Watch.
6: 2   Human Oversight Against Article 14
7: Where a human, not a deterministic component, is the check on a learned component's output, Article 14 names five distinct capabilities. The platform's own ruling loop — every decision recorded across this programme, from the four owner rulings at the start through every parked ruling since — is mapped against each separately, because a loop that serves one well does not thereby serve all five.
8: 3   Findings
9: Sixteen components classified without ambiguity. One genuinely mixed case — the DAP-32 trigger scan — carried forward from the amendment that created it rather than forced to a single verdict here. Of Article 14's five capabilities, one (override) is strongly evidenced by this canon's own working method; one (automation bias) is directly and deliberately addressed by a named requirement; two (understand-and-monitor, correct interpretation) are plausible but unconfirmed by design intent or by test; and one (halt-to-safe-state) has a specific, named, still-open question — whether CIF can be stopped independent of the run it feeds.
10: DET-1  Confirm or build a halt mechanism for CIF independent of halting the Targeta run it feeds — closing capability (e) fully rather than leaving it partially evidenced.
11: DET-2  Where an AI-assisted classification capability is built into Mtafiti, name the deterministic confirmation step before it ships — not after, per this inventory's own method for every other learned component.
12: This inventory itself should be re-run, not assumed permanent, whenever a new component is added to the platform — consistent with tcb_enumeration_v1's own standing clause. The two share a maintenance obligation because they share almost all their evidence.
13: [TABLE 0]
14: Scope | Every component on the platform — broader than tcb_enumeration_v1, which asks a narrower, conjunctive question (deterministic AND protection-critical). This document asks one question only — deterministic, or learned — of everything, whether or not it's protection-critical.
15: Basis | Attribute 10's own rule, verified: decision authority is held only by deterministic components; a learned component may detect, score, rank, propose, or draft, never decide.
16: Second half | Maps the platform's existing ruling loop — the pattern of proposal, scrutiny, and explicit ratification this entire canon runs on — against EU AI Act Article 14's five human-oversight capabilities, verified verbatim, rather than asserting “a human is in the loop” as if that were one thing.
17: Reuses | tcb_enumeration_v1's classification work directly — the two questions share almost all their evidence. Not re-derived from scratch.
18: Date | 9 September 2026
19: [/TABLE]
20: [TABLE 1]
21: Component | Class | Structural mechanism denying decision authority (if Learned)
22: SyniSense — chokepoint, custody sequence | Deterministic | — holds decision authority directly
23: Solva — assertion-boundary seam | Deterministic | — holds decision authority over what may be asserted
24: Solva — reasoning / generation | Learned | The assertion-boundary seam refuses anything the reasoning produces that isn't independently evidenced. The seam decides; Solva proposes.
25: Northena — objective-freeze mechanism | Deterministic | —
26: Mtafiti — registry storage/query | Deterministic | —
27: Mtafiti — any AI-assisted classification suggestion (if present) | Learned | Not confirmed as existing in canon. If built, it proposes a classification; a deterministic confirmation step (undefined — flagged) would need to decide.
28: Targeta — yield wall / MOAC | Deterministic | — holds acceptance authority directly
29: Targeta — the model being trained | Learned | Cannot accept or refuse its own output. MOAC, downstream and deterministic, decides.
30: Mkondo — hand-off registry | Deterministic | —
31: The Watch — Mkono (response) | Deterministic | — holds containment authority directly
32: The Watch — Grey Mirror (detection) | Learned | Mkono acts only on a signed verdict Grey Mirror cannot itself produce authority over — Grey Mirror asserts facts; Mkono decides (A2, verified verbatim).
33: The Ledger — writer | Deterministic | —
34: CIF — ideation faculty | Learned | Single-experiment principle: existence unconditional, but every adopted idea passes a deterministic acceptance point before affecting a run (BR-9.2, already on record).
35: Critic Seam — RV-tier | Deterministic | —
36: Critic Seam — QA-tier | Learned | QA-1's own rule: findings route to RV-tier or a human; a QA finding cannot block execution on its own.
37: Rules Service — ceremony engine | Deterministic | —
38: Rules Service — AI-assisted drafting | Learned | RBM-2: proposes; the named human author confirms before a rule enters PROPOSED. The confirmation is the deterministic decision point.
39: Whitepaper Wizard — eligibility gate | Deterministic | —
40: Whitepaper Wizard — prose assembly | Learned | Draws only on Tier 1/2 artefacts (WPW-13); the eligibility gate, not the prose engine, decides whether a paper may publish.
41: DAP — release budget, distance gate, output-content gate | Deterministic | — each holds its own admit/refuse authority directly
42: DAP — admission-probe trigger scan (backdoor detection half) | Mixed — flagged | Where the technique is statistical, it informs; the canary-touch half of the same probe (on A5.2's closed registry) is what actually decides admission.
43: Deck Rendering Engine | Deterministic | — not a decision authority in the governance sense; included for completeness
44: [/TABLE]
45: [TABLE 2]
46: Capability | State | Evidence
47: (a) Understand & monitor | Partially evidenced | STATE/NEXT.md-style tracking and the Rules Registry (once built) give an overseer a current, queryable view. Not confirmed as designed for this specific purpose — it was built for change-control, and happens to serve oversight.
48: (b) Aware of automation bias | Directly addressed | A5.16 (recommendation provenance) exists specifically because a human acting on an agent's advice without knowing it was advice is the automation-bias failure mode. The action record surfaces the recommendation at the point of action — not after.
49: (c) Correctly interpret output | Evidenced by design, not tested | Every claim traces to evidence in one step (A8, “Walk this →”). Whether a given overseer actually interprets correctly, given that trace, has never been tested with a real reviewer.
50: (d) Override, disregard, reverse | Strongly evidenced | The best-evidenced capability on this list. Every ruling in this canon's own history is an instance of exactly this — including several that reversed or corrected a prior proposal, this document's own predecessors among them.
51: (e) Halt to a safe state | Partially evidenced, one confirmed gap | The Watch can stop anything (A5.3, “destroy does not exist in the Watch”). Whether CIF's ideation can be halted independently of halting the Targeta run it feeds — named as unconfirmed when W-3 through W-8 were drafted — remains unconfirmed here too.
52: [/TABLE]

# SOURCE: assessment_workspace/canon/drops/20260909/extracted/text/Failure_Posture_Enumeration_v1.txt
Coordinate: source line

1: AKKI PLATFORM  ·  ENGINE SPECIFICATION  ·  5 OF 9
2: Failure Posture Enumeration
3: failure_posture_v1 — Draft for owner ratification · Closes Document 0 G-11
4: 1   The Platform Default
5: FP-1  Every component in the Trusted Computing Base fails closed by default. An evaluation that cannot complete — configuration unset, a dependency unreachable, a check erroring — refuses the operation it governs. This is the default; §3 lists the components that correctly depart from it, and why.
6: FP-2  A gate whose governing configuration is unset or fails integrity verification at load refuses by default rather than passing by default. This absorbs security_architecture_v1's SEC-4 (MOAC), SEC-6 (the distance gate), and SEC-7 (the admission probe) as one rule rather than three restatements of it — an unconfigured gate is a closed gate, platform-wide, not per-component.
7: 2   Per-Component Enumeration
8: 3   The Departures — Where Fail-Safe-Open Is Correct
9: Two departures from §1's default, both already correct in the system as built, now stated as deliberate rather than left to be discovered.
10: FP-3  Mtafiti's read path fails safe-open: a write failure never blocks a query against already-committed estate composition. The alternative — refusing to answer “what exists” because “what changed most recently” cannot be confirmed — would make an outage indistinguishable from data loss to everyone reading the registry, which is a worse failure than serving slightly stale data marked as such.
11: FP-4  The Watch's already-active containments persist through a Watch outage rather than lapsing. This is fail-closed for new decisions and explicitly not fail-open for standing ones — the two are evaluated separately, and conflating them would silently release every contained actor the moment the Watch itself failed, which is precisely when containment matters most.
12: Recovery time objective and recovery point objective for the Ledger writer specifically are covered in the Business Continuity Annex (document 8 of this set), not restated here — this document specifies posture per component; that one specifies how long a failure may last and how much may be lost before it is a breach in its own right.
13: 4   Standing
14: A component added to the Trusted Computing Base under tcb_enumeration_v1's own standing clause is added here in the same turn — posture, failure types, and preserved state, not deferred to a later pass. §1's default applies until stated otherwise; a new TCB member that departs from it states so explicitly, the way §3 does for Mtafiti and the Watch.
15: [TABLE 0]
16: Requirement answered | CC FPT_FLS.1: preserve a secure state for an enumerated list of failure types — the enumeration is the requirement, not a general commitment. NIST SC-24: fail to a known state, preserving defined state information.
17: Scope | Every component in tcb_enumeration_v1's IN column, plus DAP's already-specified posture (DAP-28–30), carried here rather than re-derived, and the three unconfigured-gate defaults flagged in security_architecture_v1 (SEC-4, SEC-6, SEC-7), absorbed as one platform-wide rule rather than three separate clauses.
18: Finding, stated up front | The platform already gets this right in the cases that have been examined closely — the chokepoint fails closed, the consumption levers correctly fail safe-open toward recomputation. What was missing was the enumeration, not the behaviour.
19: Date | 9 September 2026
20: [/TABLE]
21: [TABLE 1]
22: Component | Failure types | Posture | Preserved state
23: SyniSense — chokepoint | Custody policy unreadable; de-identification step errors; re-identification key unavailable | Fail-closed | The crossing attempt itself — who, what, when — written before the attempt, so a failed crossing is still evidenced
24: SyniSense — closed network | Allowlist configuration unreachable | Fail-closed | No outbound connection attempted; the refusal reason
25: Solva — assertion-boundary seam | Anchor map cannot be computed; source material unreachable | Fail-closed | The unanchored draft is discarded, not served; the refusal with structured reason (A5.5)
26: Northena — objective-freeze | Freeze record unreadable at a hand-off point | Fail-closed | The job halts rather than proceeding on an unverifiable scope
27: Mtafiti — registry | Write path unavailable | Fail-closed for writes; fail-safe-open for reads of already-committed data | Last successfully committed state remains queryable even while writes are refused
28: Targeta — yield wall / MOAC | Criteria configuration unset or unverifiable | Fail-closed | The run's own artefacts remain intact; nothing is marked accepted
29: Mkondo — hand-off registry | Registry write fails mid-handoff | Fail-closed | Neither side treats the hand-off as complete; the attempt is recorded as failed, not silently retried as success
30: The Watch — Mkono | Verdict cannot be read; policy table unreachable | Fail-closed on new actions; already-active containments persist | Every action already in force stays in force — a Watch outage does not release a contained actor
31: The Ledger — writer | Storage unreachable; hash-chain verification fails on write | Fail-closed — and everything that depends on writing to it (§1 FP-1) fails closed in consequence | The chain up to the last verified entry; no entry is ever appended out of order to “catch up”
32: MOAC | As Targeta's wall — same component, listed once above | — | —
33: Critic Seam — RV-tier | A deterministic check cannot execute | Fail-closed — escalates to a human rather than passing unchecked | The submission awaiting review; nothing is marked reviewed
34: Rules Service — ceremony engine | Countdown timer or countersign verification unreachable | Fail-closed — no rule reaches CANON on an unverifiable ceremony | The rule remains PROPOSED; the ceremony's partial progress, so it can resume rather than restart

# SOURCE: assessment_workspace/canon/drops/20260909/extracted/text/Handoff_Generalisation_v1.txt
Coordinate: source line

1: AKKI PLATFORM  ·  ENGINE SPECIFICATION  ·  7 OF 9
2: Hand-Off Generalisation
3: handoff_registry_v1 — Draft for owner ratification · Closes Document 0 G-13
4: 1   The Registry
5: HR-1  Mkondo owns a hand-off registry. Every job passed from one subsystem to another — not only ThinkLab to Task Manager — writes an entry before the receiving subsystem may act on it.
6: HR-2  A hand-off entry carries: the commissioning subsystem's identity; the receiving subsystem's identity; the job's frozen objective, from Northena's existing mechanism (BR-3.1); the shape of what is being handed off (a reasoning session, a training commission, an extraction request, a rule proposal — whatever the job class); a timestamp from the platform's reliable time source; and a receipt once the receiving subsystem acknowledges.
7: HR-3  A receiving subsystem MUST refuse to act on a hand-off that has no registry entry. This is the generalisation of the one existing guarantee (Promise #32: a malformed hand-off surfaces as a finding at the point of hand-off) to every crossing, not only the instantiated one.
8: HR-4  The no-dual-hatted-task rule (Promise #32) is enforced at registration: a hand-off entry naming a job already open under a different receiving subsystem is refused, not merely discouraged. This moves the rule from convention (as BR-6.3 found it) to a registry-level check.
9: HR-5  Objective freeze applies at the point of registration, not at the point of eventual action — a receiving subsystem inherits the frozen scope Northena set at hand-off, and cannot itself widen it. This is the same discipline DAP-18 already applies to commissioned jobs, generalised to every internal hand-off, not only DAP's external-facing ones.
10: HR-6  The registry is queryable by either end of a hand-off, by job, by subsystem pair, or by time range — so “what did we hand this subsystem, and when” has an answer without reconstructing it from each engine's own logs.
11: 2   Failure Posture
12: HR-7  A hand-off registry write that fails leaves the job un-commissioned on the receiving side — fail-closed, consistent with failure_posture_v1's platform default and its own treatment of Mkondo's registry (“neither side treats the hand-off as complete; the attempt is recorded as failed, not silently retried as success”).
13: 3   What This Does Not Change
14: ThinkLab's hand-off to Task Manager is not re-specified — it already meets HR-1 through HR-6 by construction, having been the pattern this document generalises from. No existing behaviour changes for that one crossing; every other crossing now has to meet the same bar it already does.
15: 4   Standing
16: A new subsystem, or a new job class passed between existing ones, registers its hand-off shape here at the point it is built — not discovered later as a second uninstantiated guarantee the way this one was.
17: [TABLE 0]
18: Problem | Promise #32's guarantee — clean hand-offs, no dropped context, no silently recalibrated objective — is instantiated exactly once: ThinkLab handing a completed reasoning session to Task Manager. Every other subsystem-to-subsystem hand-off has no registered contract at all, per BR-6.1 and the Security Amendments' G-13 finding.
19: What already exists to build on | Two ingredients, both already shared mechanisms: Northena's objective-freeze (BR-3.1, “a single, shared implementation invoked identically by every subsystem that hands off a job”) and the registered-handoff-contract shape the one working instance already uses — what was commissioned, its shape, the identity of both ends, a receipt.
20: What this document adds | The missing half: a hand-off registry every crossing writes to and every receiving subsystem checks, owned by Mkondo, generalising the one instance to all of them.
21: Date | 9 September 2026
22: [/TABLE]

# SOURCE: assessment_workspace/canon/drops/20260909/extracted/text/Pruning_Unlearning_Amendment_v1.txt
Coordinate: source line

1: AKKI PLATFORM  ·  CHANGE REGISTER  ·  SECURITY  ·  9 OF 9
2: Pruning & Unlearning Amendment
3: 2 amendments · 1 new promise · 1 ruling · 9 September 2026
4: T-3   Artefact Pruning Before Egress
5: TARGET  dap_backend_spec_v1 — new DAP-37, extending DAP-31 and DAP-36.
6: CURRENT  DAP-31 gates egress on a reproduction probe. DAP-36 trains with differential privacy by default. Neither addresses reducing an artefact's size or memorisation surface between acceptance and egress — an artefact either passes DAP-31 as trained, or it doesn't.
7: AMENDED — normative text
8: DAP-37  A fine-tuned artefact MAY be pruned — magnitude pruning or an equivalent structural reduction — between MOAC acceptance and DAP-31's distance gate, as a ruled optional step. Pruning is a second, empirical reduction in memorisation surface on top of DAP-36's differentially private training; it is never a substitute for it, and this document does not present it as one. A pruned artefact MUST re-pass MOAC's acceptance criteria — pruning can degrade performance below the accepted bar, and acceptance is re-evaluated, not assumed to survive the change. A pruned artefact's hash differs from its pre-pruning hash; it is a new artefact for every purpose DAP-10 and DAP-31 govern, including a fresh pass through the distance gate at the ruled threshold. Pruning ratio and method are ruled values, ratified alongside DAP-31's own probe parameters.
9: MECHANISM  Magnitude pruning removes the weights contributing least to model output, which empirically also reduces the model's capacity to have memorised specific training examples — a smaller, sparser artefact has less room to encode any one unit's content precisely. This is a capacity reduction, not a guarantee; DAP-31's probe, re-run on the pruned artefact, is what actually confirms the result.
10: DERIVATION  Han, Mao, and Dally, “Deep Compression” (2015) — magnitude pruning and its empirical effect on memorisation capacity. DAP-31 (the gate this feeds back through). DAP-36 (the guarantee this does not replace).
11: PRINCIPLE  A smaller artefact is not a safer artefact by assertion. It is a candidate for re-testing, and DAP-31 is what turns the candidacy into a fact.
12: T-4   Unlearning on Rights Withdrawal
13: TARGET  dap_backend_spec_v1 — new DAP-38. Rules Service (registry query, RBM-20) as the mechanism that makes affected artefacts findable.
14: CURRENT  No requirement addresses what happens when a contributor withdraws consent, or a unit's licence expires, after an artefact trained on that unit has already been registered or has already egressed under DAP-10. DAP-31 gates what leaves; nothing governs what happens to what already left.
15: AMENDED — normative text
16: DAP-38  When a unit's rights status changes to withdrawn — consent revoked, licence expired, or an equivalent event — every artefact whose training manifest cites that unit is identified via the registry (a query, per RBM-20's design, not a search) and is either re-derived without the unit or recalled. Re-derivation trains a replacement artefact excluding the withdrawn unit, using the same run configuration recorded in the original training manifest, and passes it through DAP-31 and MOAC as a new artefact before it replaces the original in the registry. Recall withdraws the original artefact's registry entry and, where the artefact was already delivered under DAP-10, notifies the receiving party that the artefact's rights basis has changed. A unit's contribution to the estate release budget (DAP-35) is NOT refunded on unlearning — the privacy loss from the original release already occurred; unlearning restores the artefact's cleanliness going forward, not the budget already spent.
17: MECHANISM  Sharded, isolated training (SISA — Sharded, Isolated, Sliced, Aggregated) makes re-derivation tractable by limiting retraining to the shard containing the withdrawn unit rather than the whole model; DAP-36's DP-SGD defaults make the retrained shard's own privacy accounting straightforward, since the accountant already runs per training job. Where SISA-style sharding was not used for the original run, re-derivation means a full retrain, and §5 R-12 rules whether that is mandatory or whether recall alone suffices in that case.
18: DERIVATION  Bourtoule et al., “Machine Unlearning” — SISA (2021). Guo et al., “Certified Data Removal from Machine Learning Models” (2020) — the formal standard re-derivation approximates. Kenya Data Protection Act 2019 s.40 (erasure). GDPR Art. 17 (right to erasure). CA1-N3, already ruled: raw source and five-ring units get real erasure; a trained model is flagged via A17.15's rights-lapse mechanism rather than untrained on demand — DAP-38 is that same discipline's extension to artefacts DAP now governs.
19: PRINCIPLE  The erasure right does not stop at the database. A model that carries a unit's influence is still carrying it, whatever the registry says about the source record.
20: This generalises CA1-N3's model-flagging answer, already ruled for the platform's own trained models, to every artefact DAP-9/DAP-10 admits an external party's model into or egresses — not a new principle, an extension of one already decided.
21: 3   New Promise
22: 4   Ruling
23: R-12  When the original training run was not sharded for isolated retraining, is re-derivation mandatory regardless of cost, or does recall alone satisfy DAP-38 where re-derivation is uneconomic? Neither this document nor CA1-N3 answers this; it is a genuine owner decision, not a technical one.
24: Nothing above is blocked by R-12. Where sharding was used, re-derivation is the norm and inexpensive enough that the question doesn't arise. R-12 matters only for the harder case, and DAP-38's recall path is fully specified either way — it is available now, pending only the ruling on when it's sufficient versus when re-derivation is required.
25: [TABLE 0]
26: Applies to | dap_backend_spec_v1 (new DAP-37, DAP-38) · Security Assurance Promise Set (S-26)
27: What this closes | Two questions raised while defining artefact egress that DAP-31/DAP-36 did not answer: can a fine-tuned model be made smaller and cleaner before it leaves, and what happens to an artefact already registered or egressed when the right to a unit it trained on is later withdrawn.
28: Honesty condition stated up front | Pruning reduces memorisation empirically; it does not prove its absence. DP-SGD (DAP-36) is the guarantee; pruning is a second reduction on top of it. This amendment does not present pruning as a substitute for differential privacy, and DAP-37 says so explicitly.
29: [/TABLE]
30: [TABLE 1]
31: ID | Promise | Rests on
32: S-26 | The system will remove a unit's influence from every artefact that carried it when the right to that unit ends — by re-derivation or recall, findable by registry query, with the release budget's prior consumption left unrefunded. | T-3, T-4 (DAP-37, DAP-38). CA1-N3. SISA; certified removal; DPA s.40; GDPR Art. 17.
33: [/TABLE]

2: Security Architecture Description
3: security_architecture_v1 — Draft for owner ratification · Closes Document 0 G-6
4: 1   SyniSense — The Chokepoint
5: 1.1. The Chokepoint
6: Verdict: Three of four fully met. Self-protection is partial — build-time gates exist; runtime tamper-resistance for the loaded policy is proposed below, not yet built.
7: SEC-1  SyniSense's custody-sequence policy and network allowlist MUST be integrity-verified at load — a signature or hash comparison against the value recorded in the Rule Registry — so that a runtime modification is detected, not merely prevented by the absence of an edit path.  [Closes the remaining gap in 1.1]
8: 2   The Watch — Mkono (Response)
9: 2.1. Mkono, the deterministic response half
10: Verdict: All four met, directly from canon text. The strongest-evidenced monitor on the platform after the chokepoint.
11: 3   The Watch — Grey Mirror (Macho)
12: Grey Mirror is not itself evaluated as a reference monitor. Per tcb_enumeration_v1, Macho is learned and holds no decision authority — “it cannot block, throttle, mark, reroute, or notify. Its sole output is a verdict” (A2, verified verbatim). ADV_ARC.1 applies to components that mediate and decide; Macho detects and proposes. Its self-protection is covered separately, under C3 below, as the subject the witness watches — not as a monitor in its own right.
13: 4   The External Witness (C3)
14: 4.1. The witness — the mechanism that makes 2.1's self-protection checkable
15: Verdict: Structurally sound and directly evidenced. The one open item is the schedule's actual cadence — a ruling, not a design gap.
16: 5   MOAC
17: 5.1. The acceptance gate
18: Verdict: Non-bypassability asserted, not demonstrated. The other three properties do not exist in canon and are specified fresh immediately below.
19: SEC-2  MOAC's acceptance criteria MUST be held in versioned, Rules-Service-governed configuration — the same discipline as SyniSense's custody policy — with integrity verified at load. No criterion is editable by the run it measures, by construction rather than by convention.  [Self-protection]
20: SEC-3  MOAC operates entirely within Targeta's boundary and reads only the run artefacts Targeta produces. It does not query Solva, Mtafiti, or any other engine to reach its decision.  [Domain separation]
21: SEC-4  MOAC MUST refuse to evaluate — not default-accept, not skip — if its criteria configuration is unset or fails integrity verification at load, on the same pattern as A17.9's execution-mode raise.  [Secure initialisation]
22: SEC-5  Every path by which a run's result could be treated as accepted MUST be enumerated and shown to pass through MOAC's evaluation, in a build-time test comparable to SyniSense's negative-scan gate.  [Non-bypassability, demonstrated not asserted]
23: 6   DAP-31 — The Artefact Egress Distance Gate
24: 6.1. The distance gate
25: Verdict: Three of four met by the amendment that created it. Secure initialisation is the one gap.
26: SEC-6  DAP-31's probe MUST refuse to run — and MUST refuse egress by default in that state — if the reproduction threshold, sample size, or probe design values are unset. Absence of configuration is a refusal condition, not a bypass.  [Secure initialisation]
27: 7   DAP-32 — Admission-Integrity Probe
28: 7.1. The mirage battery
29: Verdict: Three of four met, inherited directly from the mirage's own established properties. Secure initialisation is the gap, same shape as 6.1's.
30: SEC-7  DAP-32's battery MUST refuse to admit a model — default to refusal, not default to pass — if battery composition or deviation thresholds are unset.  [Secure initialisation]
31: SEC-4, SEC-6, and SEC-7 are the same rule applied three times: an unconfigured gate refuses. Worth ratifying once, as a platform-wide default under Attribute 11 (Failure Posture), rather than as three separate clauses that happen to say the same thing — flagged for the Failure Posture Enumeration (document 5 of this set) to absorb.
32: 8   QA-2 — The Format Gate
33: 8.1. Schema-completeness check
34: Verdict: Non-bypassability and domain separation reasonably inferred from its position in the loop; self-protection and initialisation are unspecified. Lowest priority to close — QA-2 gates form, not access or disclosure.
35: 9   Summary
36: Seven requirements (SEC-1 through SEC-7) close every proposed gap above except QA-2's self-protection and initialisation, left open as the lowest-consequence item on this list — named rather than silently dropped.
37: [TABLE 0]
38: Requirement answered | Common Criteria ADV_ARC.1: for every reference monitor, demonstrate non-bypassability, self-protection, domain separation, and secure initialisation — as a description, since these properties “largely have no directly observable interface” (the CC v2→v3.1 transition rationale, verified earlier this programme).
39: Scope | Every candidate reference monitor named in tcb_enumeration_v1: SyniSense's chokepoint, the Watch's Mkono, MOAC, the DAP-31 distance gate, the DAP-32 admission probe, and QA-2's format gate. Each treated separately — meeting the properties for one does not transfer to another.
40: Method | Each property is demonstrated by citation where canon text already establishes it, and specified fresh where it does not. Fresh specification is marked as such — this document does not claim as existing what it is proposing for the first time.
41: Date | 9 September 2026

45: Non-bypassability | Exactly one function may invoke the external model client; a negative-scan build test fails the build if any second path is introduced. Demonstrated at build time, on every build, not asserted once.
46: Self-protection | Custody-sequence logic and the closed-network allowlist are held in configuration outside the reach of any subject the crossing mediates. Runtime integrity verification of the loaded policy is not yet specified — the one property this monitor does not yet fully meet.
47: Domain separation | The chokepoint operates entirely within SyniSense's own boundary; it does not reach into Solva, Targeta, or Mtafiti to make its decision.

It reaches behind the verdict seam for nothing; there is no surface for a mediated party to tamper with beyond the seam itself.

76: # SHEET: Legend
77: Security Assurance Promise Set — Legend | 
78: Scope of this set | S-1–S-26 are entirely scoped to Document 3 (the Watch). They do not cover SyniSense's Document 1 domain — stated explicitly because of the finding immediately below.
79: “A5.7” — a citation warning, not an error | Positional IDs (rule_criteria_spec_v1 ROC-3) are document-scoped by design: Document 1 has its own A5.7 (the trust receipt — custody status, signature, organisation-binding) and Document 3 has a separate, unrelated A5.7 (non-conformance ceiling, S-15 in this set, “never convict on non-conformance”). Both are correct within their own document. Citing “A5.7” without naming the document is how the two get conflated — caught here on a direct re-check while updating this file, not before.
80: G-8 and G-9 — why neither has a row here | Document 0's G-8 (Governance Architecture) concerns Document 1's A5.7, the trust receipt — outside this set's scope. Its fix lives in Security_Promise_Set_Amendments.docx, Amendment 3, and in akki_governance_architecture_v1's own G-8 entry, not as an S-row. G-9 (system-rule change control) is a Rules Service / Attribute 9 matter, not a Watch conduct promise, and likewise has no natural S-row. Neither omission is an oversight; both are stated here so the absence reads as scoped, not missed.
81: Scope | Decomposes Promise #6 (Doc 3) into 21 assurance statements (S-1–S-21), plus S-22–S-25 added by the Security Amendments — Trojan Artefacts and Whisper Threats (5 Sep 2026). S-10, S-11 are sourced from Wave E rulings with no document home yet. Promises #7 and #26 are unchanged and cited, not reproduced.
82: Standard column | The clause each promise answers to. [V]/[K]/[P] confidence not marked per-cell here; treat citations as [K] (established knowledge, stable clause reference) unless a document says otherwise.
83: Bound / Ruling column | Structural = no numeric bound applies. Ruled = a specific value is set (cites the ruling). Baseline-period-deferred = Doc 3's own mechanism: conservative default until a defined observation period, then set by evidence. Unruled = a bound is named in A5 text with no value confirmed — a real gap, not a placeholder.
84: Status colours | Green = Present, built and grounded in canon text. Blue = Absent → new, a ruled value with no document promise yet. Amber = Absent → gap, no mechanism specified anywhere. Grey = By design, composite/umbrella row.
85: S-7 | The one promise in this set marked as a specification gap rather than asserted. Doc 3 constrains learning in three places (A5.7, A5.8, A5.12) and specifies a learning mechanism in none. See amendments document, Item 1.
86: Removed from this set | “Never run in shadow” (A5.4) — deployment doctrine, not runtime assurance. Relocated to Document 0, Attribute 9 build requirements. See amendments document, Item 3.

# SOURCE: assessment_workspace/canon/drops/20260909/extracted/text/Security_Function_Policies_v1.txt
Coordinate: source line

1: AKKI PLATFORM  ·  ENGINE SPECIFICATION  ·  4 OF 9
2: Named Security Function Policies
3: security_function_policies_v1 — Draft for owner ratification · Closes Document 0 G-7
4: 1   A Correction Before the Substance
5: G-7, as originally stated in akki_governance_architecture_v1, characterised “the evidence floor's lower-the-standard path” as subject-alterable — a party being measured able to weaken the bar it is held to — and R-2 offered two options to fix it. Re-checking the source text this document was supposed to fix shows that characterisation is wrong.
6: “Lower the standard” is Document 4 A5.5, Solva's refusal mechanism, verified verbatim: when a conclusion cannot be supported at the class an objective asked for, the platform refuses visibly and offers the person asking three actions — accept the result as recorded at the class it did achieve, narrow the objective, or lower the standard being asked for. This is a query-recalibration option for the party asking a question. It is not a mechanism by which a party under evaluation weakens the evaluation it is subject to.
7: The mechanism this was conflated with — the Watch's own binding of certainty to evidence — is A5.2 (Doc 3), verified verbatim: severance may be unlocked only by signals “an outsider cannot fabricate,” computed by “a function with no parameter through which a detector's confidence can enter,” explicitly built by transplanting “the same assertion-boundary discipline Solva uses.” A5.2 is not alterable by the party it measures. It is the opposite of the gap G-7 described.
8: R-2 is therefore closed with a different finding than either option it originally offered: no violation exists. What remains genuinely open — and is the actual substance of G-7 — is that no mandatory baseline in the system, A5.2 included, has ever been written as a named security function policy in the form Attribute 7 and FDP_ACC.1 require. That work was never blocked by the lower-the-standard question. It proceeds below.
9: Standing correction to R-2's entry in akki_governance_architecture_v1 §3 and to the Security Amendments' G-7 row: both should read “RESOLVED — no violation found on re-examination of Doc 4 A5.5 and Doc 3 A5.2” rather than carrying two unresolved options. Update 11 of this batch applies this correction to the governance architecture directly.
10: 2   Method
11: FDP_ACC.1's form, applied to every mandatory baseline found across the canon: the TSF enforces a named policy on a stated set of subjects, objects, and operations. Each entry below states that triple explicitly — the thing G-7 actually found missing — and cites the floor's own source text.
12: 3   The Policies
13: 4   What Was Deliberately Not Named as a Policy
14: Solva's “lower the standard” option (A5.5) is not listed above, on the finding in §1: it is not a policy constraining a subject, because nothing is being measured against it in the Attribute 7 sense. It remains exactly as specified in Document 4, unchanged by this document.
15: 5   Standing
16: These seven are the platform's complete set of mandatory baselines as currently identified. A future floor — any new “no X without Y” rule — is added here in the same form, with its own subject/object/operation triple, at the point it is ratified, rather than left implicit in whichever document first states it.
17: [TABLE 0]
18: ID | Name | Policy
19: SFP-1 | Assertion Floor | Subjects: any principal requesting a composed answer. Objects: the claim being composed. Operations: assert, compose, refuse. Rule: no sentence enters a composed answer without a per-sentence anchor to material; an unanchorable sentence is refused, not weakened (Doc 4 A2, A5.5).
20: SFP-2 | Certainty-to-Evidence Binding | Subjects: the Watch's response function (Mkono). Objects: severance authority. Operations: unlock, withhold. Rule: severance unlocks only from the closed six-signal registry; no confidence score, however high, is an eligible input (Doc 3 A5.2).
21: SFP-3 | Acceptance Floor | Subjects: any training run. Objects: model output. Operations: accept, refuse. Rule: every stated criterion satisfied or the run is refused in full; no partial acceptance (Promise #22, MOAC).
22: SFP-4 | Custody Floor | Subjects: any data crossing the chokepoint. Objects: the crossing itself. Operations: cross, de-identify, re-identify. Rule: no asset crosses without de-identification appropriate to its custody class (Promise #1, A5.1–A5.3).
23: SFP-5 | Non-Conformance Ceiling | Subjects: any actor whose behavioural signature drifts from its declared conduct. Objects: the actor's trust discount. Operations: reduce, revoke. Rule: loss of conformance alone returns an actor to baseline verification; it is never, by itself, grounds for conviction (Doc 3 A5.7).
24: SFP-6 | Release Budget | Subjects: all external parties, jointly and severally. Objects: the estate's total information release. Operations: release, refuse. Rule: total release across all parties, operations, and time is bounded; exceeding it is a floor violation, not a negotiable ceiling (DAP-35).
25: SFP-7 | Reproduction Ceiling | Subjects: any artefact or output leaving a component boundary. Objects: controlled-unit content. Operations: egress, refuse. Rule: no artefact or output passes carrying reproduction of a controlled unit above the ruled threshold (DAP-31, A5.15).
26: [/TABLE]

# SOURCE: assessment_workspace/canon/drops/20260909/extracted/text/TCB_Enumeration_v1.txt
Coordinate: source line

1: AKKI PLATFORM  ·  ENGINE SPECIFICATION  ·  1 OF 9
2: The Trusted Computing Base — Enumeration
3: tcb_enumeration_v1 — Draft for owner ratification · Closes Document 0 G-1
4: 1   The Test, Applied Literally
5: BA-1.1 sets a conjunction, not a list of examples: deterministic, and protection-critical. A component can be highly consequential and still fail the test if it is learned — CIF is the standing example, excluded under BR-9.1 regardless of how central its ideation is. A component can be perfectly deterministic and still fail the test if nothing depends on it — deterministic housekeeping code that no guarantee cites is not TCB by virtue of being predictable.
6: “Deterministic” is evaluated at the level of the mechanism actually making a decision, not the subsystem that hosts it. Several entries below split a subsystem in two for exactly this reason: the decision point inside it is deterministic even where the subsystem's broader function is not.
7: “Protection-critical” is evaluated by BA-1.1's own clause: would this component's failure falsify a stated guarantee. Each row below names the guarantee.
8: 2   The Enumeration
9: 3   Minimisation — What Was Kept Out, and Why That's Correct
10: TA-1.2 requires the TCB stay small by design, excluding a learned or non-critical component “even where it is operationally central.” Four exclusions above are worth stating plainly rather than leaving as table rows, because each is operationally central and excluded anyway: Solva's actual reasoning — the platform's most visible capability — is not TCB; CIF, the self-improving core of the training story, is not TCB; Grey Mirror, the detection half of the platform's own security layer, is not TCB; and the Deck Rendering Engine, despite being genuinely, verifiably deterministic, is excluded because determinism alone was never the bar.
11: This is the minimisation property working as intended, not a set of gaps. A small TCB is a stronger guarantee than a large one — it is what makes G-2's forthcoming architecture description and G-6's security architecture description tractable to write and to verify.
12: 4   What This Unblocks
13: Recommendation, not a ruling this document makes unilaterally: ratify this list as the TCB, formally closing R-3 as stated in §2. The Owner's sign-off is the ceremony act (RBM-8, once the Rules Service is built); this document is the evidence that ceremony would ratify.
14: [TABLE 0]
15: Applies BA-1.1 | “A component is in the TCB if and only if it is deterministic and its failure would falsify a guarantee this document or a document it governs makes.” Two conditions, both required. Neither alone qualifies.
16: Method | Every component named in akki_governance_architecture_v1 Part 2, plus every mechanism added since by dap_backend_spec_v1 and the Security Amendments, evaluated against both conditions separately. Where a component is internally mixed — part deterministic, part learned — it is split rather than given one verdict for the whole.
17: Resolves | Document 0 Ruling R-3 (the Watch's TCB membership) — not by new policy, but as the mechanical output of applying BA-1.1 consistently. Confirmed compatible with BR-9.1 (CIF) and BR-7.4 (Grey Mirror), both already on record.
18: Status | Draft v1. This list is itself TCB-tier content per BA-1.2 — its own future changes go through the Rules Service's system-TCB ceremony (RBM-8) once ratified.
19: Date | 9 September 2026
20: [/TABLE]
21: [TABLE 1]
22: Component / mechanism | Guarantee at risk if it fails | Deterministic? | Verdict | Reasoning
23: SyniSense — chokepoint (custody sequence) | No leakage of confidential information (#1) | Yes | IN | Sole invoking function, negative-scan build test. Deterministic and directly protection-critical — the platform's founding guarantee.
24: SyniSense — closed outbound network | No leakage; no path around the crossing | Yes | IN | Allowlist and static-analysis gate. Removing it doesn't change behaviour probabilistically — it removes the boundary.
25: Solva — assertion-boundary seam (import assertion) | Assertion floor (Doc 4) | Yes | IN | The enforcement mechanism is deterministic even though what it constrains — Solva's generated reasoning — is not. Split below.
26: Solva — reasoning / generation itself | — | No | OUT | Learned. Informs; the seam decides what may be asserted. Excluded by the same logic as CIF.
27: Northena — objective-freeze mechanism | No silent scope recalibration (#32) | Yes | IN | A shared, deterministic lock on a job's declared scope.
28: Mtafiti — registry write/query path | Estate composition is what it's recorded to be | Yes | IN | Storage and retrieval logic. Any AI-assisted classification suggestion feeding it is a separate, learned input — not itself TCB.
29: Targeta — yield wall / acceptance gate (MOAC) | No result accepted without every criterion (#22) | Yes | IN | Fixed criteria evaluated mechanically. No human, and no model, decides acceptance.
30: Targeta — the training process itself | — | Partial | OUT | Reproducible under a fixed seed, but not a decision point — nothing is admitted or refused by training running. The wall, not the run, is TCB.
31: Mkondo — hand-off registry | Clean hand-offs, no dropped context (#32) | Yes | IN (pending build) | Deterministic by design once built (BR-6.1). Included now so the enumeration doesn't need revisiting the day it ships.
32: The Watch — Mkono (response: annotate/shape/contain/sever) | Nothing is misused (#6/#7), acted on before a human wakes | Yes | IN | Executes signed policy against the certainty registry (A5.2). Resolves R-3: the response half qualifies on its own terms.

36: Critic Seam — RV-tier (deterministic record checks) | Evidence integrity (Doc 19A) | Yes | IN | Six mechanical verification checks against the record itself.
37: Critic Seam — QA-tier (model-based judgement) | — | No | OUT | QA-1's own rule: detect, never decide. Findings route to RV-tier or a human.
38: MOAC — acceptance-criteria evaluation | No result accepted without every criterion (#22) | Yes | IN | Same guarantee as Targeta's wall; MOAC is the mechanism that evaluates it.

45: Deck Rendering Engine — determinism contract (DR-R2) | — | Yes | OUT | Genuinely deterministic, verified by build test — but not protection-critical to governance. Nothing on this platform's security or access guarantees depends on deck rendering. Deterministic is necessary, not sufficient.
46: DAP — estate release budget (DAP-35) | No party or coalition exceeds the ruled total (Attribute 7 instance) | Yes | IN | Accumulator and threshold check. A floor violation under A5.2 — among the platform's least tunable mechanisms by design.
47: DAP — artefact egress distance gate (DAP-31) | No artefact carries controlled-unit content past a ruled threshold | Yes | IN | Under a fixed seed the probe is deterministic — stated explicitly in the amendment that introduced it.
48: DAP — output-content gate (A5.15) | No permitted output carries controlled content undetected | Yes | IN | Already specified as “a deterministic classifier held in the TCB” in the amendment itself. This entry confirms rather than newly decides it.
49: DAP — admission-integrity probe, canary check (DAP-32, A5.2 half) | No trojaned model touches estate data (T-2) | Yes | IN | Canary touch is on A5.2's closed registry — unfakeable by construction.
50: DAP — admission-integrity probe, trigger scan (DAP-32, capability-comparison half) | — | Mixed | SPLIT | Backdoor trigger-scanning commonly uses statistical methods in the literature this probe implements. Where it does, that half informs; the canary-touch half decides. Flagged for the build to confirm which technique is used.
51: [/TABLE]
52: [TABLE 2]
