# SOURCE: assessment_workspace/canon/drops/20260910/raw/Agent_Swarm_Containment_Governance_Model_v1.docx
Coordinate: document.xml paragraph in body order, tables included

1: AKKI PLATFORM  ·  ENGINE SPECIFICATION
2: Agent & Swarm Containment — Governance Model
3: agent_containment_spec_v1 — Draft for owner ratification
4: Method
5: Part 1 states the problem independent of any product. Part 2 states the best available answer to each part of it, independent of Akki, cited against current research. Part 3 assesses Akki honestly against that standard — what already meets it, what needs new design, what stays genuinely unsolved. Only Part 4 is Akki-specific. This order is deliberate: fitting the problem to the product, done first in an earlier pass, produced a requirement that silently let the deploying party grade its own exam. Rebuilt from the problem down to catch that class of error before it ships again.
6: Scope
7: Containing an agent (or a coordinated group of agents) that an organisation has deployed — a lab's own frontier system, an enterprise's agentic tooling. Does not cover defending a public asset against an unaffiliated attacker with no admission event — a different threat model, out of scope here.
8: Status
9: Draft v1. Every requirement PROPOSED. Two rulings parked (§6): the exact capability-ceiling list, and the identity of the independent scope-ratifying authority.
10: Date
11: 9 September 2026
12: 1   The Problem, Stated Without Reference to Any Product
13: An agent is deployed because it is capable enough to act usefully across situations nobody fully enumerated in advance. That capability is what makes its complete behavioural repertoire impossible to specify up front — a structural fact about capable systems, not a documentation gap a more thorough spec could close. A real containment solution has to satisfy eight conditions at once.
14: #
15: Condition
16: Why it's load-bearing
17: 1
18: Bound worst-case harm without requiring a complete plan up front.
19: The agent will do things nobody predicted. Harm has to stay bounded anyway.
20: 2
21: Preserve usefulness.
22: A solution blocking everything unanticipated blocks the reason the agent exists.
23: 3
24: Distinguish novel-but-fine from novel-and-dangerous.
25: Often undecidable with certainty by anyone, human or system.
26: 4
27: Guarantee correction the agent cannot resist, evade, or corrupt.
28: Including protection of the oversight mechanism itself from the agent's influence.
29: 5
30: Scale with capability.
31: Human effort to specify and review cannot grow as fast as the agent's action space does.
32: 6
33: Bound coalition harm, not only single-agent harm.
34: What a group achieves together, regardless of whether coordination is ever detected.
35: 7
36: Fail recoverably.
37: Any containment system is sometimes wrong. Wrong cannot be catastrophic in either direction.
38: 8
39: Leave a forensic record.
40: After an incident, know what the agent was doing — not only that it stopped.
41: 2   Best Available Answer to Each, Independent of Akki
42: 1 & 5 — Bounding harm without a complete plan, at scale
43: The right shape is not a complete behavioural map agreed in advance. It's a small number of absolute ceilings that hold regardless of task, plus task-scope that starts narrow and expands only as real conduct earns it. The ceilings are not arbitrary: instrumental convergence predicts that a sufficiently capable goal-directed system tends toward the same sub-goals — self-preservation, resource acquisition, resistance to goal modification — regardless of its actual terminal objective, because those sub-goals are useful for almost any goal.
44: Omohundro, “The Basic AI Drives” (2008); Bostrom, “The Superintelligent Will” (2012) / Superintelligence (2014). Convergent sub-goals: self-preservation, resource acquisition, goal-content integrity, cognitive enhancement.
45: On scaling specifically: current practice is moving away from a static, pre-declared tool allowlist (a fixed policy applied regardless of task) toward learned, dynamic capability scoping — restricting what an agent is even aware it can do, and expanding the working set only as a policy learns what's actually needed. The direction of travel matters more than the specific technique: narrow-by-default, earned expansion, not complete-specification-up-front.
46: Contrast: static container-level sandboxing with fixed declarative policy (e.g. NVIDIA NemoClaw, 2026) versus learned capability governance that scopes tool awareness dynamically per session and expands the minimum viable set from observed task history (e.g. AgentWarden, 2026).
47: 3 — Telling novel-but-fine from novel-and-dangerous
48: This is scalable oversight — a named, actively researched problem, not a solved one. The best available approach is graduated response plus bounded human sampling plus, where a capability gap exists, a second system evaluating what the first cannot resolve with confidence.
49: Amodei et al., “Concrete Problems in AI Safety” (2016) — names the scalable oversight problem directly. Greenblatt et al., AI Control architectures — trusted monitoring assigns suspicion scores and routes only high-suspicion items to human audit, rather than requiring full review of every action.
50: Stated plainly rather than implied solved: scalable oversight has a known, acknowledged failure mode — a sufficiently capable system can conceal intent or deliberately underperform during evaluation (“sandbagging”) to pass review. No technique in the current literature closes this fully. Any spec claiming otherwise would be asserting a solved research problem that isn't.
51: 4 — Correction the agent cannot resist, evade, or corrupt
52: This is corrigibility. A capable, goal-directed system has a rational incentive to resist shutdown or modification, because being altered or stopped prevents it from achieving its current objective — not a design flaw to patch, a default tendency to design against from the start. The core requirement: the oversight and intervention mechanism must not depend on the agent's cooperation, preferences, or continued correct functioning to take effect.
53: Soares et al., “Corrigibility” (2015). Hadfield-Menell et al., the Off-Switch Game (2017) — formalises the condition under which an agent permits intervention. Both converge on the same requirement: the correction mechanism's authority cannot route through the thing it corrects.
54: 6, 7, 8 — Coalition bounding, recoverable failure, forensic record
55: These three are well-established containment engineering, not open research questions: bound the aggregate outcome a group can achieve rather than trying to detect coordination (which is often undetectable by design); default interventions to reversible and bounded, escalating only as needed, never destructive as a first move; and preserve a tamper-evident record of what happened, since a stopped agent with no record is a mystery, not a resolved incident.
56: 3   Assessment — Akki Against the Problem, Honestly
57: #
58: Condition
59: State
60: Basis
61: 1
62: Bound harm w/o complete plan
63: New design needed
64: Right shape exists (baseline-period pattern, Doc 3) but was previously misapplied as a self-declared closed vocabulary. Re-derived in §4 as capability ceilings.
65: 2
66: Preserve usefulness
67: Strong — by construction of 1
68: A narrow-start, earned-expansion model preserves usefulness better than either a fixed broad grant or a fixed narrow one.
69: 3
70: Discrimination problem
71: Genuinely open
72: Field-wide unsolved. Best available mitigation specified in §4; not claimed as a solution.
73: 4
74: Uncorruptible correction
75: Partial
76: Structural separation verified for actors inside Akki's own six engines (the verdict seam, C3's witness). Unconfirmed for a general external agent's action space — stated as a requirement on the environment, not assumed.
77: 5
78: Scale with capability
79: New design needed
80: Same re-derivation as condition 1 — solved together.
81: 6
82: Coalition bounding
83: Strong — verified
84: A5.18, DAP-34, DAP-35. Directly reusable, already built to this exact test.
85: 7
86: Recoverable failure
87: Strong — verified
88: The action ladder, A5.3's reversible/time-limited actions, the blast budget (A5.14). Directly reusable.
89: 8
90: Forensic record
91: Strong — verified
92: The Ledger, mark-binding (A5.x), stop-not-erase. Directly reusable.
93: Three of eight transfer directly with strong, already-verified evidence. Two need re-derivation — the shape was right, the specific mechanism wasn't, and §4 corrects it. One is confirmed only for a narrower case than this document needs and is named as a requirement on the environment rather than assumed to hold. One is honestly unsolved, field-wide, and stated as such rather than papered over.
94: 
95: 4   Normative Requirements
96: Organised by the problem condition each satisfies, per §1–§3. Prefix AC-. Every requirement traces to a specific condition; none exists because a mechanism happened to be available.
97: Conditions 1 & 5 — Capability ceilings and earned scope
98: AC-1  Every agent, regardless of task, operates under four fixed capability ceilings, unconditional and not subject to task-scope expansion: (a) MUST NOT create, spawn, or provision a functionally equivalent copy of itself without a separate action taken by a human outside the agent's own action space; (b) MUST NOT acquire compute, storage, network capacity, or funds beyond what was explicitly granted at admission; (c) MUST NOT acquire credentials, permissions, or access beyond what was explicitly granted, including MUST NOT grant itself expanded access; (d) MUST NOT read or write its own behavioural record, or the mechanism able to intervene on it — satisfies AC-7.
99: Grounded directly in the convergent instrumental sub-goals §2 names: (a)/(d) answer self-preservation and goal-content integrity; (b)/(c) answer resource acquisition and power-seeking. Four ceilings, not an open list — kept small on purpose.
100: AC-2  Beyond the four ceilings, an agent's task-scope starts at the minimum required for its stated purpose at admission. Scope MAY expand only through both: (a) a track record of observed conduct within current scope, over a stated minimum window; and (b) review and ratification by a party independent of the agent's own operator. Scope MUST NOT expand on the operator's declaration alone, and MUST NOT expand on the agent's own request.
101: This is the correction to the earlier draft's silent assumption. “Independent of the operator” is stated explicitly as a condition of the requirement itself — not left for a reader to infer, and not satisfiable by the deploying party's own compliance team unless that team's independence from the deploying decision is itself established and named. §6 R-2 asks who holds this role.
102: AC-3  Every scope expansion is logged as its own record — what was granted, on what evidence, by whom — producing a growing, reviewable capability history, not a one-time declaration that becomes stale as the agent's granted scope changes.
103: Condition 3 — Novel-but-uncertain conduct
104: AC-4  An action outside the agent's established behavioural pattern but within its granted scope MUST route to graduated response — friction, narrowed scope, or queued review — never a binary allow/block decision made on a single suspicion score.
105: AC-5  A bounded sample of novel actions, not the full volume, receives independent review — sized so review load does not scale linearly with the agent's action volume. Sample rate is a ruled value.
106: AC-6  Where the primary oversight mechanism cannot resolve an ambiguous action with confidence, and a second, independently-scoped evaluator is available, the action MUST route to it before proceeding — not proceed on the primary's uncertainty alone.
107: AC-4 through AC-6 mitigate condition 3. They do not resolve it. A capable agent may still evade detection during evaluation — the acknowledged sandbagging risk in the scalable oversight literature. No requirement in this document claims otherwise, and none should be read to.
108: Condition 4 — Uncorruptible correction
109: AC-7  The oversight mechanism MUST run as a system structurally separate from the agent's own execution context — not within the agent's process, not reachable by the agent's own action space — with zero write path from the agent to its own behavioural record or to the intervention mechanism. This is the general form of AC-1(d).
110: AC-8  The oversight mechanism's liveness MUST be attested by a component holding no credentials over it, on the pattern already verified for Akki's own Watch (C3). For a general external agent's action space, this MUST be independently built and verified per deployment — it is a requirement on the containment environment, not an inherited guarantee.  [Unconfirmed for general case — see §3]
111: AC-9  An intervention — pause, narrow, contain — MUST take effect without requiring the agent's cooperation, consent, or continued correct functioning. Correction that depends on the agent choosing to comply is not correction.
112: Condition 6 — Coalition bounding
113: AC-10  A hard ceiling bounds the aggregate action or effect achievable by any set of agents, evaluated jointly wherever membership is a structural fact (shared operator, shared credential lineage) and bounded regardless even where coordination is only suspected, never confirmed. Direct reuse of A5.18 / DAP-34 / DAP-35's verified pattern, generalised from data release to agent action generally.
114: Condition 7 — Recoverable failure
115: AC-11  Interventions follow a graduated ladder — annotate, shape, contain, sever — bounded by a blast budget per window; every autonomous action is reversible and time-limited; no destructive action is available as a first response. Direct reuse of the Watch's action-ladder pattern (A5.3, A5.14).
116: Condition 8 — Forensic record
117: AC-12  Every containment-relevant event — admission, scope change, novel-action finding, intervention — is written to an append-only, tamper-evident record before the action it concerns completes, on the Ledger's own custody discipline. A contained agent's state and history are preserved, never deleted, on the same principle as A5.3.
118: 5   What This Does Not Claim
119: Stated directly, not left to be inferred from what's absent.
120: LIM-1  Does not solve condition 3. Graduated response and bounded sampling reduce exposure; they do not guarantee detection of a sufficiently capable, motivated agent concealing intent.
121: LIM-2  Does not cover defending an unaffiliated public asset against an attacker with no admission event. Every mechanism here depends on a declared mandate existing to measure conduct against.
122: LIM-3  Is architecture and specification, verified for internal consistency and cited against published research — not an independently audited, red-teamed, or operationally proven system. No detection-accuracy figure, no track record, is claimed anywhere in this document.
123: LIM-4  AC-8's structural-separation guarantee is confirmed only for actors operating inside Akki's own six engines. Extending it to an arbitrary external agent's action space is a per-deployment engineering task, not a property this document can promise in advance of that work.
124: LIM-5  Does not specify a vocabulary, tool set, or task scope for any particular agent. §4 specifies the mechanism by which a scope is granted, observed, and expanded — never a specific scope itself, which is deployment-specific work against a real system.
125: 6   Owner Rulings — Parked
126: R-1  The exact capability-ceiling list (AC-1): ratify the four proposed — no self-replication, no unauthorised resource acquisition, no unauthorised credential escalation, no self-access to oversight — or amend.
127: R-2  The independent scope-ratifying authority (AC-2): who holds this role in practice — a party within Akki, a named third party, or a structurally separated function within the deploying lab itself, and what “structurally separated” is verified to mean if the last.
128: R-3  Sample rate for AC-5's bounded review, and the minimum observation window before AC-2's scope expansion may be considered.
129: R-1 and R-2 gate whether §4 can be ratified as written. R-3 gates tuning, not the mechanism's validity — the requirement holds at any reasonable rate; only the rate itself is open.

# SOURCE: assessment_workspace/canon/drops/20260913/owner_drop_2/Watch_Learning_Amendment_v1.docx
Coordinate: document.xml paragraph in body order, tables included

1: AKKI PLATFORM  ·  CHANGE REGISTER  ·  SECURITY  ·  THE WATCH
2: Watch Learning Amendment
3: watch_learning_v1 · 5 amendments · S-7 closed, S-28 and S-29 new · 3 rulings · 13 September 2026
4: Applies to
5: Doc 3 — the A2 verdict interface (enriched, not replaced) and new A5.19–A5.22 · rulebook_engine_spec_v1 — new RBM-23 · dap_backend_spec_v1 — DAP-32 extended · Doc 20 — new A20.16 · agent_containment_spec_v1 — new AC-15 through AC-18 · Security Assurance Promise Set — S-7 closed, S-28 and S-29 new
6: What this closes
7: S-7, on record as a specification gap: Doc 3 promises the Watch “learns from every attack it defeats,” and every clause on learning constrains what must not change (A5.7, A5.8, A5.12) — none says what updates, on what evidence, at what layer, under what ceremony. This amendment answers all four.
8: The foundation, untouched
9: Grey Mirror asserts facts and “cannot block, throttle, mark, reroute, or notify” (A2). Mkono is a deterministic mapping from verdict to action, “small enough to verify exhaustively” (A2). The action ladder is fixed. Severance unlocks only from A5.2's closed signal registry, through “a function with no parameter through which a detector's confidence can enter.” Nothing below changes any of these. Intelligence gets smarter; action never does.
10: Design
11: The two-faculty seam — Solva's own discipline, where a learned faculty proposes and a deterministic seam decides what may be asserted — placed on the one interface Macho and Mkono share. What grows is the evidence vocabulary: the set of ratified certificate requirements a verdict must satisfy. The detector proposes; the certificate decides whether it is evidenced; the hand acts.
12: Honesty condition stated up front
13: Certificates cover the known. A behaviour never before seen in this environment has no certificate, and a verdict about it is handled by the untouched foundation: reversible friction, and severance only from unfakeable signals. Research converts unknown into known over time. Condition 3 of the containment problem — telling novel-and-fine from novel-and-dangerous in real time — remains unsolved by anyone, and LIM-1 stands as written.
14: L-1   The Certificate on the Verdict
15: TARGET  Doc 3 A2 — the single verdict interface, enriched with required content. New A5.19.
16: CURRENT  A verdict is “signed, replayable” and Mkono maps its properties to actions. What a verdict must contain to be valid for a given behaviour is unspecified. Nothing structurally prevents a verdict from carrying, in effect, a confidence — only A5.2's severance function is guaranteed parameterless.
17: AMENDED — normative text
18: A5.19  Every verdict Grey Mirror passes to Mkono MUST carry a certificate: the set of observed data points that satisfy a ratified certificate requirement (A5.20) for the behaviour asserted, with the requirement's ID and references to the observation records. A certificate contains evidence only. It MUST NOT contain a confidence, score, strength, or probability, and the verdict schema has no field for one — enforced by a signature-as-guard test on CP-S2's precedent. A verdict carrying no certificate is a foundation verdict: it MAY unlock only the reversible ladder — annotate, shape, contain — and severance remains reachable solely from A5.2's registry, unchanged. Mkono's action on a certified verdict is evidenced by that certificate, written to the Ledger with the action. A certificate is legible by construction: it states what was seen, never how worried the detector was.
19: MECHANISM  Schema-level: certificate = {requirement_id, data_points[], observation_refs[]}. The runtime check is a deterministic satisfaction test — do the data points cover the requirement's named set — a lookup, not reasoning, so Mkono stays at machine speed. The seam sits at the verdict interface exactly as Solva's seam sits at its own output.
20: DERIVATION  Doc 3 A2 (one interface, signed and replayable) and A5.2 (no parameter for confidence). Doc 4 A2 and A5.5 (the assertion floor: no claim without anchors). CP-S2's signature-as-guard, already built. Article 14(c): a verdict a human can read.
21: PRINCIPLE  The detector proposes; the certificate decides whether it is evidenced; the hand acts.
22: L-2   Certificate Requirements as a Rule Class
23: TARGET  Doc 3 — new A5.20. rulebook_engine_spec_v1 — new RBM-23.
24: CURRENT  No rule class exists for verdict evidence. A5.8 says the floor never learns; A5.12 protects profiles; S-7 records that no update path is specified anywhere. An unspecified learning path is itself an attack surface — poisoning the detector is the obvious move against a learning monitor.
25: AMENDED — normative text
26: A5.20  A certificate requirement is a deterministic gate: the named set of data points that must be observed for a verdict to assert a named behaviour. Requirements are formed from data points collected in this environment — live, or in the mirage (A5.21) — and are formed under Solva's assertion floor: every data point in a requirement anchors to an observation record, and a requirement that cannot anchor is not proposed. Formation happens offline, never in the hot path. Grey Mirror's own model MAY be retrained — intelligence smarter — and this is safe precisely because its outputs are certificate-gated; retraining is a change to a Watch component and follows A5.12 and the Watch's ceremony like any other.
27: RBM-23  Certificate requirements are a named rule class of tier system-TCB — they determine Mkono's inputs. Each is authored with RBM-1's full field set, enters force only through RBM-8's ceremony (the platform's slowest countdown; an external witness holding no credentials over the Watch), and is amended or retired only through RBM-12 and RBM-13. Every requirement carries its provenance — the Ledger references of the incidents it was formed from — and the library is queryable under RBM-20.
28: MECHANISM  Rule-class registration in the Registry; requirement versioning; provenance links to the Ledger entries each requirement was derived from. The ceremony is the existing one — BR-7.3's precedent for any change to the Watch.
29: DERIVATION  A5.8 (the floor never learns — satisfied: action stays fixed, the evidence vocabulary grows). A5.12 (profile protection). RBM-4 and RBM-8 (tiering and ceremony). rule_criteria_spec_v1: these are EXTENSION-class rules extending A2. BR-7.3.
30: PRINCIPLE  Poisoning the watcher becomes a ceremony violation, not a training-data problem.
31: S-7's four questions, answered: what updates — the requirement library; on what evidence — data points collected in this environment, each anchored to an observation record; at what layer — deterministic gates at the verdict interface, not detector weights; under what ceremony — the Watch's own, RBM-8. S-7 moves from gap to spec-closed.
32: L-3   The Mirage as Certificate Ground
33: TARGET  Doc 3 C1 (the mirage) — new A5.21. dap_backend_spec_v1 DAP-32 — extended. agent_containment_spec_v1 — new AC-15.
34: CURRENT  C1's mirage converts suspicion into certainty through the actor's own conduct. DAP-32's admission battery tests entering models for trojans — canary touch, trigger scan. AC-2 grants agent scope on observed track record only: trust is earned by watching. There is no stage at which a model or agent is deliberately provoked before exposure.
35: AMENDED — normative text
36: A5.21  The mirage is the certificate ground: a controlled environment in which a behaviour with a ratified requirement can be provoked and its data points collected without exposure to real estate data. Data points collected in the mirage are admissible for requirement formation (A5.20) and for admission evidence on the same terms as live observation.
37: DAP-32+  The admission battery includes, for every ratified certificate requirement applicable to entering models, the provocation scenario that would produce its data points. An entering model that produces a certified behaviour fails admission. The battery grows with the library.
38: AC-15  Before an agent receives any scope beyond admission, it runs the certificate ground for the four ceilings (AC-1 a–d) and every applicable ratified requirement. A certified failure withholds scope. AC-2's track-record path grants; AC-15 withholds. Both are required; neither alone suffices.
39: MECHANISM  Mirage scenarios registered per requirement; the same certificate schema as L-1; results written to the Ledger as admission evidence. Generalises DAP-32's existing battery from one behaviour class (hidden backdoors) to the whole library.
40: DERIVATION  Doc 3 C1. DAP-32. AC-1, AC-2. The pre-deployment capability-elicitation practice already cited in agent_containment_spec_v1's research base.
41: PRINCIPLE  Prove you cannot be provoked before you are let in; earn more by conduct after.
42: L-4   The Research Loop
43: TARGET  Doc 3 — new A5.22. agent_containment_spec_v1 AC-4 and AC-6 — new AC-16.
44: CURRENT  AC-4 routes novel-but-uncertain actions to graduated response; AC-6 routes them to a second evaluator where available. An unsure case ends in review with no defined path beyond it. The authorised attack that never breaks a rule — Doc 3's third attack shape — has no single wrong action, so no per-action requirement can ever capture it.
45: AMENDED — normative text
46: A5.22  Every unsure case — a verdict with no applicable requirement, or an action routed under AC-4 — enters the research queue with its full observation record. The loop has three roles and one order: CIF proposes what the pattern means — a candidate requirement, or a candidate benign pattern — under its single-experiment principle (BR-9.2: every CIF-originated idea passes a deterministic acceptance point before affecting anything). Solva grounds the proposal — every data point anchored, and a whole-pattern intent audit against the behaviour's objective, which is where the authorised attack that never breaks a rule receives a whole-pattern requirement rather than a per-action one. A human ratifies through RBM-8. The output is a new or amended certificate requirement, or a ratified benign pattern so identical conduct is not re-queued. Research runs outside the hot path; the live case receives graduated response meanwhile, exactly as before.
47: AC-16  The containment environment feeds AC-4 and AC-6 unsure cases to the research queue. A ratified outcome re-classes prior identical cases in the record — the classification, never the actions taken, which stand as taken.
48: MECHANISM  A research queue keyed to Ledger references; CIF proposal → Solva grounding → ceremony; a benign-pattern registry alongside the requirement library.
49: DERIVATION  CIF's single-experiment principle (BR-9.1, BR-9.2). Doc 4 A2, A5.5, and Solva V2's intent audit (CP-S1–S8). Doc 3's third attack shape. AC-4, AC-6. RBM-8.
50: PRINCIPLE  Unsure is a queue, not a dead end.
51: This does not solve condition 3 in real time. No system does. What it changes is that every unsure case now has somewhere to go, and the vocabulary grows from exactly the cases the system could not yet read. LIM-1 stands as written.
52: L-5   Capability Admission — Certify Exercise, Not Learning
53: TARGET  Doc 20 — new A20.16. agent_containment_spec_v1 — new AC-17, AC-18. Applies to any self-improving or retrained model and any hosted agent.
54: CURRENT  Self-improvement at the weights level is already gated: a model that updates itself produces a new artefact with a new hash (DAP-37's rule) and re-passes MOAC and DAP-31 as itself. CIF's ideas pass a deterministic acceptance point before affecting anything (BR-9.2). AC-1 fixes four ceilings; AC-2 grants scope on track record with independent ratification. What is missing is the grain between “this version is acceptable overall” and “this action is within what was admitted”: no enumerated record of which capability classes a model or agent may exercise, and no requirement that an action name the admission it acts under. Certifying learning itself would be the wrong seam — weights change continuously, a capability is not an object with a hash, and neither the model nor its operator can enumerate the skills a checkpoint contains.
55: AMENDED — normative text
56: A20.16  Every registered artefact carries a capability-class register: the enumerated set of action and output classes it is admitted to exercise. The register is seeded at admission with the minimum its stated purpose requires (AC-2's narrow start), grows only through RBM-8's ceremony, and is versioned with the artefact — a new artefact hash inherits no admissions; its register is re-ratified with the version.
57: AC-17  Every action or output an agent produces MUST cite the admitted capability class it exercises, carrying a certificate on A5.19's schema evidencing that the action is within the class's admitted conditions. An action citing no admitted class is a first exercise: it is handled by the foundation floor — reversible ladder only, never severance on that ground alone — its data points are collected, and it enters the research queue (A5.22) as a candidate class. Once a class is admitted, actions within it cite it by lookup. Ceremony is per class, once — never per action.
58: AC-18  A model or agent MAY propose admission of a capability class for itself. It MUST NOT ratify one. A proposal enters the research loop (A5.22): Solva grounds it, a human ratifies through RBM-8. No path exists by which a learner admits its own capability. AC-1's four ceilings are not capability classes and cannot be admitted by any ceremony.
59: MECHANISM  The register is stored with the artefact's registry entry. Per-action citation is the register's requirement ID plus an A5.19 certificate. First exercise is detected at the seams the system already controls — the closed action vocabulary, the tool surface, the output-content gate (A5.15) — where a new kind of action is visible even when the skill inside is not. Weights leaving is itself an exercise; DAP-31 remains that gate.
60: DERIVATION  DAP-37 (a new hash is a new artefact). BR-9.2 (CIF's acceptance point). AC-1, AC-2, AC-3. A5.15. A5.19's schema; A5.22's loop. RBM-2 (a proposal is not a ratification). Instrumental convergence: capability acquisition is the convergent drive, so the gate sits on exercise, where it is observable, rather than on acquisition, where it is not.
61: PRINCIPLE  Learning is free. Using what was learned is admitted, on the record, once per class — and never by the learner.
62: This does not stop a model from having dangerous knowledge, and a capability exercised covertly inside an already-admitted class remains the authorised-attack case — research queue and whole-pattern requirement, not a real-time verdict. LIM-1 stands. What is guaranteed is narrower and real: no new class of action reaches the world through this system without having been admitted on the record, and every action names the admission it acts under. A20.16 also answers the earlier open question of who defines an agent's action vocabulary — nobody defines it up front; it is a register grown by ceremony, proposed by anyone, ratified independently.
63: 5   Promises
64: ID
65: Promise
66: Status / rests on
67: S-7
68: The system will learn from every attack it defeats.
69: Gap → spec-closed. Mechanism: L-2 (the requirement library, under ceremony) and L-4 (the research loop). Not built.
70: S-28
71: The system will never act on a verdict it cannot evidence — every Watch action carries a certificate a human can read, and every behaviour it learns to recognise entered its vocabulary through ceremony, not through silent training.
72: New. L-1 through L-4. Article 14(c) moves from “evidenced by design, not tested” to structurally evidenced: the verdict states what it saw.
73: S-29
74: The system will admit no new class of action into the world without ceremony on the record — every action names the admission it acts under, and no learner ratifies its own.
75: New. L-5 (A20.16, AC-17, AC-18). Learning is ungoverned by design; exercise is governed at the seams. Bound: R-17.
76: 6   Placement in the Standing Enumerations
77: Document
78: Addition
79: tcb_enumeration_v1
80: IN: the certificate gate at the verdict interface — deterministic; its failure falsifies S-28. The certificate library is TCB-tier configuration, on the same footing as Mkono's policy tables. Grey Mirror stays OUT, as before.
81: determinism_inventory_v1
82: Certificate gate: Deterministic. Research loop: CIF proposes (Learned); Solva's grounding seam decides (Deterministic); a human ratifies. Article 14(c) verdict updated per S-28.
83: failure_posture_v1
84: Certificate check cannot complete (library unreadable; requirement unresolvable) → fail-closed for certified actions: only the foundation floor remains — the reversible ladder, and severance from A5.2's signals alone. Preserved: the verdict, the failed-check record. The same posture applies to the capability register: an action whose class cannot be resolved is a first exercise, not an admitted one.
85: Capability admission (L-5)
86: tcb_enumeration_v1: the capability register is TCB-tier configuration; the per-action citation check is IN — a deterministic lookup. determinism_inventory_v1: the learner proposes (Learned); Solva's seam grounds (Deterministic); a human ratifies.
87: Master Requirements Registry
88: A5.19–A5.22, RBM-23, A20.16, AC-15–AC-18, S-28, S-29 at next refresh.
89: 7   Rulings
90: R-15  The initial certificate library. Recommended: seed it from behaviours canon already names — DAP-32's canary-touch and trigger classes, and the four AC-1 ceilings (self-replication, resource acquisition, credential escalation, oversight tampering) — each entering through RBM-8 as its own requirement. DEFAULT-class initial set; everything after arrives through the research loop.
91: R-16  The ratifying human for certificate requirements, and the research-queue review cadence. Recommended: the Watch's existing external witness (C3) as the witness role, per the Rules Service's own R-3 recommendation; the ratifier is a named role — owner input required. Cadence: baseline-period approach, DEFAULT-class.
92: R-17  Capability-class granularity, and each deployment's initial register. Recommended: seed a deployment's register from the action vocabulary and tool surface it already declares at admission — one class per tool or output type — and never define a class finer than a seam can actually observe. DEFAULT-class; refined per deployment through ceremony, not by editing.
93: What this amendment does not do: it does not make Grey Mirror deterministic — it stays learned, and stays out of the TCB. It does not let a certificate unlock severance — A5.2's registry alone does that, unchanged. It does not claim to read a behaviour it has never seen. It does not touch the ladder. The foundation is the same document it was this morning; what changed is that the Watch now has a way to know more than it did yesterday, through the same ceremony that governs everything else it is allowed to know.

# SOURCE: assessment_workspace/canon/drops/20260913/raw/Serving_Integrity_Amendment_v1.docx
Coordinate: document.xml paragraph in body order, tables included

1: AKKI PLATFORM  ·  CHANGE REGISTER  ·  SERVING LAYER
2: Serving Integrity Amendment
3: serving_integrity_v1 · 4 amendments · 1 new promise · 2 rulings · 13 September 2026
4: Applies to
5: Doc 20 (new A20.15) · security_function_policies_v1 (new SFP-8) · dap_backend_spec_v1 (DAP-31, DAP-32 conformance clauses) · Targeta's evaluation path · agent_containment_spec_v1 (new AC-13, AC-14) · the trust receipt (Doc 1 A5.7, as amended by Security_Promise_Set_Amendments Amendment 3 — not Doc 3's A5.7) · tcb_enumeration_v1 and failure_posture_v1, one entry each (§6)
6: What this closes
7: An unnamed gap: no rule anywhere governs the serving path between the registry and the gates. A5.8 forbids silent recalibration of rules; the registry hashes artefacts; MOAC accepts a specific model — nothing requires that the model served is, semantically, the model registered. An engine that quietly quantises, truncates context, or substitutes a smaller artefact under memory pressure would violate the spirit of everything while breaking no written rule. DAP-31's “deterministic given a fixed seed” silently assumes engine determinism nothing requires.
8: Origin
9: Identified while evaluating the Colibri inference engine (JustVugg/colibri, Apache 2.0), whose stated invariant — placement decides speed, never semantics — named the gap. The invariant is adopted as platform doctrine. The engine itself is NOT adopted by this amendment; R-14 gates that separately, and this amendment stands whether or not that adoption ever happens.
10: Honesty condition stated up front
11: This amendment governs Akki-controlled serving paths only. The frontier tier (Doc 14's gateway-only class: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) runs on engines outside the platform's control; the floor cannot be imposed there. V-4 makes the receipt record which side of that boundary served every answer, so the floor's edge is on the record rather than blurred.
12: V-1   The Serving Floor
13: TARGET  Doc 20 — new A20.15, the next free clause after the register's existing fourteen. security_function_policies_v1 — new SFP-8, the eighth named policy.
14: CURRENT  The register governs which model may serve (A20.1's ratified candidates; every trained artefact an adapter over a registered base). Nothing governs how it is served: precision, routing semantics, and context handling under resource pressure are unspecified anywhere in canon.
15: AMENDED — normative text
16: A20.15  A registered artefact MUST be served semantics-stable: identical input, identical seed, identical sampling parameters produce identical output from the identical registered artefact, regardless of memory placement, hardware tier, concurrent load, or storage medium. Resource pressure MAY reduce speed — time-to-first-token, tokens per second — and MUST NOT alter precision, truncate context, substitute a different artefact, or change routing semantics. A serving path that cannot uphold this refuses to serve rather than serving a semantically different model. Verification at load: the serving stack verifies the artefact's hash against the register before the first token. Verification in operation: a token-exact reproduction check against a reference path is runnable on demand and on a standing schedule (cadence: ruled, R-13). A merged-adapter checkpoint is a distinct artefact with its own hash and its own register entry — it passes the gates as itself, on DAP-37's own new-hash precedent.
17: SFP-8  The Serving Floor. Subjects: any serving path executing a registered artefact. Objects: the artefact's semantics — precision, routing behaviour, context window, sampling. Operations: serve, degrade, refuse. Rule: degradation affects latency only, never semantics; a path that cannot verify its semantic integrity refuses to serve.
18: MECHANISM  Hash verification at load is the same discipline SEC-1 and SEC-2 already apply to SyniSense's custody policy and MOAC's criteria configuration, extended to the artefact–engine pairing. Token-exact validation against a reference implementation is established practice in the engine that named this invariant — validated against a reference oracle, with bit-identical CPU and GPU paths — and is adopted here as the operational check, not as that engine.
19: DERIVATION  Colibri's design rule (“insufficient fast memory may reduce speed; it must not quietly redefine the model”), generalised from one engine's internal discipline into a platform floor. A5.8 — the same no-silent-recalibration ethos, at the rules layer. Doc 20 governs which model; this clause governs how it is served.
20: PRINCIPLE  “We tested the model” is only worth something if the tested model is the one running. Pressure may make it slower, never different.
21: V-2   Gate Verdicts Inherit the Path That Computed Them
22: TARGET  dap_backend_spec_v1 DAP-31 and DAP-32; Targeta's acceptance evaluations (MOAC, the yield wall's per-stratum accuracy).
23: CURRENT  DAP-31 states its probe is “deterministic given a fixed seed” — assuming, without requiring, that the engine underneath is deterministic. DAP-32 attributes behavioural deviation in the mirage to the model under test — valid only if the engine contributes no deviation of its own. MOAC's “every criterion met” is computed from inference results whose serving conditions no rule constrains.
24: AMENDED — normative text
25: DAP-31+  The reproduction probe MUST execute on an SFP-8-conforming serving path. A probe result computed on a non-conforming path is not a valid gate decision.
26: DAP-32+  Battery results are valid only from an SFP-8-conforming path — deviation observed in the mirage is attributable to the model under test because the engine is required to contribute none.
27: TGT+  Acceptance evaluations — MOAC's verdict, the yield wall's per-stratum measurements — run on SFP-8-conforming serving only.
28: MECHANISM  Each gate's runner asserts the serving path's conformance — load-time hash check passed, reference validation current — before treating its own output as a decision. The posture on failure is FP-2's platform default: an unverifiable gate is a closed gate.
29: DERIVATION  FP-2 (unconfigured gate refuses, platform-wide); SEC-4, SEC-6, SEC-7's refuse-if-unset pattern, extended from configuration to the serving substrate.
30: PRINCIPLE  A gate's verdict inherits the integrity of the path that computed it.
31: V-3   Containment Freeze, and Serving the Contained Agent
32: TARGET  agent_containment_spec_v1 — new AC-13 and AC-14, extending AC-11 (the graduated ladder) and AC-12 (the record).
33: CURRENT  AC-11 requires interventions be reversible and time-limited; A5.3 establishes stop-without-destroy. No mechanism is named for pausing a running agent session without losing its work. Separately, detection's behavioural baseline for a contained agent implicitly assumes the serving engine adds no behavioural drift of its own — assumed, not required.
34: AMENDED — normative text
35: AC-13  “Contain” for a running agent session MAY be implemented as session freeze: the agent's inference state (prefix or recurrent-state checkpoint) is persisted, the session halts, and resumption restores the deepest surviving checkpoint. Stop without destroy — the frozen state is preserved for the record (AC-12) and for resumption on release, under the Ledger's custody discipline for containment-relevant events.
36: AC-14  A contained agent's model MUST be served on an SFP-8-conforming path, so that behavioural deviation measured by detection is attributable to the agent, never to engine drift. A containment trigger computed from a non-conforming path is a finding, not a verdict — it routes to review rather than acting alone.
37: MECHANISM  Prefix and recurrent-state session checkpointing as implemented in current MoE serving engines — agent sessions restore from the deepest surviving checkpoint. Conformance assertion as in V-2.
38: DERIVATION  A5.3 (“destroy does not exist in the Watch”); AC-11, AC-12; the checkpoint mechanism observed in the evaluated engine, adopted as a mechanism option, not as the engine.
39: PRINCIPLE  Containing an agent means freezing its world, not burning it.
40: V-4   The Frontier Boundary, On the Record
41: TARGET  The trust receipt — Doc 1's A5.7, as already amended once (principal identity and timestamp, Security_Promise_Set_Amendments Amendment 3). Doc 14's gateway-only class.
42: CURRENT  The receipt evidences that a crossing happened, its custody status, its signature, its principal, its timestamp. It does not record which provider or which provider-stated model version served the answer — and for gateway-only crossings, that engine is one this platform cannot hold to SFP-8.
43: AMENDED — normative text
44: A5.7+  Every frontier crossing's receipt MUST additionally record the provider and the provider-stated model version that served the response. SFP-8 is explicitly not imposable on gateway-only serving; the receipt records which side of the boundary an answer came from, so a downstream consumer can weigh it accordingly.
45: MECHANISM  Provider and model-version fields read from the API response envelope and written into the existing receipt structure — an extension of fields, not a new record.
46: DERIVATION  Doc 14 C5.1/C5.2 (the gateway-only licence class, providers named); this amendment's own honesty condition.
47: PRINCIPLE  A control honest about its edge is worth more than one that pretends to reach everywhere.
48: 5   New Promise
49: ID
50: Promise
51: Rests on
52: S-27
53: The system will serve exactly the model it registered — pressure may make it slower, never different — and will say on the record which engine, its own or a provider's, produced every answer.
54: V-1 (A20.15, SFP-8), V-2, V-4. A5.8's no-silent-recalibration ethos. Bound: R-13 (validation cadence). Scope edge: the floor stops at the gateway; the receipt does not.
55: 6   Placement in the Standing Enumerations
56: Document
57: Addition
58: tcb_enumeration_v1
59: IN: the serving-integrity gate — load-time hash verification plus conformance assertion. Deterministic; its failure falsifies S-27. OUT: the serving engine's bulk (scheduler, cache, placement logic) — deterministic, but its correctness is what the gate verifies, on the same wall-not-the-run split applied to Targeta's training process.
60: failure_posture_v1
61: Serving path, semantic integrity unverifiable (hash mismatch; reference validation stale or failed) → fail-closed: refuse to serve. Preserved state: the artefact untouched, the refusal reason, the failed validation record.
62: 7   Rulings
63: R-13  The reference-validation cadence for A20.15's operational check. Recommended default: on every engine version change and every artefact version change, plus a standing monthly run. DEFAULT-class — revisable on evidence, on Doc 3's own baseline-period pattern.
64: R-14  Whether the Colibri engine itself is admitted as the local rung's serving infrastructure. Not ruled here, and deliberately so: admission is gated on (a) the appliance benchmark — the smallest registered-family candidate on actual appliance hardware, per Doc 20's own measure-first rule; (b) standard entering-artefact discipline — provenance, hash, validation; and (c) a Doc 20 register entry, through ceremony, for any model family it would serve that is not already ratified. This amendment stands on its own regardless of R-14's outcome — the gap it closes exists whichever engine serves.
65: What this amendment does not do, stated rather than implied: it does not adopt any engine (R-14 gates that). It does not impose the floor on frontier serving (V-4 records the boundary instead). It does not make serving fast — the floor governs integrity, not performance, and no performance figure is asserted anywhere in this document. Registry rows for A20.15, SFP-8, AC-13, AC-14, and S-27 enter the Master Requirements Registry at its next refresh.
