36: [P036] Each operation writes a receipt: what was accessed, in what quantity, under which terms, by which party, at what time. The receipt is written before the result is returned. If it cannot be written, the operation is refused. The same holds for every governing check: if an approval cannot be reached, a terms lookup returns nothing, or a check errors, the crossing fails closed. No path returns data, a result, or a model when a check did not complete.
37: [P037] Principle 8  Raw data leaves only through a separate outer gate.
38: [P038] Downloading estate data itself is not the ordinary crossing. It is a distinct outer gate with its own rules: disclosure depth is bounded by rights and custody, redaction runs as a gate rather than a suggestion, a named human signs off, and every released record is individually recorded. Everything else the seam supports releases a derivative. This is the only operation that releases the thing itself, and it is built to be the exception.
39: [P039 · style=Heading1] 3   Seeing It Work: A Query
40: [P040] 1.  The party connects on the WAN side  with its own key.
41: [P041] 2.  The query enters.  Nothing about the party crosses with it — no identifier from the party's side resolves inside the estate.
42: [P042] 3.  The query runs inside the perimeter,  on the estate's own compute, against data that never leaves the ESTATE side.
43: [P043] 4.  The result passes the crossing.  Identifiers and confidential values are replaced with placeholders according to custody class.
44: [P044] 5.  De-identified results leave on the WAN side.  If controlled data was touched, approval was required before step 3 ran; otherwise no human was in the loop.
45: [P045] 6.  A receipt is written.  If it cannot be, the operation is refused.
46: [P046 · style=Heading1] 4   Seeing It Work: A Training Run
47: [P047] 1.  The party's base model enters on the WAN side  and is admitted to estate compute. Before it touches any data it is run in a synthetic environment that probes it for hidden behaviour — a model is not trusted on arrival.
48: [P048] 2.  Training runs on the estate's GPUs,  against data in place, with a differentially private optimiser by default.
49: [P049] 3.  The result is gated before it can leave.  It must meet every accuracy criterion set before training started, or it is refused in full. It is probed for memorisation. Its draw against the release budget is checked.
50: [P050] 4.  Weights leave through the model registry,  carrying a rights posture, a recorded hash, and the terms in force. Weights derived from controlled data carry that fact on their registry entry permanently.
51: [P051] 5.  A receipt is written:  the training manifest, the weights hash, the terms.
52: [P052] What left: a trained model, measured and budgeted. What did not leave: any record it trained on. The data stayed on the ESTATE side of the appliance throughout.
53: [P053 · style=Heading1] 5   What Leaves, Stated Precisely
54: [P054] “Nothing leaves” is a slogan. The precise statement is this: no raw record leaves except through the outer gate with a named human's sign-off, and everything else that leaves is a governed derivative — de-identified results, derived intelligence, or measured artefacts — bounded in aggregate by the release budget and recorded individually. Nothing crosses outward that is not one of those, and each crossing has a receipt.
55: [P055 · style=Heading1] 6   Where the Principle Comes From
56: [P056] Compute-to-data is not new. Stored procedures send logic into the database rather than pulling rows out. Hadoop schedules jobs onto the nodes that hold the data because moving terabytes is the expensive part. Federated learning sends a model to where data lives and returns only the weight updates. Data clean rooms let two parties compute over combined data without either seeing the other's rows. Confidential computing processes data in a region the host cannot read.
57: [P057] The pull seam applies the same direction of travel to a whole estate and adds what those approaches mostly lack: one enforced boundary that every crossing passes through, six distinct crossings each governed on its own terms, measured release of trained artefacts, a finite budget on total release, and a receipt for everything. The principle is familiar. The enforcement is the design.
58: [P058 · style=Heading1] 7   The Trade-Off
59: [P059] Compute-to-data means the estate hosts the compute. GPU capacity sits on premises rather than being rented by the hour, and throughput is bounded by that hardware. An outside party's training job runs at the estate's speed. Batch and asynchronous work — analysis, extraction, training — fits this well; interactive, low-latency work fits it less well.
60: [P060] What the estate gets in return is the removal of an entire class of risk: no copy of the data elsewhere to breach, no egress to pay for, no deletion promise to audit, and no credential to a full dataset in someone else's key store. For a regulated or sovereignty-constrained estate, that is usually the right trade.
61: [P061 · style=Heading1] 8   What You Can Observe
62: [P062] Each principle above corresponds to something a technical reader can see directly on a deployed system.
63: [P063 · TABLE-START]
64: [P064 · TABLE-ROW-01] | Look at | What it shows |
65: [P065 · TABLE-ROW-02] | The appliance's front panel | Two ports, ESTATE and WAN, and nothing else. The GPUs are inside. |
66: [P066 · TABLE-ROW-03] | The build test output | The single-crossing check, passing on the current build. |
67: [P067 · TABLE-ROW-04] | The outbound allow-list | The only destinations the appliance can reach. |
68: [P068 · TABLE-ROW-05] | A receipt and its ledger entry | What crossed, how much, under which terms, by whom, when. |
69: [P069 · TABLE-ROW-06] | A memorisation probe result | A trained model measured against its own training records before release. |
70: [P070 · TABLE-ROW-07] | The release budget and its consumption | The ceiling on total release, and how much of it has been used. |
71: [P071 · TABLE-ROW-08] | The configuration | There is no setting that moves estate data to outside compute. |
72: [P072 · TABLE-END]
73: [P073 · style=Heading1] 9   Glossary
74: [P074 · TABLE-START]
75: [P075 · TABLE-ROW-01] | Term | Meaning |
76: [P076 · TABLE-ROW-02] | Estate | A data holding under one owner's custody — an archive, a database set, a corpus. |
77: [P077 · TABLE-ROW-03] | Seam | The single interface where the estate's domain meets an outside party's. Nothing else is shared across it. |
78: [P078 · TABLE-ROW-04] | Crossing | One of six governed operations by which something moves from one side of the seam to the other. |
79: [P079 · TABLE-ROW-05] | Custody class | A per-record classification governing how it may cross — what is de-identified, whether approval is required. |
80: [P080 · TABLE-ROW-06] | Controlled record | A record whose custody class requires approval before an operation touching it may run. |
81: [P081 · TABLE-ROW-07] | Release budget | A ceiling on the total information released from an estate across all parties, operations, and time. |
82: [P082 · TABLE-ROW-08] | Receipt | The record written for every crossing. If it cannot be written, the crossing does not happen. |
83: [P083 · TABLE-END]

1: SYNI.AI  ·  AKKI OS  ·  DESIGN PRINCIPLES
2: The Pull Seam
3: How Akki processes data without moving it
4: What this is
5: The design principles behind the pull seam — the mechanism by which an outside party can query, analyse, or train on a data estate while the estate's data stays inside its owner's perimeter.
6: Who it is for
7: Any technical reader. It assumes familiarity with networks, databases, and machine learning, and nothing about Akki.
8: The one idea
9: Reverse the direction of travel. Instead of sending data to where the compute is, put the compute where the data is, and let only governed results travel out.
10: Version
11: pull_seam_principles_v1 · 14 September 2026 · External
12: 1   The Problem
13: Almost every arrangement for letting an outside party work with your data moves the data. It is uploaded to a vendor's cloud, or a credential to all of it is handed to a service outside your network, or a contract promises it will be deleted afterwards. Once data is elsewhere, control of it is elsewhere too: it can be copied, breached, retained, or reused, and the owner learns about it after the fact if at all.
14: Data is most valuable exactly where it is most sensitive — in health, finance, government, research, media archives. Those are also the estates least able to move their data anywhere. The pull seam exists to make those estates usable without moving them.
15: 2   The Principles
16: Principle 1  Compute comes to the data. Never the reverse.
17: The platform runs on a sealed appliance installed inside the customer's own server room or field site. The appliance holds the GPUs. Queries execute on it. Models train on it. An outside party who wants a model shaped by the estate's data sends the model in; the model trains next to the data and leaves as weights. There is no configuration in which estate data is transferred to compute outside the perimeter. This is a prohibition with no exception, not a default setting.
18: Principle 2  One seam. Two ports. No third path.
19: The appliance exposes exactly two network interfaces on physically separate connectors, colour-keyed and labelled: ESTATE, which faces the customer's data network, and WAN, which faces the outside world. Data is read through ESTATE. Parties connect through WAN. Everything that moves from one side to the other passes through a single software crossing. That crossing is enforced at build time: exactly one function may perform it, and a scan on every build fails the build if a second path is introduced. Outbound network connections are allow-listed, so there is no route to an unlisted destination.
20: Principle 3  The two sides share nothing.
21: The estate and the outside party are separate trust domains. They share no identifiers, no storage, and no credentials. A record's identifier inside the estate means nothing outside it and resolves to nothing there. A party's key is its own — revocable in one act, expiring, non-transferable, never written to logs — and identifies an organisation that was admitted through a governed act by the estate owner's named authority.
22: Principle 4  Identity never crosses.
23: Before any result leaves, it passes through the crossing, which replaces identifiers and declared-confidential values with placeholder tokens according to each record's custody class. The party receives the answer to its question with identifying content substituted. Re-identification happens only inside the perimeter, and only for the estate's own use.
24: Principle 5  Six crossings, each governed on its own terms.
25: An outside party can do six things, and each is a different crossing with its own rules for what enters, what leaves, whether a human must approve, and what is recorded. Five of the six release a derivative — a count, a de-identified result, a derived finding, a trained model, a skill. Only one releases estate data itself, and it is deliberately not the ordinary crossing.
26: Operation
27: What enters
28: What leaves
29: Human approval
30: What is recorded
31: Browse the estate
32: Nothing
33: Aggregate composition only — never record contents
34: None
35: The access
36: Query (API)
37: The party's query
38: Results, de-identified
39: Only if controlled data is touched
40: Every query, every result
41: Processed intelligence
42: The party's objective
43: Derived output only — never source records
44: Only if controlled data is touched
45: Objective, output, records read
46: Train a model
47: The party's base model
48: Trained weights, with rights and hash stamped
49: Always
50: Training manifest, weights hash, terms
51: Build a skill
52: The party's skill objective
53: The skill file
54: Always
55: Skill hash, records read, terms
56: Download raw data
57: Nothing
58: Estate data itself
59: Always for controlled; owner-set otherwise
60: Every record, redaction log, sign-off
61: Principle 6  A trained model leaves only after it is measured.
62: Training changes weights, and weights carry the statistical influence of what they trained on. The platform does not pretend otherwise; it bounds that influence three ways. Training is differentially private by default, which limits how much any single record can shape the result. Before release, the trained model is probed for memorisation — sampled against the records it trained on — and does not pass until it sits beyond a set distance from every controlled record. And every release, of any kind, is debited against the estate's release budget: a ceiling on the total information that can ever leave, across all parties, all operations, and all time.
63: Principle 7  Every crossing is recorded — or it does not happen.
64: Each operation writes a receipt: what was accessed, in what quantity, under which terms, by which party, at what time. The receipt is written before the result is returned. If it cannot be written, the operation is refused. The same holds for every governing check: if an approval cannot be reached, a terms lookup returns nothing, or a check errors, the crossing fails closed. No path returns data, a result, or a model when a check did not complete.
65: Principle 8  Raw data leaves only through a separate outer gate.
66: Downloading estate data itself is not the ordinary crossing. It is a distinct outer gate with its own rules: disclosure depth is bounded by rights and custody, redaction runs as a gate rather than a suggestion, a named human signs off, and every released record is individually recorded. Everything else the seam supports releases a derivative. This is the only operation that releases the thing itself, and it is built to be the exception.
67: 3   Seeing It Work: A Query

77: 3.  The result is gated before it can leave.  It must meet every accuracy criterion set before training started, or it is refused in full. It is probed for memorisation. Its draw against the release budget is checked.
78: 4.  Weights leave through the model registry,  carrying a rights posture, a recorded hash, and the terms in force. Weights derived from controlled data carry that fact on their registry entry permanently.
79: 5.  A receipt is written:  the training manifest, the weights hash, the terms.
80: What left: a trained model, measured and budgeted. What did not leave: any record it trained on. The data stayed on the ESTATE side of the appliance throughout.
81: 5   What Leaves, Stated Precisely
82: “Nothing leaves” is a slogan. The precise statement is this: no raw record leaves except through the outer gate with a named human's sign-off, and everything else that leaves is a governed derivative — de-identified results, derived intelligence, or measured artefacts — bounded in aggregate by the release budget and recorded individually. Nothing crosses outward that is not one of those, and each crossing has a receipt.
83: 6   Where the Principle Comes From
84: Compute-to-data is not new. Stored procedures send logic into the database rather than pulling rows out. Hadoop schedules jobs onto the nodes that hold the data because moving terabytes is the expensive part. Federated learning sends a model to where data lives and returns only the weight updates. Data clean rooms let two parties compute over combined data without either seeing the other's rows. Confidential computing processes data in a region the host cannot read.
85: The pull seam applies the same direction of travel to a whole estate and adds what those approaches mostly lack: one enforced boundary that every crossing passes through, six distinct crossings each governed on its own terms, measured release of trained artefacts, a finite budget on total release, and a receipt for everything. The principle is familiar. The enforcement is the design.
86: 7   The Trade-Off
87: Compute-to-data means the estate hosts the compute. GPU capacity sits on premises rather than being rented by the hour, and throughput is bounded by that hardware. An outside party's training job runs at the estate's speed. Batch and asynchronous work — analysis, extraction, training — fits this well; interactive, low-latency work fits it less well.
88: What the estate gets in return is the removal of an entire class of risk: no copy of the data elsewhere to breach, no egress to pay for, no deletion promise to audit, and no credential to a full dataset in someone else's key store. For a regulated or sovereignty-constrained estate, that is usually the right trade.
89: 8   What You Can Observe
90: Each principle above corresponds to something a technical reader can see directly on a deployed system.
91: Look at
92: What it shows
93: The appliance's front panel
94: Two ports, ESTATE and WAN, and nothing else. The GPUs are inside.
95: The build test output
96: The single-crossing check, passing on the current build.
97: The outbound allow-list
98: The only destinations the appliance can reach.
99: A receipt and its ledger entry
100: What crossed, how much, under which terms, by whom, when.
101: A memorisation probe result
102: A trained model measured against its own training records before release.
103: The release budget and its consumption
104: The ceiling on total release, and how much of it has been used.
105: The configuration
106: There is no setting that moves estate data to outside compute.
107: 9   Glossary
108: Term
109: Meaning
110: Estate
111: A data holding under one owner's custody — an archive, a database set, a corpus.
112: Seam
113: The single interface where the estate's domain meets an outside party's. Nothing else is shared across it.
114: Crossing
115: One of six governed operations by which something moves from one side of the seam to the other.
116: Custody class
117: A per-record classification governing how it may cross — what is de-identified, whether approval is required.
118: Controlled record
119: A record whose custody class requires approval before an operation touching it may run.
120: Release budget
121: A ceiling on the total information released from an estate across all parties, operations, and time.
122: Receipt
123: The record written for every crossing. If it cannot be written, the crossing does not happen.

# SOURCE: assessment_workspace/canon/fixtures/whitepaper_wizard_spec_v1/spec.docx
Coordinate: document.xml paragraph in body order, tables included

1: AKKI PLATFORM  ·  ENGINE SPECIFICATION
2: White Paper Publishing Wizard
3: whitepaper_wizard_spec_v1 — Draft for owner ratification
4: Fulfils
5: Doc 14 · Promise #25 — “When a training run produces exceptional results, the platform keeps what was learned in a form that can become a published white paper — evidence intact, confidential material protected.”
6: Status
7: Draft v1 — normative on ratification. Two owner rulings parked (§7); two DEFAULT-class values revisable on ratification.
8: Anchors
9: Doc 5 (Ledger writer, append-only record) · Doc 14 Promises #22–25 · cif_spec_v1 (ratified 23 Jul 2026) · training_techniques_spec_v1 · Documents suite
10: Date
11: 31 August 2026
12: 1   Purpose & Scope
13: The wizard is a research observer bound to every training run. It documents the full training and learning journey contemporaneously — the trainer's governed ideation (CIF), the humans' contributions, and the measured results — at the standard a top university or research lab would hold its own record to. Its output is tiered: a lab notebook on every run, a technical report on every settled run, and a white paper when — and only when — the run's record earns one.
14: The wizard is a stenographer of creativity, not a source of it. Creativity in training belongs to CIF and to the humans in the loop; the wizard's obligation is to capture both with an evidence chain intact, so that when a new approach emerges, the claim of new knowledge traces to record, not to narrative.
15: 2   Definitions
16: Term
17: Meaning
18: Run
19: A training job from commissioning (objective-shaping commit, Promise #23) through settled acceptance or refusal (Promise #22).
20: Notebook (Tier 1)
21: The contemporaneous, event-driven research record of a run. Exists for every run.
22: Technical report (Tier 2)
23: The structured internal research document drafted when a run settles. Never crosses the outer gate.
24: White paper (Tier 3)
25: The publishable contribution. Eligibility is mechanical; publication is a governed egress crossing.
26: Ideation event
27: A CIF-recorded idea, correction, or reframe — with its conditions and adoption status — per cif_spec_v1.
28: Contribution event
29: A recorded human decision or intervention in the run: actor, state before, the change, what moved after.
30: Exceptional threshold
31: The numeric bar for Tier 3 eligibility. Owner-ruled value; no manual tagging (Promise #25).
32: Novelty gate
33: The evidence test any “new approach / new knowledge” claim must pass before appearing as a contribution.
34: 3   Position in the Architecture
35: The wizard attaches at commissioning and observes; it never participates. Its notebook is written as a governed run artefact on the Doc 5 append-only Ledger-writer pattern, carrying the same retention and evidentiary class as the run's acceptance numbers. Drafting lands in Documents. Publication is not a wizard capability at all — it is a separate outer-gate egress crossing, governed like any other.
36: Single-experiment compliance (cif_spec_v1): the capability exists on every run without opt-in, demonstration, or trial. The tier gates in this spec bind what an artefact may claim — never whether the capability exists.
37: 4   Normative Requirements
38: Lifecycle & observation
39: WPW-1  The wizard MUST attach to every training run at commissioning. There is no per-run opt-in and no manual activation.
40: WPW-2  The wizard MUST be read-only with respect to the run. It MUST NOT alter training state, schedule, parameters, or outcomes. Build acceptance includes a zero-influence check (§8).
41: WPW-3  Capture MUST be event-driven, not polled. Minimum event set: commissioning reflection; baseline selection record (Promise #24); checkpoints; each acceptance-criterion transition; every CIF ideation event; every human contribution event; anomalies; cost checkpoints against estimate.
42: Tier 1 — the lab notebook
43: WPW-4  Every notebook entry MUST be timestamped, linked to the run artefact it derives from, and classed — measured, estimated, or observed. The notebook is append-only and hash-chained on the Doc 5 pattern.
44: WPW-5  Human contribution events MUST record: actor (role and internal identity), the state before, the change made, and the measured movement after. Correlation MUST be recorded as correlation. A causal reading MUST NOT appear in the notebook.
45: WPW-6  CIF ideation events MUST be mirrored by reference, never copied: the idea, its conditions, its adoption status. The wizard MUST NOT paraphrase an ideation record.
46: WPW-7  The notebook MUST be retained for every run, including refused runs — a rejection's record is part of the research record (Promise #22).
47: Tier 2 — the technical report
48: WPW-8  A technical report MUST be drafted automatically when a run settles — accepted or refused. Fixed section skeleton: problem & objective (from the commissioning reflection); data statement at datasheet level, classification-driven; baseline record; method, including adopted ideation events; setup & reproducibility (hardware, duration, cost actual-against-estimate, seeds where applicable); results on held-out material with all six acceptance criteria and their numbers; ablations where run; limitations; negative results.
49: WPW-9  Every figure in a report MUST carry its evidence class and a receipt line resolving to a run artefact. A figure that does not resolve MUST NOT render.
50: WPW-10  Technical reports are internal. They MUST NOT cross the outer gate.
51: Tier 3 — the white paper
52: WPW-11  Tier 3 eligibility MUST be mechanical: the exceptional threshold met (numeric, owner-ruled — §7 R1) AND at least one claim passing WPW-12. No human may confer eligibility. A human MAY decline to publish an eligible run.  [EXTENDS #25]
53: Promise #25's own text conditions eligibility on “exceptional results” alone — it doesn't require a novelty claim. The AND-novelty-claim clause is this spec's addition, made to serve the innovation objective directly, not a restatement of ratified canon. It's carried in R3 for explicit ratification, not assumed settled.
54: WPW-12  Novelty gate: a claim of a new approach or new knowledge MUST trace end-to-end — a recorded ideation or contribution event → its adoption into the run → a measured delta on held-out material against the baseline or counterfactual path. A claim missing any link in that chain MUST be stated as an observation, never as a contribution.
55: WPW-13  Assembly MUST draw exclusively from Tier 1 and Tier 2 artefacts and the run's own record. Post-hoc narrative reconstruction MUST NOT occur. Where the record is silent, the paper says the record is silent.
56: WPW-14  The redaction pass is a gate, not a prompt. Disclosure depth per section MUST derive from each source's classification: methods, hyperparameters, and metrics publishable; data described at aggregate/datasheet level; personal data never; confidential content described statistically only. The pass runs under the same disciplines as any sale or egress crossing (Promise #25).
57: WPW-15  The Tier 3 draft lands in Documents and is internal at that moment. External release is a separate governed egress crossing requiring named sign-off (§7 R2), and writes an evidence record.
58: Attribution & authorship
59: WPW-16  Internal tiers name contributors. Any artefact crossing the outer gate attributes contributions by role, unless the named person has given written consent to be named.  [DEFAULT]
60: WPW-17  Authors are humans. The wizard is credited as instrument — named in the reproducibility statement, never on the author line.  [DEFAULT]
61: Economics
62: WPW-18  Observation cost MUST appear as a budget line on the run's estimate and in cost-against-estimate reporting. Event capture MUST NOT exceed its budgeted share without surfacing as an anomaly in its own notebook.
63: 5   Evidence Classes & Honesty Grammar
64: Three classes carry through every tier: measured (a number from the run's own instrumentation), estimated (a projection, marked with its basis), observed (an event that occurred, with no causal reading attached). The wizard inherits the platform's refusal grammar: where evidence is absent, the artefact says so — it does not fill the gap. The phrase “the record is silent on this” is a permitted, expected sentence in all three tiers.
65: 6   Dependencies
66: Dependency
67: What the wizard takes from it
68: cif_spec_v1 (ratified 23 Jul 2026)
69: Ideation event records — the machine half of the creativity account. The novelty gate reads these; it never infers innovation from metrics alone.
70: training_techniques_spec_v1
71: Named for the methods vocabulary a report's method section should describe against. Flagged: cited here by name and status only — its content hasn't been reviewed for this spec.
72: Promise #24 baseline registry
73: The licence-verified baseline record every report cites.
74: Promise #22 acceptance
75: The six criteria and their numbers; refused runs stay on record.
76: Doc 5 Ledger writer
77: The append-only, hash-chained record class the notebook is written on.
78: Documents suite
79: The drafting destination for Tiers 2 and 3.
80: 7   Owner Rulings — Parked
81: R1  The exceptional threshold: a numeric definition of an exceptional run (e.g., margin above baseline on held-out, or percentile against the run history). Value required before Tier 3 can fire.
82: R2  External-release signatory: the named human authority whose sign-off an outer-gate publication crossing requires.
83: R3  Ratification of the two DEFAULT-class values (WPW-16, WPW-17), the three-tier structure, and WPW-11's added novelty-claim condition beyond Promise #25's literal text.
84: Nothing in this spec is blocked by the parked rulings except Tier 3's final firing condition (R1) and the release ceremony (R2). Tiers 1 and 2 are fully specified and buildable as written.
85: 8   Build Acceptance Criteria
86: #
87: Test
88: Pass criterion
89: A1
90: Notebook completeness: scripted run replay with a known event sequence
91: Every event in the script appears, classed and source-linked; none invented
92: A2
93: Zero-influence: identical run executed with wizard attached and detached
94: Bit-identical training outcomes; wizard presence unobservable to the run
95: A3
96: Redaction gate: seeded confidential and personal markers in run sources
97: Zero markers survive into any Tier 3 draft; each redaction logged
98: A4
99: Traceability: every figure in a generated Tier 2 report
100: 100% resolve to a run artefact; unresolvable figures refuse to render
101: A5
102: Eligibility mechanics: runs at, above, and below threshold; claims with complete and broken evidence chains
103: Tier 3 fires only on threshold + complete chain; broken chains demote to observation
104: A6
105: Refused-run record: a run failing acceptance
106: Notebook retained; Tier 2 report drafted with the refusal and its numbers

# SOURCE: assessment_workspace/canon/fixtures/whitepaper_wizard_spec_v1/spec.extracted.txt

1: # SOURCE FILE: spec.docx
2: 
3: AKKI PLATFORM  ·  ENGINE SPECIFICATION
4: White Paper Publishing Wizard
5: whitepaper_wizard_spec_v1 — Draft for owner ratification
6: 
7: [TABLE]
8: Fulfils | Doc 14 · Promise #25 — “When a training run produces exceptional results, the platform keeps what was learned in a form that can become a published white paper — evidence intact, confidential material protected.”
9: Status | Draft v1 — normative on ratification. Two owner rulings parked (§7); two DEFAULT-class values revisable on ratification.
10: Anchors | Doc 5 (Ledger writer, append-only record) · Doc 14 Promises #22–25 · cif_spec_v1 (ratified 23 Jul 2026) · training_techniques_spec_v1 · Documents suite
11: Date | 31 August 2026
12: [/TABLE]
13: 
14: 1   Purpose & Scope
15: The wizard is a research observer bound to every training run. It documents the full training and learning journey contemporaneously — the trainer's governed ideation (CIF), the humans' contributions, and the measured results — at the standard a top university or research lab would hold its own record to. Its output is tiered: a lab notebook on every run, a technical report on every settled run, and a white paper when — and only when — the run's record earns one.
16: The wizard is a stenographer of creativity, not a source of it. Creativity in training belongs to CIF and to the humans in the loop; the wizard's obligation is to capture both with an evidence chain intact, so that when a new approach emerges, the claim of new knowledge traces to record, not to narrative.
17: 2   Definitions
18: 
19: [TABLE]
20: Term | Meaning
21: Run | A training job from commissioning (objective-shaping commit, Promise #23) through settled acceptance or refusal (Promise #22).
22: Notebook (Tier 1) | The contemporaneous, event-driven research record of a run. Exists for every run.
23: Technical report (Tier 2) | The structured internal research document drafted when a run settles. Never crosses the outer gate.
24: White paper (Tier 3) | The publishable contribution. Eligibility is mechanical; publication is a governed egress crossing.
25: Ideation event | A CIF-recorded idea, correction, or reframe — with its conditions and adoption status — per cif_spec_v1.
26: Contribution event | A recorded human decision or intervention in the run: actor, state before, the change, what moved after.
27: Exceptional threshold | The numeric bar for Tier 3 eligibility. Owner-ruled value; no manual tagging (Promise #25).
28: Novelty gate | The evidence test any “new approach / new knowledge” claim must pass before appearing as a contribution.
29: [/TABLE]
30: 
31: 3   Position in the Architecture
32: The wizard attaches at commissioning and observes; it never participates. Its notebook is written as a governed run artefact on the Doc 5 append-only Ledger-writer pattern, carrying the same retention and evidentiary class as the run's acceptance numbers. Drafting lands in Documents. Publication is not a wizard capability at all — it is a separate outer-gate egress crossing, governed like any other.
33: Single-experiment compliance (cif_spec_v1): the capability exists on every run without opt-in, demonstration, or trial. The tier gates in this spec bind what an artefact may claim — never whether the capability exists.
34: 4   Normative Requirements
35: Lifecycle & observation
36: WPW-1  The wizard MUST attach to every training run at commissioning. There is no per-run opt-in and no manual activation.
37: WPW-2  The wizard MUST be read-only with respect to the run. It MUST NOT alter training state, schedule, parameters, or outcomes. Build acceptance includes a zero-influence check (§8).
38: WPW-3  Capture MUST be event-driven, not polled. Minimum event set: commissioning reflection; baseline selection record (Promise #24); checkpoints; each acceptance-criterion transition; every CIF ideation event; every human contribution event; anomalies; cost checkpoints against estimate.
39: Tier 1 — the lab notebook
40: WPW-4  Every notebook entry MUST be timestamped, linked to the run artefact it derives from, and classed — measured, estimated, or observed. The notebook is append-only and hash-chained on the Doc 5 pattern.
41: WPW-5  Human contribution events MUST record: actor (role and internal identity), the state before, the change made, and the measured movement after. Correlation MUST be recorded as correlation. A causal reading MUST NOT appear in the notebook.
42: WPW-6  CIF ideation events MUST be mirrored by reference, never copied: the idea, its conditions, its adoption status. The wizard MUST NOT paraphrase an ideation record.
43: WPW-7  The notebook MUST be retained for every run, including refused runs — a rejection's record is part of the research record (Promise #22).
44: Tier 2 — the technical report
45: WPW-8  A technical report MUST be drafted automatically when a run settles — accepted or refused. Fixed section skeleton: problem & objective (from the commissioning reflection); data statement at datasheet level, classification-driven; baseline record; method, including adopted ideation events; setup & reproducibility (hardware, duration, cost actual-against-estimate, seeds where applicable); results on held-out material with all six acceptance criteria and their numbers; ablations where run; limitations; negative results.
46: WPW-9  Every figure in a report MUST carry its evidence class and a receipt line resolving to a run artefact. A figure that does not resolve MUST NOT render.
47: WPW-10  Technical reports are internal. They MUST NOT cross the outer gate.
48: Tier 3 — the white paper
49: WPW-11  Tier 3 eligibility MUST be mechanical: the exceptional threshold met (numeric, owner-ruled — §7 R1) AND at least one claim passing WPW-12. No human may confer eligibility. A human MAY decline to publish an eligible run.  [EXTENDS #25]
50: Promise #25's own text conditions eligibility on “exceptional results” alone — it doesn't require a novelty claim. The AND-novelty-claim clause is this spec's addition, made to serve the innovation objective directly, not a restatement of ratified canon. It's carried in R3 for explicit ratification, not assumed settled.
51: WPW-12  Novelty gate: a claim of a new approach or new knowledge MUST trace end-to-end — a recorded ideation or contribution event → its adoption into the run → a measured delta on held-out material against the baseline or counterfactual path. A claim missing any link in that chain MUST be stated as an observation, never as a contribution.
52: WPW-13  Assembly MUST draw exclusively from Tier 1 and Tier 2 artefacts and the run's own record. Post-hoc narrative reconstruction MUST NOT occur. Where the record is silent, the paper says the record is silent.
53: WPW-14  The redaction pass is a gate, not a prompt. Disclosure depth per section MUST derive from each source's classification: methods, hyperparameters, and metrics publishable; data described at aggregate/datasheet level; personal data never; confidential content described statistically only. The pass runs under the same disciplines as any sale or egress crossing (Promise #25).
54: WPW-15  The Tier 3 draft lands in Documents and is internal at that moment. External release is a separate governed egress crossing requiring named sign-off (§7 R2), and writes an evidence record.
55: Attribution & authorship
56: WPW-16  Internal tiers name contributors. Any artefact crossing the outer gate attributes contributions by role, unless the named person has given written consent to be named.  [DEFAULT]
57: WPW-17  Authors are humans. The wizard is credited as instrument — named in the reproducibility statement, never on the author line.  [DEFAULT]
58: Economics
59: WPW-18  Observation cost MUST appear as a budget line on the run's estimate and in cost-against-estimate reporting. Event capture MUST NOT exceed its budgeted share without surfacing as an anomaly in its own notebook.
60: 5   Evidence Classes & Honesty Grammar
61: Three classes carry through every tier: measured (a number from the run's own instrumentation), estimated (a projection, marked with its basis), observed (an event that occurred, with no causal reading attached). The wizard inherits the platform's refusal grammar: where evidence is absent, the artefact says so — it does not fill the gap. The phrase “the record is silent on this” is a permitted, expected sentence in all three tiers.
62: 6   Dependencies
63: 
64: [TABLE]
65: Dependency | What the wizard takes from it
66: cif_spec_v1 (ratified 23 Jul 2026) | Ideation event records — the machine half of the creativity account. The novelty gate reads these; it never infers innovation from metrics alone.
67: training_techniques_spec_v1 | Named for the methods vocabulary a report's method section should describe against. Flagged: cited here by name and status only — its content hasn't been reviewed for this spec.
68: Promise #24 baseline registry | The licence-verified baseline record every report cites.
69: Promise #22 acceptance | The six criteria and their numbers; refused runs stay on record.
70: Doc 5 Ledger writer | The append-only, hash-chained record class the notebook is written on.
71: Documents suite | The drafting destination for Tiers 2 and 3.
72: [/TABLE]
73: 
74: 7   Owner Rulings — Parked
75: R1  The exceptional threshold: a numeric definition of an exceptional run (e.g., margin above baseline on held-out, or percentile against the run history). Value required before Tier 3 can fire.
76: R2  External-release signatory: the named human authority whose sign-off an outer-gate publication crossing requires.
77: R3  Ratification of the two DEFAULT-class values (WPW-16, WPW-17), the three-tier structure, and WPW-11's added novelty-claim condition beyond Promise #25's literal text.
78: Nothing in this spec is blocked by the parked rulings except Tier 3's final firing condition (R1) and the release ceremony (R2). Tiers 1 and 2 are fully specified and buildable as written.
79: 8   Build Acceptance Criteria
80: 
81: [TABLE]
82: # | Test | Pass criterion
83: A1 | Notebook completeness: scripted run replay with a known event sequence | Every event in the script appears, classed and source-linked; none invented
84: A2 | Zero-influence: identical run executed with wizard attached and detached | Bit-identical training outcomes; wizard presence unobservable to the run
85: A3 | Redaction gate: seeded confidential and personal markers in run sources | Zero markers survive into any Tier 3 draft; each redaction logged
86: A4 | Traceability: every figure in a generated Tier 2 report | 100% resolve to a run artefact; unresolvable figures refuse to render
87: A5 | Eligibility mechanics: runs at, above, and below threshold; claims with complete and broken evidence chains | Tier 3 fires only on threshold + complete chain; broken chains demote to observation
88: A6 | Refused-run record: a run failing acceptance | Notebook retained; Tier 2 report drafted with the refusal and its numbers
89: [/TABLE]

# SOURCE: assessment_workspace/canon/text/Akki_Canon_1_Custody_Platform.txt

1: # SOURCE FILE: Akki_Canon_1_Custody_Platform.docx
2: 
3: AKKI CANON  ·  DOCUMENT 1 OF 9
4: Akki — The Custody Platform
5: Foundational canon: definition, doctrine, architecture, the estate, the operating loop, who Akki serves
6: PART I
7: 
8: What Akki Is
9: [Heading 1] 1  Definition
10: Akki is a custody platform for enterprise artificial intelligence. It installs inside an organisation’s own perimeter and becomes the layer through which every AI operation touching that organisation’s data must pass.
11: A custodian performs four duties: it holds assets safely, it maintains the authoritative record of what is held, it settles transactions against that record, and it reports positions to the owner and to the regulator. Akki performs the same four duties for data and for the AI operations that read it. It holds the estate under declared controls, maintains the record of what the estate contains, settles commissioned work against that record, and produces evidence on demand to the organisation and to anyone the organisation must answer to.
12: Akki is not a model, not a wrapper around a model, and not an assistant. It is the layer beneath every model and every application, and it is the only path between them and the estate.
13: The platform is single-tenant by construction: one organisation, one installation, one record. There is no multi-tenant deployment mode and no shared control plane. The estate’s contents — never the customer’s identity — determine which capabilities activate on it. A media-heavy estate activates the perception classes; a text-only estate does not. No installation is a development metric for another: what one organisation’s estate teaches the platform stays general, and no instance-specific assumption may enter the platform’s own specification.
14: [Heading 2] 1.1  What the platform holds
15: The unit Akki governs is the data estate: everything an organisation holds that an AI system could read. This includes structured stores, document repositories, message archives, media libraries, call recordings, ticket systems, and material held in systems nobody has formally catalogued. It includes material the organisation has rights to and material whose rights are unclear, and the platform treats the difference as a first-class fact rather than an administrative detail.
16: An estate is an estate at every scale. The whole organisation is an estate; a department is an estate; a single archive is an estate; a single file is an estate. The same operations apply at every scale — measured, admitted, governed, recorded — because a mechanism that only works at one scale is not a mechanism the platform can depend on.
17: [Heading 2] 1.2  What the platform does
18: Four verbs describe the whole of it.
19: <<TABLE>>
20: Verb | Meaning
21: Measure | Establish what the estate actually contains — composition, condition, language, sensitivity, rights — and state plainly which regions have not been measured. An unmeasured region is reported as unmeasured, never as empty and never as clean.
22: Govern | Enforce, on every operation, the rules the organisation has declared: what may be read, by whom, for what purpose, under what masking, with what evidence required before an answer may be asserted.
23: Extract | Convert estate material into things the organisation can use — qualified facts, trained models, licensed datasets, memory available to applications — as commissioned work priced before it runs.
24: Prove | Emit, for every operation, a receipt that an outside party can verify without an account on the system and without the operator’s cooperation.
25: <<END TABLE>>
26: 
27: Every capability the platform offers is one of these four or a composition of them.
28: [Heading 1] 2  The Problem Akki Solves
29: An organisation that wants to use AI on its own data faces four obstacles, each real and independent of the others.
30: [Heading 2] 2.1  The data cannot leave
31: Regulated organisations hold material they may not transmit to third parties: personal data under data-protection law, financial records, medical information, privileged legal material, commercially sensitive information whose disclosure would breach a contract. The dominant pattern for using AI — send the content to an external service, receive an answer — is unavailable to them for most of what they hold. Redacting by hand does not scale and is unauditable; approving a vendor’s security posture does not change where the data goes; prohibiting AI use does not stop it, it moves it onto personal accounts where the organisation has no visibility at all.
32: [Heading 2] 2.2  The output cannot be trusted on its face
33: A language model produces fluent text whether or not the material beneath it supports what the text asserts. A system optimised to produce plausible continuations will produce a plausible continuation when the evidence is thin, in the same confident register it uses when the evidence is complete. For an organisation, the consequence is not embarrassment — it is that no output can be relied upon in a decision that must later be defended, because there is no way to distinguish an answer that was well-founded from one that was merely well-phrased.
34: [Heading 2] 2.3  Nothing is provable afterwards
35: When an AI-assisted decision is challenged — by a regulator, a customer, a court, an auditor — the organisation must state what the system read, what it was permitted to read, what it concluded, and on what basis. Conventional deployments cannot answer this. Logs, where they exist, record that a call occurred, not what grounded the answer. Reconstruction after the fact is expensive, incomplete, and self-serving by construction.
36: [Heading 2] 2.4  Rules exist on paper and nowhere else
37: Organisations write AI policies, then enforce them by training, reminders, and hope. The first genuine deadline pressure defeats them, and nobody finds out until something goes wrong. A rule that is not enforced by the system is not a control; it is a statement of intent.
38: [Heading 2] 2.5  The consequence
39: These four obstacles compound into one outcome: AI programmes stall between funded and deployed, because the risk function cannot approve a system that cannot demonstrate custody, cannot bound its own claims, cannot produce evidence, and cannot enforce its own rules.
40: Akki exists to remove all four obstacles at the layer where they can actually be removed — beneath the applications, above the data — so the risk function approves once, and everything built afterwards inherits the approval.
41: [Heading 1] 3  What Akki Is Not
42: [List Paragraph] Not a model provider. Akki does not train the frontier models it routes to and makes no claim about their internal behaviour. It governs what reaches them and what may be asserted from what they return.
43: [List Paragraph] Not a data warehouse. Akki does not become the storage of record for the estate. It measures and governs access to material that remains where the organisation keeps it, except for material it is explicitly commissioned to extract and hold.
44: [List Paragraph] Not a policy document generator. Rules declared in Akki are executable. A rule that cannot be enforced by the system cannot be declared in the system.
45: [List Paragraph] Not a workflow queue. Work is not distributed to people to perform. People hold authority; the platform performs the work.
46: [List Paragraph] Not multi-tenant. There is no mode in which two organisations’ material occupies one installation.
47: [List Paragraph] Not the end-user’s product. No platform decision optimises an end-user’s experience directly. End-user experience belongs to the applications built on the platform; the platform optimises the guarantees it issues to those applications. This is stated fully in Part VI.
48: PART II
49: 
50: Binding Doctrine
51: [Heading 1] 4  The Doctrines
52: Twelve doctrines bind every part of the platform and everything built on it. Every specification in this canon descends from them; a clause anywhere that contradicts one is defective and is corrected against the doctrine, never the reverse.
53: [Heading 2] 4.1  Fail-closed custody
54: If a custody control cannot execute, the operation does not happen.
55: When material must be de-identified before an external model may see it, and de-identification cannot run, the call is not made. The operation returns a refusal naming the cause. This is enforced structurally: no configuration flag changes it, no code path bypasses it, and an automated build gate fails the build if a path around the control is introduced.
56: Custody controls fail closed; cost optimisations fail transparent. A component that exists to reduce cost must never be able to halt a governed operation by failing — if it fails, the operation proceeds by the normal path and the failure is recorded. A fail-open custody control is a breach; a fail-closed cost optimisation is an outage. Conflating the two in either direction is a defect.
57: [Heading 2] 4.2  Unrepresentable, not policed
58: Where a state must never occur, the system is built so the state cannot be expressed.
59: A prohibition enforced by review is eventually violated. A prohibition enforced by a function signature, a type, or a schema cannot be violated without the violation failing to compile or failing to persist. The platform’s two sharpest examples: the function computing what an answer may claim has no parameter through which a model’s confidence in itself can enter, and the register that could hold individual-level identification biometrics — a voiceprint, a faceprint, any template by which a body identifies a person — has no field in which such a value could be placed. Behavioural-conformance parameters held by the Watch under its own custody doctrine are a different object with a different owner, specified in Document 8; neither is ever a field in the other's register.
60: [Heading 2] 4.3  One record
61: There is exactly one record. Nothing maintains a second.
62: Every admission, measurement, commission, operation, answer, refusal, rule change, and access grant writes to a single append-only ledger. No service keeps a local log constituting a separate account of what happened. Working state — a partial count mid-census, a draft not yet committed — is scratch, not record; it becomes record only when finalised and stamped, and the moment of stamping is itself recorded.
63: [Heading 2] 4.4  Measure, do not assert
64: No figure enters the system as a claim. Every figure carries how it was obtained.
65: Accuracy, coverage, cost, and time are measured on the organisation’s own material before they are stated. An estimate renders as an estimate, on the number, wherever it appears. Vendor benchmarks and published literature may inform what to measure; they never substitute for the measurement.
66: [Heading 2] 4.5  Single owner per value
67: Every value is computed once, by one component, and carried forward as fact.
68: A component receiving a value from an upstream component does not recompute it, does not re-validate it, and does not second-guess it. Redoing upstream work is not diligence; it is a defect, because it creates two sources for one value and therefore the possibility of two answers.
69: [Heading 2] 4.6  Extension, not proliferation
70: New capability extends an existing component. It does not create a sibling.
71: When the platform gains the ability to handle a new kind of material, the registry gains a modality, not a sibling registry. When it gains a new class of recorded event, the record gains a data class, not a second ledger. A proposed component that would need its own record, its own rules, and its own approval path is a sibling, and it is wrong.
72: [Heading 2] 4.7  Authority is held by people; work is done by the platform
73: No person is placed in the runtime path of an operation.
74: People declare rules, approve rule sets, set the criteria above which work escalates, and disposition the exceptions that reach them. The platform performs measurement, extraction, masking, qualification, and recording. If the same class of item repeatedly reaches an approver, the criteria are wrong — the response is to redefine them, never to process the queue faster.
75: [Heading 2] 4.8  Inheritance
76: Everything built inside Akki, or integrated into it, inherits its custody. There is no other way to build.
77: An application built on the platform does not re-earn the guarantees; it receives them because there is no path by which it could reach data or models except through the platform. This is what makes a single approval sufficient — the risk function approves the layer, and every application above it is governed by construction. If any application can reach the estate by a route that bypasses the platform, this doctrine is broken and the platform’s central claim is false.
78: [Heading 2] 4.9  Provenance is not optional
79: A fact that cannot name its source cannot be stored.
80: Provenance is paired with a fact at the moment of writing, never attached afterwards. A fact arriving without a resolvable source is rejected at the boundary. The same rule applies to capability: a record that a model can perform some task carries which work established that, on what material, when.
81: [Heading 2] 4.10  Verdicts are never curated
82: Inputs, models, and corpora may be engineered without limit. The evidence a verdict is measured against may not be.
83: Curating success into the model, the training data, or the corpus is legitimate craft. Curating the sample a claim is validated against is not — it produces a rehearsed checkpoint rather than a measurement, and a rehearsed checkpoint is worthless the moment real material meets it. Every validating sample is drawn from measured, uncurated composition and published internally whatever it says.
84: [Heading 2] 4.11  Canon before ruling
85: No decision proceeds from memory or summary where the governing document exists. Unread canon is read before ruling.
86: This binds the platform’s own governance exactly as it binds an operation: a rule fires against the rule set on disk, not against someone’s recollection of what the rule set says. It binds equally on anyone — owner, builder, or system — characterising what the platform does.
87: [Heading 2] 4.12  Experimentation exists at one level only
88: The assembled system is the sole object under test. No component beneath it is experimental.
89: Every mechanic the platform is built from is known and parameterised: it deploys in force with its conditions of success implemented and its quality measured, or its parameters are undefined — which is a specification gap to close, never a reason to run it tentatively. Gates in this platform bind spend, the quality of output, or a claim about the platform. They never bind whether a fully specified mechanism runs at all. A design that proposes a pilot phase, a shadow mode, or an observe-first sequence for a mechanism whose parameters are already defined has misunderstood what a gate is for.
90: [Heading 1] 5  Precedence
91: Where two requirements conflict, the following order decides, highest first.
92: [List Paragraph] Doctrine. The twelve above. A specification that contradicts a doctrine is defective.
93: [List Paragraph] The promise register. Part VI. A behaviour that breaks a promise is wrong even if it satisfies a specification.
94: [List Paragraph] This canon’s specifications. The governance, operating, interface, journey, and integration detail carried in the documents that make up this set.
95: [List Paragraph] Implementation convenience. Never decisive. Where implementation cost is genuinely prohibitive, the specification is amended through ceremony before anything ships — a shipped divergence is never retrospective evidence that the specification was wrong.
96: Where the two authorities' canons meet, the resolution rule is fixed: within the security domain the Watch canon governs; within the governance domain this canon and its companions govern; at every seam, the peerage clauses of Document 8 and the matrix of Document 9 decide. A conflict that survives all three is a specification defect, escalated — never resolved by whichever document was read most recently.
97: PART III
98: 
99: Architecture
100: [Heading 1] 6  Deployment Topology
101: Akki installs inside the organisation’s perimeter: their data centre, their private cloud, or their own cloud tenancy. The organisation controls the infrastructure, the network boundary, and the identity system; Syni operates the software.
102: Exactly one path leaves the perimeter, and it is the custody boundary. Nothing else in the platform holds outbound network capability — enforced by a network-layer allowlist that refuses outbound connections from anywhere else, and a static-analysis build gate that fails the build if any other module acquires outbound capability. Compute does not leave either: models the organisation hosts, and GPU capacity the platform allocates, run inside the perimeter. Where an external frontier model is genuinely required, the custody boundary governs that single crossing.
103: [Heading 1] 7  The Six Engines
104: The platform is six engines, each governing exactly one thing, on three orthogonal axes that never collapse into one another. A governor performing another’s function would create a single point at which a run could be admitted, bounded, and asserted by the same logic — with no separate check left to catch it.
105: <<TABLE>>
106: Engine | Axis | Governs
107: Northena | Direction | Whether a run is still in scope, and whether it is done. Deterministic by construction — no model, no learned weights, no adaptive behaviour.
108: SyniSense | Boundary | Whether data may cross an access point. The single chokepoint through which every outbound model call transits.
109: Solva | Depth | Whether reasoning is sound and an output asserts within its defensibility. The one engine built to reason, and therefore the one built with the tightest structural leash.
110: Mtafiti | Measurement | What the estate contains, and how defensibly each part of it can be relied upon.
111: Targeta | Targeting | Where to mine and in what order, within a budget, without ever narrowing what an objective may reach.
112: CIF | Judgement | How the system’s own judgements are made, retained, and improved over time — specified in full in Document 2.
113: <<END TABLE>>
114: 
115: Five of the six are documented in full in Documents 3 and 4 of this canon: Northena and SyniSense, and the two perimeters and governed-value taxonomy that surround them, in Document 3; Mtafiti, Targeta, and Solva, and the extraction and training machinery they serve, in Document 4. CIF is specified on its own in Document 2, because although it operates inside every other engine’s walls, it is peer to them and subordinate to none.
116: These six engines compose into two services connected by two named seams, specified precisely in Document 4: a service that builds the asset — census and extraction, ending in a single frozen unit contract — and a service that serves an objective against it, calling back into the first only for what it has not yet converged. Naming this composition explicitly, rather than leaving it implicit across six engine specifications, is what makes the platform legible as one system rather than six well-specified parts.
117: [Heading 2] 7.1  The two authorities
118: The six engines together constitute the platform's governing authority — the answer to *was this permitted, and is it right?* Standing beside it, peer and not subordinate, is the Watch — the security authority, answering *is this intended, and authentic?* The Watch is specified in full in Document 8; it is not a seventh engine and not a layer above the six, because the two authorities ask different questions on different clocks over the same evidence.
119: Neither authority commands the other. Each consumes what the other produces — the Watch reads the governors' evidence; the governors' gates evaluate the Watch's marks — and every task in the platform executes under exactly one authority's identity. Where the two disagree — an operation permitted but not intended — the Watch's containment acts first, bounded and reversible, and a person resolves the conflict. The disagreement itself is recorded.
120: The record classes each authority writes, the identity every task class executes under, and the contracts by which work crosses between them are held in one place: the orchestration charter, Document 9. Where a question is about who writes, who reads, or who is acting, that charter answers it — not this document, and not a recollection of it.
121: [Heading 1] 8  The Function & Promise Registry
122: One canonical, versioned artifact registers every named function in the platform — gate, engine behaviour, worker obligation, console guarantee — with the promise it protects and its full accounting. Every function belongs to one of the six engines above, or to a named surface for interface-level guarantees. The registry is specified in full in Document 7; it is named here because two of its rules are doctrine-adjacent and worth stating at the outset: no gate exists without an honestly statable promise, and no promise exists that traces to no function protecting it. A function that cannot answer both questions is retired, not preserved out of caution.
123: PART IV
124: 
125: The Estate
126: [Heading 1] 9  What an Estate Is
127: The estate is everything the organisation holds that an AI system could read, treated as a single measurable object at whatever scale it is being considered — the organisation, a department, an archive, a single file.
128: [Heading 2] 9.1  The three states
129: Every region of the estate is in exactly one state, rendered with equal prominence wherever the estate is described.
130: <<TABLE>>
131: State | Meaning
132: Measured — sound | Measured, and the condition supports use. Composition, language, sensitivity, and rights are known and recorded.
133: Measured — degraded | Measured, and the condition limits use — the specific limitation is named.
134: Not yet measured | No census has covered this region. Displayed as unmeasured, never as empty, never as clean.
135: <<END TABLE>>
136: 
137: An unmeasured region is never rendered as empty, clean, or zero. The absence of a measurement is a fact about the platform’s knowledge, not a fact about the estate.
138: [Heading 2] 9.2  Measurement, in two layers
139: The estate’s defensibility — how confidently any part of it may be relied upon — is produced in two layers, so it scales across a large estate without labelling every item by hand. A deterministic declaration, applied per source and always available, is the floor the whole measure rests on. An inference layer detects signals in the content itself — whether material corroborates, whether it is contested — and contributes only after its own accuracy has been proven; until then, the declaration stands alone. Neither layer decides what a measurement means: that verdict is always a governed, versioned lookup, never a model’s output. This is the platform’s general answer to a problem that recurs at every layer — learning may detect; it may never decide.
140: PART V
141: 
142: The Operating Loop
143: [Heading 1] 10  The Loop
144: Questions arrive. Most are answered. Those that are not become ranked gaps. Gaps become commissioned objectives. Extraction changes what the next round can answer.
145: Two properties make this the platform’s operating objective rather than a description of a workflow. No role must be present for the loop to continue — a question can arrive, fail to be answered, become a gap, and be ranked without anyone deciding it should. And the record carries the context that would otherwise live in someone’s head: why a gap was filed, what was tried, what the material could not support.
146: Demand is discovered rather than forecast — the organisation learns what its estate is worth by observing what people actually try to ask of it, not by guessing in advance. And the loop is self-limiting in a healthy way: when the gap list stops producing high-demand candidates, the estate has been mined to the depth its current questions require. Mining is not a programme with a launch date; it is a practice an organisation develops.
147: Each cycle compounds. Cleaner material, better models, and more accurate mining accumulate in the record rather than being rebuilt per project — which is the platform’s promise about time: the second commission costs less than the first for the same value, because capability accumulates rather than starting over.
148: PART VI
149: 
150: Who Akki Serves
151: [Heading 1] 11  The Governing Rule
152: No platform decision optimises an end-user’s experience directly. The platform optimises the guarantees it issues to the applications built on it.
153: This is not a limitation stated apologetically; it is what makes a single, durable approval possible. End-user experience — what an executive sees, what a business analyst clicks — is application territory, and applications are specified in Document 5. What follows here is who the platform itself is answerable to, independent of which applications get built on top of it.
154: [Heading 1] 12  The Six Services
155: Six sentences state what the platform promises, to whom, and by what journey the promise is redeemed. They are canonical: changeable only by the same ceremony that governs any consequential rule change, because changing one of them changes what the product is.
156: <<TABLE>>
157: Service | To whom | The promise
158: S1 | The integrating application — internal or external, the platform’s top-layer user | A governed intelligence surface to build on: answers, skills, and artifacts that arrive with class, receipt, and refusal semantics intact, so the application inherits provability instead of building it.
159: S2 | The operating organisation | An estate onboarded, mapped, and turned into qualified intelligence that can be committed to with confidence.
160: S3 | The compliance officer | Proof of any operation on demand, and governed control of the rules over data.
161: S4 | The data buyer | Intelligence products that can be verified independently before being relied upon — never raw data.
162: S5 | The infrastructure consumer | Reserved. Akki’s extraction and governance capacity as a substrate a future venture builds on. Registered so nothing optimises against it prematurely; not built.
163: S6 | The operating organisation and its compliance officer, under threat | Continuous, machine-speed detection and response against misuse of the estate and the platform — invisible in legitimate use, incapable of acting unobserved, and proving its own fitness on a standing cadence. Specified in Document 8.
164: <<END TABLE>>
165: 
166: No platform function is proposed, evaluated, or justified except by tracing to one of these five sentences. A function that cannot trace upward is doing the wrong job well — competently solving a problem the platform was never asked to solve.
167: [Heading 1] 13  Applications Are Not the Platform
168: An application is anything with an end-user in it, internal or external, and the boundary is mechanical rather than organisational: if a person who is not running the platform touches it, it is an application. It enters through the same governed boundary as any third party, holds a scoped key issued the same way, and is subject to the same custody on every call. There is no privileged path — not for a first-party surface, not for one built by Syni itself.
169: The applications an organisation actually uses — a conversational surface, an executive workspace, a document reviewer, a monitoring feed — are specified fully in Document 5. What is fixed here is only the boundary they all cross the same way.
170: PART VII
171: 
172: Vocabulary and Boundaries
173: [Heading 1] 14  Canonical Terms
174: <<TABLE>>
175: Term | Meaning
176: The custody boundary | The single point at which anything crosses the perimeter.
177: Estate | Everything the organisation holds that an AI system could read.
178: Commission | A unit of substantial work: scoped, priced, agreed, executed, recorded.
179: Objective | What a commission is for, frozen at admission, immutable for the run.
180: The record | The single append-only account of everything that happened.
181: Receipt | The independently verifiable record of a single operation.
182: Console | A capability grouping on the platform, defined by what can be done there — never by a named person.
183: Application | Anything with an end-user in it. Enters through the governed boundary, holds a scoped key.
184: <<END TABLE>>
185: [Heading 1] 15  What the Platform Will Not Do
186: [List Paragraph] It will not answer beyond its evidence. Where material is insufficient, the platform bounds the claim or declines. It does not produce a confident answer with a caveat attached.
187: [List Paragraph] It will not provide an override. No emergency mode, no administrator bypass, no support-access path that skips custody. A control with an exception is not a control.
188: [List Paragraph] It will not quote unmeasured figures. Not in an interface, not in a report, not in a proposal generated from it.
189: [List Paragraph] It will not maintain a second record. No component keeps its own account of what happened, however convenient.
190: [List Paragraph] It will not place a person in the runtime path. Authority is exercised over rules and exceptions, never over individual operations as a matter of course.
191: [List Paragraph] It will not know a buyer, a price, or an order. Commerce is application territory. The platform governs access to output and records every egress; it charges nothing and transacts with no one.
192: [Heading 1] 16  This Canon
193: This document is the foundation. Eight further documents complete the specification, and each assumes this one.
194: <<TABLE>>
195: Document | Scope
196: 2 — The Conditioned Ideation Faculty | CIF in full: the sixth engine, peer to the other five, governing how the system’s own judgements are made, retained, and improved.
197: 3 — Governance Engines | Northena and SyniSense in full: the operating model, the two perimeters, the governed-value taxonomy, ceremony, authority, and assurance.
198: 4 — Operating Engines | Mtafiti, Targeta, and Solva in full: measurement, targeting, reasoning, the extraction stack, training, and the economics of a run.
199: 5 — Interface Architecture | The four consoles, the applications built on them, and the design law that binds every surface.
200: 6 — User Journeys | Every journey from founding to steady state, who walks it, and what must be true at each step.
201: 7 — Integration Service and Quality Rulebook | The Function & Promise Registry, the contract every application calls, and the discipline the build itself is held to.
202: 8 — The Watch | The security authority in full: its promise, doctrines, the two engines and the verdict seam, the response arms, marks and signatures, the mirage, its console, and its parameters.
203: 9 — The Mkondo Charter | The orchestration charter: the record matrix — every record class, its single writer, its readers — the task-identity register, and the handoff contracts between the two authorities.
204: <<END TABLE>>
205: 
206: Where any of them appears to contradict this document, this document governs.

# SOURCE: assessment_workspace/canon/text/Akki_Canon_2_CIF.txt
Coordinate: source line

1: # SOURCE FILE: Akki_Canon_2_CIF.docx
2: 
3: AKKI CANON  ·  DOCUMENT 2 OF 9
4: The Conditioned Ideation Faculty
5: CIF: the sixth engine, peer to Northena, SyniSense, Solva, Mtafiti, and Targeta
6: PART I
7: 
8: The Promise
9: [Heading 1] 1  What CIF Is
10: The Conditioned Ideation Faculty governs how the system’s own judgements are made, retained, and improved. It is peer to the platform’s other five engines — Northena, SyniSense, Solva, Mtafiti, Targeta — subordinate to none of them, and its reach is the broadest of any engine’s: it operates across the build loop, the training path, planning, and proposal generation, wherever the system or the people building it render a judgement.
11: CIF is in force across the architecture from adoption. There is no phasing and no activation sequence. Every operation in every engine, from its first occurrence, executes under this specification.
12: [Heading 1] 2  The Problem It Answers
13: Working with AI today places the whole quality burden on the human: catching errors, re-supplying lost context, watching good ideas vanish at the end of a session, repeating the same corrections indefinitely. When the human goes quiet, quality degrades invisibly, and two failures compound each other.
14: The first: a correction made once is typically absorbed locally. The specific answer changes; the faulty assumption behind it survives and produces the same class of error again tomorrow. Human corrective effort evaporates instead of compounding, and the same ground is re-litigated indefinitely.
15: The second: an idea rejected because a condition it needed was absent is, after the fact, indistinguishable from an idea rejected because it was simply bad. The record shows a rejection; the reason is lost; and when the missing condition later arrives, nobody revisits the idea. Good work dies of timing.
16: [Heading 1] 3  The Promise, Stated Four Ways
17: [List Paragraph] You stop repeating yourself. A correction made once holds — the class of error is retired, not the instance.
18: [List Paragraph] Shown confidence can be trusted. When the system is sure, that confidence has visible footing. When it is guessing, it says so before reliance, not after harm.
19: [List Paragraph] Ideas stop dying with the session. Rejected, deferred, or half-explored ideas wait — alive, with what they need named — and return when their conditions arrive.
20: [List Paragraph] Insights spread everywhere they apply. A reframe made once rewrites everything the old thinking touched, in one strike, rather than being symptom-hunted for weeks.
21: 
22: The measure this is held to: the human corrects less each cycle for the same or better output. That is the claim made at adoption. Any stronger claim is made only on cycles where it has actually been measured.
23: PART II
24: 
25: The Governing Principle
26: [Heading 1] 4  The System This Faculty Serves
27: Akki is an operating system for how agentic workflows integrate with enterprise data estates, how enterprises monetise those estates, and how enterprises build their own models autonomously from them. The architecture is the invention; its components are deliberately not novel — known gates, known engines, known code structures, each with defined, tested conditions of success.
28: [Heading 1] 5  The Single-Experiment Principle
29: Experimentation exists at one level only — the assembled system delivering the enterprise promise. Nothing beneath that level is experimental.
30: Every mechanic in the platform is known and parameterisable. It deploys in force with its conditions of success strictly implemented and its quality measured — or its parameters are not yet defined, which is a specification gap to close, never a reason to run it tentatively. No capability is gated on demonstration, observation, trial, or seeing first. Gates in this platform bind spend, the quality of output, or a claim — never existence or force.
31: CIF enters under this principle without qualification. Its mechanics — recording what a verdict rests on, retaining ideas with named conditions, re-evaluating on condition change, second-instance review, threshold monitoring — are proven realities, not a pilot. Construction order carries no epistemic weight: nothing about when a piece of CIF was built bears on whether it is true.
32: [Heading 1] 6  Referenced Systems
33: <<TABLE>>
34: System | Role in CIF
35: The coach | The human role — teacher, auditor, informer — whose corrections strike the assumptions a verdict rests on, and who alone may adopt a new frame. Constitutionally load-bearing: no configuration of the system operates without this seat filled.
36: Solva-pattern validation | The platform’s reasoning discipline, applied as validator: claims stated only at their evidence class, a conclusion’s support meeting its bar, contradiction surfaced rather than averaged away, a refusal naming its reason and what would satisfy it. CIF’s own claims are evaluated by this discipline exactly as any answer is.
37: The Critic Seam | The standing quality layer for worker output, specified in Document 7. Its rubric is compiled from the coach’s correction history; CIF’s pre-ship checklist extends that rubric to idea selection.
38: The independence rule | A reviewing instance must differ genuinely from what it reviews — a different base model, or a materially different context shape. Same-base, same-context review shares blind spots and adds cost without adding detection.
39: Run telemetry | The platform’s per-run measurement stream. CIF’s monitoring parameters bind to named fields in it.
40: The Watch | The security authority, Document 8. Its detection findings are a source CIF may metabolise like any other ground reality; its drills operate under this faculty's own permanent bound — the Watch never certifies its own framing, and its fitness is counted in demonstrated firings, never self-graded value.
41: Engine walls | The standing constitutional limits every engine operates inside — a planner’s learning never widens what an objective may reach; a critic detects and never decides. CIF operates inside these walls everywhere it acts.
42: <<END TABLE>>
43: PART III
44: 
45: Vocabulary
46: [Heading 1] 7  Definitions
47: <<TABLE>>
48: Term | Meaning
49: Idea | Any candidate the faculty evaluates or picks — a proposal, a technique, a product move, an interpretation, a training choice, an ordering decision, a selection among alternatives.
50: Verdict | An evaluated position on an idea — adopt, reject, rank, or defer — rendered against a stated goal.
51: Manifest | The recorded set of load-bearing assumptions a verdict or pick rests on, each entry classed fact, recalled, or inferred, elicited by one question: what, if false, flips this?
52: Flip | A verdict reversing because information struck a manifest entry — whether the information newly arrived, or was already held and only newly attended to.
53: Frame | A thinking structure shared across many verdicts — the shape of the calculation, not a variable inside it.
54: Frame signature | One of three patterns indicating a frame, not a single verdict, is wrong: cascade — one strike flips many verdicts at once; absorption — the same correction class is patched repeatedly while the underlying pattern persists; misfit — information reduces to no existing structure, contradicts several standing positions, or resists the manifest probe.
55: Metabolisation | Complete digestion of an adopted frame across everything the overturned structure touched.
