380: | **Language ID** | segment → { languages[], confidences, switch_points }; written to provenance. |
381: | **Occurrence index (ext.)** | dedup item → + instance condition map. |
382: | **Character Register** | Write path: schema cannot represent instance-level identity (§6.3). Read path: strata queries for planner and evaluation. |
383: | **Objective Wizard** | session → { TargetOutcome, CollectionSchema }; deterministic compile; compile-time rejection of contract-violating artifacts; session stamped to ledger. |
384: | **TargetOutcome** | Rejected without existing test_set_ref; acceptance per stratum; gate_policy recorded at definition. |
385: | **Training Planner** | Outcome → { coverage report, curriculum, milestone list, quote ± interval }; reproducible plan_id; plan without calibration stage rejected. |
386: | **Training run** | Commissioned-job contract; completion certificate incl. manifest hash and per-stratum results. |
387: | **Voice identity** | register strata + constructed organic parameters → identity; distance gate mandatory, fail-closed; certificate issued on pass; versioned; change by ceremony. |
388: | **Commission View** | Reads milestones, statuses, spend, and existing artifacts only; introduces no new backend computation. |
389: 
390: # **15  ****Build Sequence**
391: 
392: Ordered by dependency and cost-of-deferral, not by size.
393: 
394: | **#** | **Item** | **Rationale for position** |
395: | --- | --- | --- |
396: | **1** | Ingestion capture: language ID, code-switch points, condition profile, synthesis attributes (§4.1–4.4) | Everything downstream consumes these; only cheap at first ingestion. Deferral cost is a full re-pass over the estate. |
397: | **2** | Dedup instance condition map (§4.5) | Contract change to existing machinery; near-zero new detection work. |
398: | **3** | Character Register schema + custody invariant harness (§6) | The boundary must exist before the first cluster is stored; retrofitting means rebuilding from source. |
399: | **4** | Codec service (§3) | Unsupervised pretraining starts on unlabelled audio while labelled work proceeds elsewhere. |
400: | **5** | Clustering + sampled human validation (§5.3) | Requires 1–4. |
401: | **6** | Objective Wizard variant + Collection Schema type + registry namespace (§8, §9, §12.1) | The planner must never accept a hand-authored Outcome once the wizard exists; building the planner first invites the malformed-input class the compile stage makes impossible. |
402: | **7** | TargetOutcome type + planner core (§10, §11.1, §11.4) | Requires register strata to plan against and the wizard to author Outcomes. |
403: | **8** | Sampling & Reflection machinery + milestone records (§11.2–11.3) | Requires 7 and a test set. |
404: | **9** | Commission View (§13) | Reads records created in 8; by §13.4 it cannot precede them. |
405: | **10** | Full training runs under the commissioned-job contract (§11.6) | Last by construction — the planner refuses to run earlier. |
406: | **P2** | Voice identity rendering; music register | Phase 2. Non-foreclosure is guaranteed by item 1 and §7.5. |
407: 
408: # **16  ****Verification Register and Open Decisions**
409: 
410: ## **16.1  ****Items to verify against current code before build**
411: 
412: - Perception router contract — model registration point; whether a second output stream per segment is carried or the character stream needs its own artifact type (§3.2).
413: 
414: - Ingestion segment boundaries — the unit a language label attaches to (§4.1).
415: 
416: - Wizard B-2/B-3 landing state — extend the existing state machine with an objective variant, or stand a sibling machine on the shared agent interface and ledger sidecar (§8.5).
417: 
418: ## **16.2  ****Open decisions (owner: product)**
419: 
420: - N for the shared-attribute condition (§6.2.2): inherit the platform minimum-group-size seam value, or set a register-specific one.
421: 
422: - Platform default for gate_policy (§10.1) where an Outcome does not set it: missed stratum gates release, or ships documented. This default silently decides how minority-variant quality is treated under schedule pressure.
423: 
424: - Cluster naming validation: commissioned internally or delegated to an external evaluation partner where one exists (§5.3).
425: 
426: - Codec choice: adopt an existing open codec versus training estate-specific — a trade the Sampling & Reflection machinery can itself answer once built (§3, §11.2).
427: 
428: - Baseline tier contents (§9.2): the v1.0 set is the proposal; every addition is paid on every hour ingested, every omission is paid at re-ingestion.
429: 
430: *End of specification. This document is the single build reference for the Audio Intelligence Plane; the working drafts it consolidates are retired.*
431: 
432: Akki OS · Audio Intelligence Plane · Specification v1.0   ·

# SOURCE: assessment_workspace/canon/unpacked/Akki_Canon_1_Custody_Platform.docx
Coordinate: document.xml paragraph in body order, tables included

1: AKKI CANON  ·  DOCUMENT 1 OF 9
2: Akki — The Custody Platform
3: Foundational canon: definition, doctrine, architecture, the estate, the operating loop, who Akki serves
4: PART I
What Akki Is
5: 1  Definition
6: Akki is a custody platform for enterprise artificial intelligence. It installs inside an organisation’s own perimeter and becomes the layer through which every AI operation touching that organisation’s data must pass.
7: A custodian performs four duties: it holds assets safely, it maintains the authoritative record of what is held, it settles transactions against that record, and it reports positions to the owner and to the regulator. Akki performs the same four duties for data and for the AI operations that read it. It holds the estate under declared controls, maintains the record of what the estate contains, settles commissioned work against that record, and produces evidence on demand to the organisation and to anyone the organisation must answer to.
8: Akki is not a model, not a wrapper around a model, and not an assistant. It is the layer beneath every model and every application, and it is the only path between them and the estate.
9: The platform is single-tenant by construction: one organisation, one installation, one record. There is no multi-tenant deployment mode and no shared control plane. The estate’s contents — never the customer’s identity — determine which capabilities activate on it. A media-heavy estate activates the perception classes; a text-only estate does not. No installation is a development metric for another: what one organisation’s estate teaches the platform stays general, and no instance-specific assumption may enter the platform’s own specification.
10: 1.1  What the platform holds
11: The unit Akki governs is the data estate: everything an organisation holds that an AI system could read. This includes structured stores, document repositories, message archives, media libraries, call recordings, ticket systems, and material held in systems nobody has formally catalogued. It includes material the organisation has rights to and material whose rights are unclear, and the platform treats the difference as a first-class fact rather than an administrative detail.
12: An estate is an estate at every scale. The whole organisation is an estate; a department is an estate; a single archive is an estate; a single file is an estate. The same operations apply at every scale — measured, admitted, governed, recorded — because a mechanism that only works at one scale is not a mechanism the platform can depend on.
13: 1.2  What the platform does
14: Four verbs describe the whole of it.
15: Verb
16: Meaning
17: Measure
18: Establish what the estate actually contains — composition, condition, language, sensitivity, rights — and state plainly which regions have not been measured. An unmeasured region is reported as unmeasured, never as empty and never as clean.
19: Govern
20: Enforce, on every operation, the rules the organisation has declared: what may be read, by whom, for what purpose, under what masking, with what evidence required before an answer may be asserted.
21: Extract
22: Convert estate material into things the organisation can use — qualified facts, trained models, licensed datasets, memory available to applications — as commissioned work priced before it runs.
23: Prove
24: Emit, for every operation, a receipt that an outside party can verify without an account on the system and without the operator’s cooperation.
25: 
26: Every capability the platform offers is one of these four or a composition of them.
27: 2  The Problem Akki Solves
28: An organisation that wants to use AI on its own data faces four obstacles, each real and independent of the others.
29: 2.1  The data cannot leave
30: Regulated organisations hold material they may not transmit to third parties: personal data under data-protection law, financial records, medical information, privileged legal material, commercially sensitive information whose disclosure would breach a contract. The dominant pattern for using AI — send the content to an external service, receive an answer — is unavailable to them for most of what they hold. Redacting by hand does not scale and is unauditable; approving a vendor’s security posture does not change where the data goes; prohibiting AI use does not stop it, it moves it onto personal accounts where the organisation has no visibility at all.
31: 2.2  The output cannot be trusted on its face
32: A language model produces fluent text whether or not the material beneath it supports what the text asserts. A system optimised to produce plausible continuations will produce a plausible continuation when the evidence is thin, in the same confident register it uses when the evidence is complete. For an organisation, the consequence is not embarrassment — it is that no output can be relied upon in a decision that must later be defended, because there is no way to distinguish an answer that was well-founded from one that was merely well-phrased.
33: 2.3  Nothing is provable afterwards
34: When an AI-assisted decision is challenged — by a regulator, a customer, a court, an auditor — the organisation must state what the system read, what it was permitted to read, what it concluded, and on what basis. Conventional deployments cannot answer this. Logs, where they exist, record that a call occurred, not what grounded the answer. Reconstruction after the fact is expensive, incomplete, and self-serving by construction.
35: 2.4  Rules exist on paper and nowhere else
36: Organisations write AI policies, then enforce them by training, reminders, and hope. The first genuine deadline pressure defeats them, and nobody finds out until something goes wrong. A rule that is not enforced by the system is not a control; it is a statement of intent.
37: 2.5  The consequence
38: These four obstacles compound into one outcome: AI programmes stall between funded and deployed, because the risk function cannot approve a system that cannot demonstrate custody, cannot bound its own claims, cannot produce evidence, and cannot enforce its own rules.
39: Akki exists to remove all four obstacles at the layer where they can actually be removed — beneath the applications, above the data — so the risk function approves once, and everything built afterwards inherits the approval.
40: 3  What Akki Is Not
41: Not a model provider. Akki does not train the frontier models it routes to and makes no claim about their internal behaviour. It governs what reaches them and what may be asserted from what they return.
42: Not a data warehouse. Akki does not become the storage of record for the estate. It measures and governs access to material that remains where the organisation keeps it, except for material it is explicitly commissioned to extract and hold.
43: Not a policy document generator. Rules declared in Akki are executable. A rule that cannot be enforced by the system cannot be declared in the system.
44: Not a workflow queue. Work is not distributed to people to perform. People hold authority; the platform performs the work.
45: Not multi-tenant. There is no mode in which two organisations’ material occupies one installation.
46: Not the end-user’s product. No platform decision optimises an end-user’s experience directly. End-user experience belongs to the applications built on the platform; the platform optimises the guarantees it issues to those applications. This is stated fully in Part VI.
47: PART II
Binding Doctrine
48: 4  The Doctrines
49: Twelve doctrines bind every part of the platform and everything built on it. Every specification in this canon descends from them; a clause anywhere that contradicts one is defective and is corrected against the doctrine, never the reverse.
50: 4.1  Fail-closed custody
51: If a custody control cannot execute, the operation does not happen.
52: When material must be de-identified before an external model may see it, and de-identification cannot run, the call is not made. The operation returns a refusal naming the cause. This is enforced structurally: no configuration flag changes it, no code path bypasses it, and an automated build gate fails the build if a path around the control is introduced.
53: Custody controls fail closed; cost optimisations fail transparent. A component that exists to reduce cost must never be able to halt a governed operation by failing — if it fails, the operation proceeds by the normal path and the failure is recorded. A fail-open custody control is a breach; a fail-closed cost optimisation is an outage. Conflating the two in either direction is a defect.
54: 4.2  Unrepresentable, not policed
55: Where a state must never occur, the system is built so the state cannot be expressed.
56: A prohibition enforced by review is eventually violated. A prohibition enforced by a function signature, a type, or a schema cannot be violated without the violation failing to compile or failing to persist. The platform’s two sharpest examples: the function computing what an answer may claim has no parameter through which a model’s confidence in itself can enter, and the register that could hold individual-level identification biometrics — a voiceprint, a faceprint, any template by which a body identifies a person — has no field in which such a value could be placed. Behavioural-conformance parameters held by the Watch under its own custody doctrine are a different object with a different owner, specified in Document 8; neither is ever a field in the other's register.
57: 4.3  One record
58: There is exactly one record. Nothing maintains a second.
59: Every admission, measurement, commission, operation, answer, refusal, rule change, and access grant writes to a single append-only ledger. No service keeps a local log constituting a separate account of what happened. Working state — a partial count mid-census, a draft not yet committed — is scratch, not record; it becomes record only when finalised and stamped, and the moment of stamping is itself recorded.
60: 4.4  Measure, do not assert
61: No figure enters the system as a claim. Every figure carries how it was obtained.
62: Accuracy, coverage, cost, and time are measured on the organisation’s own material before they are stated. An estimate renders as an estimate, on the number, wherever it appears. Vendor benchmarks and published literature may inform what to measure; they never substitute for the measurement.
63: 4.5  Single owner per value
64: Every value is computed once, by one component, and carried forward as fact.
65: A component receiving a value from an upstream component does not recompute it, does not re-validate it, and does not second-guess it. Redoing upstream work is not diligence; it is a defect, because it creates two sources for one value and therefore the possibility of two answers.
66: 4.6  Extension, not proliferation
67: New capability extends an existing component. It does not create a sibling.
68: When the platform gains the ability to handle a new kind of material, the registry gains a modality, not a sibling registry. When it gains a new class of recorded event, the record gains a data class, not a second ledger. A proposed component that would need its own record, its own rules, and its own approval path is a sibling, and it is wrong.
69: 4.7  Authority is held by people; work is done by the platform
70: No person is placed in the runtime path of an operation.
71: People declare rules, approve rule sets, set the criteria above which work escalates, and disposition the exceptions that reach them. The platform performs measurement, extraction, masking, qualification, and recording. If the same class of item repeatedly reaches an approver, the criteria are wrong — the response is to redefine them, never to process the queue faster.
72: 4.8  Inheritance
73: Everything built inside Akki, or integrated into it, inherits its custody. There is no other way to build.
74: An application built on the platform does not re-earn the guarantees; it receives them because there is no path by which it could reach data or models except through the platform. This is what makes a single approval sufficient — the risk function approves the layer, and every application above it is governed by construction. If any application can reach the estate by a route that bypasses the platform, this doctrine is broken and the platform’s central claim is false.
75: 4.9  Provenance is not optional
76: A fact that cannot name its source cannot be stored.
77: Provenance is paired with a fact at the moment of writing, never attached afterwards. A fact arriving without a resolvable source is rejected at the boundary. The same rule applies to capability: a record that a model can perform some task carries which work established that, on what material, when.
78: 4.10  Verdicts are never curated
79: Inputs, models, and corpora may be engineered without limit. The evidence a verdict is measured against may not be.
80: Curating success into the model, the training data, or the corpus is legitimate craft. Curating the sample a claim is validated against is not — it produces a rehearsed checkpoint rather than a measurement, and a rehearsed checkpoint is worthless the moment real material meets it. Every validating sample is drawn from measured, uncurated composition and published internally whatever it says.
81: 4.11  Canon before ruling
82: No decision proceeds from memory or summary where the governing document exists. Unread canon is read before ruling.
83: This binds the platform’s own governance exactly as it binds an operation: a rule fires against the rule set on disk, not against someone’s recollection of what the rule set says. It binds equally on anyone — owner, builder, or system — characterising what the platform does.
84: 4.12  Experimentation exists at one level only
85: The assembled system is the sole object under test. No component beneath it is experimental.
86: Every mechanic the platform is built from is known and parameterised: it deploys in force with its conditions of success implemented and its quality measured, or its parameters are undefined — which is a specification gap to close, never a reason to run it tentatively. Gates in this platform bind spend, the quality of output, or a claim about the platform. They never bind whether a fully specified mechanism runs at all. A design that proposes a pilot phase, a shadow mode, or an observe-first sequence for a mechanism whose parameters are already defined has misunderstood what a gate is for.
87: 5  Precedence
88: Where two requirements conflict, the following order decides, highest first.
89: Doctrine. The twelve above. A specification that contradicts a doctrine is defective.
90: The promise register. Part VI. A behaviour that breaks a promise is wrong even if it satisfies a specification.
91: This canon’s specifications. The governance, operating, interface, journey, and integration detail carried in the documents that make up this set.
92: Implementation convenience. Never decisive. Where implementation cost is genuinely prohibitive, the specification is amended through ceremony before anything ships — a shipped divergence is never retrospective evidence that the specification was wrong.
93: Where the two authorities' canons meet, the resolution rule is fixed: within the security domain the Watch canon governs; within the governance domain this canon and its companions govern; at every seam, the peerage clauses of Document 8 and the matrix of Document 9 decide. A conflict that survives all three is a specification defect, escalated — never resolved by whichever document was read most recently.
94: PART III
Architecture
95: 6  Deployment Topology
96: Akki installs inside the organisation’s perimeter: their data centre, their private cloud, or their own cloud tenancy. The organisation controls the infrastructure, the network boundary, and the identity system; Syni operates the software.
97: Exactly one path leaves the perimeter, and it is the custody boundary. Nothing else in the platform holds outbound network capability — enforced by a network-layer allowlist that refuses outbound connections from anywhere else, and a static-analysis build gate that fails the build if any other module acquires outbound capability. Compute does not leave either: models the organisation hosts, and GPU capacity the platform allocates, run inside the perimeter. Where an external frontier model is genuinely required, the custody boundary governs that single crossing.
98: 7  The Six Engines
99: The platform is six engines, each governing exactly one thing, on three orthogonal axes that never collapse into one another. A governor performing another’s function would create a single point at which a run could be admitted, bounded, and asserted by the same logic — with no separate check left to catch it.
100: Engine
101: Axis
102: Governs
103: Northena
104: Direction
105: Whether a run is still in scope, and whether it is done. Deterministic by construction — no model, no learned weights, no adaptive behaviour.
106: SyniSense
107: Boundary
108: Whether data may cross an access point. The single chokepoint through which every outbound model call transits.
109: Solva
110: Depth
111: Whether reasoning is sound and an output asserts within its defensibility. The one engine built to reason, and therefore the one built with the tightest structural leash.
112: Mtafiti
113: Measurement
114: What the estate contains, and how defensibly each part of it can be relied upon.
115: Targeta
116: Targeting
117: Where to mine and in what order, within a budget, without ever narrowing what an objective may reach.
118: CIF
119: Judgement
120: How the system’s own judgements are made, retained, and improved over time — specified in full in Document 2.
121: 
122: Five of the six are documented in full in Documents 3 and 4 of this canon: Northena and SyniSense, and the two perimeters and governed-value taxonomy that surround them, in Document 3; Mtafiti, Targeta, and Solva, and the extraction and training machinery they serve, in Document 4. CIF is specified on its own in Document 2, because although it operates inside every other engine’s walls, it is peer to them and subordinate to none.
123: These six engines compose into two services connected by two named seams, specified precisely in Document 4: a service that builds the asset — census and extraction, ending in a single frozen unit contract — and a service that serves an objective against it, calling back into the first only for what it has not yet converged. Naming this composition explicitly, rather than leaving it implicit across six engine specifications, is what makes the platform legible as one system rather than six well-specified parts.
124: 7.1  The two authorities
125: The six engines together constitute the platform's governing authority — the answer to *was this permitted, and is it right?* Standing beside it, peer and not subordinate, is the Watch — the security authority, answering *is this intended, and authentic?* The Watch is specified in full in Document 8; it is not a seventh engine and not a layer above the six, because the two authorities ask different questions on different clocks over the same evidence.
126: Neither authority commands the other. Each consumes what the other produces — the Watch reads the governors' evidence; the governors' gates evaluate the Watch's marks — and every task in the platform executes under exactly one authority's identity. Where the two disagree — an operation permitted but not intended — the Watch's containment acts first, bounded and reversible, and a person resolves the conflict. The disagreement itself is recorded.
127: The record classes each authority writes, the identity every task class executes under, and the contracts by which work crosses between them are held in one place: the orchestration charter, Document 9. Where a question is about who writes, who reads, or who is acting, that charter answers it — not this document, and not a recollection of it.
128: 8  The Function & Promise Registry
129: One canonical, versioned artifact registers every named function in the platform — gate, engine behaviour, worker obligation, console guarantee — with the promise it protects and its full accounting. Every function belongs to one of the six engines above, or to a named surface for interface-level guarantees. The registry is specified in full in Document 7; it is named here because two of its rules are doctrine-adjacent and worth stating at the outset: no gate exists without an honestly statable promise, and no promise exists that traces to no function protecting it. A function that cannot answer both questions is retired, not preserved out of caution.
130: PART IV
The Estate
131: 9  What an Estate Is
132: The estate is everything the organisation holds that an AI system could read, treated as a single measurable object at whatever scale it is being considered — the organisation, a department, an archive, a single file.
133: 9.1  The three states
134: Every region of the estate is in exactly one state, rendered with equal prominence wherever the estate is described.
135: State
136: Meaning
137: Measured — sound
138: Measured, and the condition supports use. Composition, language, sensitivity, and rights are known and recorded.
139: Measured — degraded
140: Measured, and the condition limits use — the specific limitation is named.
141: Not yet measured
142: No census has covered this region. Displayed as unmeasured, never as empty, never as clean.
143: 
144: An unmeasured region is never rendered as empty, clean, or zero. The absence of a measurement is a fact about the platform’s knowledge, not a fact about the estate.
145: 9.2  Measurement, in two layers
146: The estate’s defensibility — how confidently any part of it may be relied upon — is produced in two layers, so it scales across a large estate without labelling every item by hand. A deterministic declaration, applied per source and always available, is the floor the whole measure rests on. An inference layer detects signals in the content itself — whether material corroborates, whether it is contested — and contributes only after its own accuracy has been proven; until then, the declaration stands alone. Neither layer decides what a measurement means: that verdict is always a governed, versioned lookup, never a model’s output. This is the platform’s general answer to a problem that recurs at every layer — learning may detect; it may never decide.
147: PART V
The Operating Loop
148: 10  The Loop
149: Questions arrive. Most are answered. Those that are not become ranked gaps. Gaps become commissioned objectives. Extraction changes what the next round can answer.
150: Two properties make this the platform’s operating objective rather than a description of a workflow. No role must be present for the loop to continue — a question can arrive, fail to be answered, become a gap, and be ranked without anyone deciding it should. And the record carries the context that would otherwise live in someone’s head: why a gap was filed, what was tried, what the material could not support.
151: Demand is discovered rather than forecast — the organisation learns what its estate is worth by observing what people actually try to ask of it, not by guessing in advance. And the loop is self-limiting in a healthy way: when the gap list stops producing high-demand candidates, the estate has been mined to the depth its current questions require. Mining is not a programme with a launch date; it is a practice an organisation develops.
152: Each cycle compounds. Cleaner material, better models, and more accurate mining accumulate in the record rather than being rebuilt per project — which is the platform’s promise about time: the second commission costs less than the first for the same value, because capability accumulates rather than starting over.
153: PART VI
Who Akki Serves
154: 11  The Governing Rule
155: No platform decision optimises an end-user’s experience directly. The platform optimises the guarantees it issues to the applications built on it.
156: This is not a limitation stated apologetically; it is what makes a single, durable approval possible. End-user experience — what an executive sees, what a business analyst clicks — is application territory, and applications are specified in Document 5. What follows here is who the platform itself is answerable to, independent of which applications get built on top of it.
157: 12  The Six Services
158: Six sentences state what the platform promises, to whom, and by what journey the promise is redeemed. They are canonical: changeable only by the same ceremony that governs any consequential rule change, because changing one of them changes what the product is.
159: Service
160: To whom
161: The promise
162: S1
163: The integrating application — internal or external, the platform’s top-layer user
164: A governed intelligence surface to build on: answers, skills, and artifacts that arrive with class, receipt, and refusal semantics intact, so the application inherits provability instead of building it.
165: S2
166: The operating organisation
167: An estate onboarded, mapped, and turned into qualified intelligence that can be committed to with confidence.
168: S3
169: The compliance officer
170: Proof of any operation on demand, and governed control of the rules over data.
171: S4
172: The data buyer
173: Intelligence products that can be verified independently before being relied upon — never raw data.
174: S5
175: The infrastructure consumer
176: Reserved. Akki’s extraction and governance capacity as a substrate a future venture builds on. Registered so nothing optimises against it prematurely; not built.
177: S6
178: The operating organisation and its compliance officer, under threat
179: Continuous, machine-speed detection and response against misuse of the estate and the platform — invisible in legitimate use, incapable of acting unobserved, and proving its own fitness on a standing cadence. Specified in Document 8.
180: 
181: No platform function is proposed, evaluated, or justified except by tracing to one of these five sentences. A function that cannot trace upward is doing the wrong job well — competently solving a problem the platform was never asked to solve.
182: 13  Applications Are Not the Platform
183: An application is anything with an end-user in it, internal or external, and the boundary is mechanical rather than organisational: if a person who is not running the platform touches it, it is an application. It enters through the same governed boundary as any third party, holds a scoped key issued the same way, and is subject to the same custody on every call. There is no privileged path — not for a first-party surface, not for one built by Syni itself.
184: The applications an organisation actually uses — a conversational surface, an executive workspace, a document reviewer, a monitoring feed — are specified fully in Document 5. What is fixed here is only the boundary they all cross the same way.
185: PART VII
Vocabulary and Boundaries
186: 14  Canonical Terms
187: Term
188: Meaning
189: The custody boundary
190: The single point at which anything crosses the perimeter.
191: Estate
192: Everything the organisation holds that an AI system could read.
193: Commission
194: A unit of substantial work: scoped, priced, agreed, executed, recorded.
195: Objective
196: What a commission is for, frozen at admission, immutable for the run.
197: The record
198: The single append-only account of everything that happened.
199: Receipt
200: The independently verifiable record of a single operation.
201: Console
202: A capability grouping on the platform, defined by what can be done there — never by a named person.
203: Application
204: Anything with an end-user in it. Enters through the governed boundary, holds a scoped key.
205: 15  What the Platform Will Not Do
206: It will not answer beyond its evidence. Where material is insufficient, the platform bounds the claim or declines. It does not produce a confident answer with a caveat attached.
207: It will not provide an override. No emergency mode, no administrator bypass, no support-access path that skips custody. A control with an exception is not a control.
208: It will not quote unmeasured figures. Not in an interface, not in a report, not in a proposal generated from it.
209: It will not maintain a second record. No component keeps its own account of what happened, however convenient.
210: It will not place a person in the runtime path. Authority is exercised over rules and exceptions, never over individual operations as a matter of course.
211: It will not know a buyer, a price, or an order. Commerce is application territory. The platform governs access to output and records every egress; it charges nothing and transacts with no one.
212: 16  This Canon
213: This document is the foundation. Eight further documents complete the specification, and each assumes this one.
214: Document
215: Scope
216: 2 — The Conditioned Ideation Faculty
217: CIF in full: the sixth engine, peer to the other five, governing how the system’s own judgements are made, retained, and improved.
218: 3 — Governance Engines
219: Northena and SyniSense in full: the operating model, the two perimeters, the governed-value taxonomy, ceremony, authority, and assurance.
220: 4 — Operating Engines
221: Mtafiti, Targeta, and Solva in full: measurement, targeting, reasoning, the extraction stack, training, and the economics of a run.
222: 5 — Interface Architecture
223: The four consoles, the applications built on them, and the design law that binds every surface.
224: 6 — User Journeys
225: Every journey from founding to steady state, who walks it, and what must be true at each step.
226: 7 — Integration Service and Quality Rulebook
227: The Function & Promise Registry, the contract every application calls, and the discipline the build itself is held to.
228: 8 — The Watch
229: The security authority in full: its promise, doctrines, the two engines and the verdict seam, the response arms, marks and signatures, the mirage, its console, and its parameters.
230: 9 — The Mkondo Charter
231: The orchestration charter: the record matrix — every record class, its single writer, its readers — the task-identity register, and the handoff contracts between the two authorities.
232: 
233: Where any of them appears to contradict this document, this document governs.

# SOURCE: assessment_workspace/canon/unpacked/Akki_Canon_2_CIF.docx
Coordinate: document.xml paragraph in body order, tables included

1: AKKI CANON  ·  DOCUMENT 2 OF 9
2: The Conditioned Ideation Faculty
3: CIF: the sixth engine, peer to Northena, SyniSense, Solva, Mtafiti, and Targeta
4: PART I
The Promise
5: 1  What CIF Is
6: The Conditioned Ideation Faculty governs how the system’s own judgements are made, retained, and improved. It is peer to the platform’s other five engines — Northena, SyniSense, Solva, Mtafiti, Targeta — subordinate to none of them, and its reach is the broadest of any engine’s: it operates across the build loop, the training path, planning, and proposal generation, wherever the system or the people building it render a judgement.
7: CIF is in force across the architecture from adoption. There is no phasing and no activation sequence. Every operation in every engine, from its first occurrence, executes under this specification.
8: 2  The Problem It Answers
9: Working with AI today places the whole quality burden on the human: catching errors, re-supplying lost context, watching good ideas vanish at the end of a session, repeating the same corrections indefinitely. When the human goes quiet, quality degrades invisibly, and two failures compound each other.
10: The first: a correction made once is typically absorbed locally. The specific answer changes; the faulty assumption behind it survives and produces the same class of error again tomorrow. Human corrective effort evaporates instead of compounding, and the same ground is re-litigated indefinitely.
11: The second: an idea rejected because a condition it needed was absent is, after the fact, indistinguishable from an idea rejected because it was simply bad. The record shows a rejection; the reason is lost; and when the missing condition later arrives, nobody revisits the idea. Good work dies of timing.
12: 3  The Promise, Stated Four Ways
13: You stop repeating yourself. A correction made once holds — the class of error is retired, not the instance.
14: Shown confidence can be trusted. When the system is sure, that confidence has visible footing. When it is guessing, it says so before reliance, not after harm.
15: Ideas stop dying with the session. Rejected, deferred, or half-explored ideas wait — alive, with what they need named — and return when their conditions arrive.
16: Insights spread everywhere they apply. A reframe made once rewrites everything the old thinking touched, in one strike, rather than being symptom-hunted for weeks.
17: 
18: The measure this is held to: the human corrects less each cycle for the same or better output. That is the claim made at adoption. Any stronger claim is made only on cycles where it has actually been measured.
19: PART II
The Governing Principle
20: 4  The System This Faculty Serves
21: Akki is an operating system for how agentic workflows integrate with enterprise data estates, how enterprises monetise those estates, and how enterprises build their own models autonomously from them. The architecture is the invention; its components are deliberately not novel — known gates, known engines, known code structures, each with defined, tested conditions of success.
22: 5  The Single-Experiment Principle
23: Experimentation exists at one level only — the assembled system delivering the enterprise promise. Nothing beneath that level is experimental.
24: Every mechanic in the platform is known and parameterisable. It deploys in force with its conditions of success strictly implemented and its quality measured — or its parameters are not yet defined, which is a specification gap to close, never a reason to run it tentatively. No capability is gated on demonstration, observation, trial, or seeing first. Gates in this platform bind spend, the quality of output, or a claim — never existence or force.
25: CIF enters under this principle without qualification. Its mechanics — recording what a verdict rests on, retaining ideas with named conditions, re-evaluating on condition change, second-instance review, threshold monitoring — are proven realities, not a pilot. Construction order carries no epistemic weight: nothing about when a piece of CIF was built bears on whether it is true.
26: 6  Referenced Systems
27: System
28: Role in CIF
29: The coach
30: The human role — teacher, auditor, informer — whose corrections strike the assumptions a verdict rests on, and who alone may adopt a new frame. Constitutionally load-bearing: no configuration of the system operates without this seat filled.
31: Solva-pattern validation
32: The platform’s reasoning discipline, applied as validator: claims stated only at their evidence class, a conclusion’s support meeting its bar, contradiction surfaced rather than averaged away, a refusal naming its reason and what would satisfy it. CIF’s own claims are evaluated by this discipline exactly as any answer is.
33: The Critic Seam
34: The standing quality layer for worker output, specified in Document 7. Its rubric is compiled from the coach’s correction history; CIF’s pre-ship checklist extends that rubric to idea selection.
35: The independence rule
36: A reviewing instance must differ genuinely from what it reviews — a different base model, or a materially different context shape. Same-base, same-context review shares blind spots and adds cost without adding detection.
37: Run telemetry
38: The platform’s per-run measurement stream. CIF’s monitoring parameters bind to named fields in it.
39: The Watch
40: The security authority, Document 8. Its detection findings are a source CIF may metabolise like any other ground reality; its drills operate under this faculty's own permanent bound — the Watch never certifies its own framing, and its fitness is counted in demonstrated firings, never self-graded value.
41: Engine walls
42: The standing constitutional limits every engine operates inside — a planner’s learning never widens what an objective may reach; a critic detects and never decides. CIF operates inside these walls everywhere it acts.
43: PART III
Vocabulary
44: 7  Definitions
45: Term
46: Meaning
47: Idea
48: Any candidate the faculty evaluates or picks — a proposal, a technique, a product move, an interpretation, a training choice, an ordering decision, a selection among alternatives.
49: Verdict
50: An evaluated position on an idea — adopt, reject, rank, or defer — rendered against a stated goal.
51: Manifest
52: The recorded set of load-bearing assumptions a verdict or pick rests on, each entry classed fact, recalled, or inferred, elicited by one question: what, if false, flips this?
53: Flip
54: A verdict reversing because information struck a manifest entry — whether the information newly arrived, or was already held and only newly attended to.
55: Frame
56: A thinking structure shared across many verdicts — the shape of the calculation, not a variable inside it.
57: Frame signature
58: One of three patterns indicating a frame, not a single verdict, is wrong: cascade — one strike flips many verdicts at once; absorption — the same correction class is patched repeatedly while the underlying pattern persists; misfit — information reduces to no existing structure, contradicts several standing positions, or resists the manifest probe.
59: Metabolisation
60: Complete digestion of an adopted frame across everything the overturned structure touched.
61: Archive state
62: One of four states every evaluated idea lands in: adopted, not-yet-conditioned (with its missing condition named), unverified-provisional (no verdict returned), or superseded. Failure is a state an idea can hold, never an identity it acquires.
63: Cycle
64: One working period between owner touchpoints — the measurement unit for the faculty’s own parameters.
65: PART IV
Core Practice
66: 8  Manifests
67: Every shipped verdict and every idea pick carries its manifest. An unmanifested verdict is a defect, not an oversight to note and move past.
68: Entries are evidence-classed. A verdict resting on inferred entries states its provisionality where it ships, not in a place a reader would have to go looking for it.
69: A selection records why the winner ranked first. The pick carries its own manifest, so selection bias is examinable rather than invisible.
70: Silence is a data state, never confirmation. A response receiving no verdict from a human is archived as unverified-provisional. It is not counted as agreed.
71: 9  The Living Archive
72: Every evaluated idea lands in an archive state the same cycle it was evaluated in. Nothing exits silently.
73: A rejection for circumstantial reasons names the missing condition specifically enough that its arrival is recognisable — not "not ready," but what, precisely, would make it ready.
74: Every entry carries rent: a review-by date and a re-qualification budget. An expired entry is re-qualified or superseded, never left to sit.
75: A resurfaced idea re-enters with zero inherited credibility. It is a new candidate, fully re-qualified against the current goal, not restored to whatever standing it once had.
76: 
77: Re-qualification is paper-first. Re-scoring under changed assumptions precedes compute; simulation runs only where the paper verdict warrants the spend.
78: 10  Selection Quality
79: 10.1  The naivety pass
80: On demand, or when a workstream stagnates, candidates may be re-qualified with their inherited constraints deliberately struck — "known not to work," "nobody does it this way," "too simple to matter" — while ground-truth constraints remain untouched: law, physics, custody, budget. Every struck constraint receives a short evidence brief answering why consensus holds it, presented for a human call. The pass never classifies autonomously, and a survivor never ships without its autopsy attached.
81: 10.2  The pre-ship checklist
82: The coach’s correction history is maintained as a readable checklist of known failure classes, applied to picks and verdicts before they ship. The checklist is replay-only: it applies known classes and never claims to cover novel ones, and it enters the Critic Seam’s standing rubric as an amendment rather than a parallel mechanism.
83: PART V
The Frame Lifecycle
84: 11  Detection
85: The three frame signatures are watched continuously from the manifest corpus, as standing practice rather than a periodic review. An observed signature escalates as a frame-candidate finding in the same cycle it is observed — not noted for later.
86: The faculty detects. It never adopts a frame on the strength of its own signature.
87: 12  Origination
88: A new frame enters only through the origination port: the coach, ground reality observed in deployment, or a genuinely outside reviewer. This seat is constitutionally load-bearing and is not a temporary limitation awaiting some future automation — it is permanent in every configuration of the system.
89: 13  Metabolisation
90: When a frame is adopted, four things follow, in order, and none is optional.
91: The adoption record names the overturned structure — the shape of thinking that was wrong — not merely the new statement that replaces it.
92: Every archived verdict whose manifest touches the overturned structure re-qualifies on paper. The sweep completes before any new verdict issues on the affected class.
93: The adopted frame enters the manifest vocabulary, so every subsequent verdict declares its position relative to it.
94: Closure holds when the absorption signature for that correction class has been quiet for three cycles. A noisy signature rules the metabolisation incomplete, and the sweep runs again.
95: 
96: A frame-adoption commit without its sweep record fails its own build check — the same discipline applied to a function landing with no registry row.
97: PART VI
Monitoring
98: 14  Three Capabilities
99: Three monitoring capabilities operate under defined parameters that govern how each runs. None is an entry condition for the faculty; all three are measured like every other quality parameter.
100: Capability
101: What it does
102: Condition watchers
103: Automated monitoring of an archived idea’s named conditions, bound only to conditions that resolve to named live telemetry fields. An unbindable condition carries a rent-date human review instead. A fired watcher re-queues its idea as a candidate; it never adopts on its own.
104: Cascade detection
105: Multi-flip identification across the manifest corpus, escalating as a frame-candidate finding under the same rule as any other detected signature.
106: Adversarial manifest elicitation
107: Second-instance interrogation of shipped verdicts, satisfying the independence rule — a genuinely different reviewer, never a same-base echo.
108: PART VII
The Permanent Bound
109: 15  Self-Certification Is Closed by Construction
110: No parameter set exists whose truth would license the faculty to validate its own framing.
111: Any evidence the faculty produced for its own independence would be evaluated inside the frame that evidence was meant to certify — which is not evidence at all. A proposal for such a path is not a feature request; it is an exhibit of the exact failure this bound exists to prevent, and it is rejected on sight rather than debated on its merits.
112: The function self-certification pretends to offer is instead held by a composite of three things acting together: the faculty detects and metabolises; the coach originates and ratifies; Solva-pattern validation keeps the evidence honest throughout. The loop closes through the coach seat. It never closes around it.
113: PART VIII
Operative and Quality Parameters
114: 16  Operative Parameters — Held Every Cycle
115: Parameter
116: Requirement
117: Manifest coverage
118: 100% of shipped verdicts and picks carry a manifest. FACT.
119: Archive completeness
120: Every evaluated idea lands in a state the same cycle it was evaluated. FACT.
121: Escalation latency
122: A frame signature escalates in the cycle it is observed. FACT.
123: Metabolisation execution
124: The four-step sweep triggers within one cycle of adoption; it completes before new verdicts issue on the affected class. FACT.
125: Rent collection
126: Archive review-by dates are honoured; expired entries are re-qualified or superseded, never left standing. FACT.
127: 17  Quality Parameters — Measured
128: A breach of any of these acts on CIF’s own practice. It is never resolved by relaxing product work elsewhere.
129: Parameter
130: Threshold
131: On breach
132: Promise metric
133: Owner-confirmed repeat-class corrections decline across cycles.
134: Flat or rising for two consecutive cycles triggers a CIF review.
135: Manifest hit-rate
136: When a flip occurs, the struck assumption was already in the manifest, ≥ 70% DEFAULT.
137: Below bar, the elicitation protocol is repaired.
138: Provisional honesty
139: Zero instances of inferred-footing content shipped into the register of fact.
140: One instance is a finding on record, not a rounding error.
141: Metabolisation closure
142: The absorption signature for an adopted frame is quiet within 3 cycles DEFAULT.
143: Noisy — the metabolisation is ruled incomplete and the sweep re-runs.
144: Overhead ceiling
145: CIF practice consumes no more than an owner-set share of cycle budget.
146: Breach shrinks CIF. Product work is never the variable that absorbs it.
147: False-escalation rate
148: Frame candidates later ruled non-events, ≤ 30% DEFAULT.
149: Above bar, detection thresholds tighten.
150: 
151: Values marked DEFAULT are operating constants — cheap to correct, revised on evidence at a cycle boundary, never mid-cycle, and never requiring this specification to be reopened.
152: PART IX
Enforcement
153: 18  How This Is Enforced
154: CIF uses the platform’s standing enforcement vehicles. It introduces no new ones — a faculty that needed its own enforcement machinery would itself be the kind of structural proliferation the platform’s doctrine forbids.
155: Mechanism
156: Enforcement
157: Manifests
158: Schema-required fields on every verdict-bearing artifact. An unmanifested verdict is rejected at submission — the standing format-gate pattern, checking form only.
159: The archive
160: Entries are append-only ledger rows. A standing query surfaces any evaluated-but-unarchived idea as a finding.
161: Evidence classing
162: CIF’s own claims are evaluated by the assertion boundary exactly as any answer is — no separate leniency for the faculty that watches everyone else.
163: Metabolisation
164: A frame-adoption commit lacking its sweep record fails its build check, the same pattern used when a function lands with no registry row.
165: Rent and monitoring
166: Review dates and watcher precision are queryable fields; expiries and breaches surface through the same standing-query machinery as everything else.
167: Selection defects
168: Enter the Critic Seam’s rubric as a named amendment class, not a parallel checklist.
169: One boundary is stated plainly because it is easy to miss: live conversational reasoning — a judgement spoken before it becomes an artifact — is governed as behavioural discipline with a mechanical audit backstop, not intercepted mid-thought. Everything that lands is gated. The ephemeral layer is audited, not policed in flight.
170: PART X
Governance
171: 19  Standing Rules
172: CIF’s yield is counted in owner-confirmed catches only. Self-graded value is inadmissible — a faculty cannot be the judge of its own usefulness.
173: No CIF output may claim coach-independence, in any configuration, permanently. The origination port is load-bearing every time, not only until some future maturity.
174: CIF is entry #1 in its own archive: manifested, rented, and revisable under exactly the rules it applies to everything else.
175: Paper precedes compute; detection never decides; engine walls hold everywhere CIF operates — with no exception carved out for the faculty itself.
176: 20  What CIF Does Not Do
177: Stated explicitly, because a mechanism this reach-heavy invites scope creep by default.
178: It does not originate frames, adjudicate its own framing, or replace the coach seat. Any output claiming otherwise is exhibiting the exact failure the permanent bound exists to prevent.
179: It does not block work, hold veto authority, or acquire a review layer above itself. There is no meta-CIF, and proposing one is itself a frame-absorption finding.
180: It does not promise a zero residual. The assumption that was never recorded is the one that flips unseen — which is exactly why human challenge remains load-bearing, and why the faculty’s value is stated as halving the residual, never eliminating it.

# SOURCE: assessment_workspace/canon/unpacked/Akki_Canon_3_Governance_Engines.docx
Coordinate: document.xml paragraph in body order, tables included

1: AKKI CANON  ·  DOCUMENT 3 OF 9
2: Akki Governance Engines
3: Northena and SyniSense: direction, boundary, entitlement, the two perimeters, governed values, ceremony, and assurance
4: PART I
Two Axes, One Discipline
5: 1  Scope
6: This document specifies two of the platform’s six engines in full: Northena, which governs direction, and SyniSense, which governs the boundary. A third axis, depth, belongs to Solva and is specified in Document 4, because the component that reasons sits inside the extraction path rather than beside it. The three never collapse into one another — a governor performing another’s function would create a single point at which a run could be admitted, bounded, and asserted by the same logic, with no separate check left to catch it.
7: Axis
8: Governor
9: The question it answers
10: Direction
11: Northena
12: Is this run still in scope, and is it done? Answered for every run, run after run, and recorded.
13: Boundary
14: SyniSense
15: May this data cross this access point? Answered for every outbound model call, every egress.
16: Depth
17: Solva
18: Is the reasoning sound, and does the output assert within its defensibility? — Document 4.
19: 2  The Accountability Standard
20: Every run must be answerable deterministically. Admitted because these fields were valid. Gated in because scope membership held. Stopped because this condition was met. Refused because this rule fired. "Admitted because the model scored it highly enough" is the unauditable outcome this standard exists to prevent.
21: The governing artifact is frozen before a run begins, so the reason for every decision made against it is fixed and inspectable after the fact. The record is a contract, not a log — versioned, append-only, and closed on every run. Refusals and drops are recorded exactly as successes are.
22: A run with no closed record is an incomplete, non-auditable run, and is invalid. This is not a reporting preference; it is the condition under which the platform’s central claim — that any run can be proved lawful and accountable on demand — remains true.
23: PART II
Northena — The Direction Governor
24: 3  What Northena Is
25: Northena keeps every run on-objective, brings it to a defined stop, and writes the durable, audit-grade record of how the run was directed. It answers two questions, run after run: is this still in scope, and is this run done — and records both answers in the Ledger. It does not extract, and it does not reason.
26: It governs two services through two artifacts: a first-contact service through a Portfolio Mandate, and a day-to-day service through an Objective Request. It governs the run’s lifecycle; it does not define what those artifacts contain.
27: 4  Deterministic by Construction
28: No machine-learning model, no learned weights, no adaptive behaviour. Trustworthy as a governor because it cannot be otherwise.
29: Northena’s behaviour varies enormously from run to run — different objectives admitted, different scopes gated, different stops reached — but every part of that variation is driven by the frozen governing artifact it reads, never by Northena itself adapting. It is dynamic the way a thermostat is dynamic: behaviour changes completely as the setpoint changes, while the mechanism neither learns nor infers. The moment a direction governor adjusts gating from past runs, or infers scope probabilistically, it stops being auditable — and auditability is its entire reason to exist.
30: Determinism is checked structurally, not by review. No Northena module imports a machine-learning library or a learned component, and an import assertion enforcing this runs in continuous integration. Where a decision genuinely needs judgement, Northena invokes the depth governor through an opaque handle and acts deterministically on the value returned; it never reads that governor’s internals and never performs inference itself.
31: 5  The Four Stages
32: In day-to-day service the stages run as a loop. Admit freezes the request; Gate routes the objective or a sub-objective warm, fresh, or refused; execution and reasoning return any gaps that remain unmet; in-scope gaps are re-tasked and out-of-scope gaps are logged and dropped; Converge stops on the done-condition or the budget. Each answered objective densifies what the next pass can serve warm.
33: Stage
34: Does
35: Decision is
36: Admit
37: Compiles a raw intent into a frozen governing artifact, validates it deterministically, and freezes it atomically.
38: A validity check — presence, completeness, membership.
39: Gate
40: Checks whether a sub-objective falls within the frozen artifact’s declared scope, and routes on the result.
41: Strict set-membership.
42: Converge
43: Decides whether the run is done.
44: A threshold check against the done-condition or the budget.
45: Ledger
46: Writes the durable, audit-grade record of the run.
47: None — it records, deterministically.
48: What happens inside "execution and reasoning" — the two services that build the asset and serve the objective, and the two named seams between them — is specified in full in Document 4 §34.1–34.3.
49: 6  Admit
50: Admit compiles, validates, and freezes. Where compilation needs judgement — resolving an ambiguous scope, setting a preservation depth or a floor — Admit invokes the depth governor and freezes the value it returns. The judgement is the reasoner’s; the freeze is Northena’s alone.
51: 6.1  The validity sequence
52: Five deterministic checks run in order, each with its own refusal reason. A failure at any point refuses the admission and writes the reason; no downstream stage runs.
53: Check
54: Refusal reason on failure
55: A lawful basis is present
56: missing_lawful_basis
57: The acting party holds a current declaration
58: missing_declaration
59: The artifact is complete against its required fields
60: incomplete_artifact
61: The declared scope resolves against the Registry
62: scope_unresolved
63: The defensibility floor is well-formed
64: floor_malformed
65: 
66: Lawful basis is enforced at Admit, before any extraction. Purpose limitation is an admission property, not a downstream filter — a run with no lawful basis never starts, so no material is ever touched under an unstated basis.
67: No actor enters undeclared. An agent is admitted against a declared objective with its capabilities and risks stated; a person is admitted against a declared role and interests. The declaration is frozen with the run's artifact, and it is the baseline every later question of intent is measured against — the Watch reconciles realised behaviour against it, per Document 8, and re-declaration through this same admission path is the legitimate exit from honest change. An undeclared actor operates under the default-restrictive envelope and nothing wider.
68: 6.2  The freeze
69: The freeze is atomic, and the artifact is immutable for the run. A changed intent is a new admission, never an edit of a live one. The frozen artifact carries its type and identity, its version, the scope set Gate will test membership against, the defensibility floor, the done-condition, the budget, and the lawful basis. Admission writes the Ledger — both admission paths, the internal work order and the external request, write a row carrying the artifact reference and the lawful-basis reference.
70: 6.3  Two admission paths
71: An external request arrives complete or is refused; a request missing any required field is refused with the validation envelope, and it carries an idempotency key so a retried submission neither double-commissions nor double-charges. A work order cannot freeze until the shaping conversation completes the envelope — the wizard is where the envelope is filled; Admit is where it is checked and frozen.
72: 7  Gate
73: Gate tests whether a sub-objective falls within the scope the frozen artifact declares, and routes on the result. Scope is a defined set; Gate checks membership, and nothing else.
74: Ambiguous membership is a compilation defect, not a Gate decision. If a scope is ambiguous, Admit should have resolved it by invoking the reasoner and freezing the answer. Gate does not decide membership by inference, and no inferential path exists in it.
75: Routing
76: When, and what is recorded
77: Refuse
78: Not in scope. A governed refusal, logged with reason out_of_scope. Recorded, never silently dropped.
79: Warm serve
80: In scope and already converged — servable from qualified intelligence already held. Answered synchronously.
81: Fresh extract
82: In scope and unconverged — requires extraction. Returns the async contract.
83: The warm/fresh determination is the same fork the objective’s execution branches on. It is made once, at the boundary, by a membership test against a frozen set and a convergence check — never re-derived downstream.
84: 8  Converge
85: Converge decides termination on two conditions fixed in the frozen artifact, both threshold checks. There is no learned stopping: done-condition met terminates as success; budget exhausted terminates on budget; neither continues.
86: Northena owns the halt. The depth governor may report that it cannot reason further soundly — that report is an input Converge acts on, but the stop decision and its record belong to Northena alone. A component that could stop a run without Northena recording why would put a termination outside the audit surface entirely.
87: The budget is a hard stop. A run halts at its ceiling and nothing past it is billed. This is what makes an open-ended extraction commissionable at all: exposure is bounded at commit, by a number the commissioner set, enforced by the governor rather than by the executor that could be tempted to keep going.
88: 9  The Ledger
89: The Ledger is Northena’s memory and the platform’s primary audit surface for direction. Because the compliance officer and the operator both read it directly, its row shape is a contract rather than an internal log: frozen, versioned, append-only, and closed on every run.
90: 9.1  What it records
91: Admission and its outcome; every Gate routing and its reason; every refusal or drop; the convergence decision; and the absorbed defensibility stamp-audit entries produced elsewhere in the run.
92: 9.2  The row
93: Field
94: What it carries
95: run_id
96: One run has one closed ledger.
97: trace_id
98: Joins the row to the units it produced and to the trace lenses that explain them.
99: stage
100: admit · gate · converge
101: decision
102: admitted · refused · warm · fresh · terminate_success · terminate_budget · continue
103: reason
104: A deterministic reason string — the same inputs produce the same string, always.
105: artifact_ref
106: The governing artifact: type, identity, version.
107: lawful_basis_ref
108: The basis under which the run was admitted.
109: stamp_audit
110: An optional absorbed side-channel entry, joined by unit and trace identity.
111: at
112: Timestamp.
113: 9.3  Append only
114: The writer exposes append and nothing else. No update path and no delete path exist within the retention window. A correction is a new entry referencing what it corrects, never an edit of what was written. Out-of-scope and refused items are recorded — a system that drops what it declined cannot show what it declined, and the ability to show that is a substantial part of what the record is for.
115: 9.4  Why the stamp-audit field is permissive
116: The absorbed side-channel is deliberately untyped, and this is a design decision rather than a lapse. It is what lets artefacts from engines built later — boundary emissions, measurement stamps, trace correlation, gate receipts, refusal envelopes — be absorbed into a ledger row without mutating the frozen contract the row itself represents. Typing it would harden it into a mutation surface and lose the property entirely.
117: The consequence is worth stating on its own: the Ledger’s semantic reach can grow across future engines while its contract stays byte-identical. The permissiveness is guarded by a snapshot test, so the decision cannot be quietly reversed later. Unit and audit stay in separate envelopes with separate lifecycles — the stamp-audit is joined by unit and trace identity rather than embedded in the unit, so an output and its audit trail can be retained, exported, and expired independently of one another.
118: 10  The Determinism Boundary, Enforced as Code
119: The depth governor is reached only through an opaque handle. Northena’s orchestration cannot read its internals and cannot reason itself; it requests a judgement — resolve this scope, set this preservation vector — and acts deterministically on the value returned.
120: Three dependency rules, each enforced by import assertion rather than by convention:
121: No module imports a machine-learning library or a learned component. Determinism is checked structurally, not by review.
122: The state machine reaches the reasoner only through the handle. No internal access, and no inference performed in place.
123: The ledger writer exposes append only. No update or delete path exists on the writer at all.
124: 11  Northena’s Invariants
125: Binding. Any implementation that violates one of these is incorrect regardless of what it otherwise does correctly.
126: Northena is deterministic: no model, no learned weights, no adaptive behaviour. Its dynamism is entirely a function of the frozen governing artifact.
127: Any decision requiring inference belongs to the depth governor, invoked through an opaque handle, acted on deterministically.
128: Every run is governed by exactly one frozen artifact, admitted by Northena, carrying a valid lawful basis.
129: The frozen artifact is immutable for the run. A changed intent is a new admission.
130: Gate is strict set-membership. Ambiguous membership is a compilation defect resolved at Admit, never a Gate-time judgement.
131: Northena owns the halt. No run closes without a closed, audit-grade ledger.
132: The Ledger is contract-grade: versioned, snapshot-asserted, append-only, immutable within the retention window.
133: Out-of-scope and refused items are recorded, never silently dropped.
134: Northena governs direction only. Boundary belongs to SyniSense; depth belongs to Solva. The axes never collapse.
135: PART III
SyniSense — The Boundary Governor
136: 12  What SyniSense Is
137: SyniSense governs the boundary: whether data may cross an access point. It is the single chokepoint through which every outbound model call transits, the enforcement point of the de-identify→invoke→re-identify custody chain, the class-honesty guard on every governed response, and the closer of the refusal taxonomy across the whole layered governance surface.
138: Its scope is every model surface, not language alone. Perception providers — speech recognition, vision — route through it as well, so material crossing a model boundary carries the same custody and the same receipt whatever its modality.
139: 13  The Chokepoint
140: One function is the only place a model is invoked. Everything else that wants a model calls that function.
141: The invariant is not that developers should route through it; the invariant is that a build fails if any other module imports the model client. Custody enforced at an orchestrator is custody a new call path can miss. Custody enforced at the invocation itself cannot be missed, because there is no other invocation to miss it through — the chokepoint pattern places the guarantee at the narrowest point in the system rather than at the most convenient one.
142: 13.1  The sequence
143: Provider selection. Resolved from configuration. Where the key is issued in sandbox mode, a deterministic fixture provider serves in its place — a declared, labelled, non-production behaviour, not an inferred fallback. Under a production credential with no provider configured, the call is refused rather than served from a fixture, because a synthetic response returned as if governed would violate the platform’s own rule that a claim and its class are never separable.
144: De-identify. The inbound payload transits the de-identifier, which strips identifiers to placeholder tokens and records the mapping in a per-request custody envelope.
145: *Between de-identification and invocation sits the Watch's input seat, specified in Document 8: every payload bound for a model is scored for hostility and provenance before the call is made. The seat is a sensor and a graded gate under the Watch's own authority; it adds no second custody chain, and its verdicts land in the record like every other emission at this boundary.*
146: Invoke with metering. The call is made and per-call metering is emitted to the telemetry stream.
147: Re-identify. Output transits the re-identifier against the same custody envelope. An unmatched token raises rather than passing through — a placeholder that cannot be resolved is an error, never a value.
148: Grounding gate. A per-sentence anchor map is enforced on composed output.
149: Class-honesty check. A structural scan bounds the governed-response boundary.
150: Trust receipt. Every invocation writes one.
151: 14  The Custody Chain
152: De-identify, invoke, re-identify, per request, with the mapping held in a per-request envelope that does not outlive the call. Tenant-scoped entity resolution supplies the entities that must be recognised for a given instance, so de-identification is never limited to what a general recogniser happens to detect.
153: The envelope is per request and does not outlive it. A mapping that persisted beyond the call would be a standing re-identification key — precisely the artefact the chain exists to avoid ever creating.
154: 15  Purpose Enforcement
155: Purpose enforcement is a property of the chokepoint, distributed across four mechanisms rather than concentrated in one validator a caller could route around.
156: Data-blind prompts. Templates cannot leak purpose-scoped data, because by construction they contain none.
157: The grounding gate as proof of purpose alignment. A claim that is ungrounded is refused; an output that cannot be anchored to material within scope does not compose.
158: The closed refusal taxonomy. The refusal modules exhaustively enumerate every governed-purpose refusal path, so a purpose violation resolves to a named refusal rather than an ad-hoc one.
159: Advisory-marker discipline. Non-fact classes carry markers at write time and at render time, so an advisory output can never be consumed as a governed one.
160: 16  Key Custody and Receipts
161: A trust receipt is emitted per invocation — the key-custody envelope: evidence that the call happened, under what custody, without exposing the credential itself. The credential is never logged; its presence surfaces only as a boolean probe at module load, and its absence selects the sandbox fixture path. Nothing downstream branches on the credential’s value.
162: Two custody pathways exist — the synthesis path through the chokepoint, and the perception path through the perception router — and both emit receipts; neither bypasses the other.
163: 17  Grounding and the Model Ladder
164: Grounding is proven, not asserted. A sentence that cannot be anchored to material is not a weaker sentence — it is a refusal.
165: Composed output carries a per-sentence anchor map, and the gate enforces it. Every model-reaching composition carries a lower-rung fallback — the mechanical composer is preserved byte-identical as that fallback — because a system whose highest rung has no floor beneath it has a single point at which output quality becomes unbounded. Advisory outputs are marked twice: at write time by the producing service, and at render time by the surface, because a marker enforced only at write can be dropped by a renderer that never knew it was load-bearing.
166: 18  SyniSense’s Invariants
167: The chokepoint function is the only module invoking the model client anywhere in the codebase, enforced by negative-scan test.
168: The contracts anchoring the boundary are frozen; a change to them is a seal event requiring explicit ratification.
169: Every model invocation transits de-identify → invoke → re-identify. No orchestrator path is authorised to skip it.
170: The refusal taxonomy is closed. No ad-hoc refusal path exists anywhere.
171: Any composition reaching the highest rung is paired with a lower-rung fallback, preserved byte-identical.
172: Prompt template files are negative-scanned against tenant data on every build.
173: PART IV
The Two Perimeters
174: 19  Inner and Outer
175: Delivery has two perimeters, and they enforce differently because they carry different risk. The inner gate governs the live path, where governance is enforced per call. The outer gate governs extract — material leaving as a hand-over that cannot be recalled once it has gone.
176: Perimeter
177: Governs
178: Enforcement mode
179: Inner gate
180: The live path: queries against a standing service, per-response answers.
181: Per call. Key scope enforced server-side. Class carried inline on every response.
182: Outer gate
183: Extract: datasets, artefacts, anything handed over.
184: Once, at export. Rights, irreversibility, cumulative disclosure, licence issue, receipt minting.
185: 20  The Outer Gate
186: Five checks run before anything leaves, and each is a distinct failure mode rather than a stage of one check.
187: Rights. Does the licence class of the material permit this delivery, to this recipient, for this purpose?
188: Irreversibility. Can what is leaving be reversed into material the organisation may not release? This is why raw media sits out of scope for direct export — irreversibility cannot be honoured on it.
189: Cumulative disclosure. Would this export, combined with everything that has already left, reconstruct what neither export alone would?
190: Licence issue. The terms under which the recipient may use what they receive, attached to the deliverable itself.
191: Receipt. The fact and the fingerprint of the transform — never anything that could aid reversal.
192: 
193: Nothing partial egresses, including on cancellation. A cancelled run is still ledgered, and the partial output does not leave — partial egress would make the perimeter probabilistic rather than absolute.
194: 21  Cumulative Disclosure
195: Single-packet refusal is live from the outset. The cumulative arm across sessions is a closed seam awaiting its thresholds — a deliberate, recorded state, not an omission.
196: The arm evaluates three thresholds across repeated exports: a minimum group size, a minimum distinct-value count within a group, and a cumulative privacy budget. Individually clean egresses that recombine to reconstruct identities are refused when any threshold is crossed or the budget is exhausted.
197: The arm is closed by construction, not by configuration accident. The admission function returns false whenever any of the three values is unset or unparseable, so it cannot half-open.
198: Opening it is a compliance decision: the thresholds are set, the arm begins admitting, and a new refusal reason path becomes reachable for the first time. From that moment the system begins persisting egress fingerprints across sessions — a material change in what the platform retains, which is why the decision belongs to the compliance officer rather than to routine configuration.
199: PART V
Governed Values
200: 22  The Four Classes
201: Four classes of governed value share one record shape and one surface, and they differ in change authority, change velocity, and verification method — which is what makes them genuinely different objects rather than one object wearing four labels. Treating them alike is how a weekly operational update ends up waiting on a multi-day ceremony, and how a platform invariant ends up editable at runtime.
202: Class
203: Develop
204: Deploy
205: Rails
206: Authored as code and contract.
207: Only through a build; never runtime-editable.
208: Rules
209: Defined with type, bounds, a recommended default.
210: Set at setup, locked at approval.
211: Engine settings
212: Declared with their conditions of success.
213: Pinned per engine version.
214: Registries
215: Schema defined once; rules reference by version.
216: Initial load at setup or first upload.
217: 
218: Class
219: Operate
220: Verify
221: Rails
222: Not operable — observable only.
223: A hard-fail check; a rail without one does not exist.
224: Rules
225: Propose, counter-sign, wait, apply, certificate.
226: Live test packs, per rule.
227: Engine settings
228: Changed by engineers, through versioned deployment.
229: The version’s evaluation verdict.
230: Registries
231: Upload, validate, difference, confirm, version.
232: A validation report and a live probe on drawn entries.
233: 22.1  Entitlement Rules
234: Rules govern more than custody and retention. They extend, by the identical mechanism, to who inside the organisation may see what — a distinct concern from what may leave the perimeter, and one this platform adopts a well-established model for rather than inventing a new one.
235: Entitlement is attribute-based access control: a decision made by matching attributes of the requester against attributes of the content, expressed as a rule and enforced the same way every other rule is. Role-based access — a decision by role alone — is the common simplified case, not a separate mechanism.
