41: An application is anything with an end-user in it, internal or external, and the boundary that decides this is mechanical rather than organisational.
42: If a person who is not running the platform touches a surface, that surface is an application, and it enters through the Integration Console like any external party. Internal privilege is a key class, never a back door, and it is enforced server-side on every call.
43: The platform’s own conversational surface — specified in full in Part VIII — is a reference application, not a platform surface. It consumes the platform through an Integration-Console-issued key and demonstrates the contract every future application follows. It is one implementation of asking, never the definition of it.
44: Commerce is an application layer in its entirety. Buying is a commercial act performed in a separate sales product; no buyer ever touches a console or the extraction machinery directly. A buyer is an end-user of that commercial product, which itself holds a scoped external key and passes the same governed boundary as any third party. There is no privileged path anywhere in this design.
45: 4  The Three Motions
46: Surfaces follow human motions, not platform modules. Three distinct motions exist, performed by different people at different moments, and they are never collapsed into one surface.
47: Motion
48: Performed by
49: Character
50: Verification
51: The compliance owner, continuously.
52: Checking that governance holds — reading the record, proving a run, watching for what has drifted.
53: Exploration
54: Business users, continuously.
55: Finding out what the estate would support before committing budget to extracting it.
56: Consumption
57: Anyone with a question.
58: Asking, and receiving an answer that carries its own defensibility.
59: 
60: Every screen belongs to exactly one motion. A screen built to serve two masters serves neither — it is the reason a design ends up with a verification page that half-explores, or an exploration page a compliance owner cannot actually trust.
61: Day-zero success is both the estate manager’s and the compliance owner’s home dashboards live and populated at the close of onboarding, simultaneously. The test objectives run at commissioning exist to verify the instance’s own parameters, not to produce value — day-zero mining is verification, never a demonstration staged for its own sake.
62: PART II
The Visual System
63: 5  The Palette
64: Values are fixed. Every colour on every surface is one of these; there are no ad-hoc values and no per-surface variants.

122: Oxblood is reserved for refusal and destruction. It never marks emphasis, branding, or a call to action. A person who sees oxblood must be able to conclude, without reading, that something was refused or is irreversible.
123: 6  State Colour
124: State
125: Token
126: Rendering

136: Fault — something broke

138: Neutral. A dashed 1px border, a retry affordance, and no colour from the refusal family.
139: Not yet measured
140: --ink-3
141: Hatched fill at 6% opacity. Present in every estate view, at full visual weight.
142: 
143: The fault rendering shares no colour, border treatment, or component with the refused rendering. A person must be able to tell at a glance whether the system said no or the system broke — the two mean entirely different things about what happened to their request.
144: 7  Typography
145: display   Georgia, serif                  — headings, artifact titles
146: body      system-ui, -apple-system, sans  — all interface text
147: mono      ui-monospace, Menlo, monospace  — identifiers, digests, receipts, contract views
148: 
149: Role
150: Size
151: Weight
152: Use

154: 24px
155: 700
156: Surface title. One per surface.
157: h2
158: 18px
159: 600
160: Section within a surface.
161: body
162: 13px
163: 400
164: Default interface text.
165: body-lg
166: 14px
167: 400
168: Prose, refusals, plain-language rule statements.
169: label
170: 11px
171: 600
172: Field labels, column headers.
173: micro
174: 10px
175: 500
176: Timestamps, counts, measurement class marks.
177: mono
178: 12px

180: Identifiers, hashes, receipts, contract fields.
181: 
182: An identifier, digest, or any value a person may need to copy or compare renders in mono. A trace identity in a proportional face cannot be compared by eye and invites a transcription error.
183: 8  Layout
184: reading measure    720px    prose, refusals, rule statements
185: content width      1280px   dense console surfaces, tables
186: panel width        380px    evidence panels, detail drawers
187: 
188: Layout
189: Structure
190: Used by
191: Register
192: 1fr 300px
193: A list with a detail panel — sources, applications, rules.
194: Ledger
195: Full width, tabular
196: Dense records — the respect record, the violation record, usage.
197: Wizard
198: 720px, centred
199: One decision at a time — commissioning, ceremony, registration.
200: Board
201: Repeat(3, 1fr)
202: Equal-weight cards — opportunity briefs, held items.
203: 
204: Prose never exceeds 720px regardless of viewport. A refusal or a plain-language rule statement rendered at full content width is harder to read, and is treated as a layout defect, not a matter of taste.
205: 9  Components
206: 9.1  Figure
207: The only permitted way to render a number that describes the estate, an artefact, or a measurement.
208: measured    1,284
209: estimated   ≈ 1,300 (est.)
210: unmeasured  — not measured
211: 
212: A number describing the estate, an artefact, or a measurement never renders as bare text. Its measurement class is part of the figure, not a footnote beside it.
213: 9.2  The refusal card
214: ┌─ 3px left rule, oxblood ─────────────────────────────┐
215: │  Not to the standard you asked for.                  │
216: │                                                       │
217: │  Accept as recorded statement · Narrow the objective │
218: │  · Lower the standard                                 │
219: │                                                       │
220: │  A refusal is the system keeping its promise.        │
221: └─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
222: 
223: The title, the three actions, and the footer are binding copy, reproduced verbatim wherever this card renders. They are never paraphrased, shortened, or restyled for a particular surface.
224: 9.3  The agent-assumed chip
225: Agent assumed — confirm or change
226: 
227: Amber, 11px label weight, attached to any field an agent filled rather than the person. It survives to the commit review unchanged — a value that was agent-assumed at draft time is never quietly reclassified as user-supplied by the act of confirming the screen it appears on.
228: 9.4  The four designed states
229: Four conditions recur throughout the product, and each has a deliberate treatment rather than an empty space where content would otherwise be.
230: State
231: Treatment
232: Not yet measured
233: Hatched fill, --ink-3. Present at true visual weight — never smaller, never omitted from a filtered view.
234: Coverage gap
235: Named specifically: what was asked, what is missing, an offer to file it as work.
236: Refused
237: The refusal card, above.
238: Dormant capability
239: Visible and named, with what would activate it — never hidden as though the capability did not exist.
240: PART III
The Surface Taxonomy
241: 10  Four Consoles, Capability-Defined
242: The platform has exactly five consoles, defined by what can be done on them rather than by a named person. A single person may work several consoles in a day; a console is a set of capabilities, not a job title, and no capability is deleted by this taxonomy — anything that once sat under a named role is rehomed to the console where it actually belongs.
243: Console
244: What it is for
245: Extraction
246: Commissioning and watching the work that turns raw estate material into governed intelligence.
247: Compliance
248: Proving that governance holds, and controlling the rules it holds by.
249: Integration
250: Provisioning and administering every application that consumes the platform.
251: Administration
252: Instance founding, roles, operational economics, and the second signature governance requires.
253: Watch
254: Standing surveillance of the estate's security — the state of the watch, its record, what is under suspicion, and the decisions reserved for people. The one console owned by the Watch authority, specified in Part VII‑A below and in Document 8.
255: 11  The Shell
256: One sidebar across the whole product, with role-based landings — each console opens to the screen its primary user needs first, not to a generic dashboard.
257: No figure appears anywhere in the product without a path to where it came from. This single rule shapes more of the interface than any aesthetic decision does: it forces every tile, table cell, and chart to carry a receipt link, and it makes the proof walk the product’s most-used interaction rather than an audit feature reached only in an emergency.
258: Every screen carries a breadcrumb, a chip stating which census the visible data reflects, and contextual access to the reference application.
259: 12  The Two Day-Zero Dashboards
260: 12.1  The Registry Dashboard — the warehouse floor
261: Inventory management for the data estate, because that is what the platform fundamentally is. The estate manager’s home screen.
262: Topline highlights about the holding, each with a descriptive note and a link to how it was measured.
263: A distribution view beside an insight card stating plainly what the composition supports.
264: The estate table: source, data type, volume, languages, rights, condition, last measured, share extracted. Any row opens to its own profile.
265: Intelligence on the inventory: standing opportunity briefs, coverage-to-objective bars for live objectives, and extraction activity showing what is mining now and what is queued.
266: 12.2  The Trust Center — the warehouse of rules
267: The identical inventory idea, applied to governance. The compliance owner’s home screen, specified fully in Part V; introduced here because the two dashboards together are what "day zero" means — both live and populated at the close of onboarding, simultaneously.
268: PART IV
The Extraction Console
269: 13  Home
270: Header. Product and role, with a Commission objective action.
271: Status line. Binding pattern: "Running normally. One item needs you."
272: Attention. At most one attention card per exceeded threshold — what happened, the number against the threshold, and one Review action.
273: Running list. Rows of objective name, entry type and stage, and budget consumed. Mining-stage visibility renders inside running status, never as a separate progress screen.
274: Capacity strip. Fleet apportionment and current consumption at a glance.
275: 
276: No dashboards or charts render by default. Exceptions appear only on threshold crossings; everything else stays quiet until it needs the reader’s attention.
277: 14  Commission — The Shaping Wizard
278: Layout: a chat pane on one side, an objective draft rail on the other.
279: Chat. The operator states intent; the agent asks for mandatory fields and never proposes on them. An estate-check chip renders inline before any feasibility-dependent question is asked.
280: Draft rail. Three dimensions — entry, reach, output — plus the envelope, each field in one of three visual states: filled with a check, open and muted, or agent-assumed with the amber chip. The envelope line lists done-condition, budget, and lawful basis until each is supplied.
281: Sample action. Run a sample becomes available once reach is drafted.
282: 
283: Mandatory fields — reach, the four output fields, done-condition, budget, lawful basis — are asked, never pre-filled. Preference fields may carry agent recommendations, but the mandatory set never does. Every turn is grounded in a real estate read; no fabricated availability, ever, under any circumstance.
284: 15  Freeze — Commit Review
285: You supplied. Rows of operator-stated values.
286: Agent assumed. Rows headed "Agent assumed — confirm or change," each carrying the amber chip and a change link.
287: Feasibility verdict. A success-treatment card. Binding pattern: "Floor feasible — {n}% of in-scope estate meets your standard."
288: Grounding marker. States whether the objective was sample-grounded or estimate-grounded.
289: Grounded by sample {sample_ref}   ·   No sample run — estimates only.
290: Envelope line. Lawful-basis reference, budget, commissioner, and the scope ceiling respected.
291: Action. Freeze objective.
292: Frozen is immutable — a changed intent is a new objective.
293: 16  Sampling
294: A sample is a first-class narrow-reach objective whose results ground the full commit. It exists because full extraction carries a real resource commitment, and because feasibility honestly returns unknown on un-censused reach — a sample converts unknown into evidence.
295: Trigger. The Run a sample action on the wizard, once reach is drafted. The operator bounds the sample.
296: Result card. Renders in the same position the feasibility verdict occupies: volume found, class distribution observed, per-hour cost observed. Recorded into the commit envelope beside the availability snapshot.
297: 
298: Sample cost draws the objective’s budget and is shown doing so. A sample result is evidence, not a promise — it grounds an estimate; it does not guarantee the full run’s eventual yield.
299: 17  Registry Administration
300: View census state by estate region; trigger or schedule census passes; un-censused regions are marked honestly as unknown, never as empty.
301: 18  Quality Observation
302: Mining-stage visibility inside running status; per-objective yield and class distribution as extraction proceeds; threshold-crossing attention cards under the Home rules stated above.
303: 19  Opportunity Briefs
304: The recommendation surface: a consumer of the registry census that proposes what the estate could be used for, grounded in census facts and real-world precedent. Advisory output — never a governed claim.
305: 19.1  The home card
306: One quiet card: "What this estate can do." One line — estate analysis current as of a date, a count of briefs, a count new since the last census — and one action: Explore. Threshold-attention rules do not apply; this card never demands attention on its own.
307: 19.2  The briefs view
308: A bordered row list. Each row carries a plain-language title, a grounding line of census facts, a precedent chip naming a real-world reference, and an amber advisory marker.
309: Advisory — not a governed claim. Verbatim on every row and every brief.
310: 19.3  The brief itself
311: Three sections. What exists — the census slice or slices, rendered from registry reads. What it could become — two or three product shapes, each with a named real-world precedent and one line on how it monetised. What is missing — honest gaps: rights, consent basis, licensing preconditions.
312: One action: Shape as objective, which pre-fills the commission wizard with the brief’s reach. The brief’s only exit is into the governed pipeline — it cannot publish, export, or transact on its own.
313: 19.4  Rules
314: Every number in a grounding line is a live registry read, rendered verbatim. The generation layer may select which facts to show; it may never produce a fact of its own.
315: No render path drops the advisory marker. Briefs sit outside the trust-receipt and trace system entirely — generation runs behind the boundary governor, and briefs regenerate on census change, stamped with their generation date and the census reference. A superseded brief is marked stale, never deleted.
316: PART V
The Compliance Console
317: 20  Home
318: Lookup. A single field: look up any run, claim, or acquisition by trace.
319: Attention. Problems stated honestly. Binding pattern: "One retention window has passed — a 2019 call-in set is fourteen days beyond its agreed hold. It has not been auto-deleted; that rule isn’t set."
320: Cards. Three, always: runs with lawful basis; refusals this month with a link to see what was refused; retention windows past due.
321: 
322: Adversarial to comfort. Overruns, unset rules, and refusals are surfaced as problems and as evidence the governance actually bites — never hidden behind an all-green summary.
323: This is the same record every user’s audit view reaches — read-only, nothing reconstructed for display.
324: 21  Prove One Run
325: Banner. The lawfulness banner: lawful-basis reference, commissioner, and the statement that the objective was frozen and immutable.
326: Record rows. Five, each resolving to the record beneath it.
327: 
328: Read-only. This is the record itself, not a summary of it. Export for a regulator on request.
329: 22  Retention and Rights
330: Banner, while unset. The honest statement, rendered before anything else on the screen.
331: No deletion rule is set. The system holds everything indefinitely and append-only until you set a retention window. This is a decision only you can make — the system won’t guess a duration.
332: Holdings rows. Within window; past due, each with a Decide action; and delivered acquisitions — irreversibly transformed, licensed, receipts on file.
333: Held classes render separately addressable. Ledger rows, wizard transcripts, and delivered artefacts each carry their own row, so the compliance owner can scope one window across all of them, or split per class as their actual policy requires.
334: Setting a retention window here becomes a governed rule — versioned, dated, and recorded like every other control change.
335: 23  The Compliance Rulebook
336: The Compliance Console owns writes to the compliance rule classes specifically: retention windows, disclosure thresholds — group size, distinct-value count, privacy budget — the lawful-basis registry, the source-standing table, and entitlement rules governing who internally may see what.
337: Rendering reuses the established plain-language rule pattern throughout: the rule as a sentence, its current behaviour, what changes, and the record of the change with its date. It is re-used, not redesigned — a second rule-editing grammar would be a second thing to learn and a second thing to get wrong. An entitlement rule is written, changed, and proven exactly this way; it is not a special case.
338: PART VI
The Integration Console
339: 24  Register an Application
340: Fields. Application name; class choice — internal or external; path choice with one-line grants stated plainly.
341: Key grants panel. A plain-terms statement of what the key permits — its class, its path, its floor, its scope — and the statement that all of it is enforced server-side on every call.
342: Async fields. An optional webhook URL, carrying the note that it receives event and status only and never content; and a sandbox toggle, which is a key mode served from fixture estate.
343: Action. Issue key. Grant issuance and revocation each emit a ledger row.
344: 25  First Call — The Contract
345: Request block. The objective endpoint with its ask, standard, and scope.
346: Response panels, side by side. Answered — outcome, trace identity, claim, defensibility inline, provenance. Refused — the identical envelope shape, distinguished only by the body discriminator, carrying what was asked, the supported class, and what would raise it.
347: Async variant, noted beneath. A fresh-extraction ask returns an accepted acknowledgement with an objective identity and a delivery estimate; status transitions appear in Administer.
348: 
349: The panel’s sample payload is clearly marked as illustration and is fixture-schema-gated — the sample parses through the platform’s own frozen contracts. An unmarked sample is a hidden mock, and it is prohibited.
350: There is no response shape in which the claim is separable from its class. Infrastructure faults return a server error and are never rendered as refusals.
351: 26  Administer
352: Attention. At most one card. Pattern: application name, refusal rate, plain-language cause, and a Review action.
353: Applications list. Rows carrying name and class badge, path and key, calls and refusal rate. Extract-path rows additionally show acquisitions and rights state; long-running objectives show their lifecycle state.
354: 
355: Refusal health reads as a signal rather than an error log. A rising refusal rate against one key says something real about that integration’s objective — its scope may be too wide, or its floor too high for what the estate holds.
356: Key scope is enforced server-side on every call.
357: 27  Dual-Actor Scoping
358: Two roles, one console, identical screens, different scope. Enforcement is server-side, never view-layer filtering alone.
359: External-scope denials are access-control class, carrying a reason and detail. They never carry an outcome key and never render through the refusal card — a denial and a refusal are different things and must never look the same.
360: The distinction that must never be conflated: an external engineer is an integrating partner’s own engineer, wiring a partner system to the governed boundary — a platform-operator action performed by an outside party, legitimately seeing a scoped console view. A buyer shaping a purchase is purely an end-user of the commercial application, and sees no console at all.
361: 28  The Governed Boundary
362: The Integration Console provisions access to the platform’s outputs; it does not itself sell, price, or transact. What it exposes is the single contract every application calls to reach that output — application registration, key issuance and scope, the bounds of which estate slices a key may reach, and usage and refusal-health monitoring.
363: The boundary enforces, for every caller, with no exception for first-party applications: the inner gate on a live query or the full outer gate on a governed extract, server-side key scope on every call, and the four response classes. An application that appears to bypass any of these is a defect, never a tier of service.
364: No price, quote, offer, catalogue, order, or buyer-account concept exists on this console or in this boundary. Those are commercial-application concerns entirely. The platform charges nothing and knows no buyer; it governs access to output and records every egress.
365: The Administration Console owns internal cost and capacity economics — fleet apportionment, cost-per-unit telemetry — because running the machine requires them. It owns no commercial price. The relationship between platform cost and any market price is a commercial concern, and commercial price never appears on a platform surface.
366: PART VII
The Administration Console
367: 29  Home
368: Pending banner. Plain language, two backing classes: governance seams awaiting values, and items awaiting counter-signature. Pattern: "Two rules are waiting on your decision before they can take effect." with a Review action. Never a placeholder count.
369: Prompt. "What do you want to do?"
370: Actions. Six buttons, binding labels: Assign a role · Change a rule · Manage keys and access · Update the taxonomy · Set pricing · Apportion capacity.
371: Footer. "See everything I’ve changed — every action is recorded."
372: 
373: Buttons and sentences only. No dashboards, no version strings, no configuration syntax anywhere on this surface.
374: 30  Change a Rule
375: The rule. One sentence stating what it does in everyday language; a short paragraph of current behaviour and what turning it on or off means; plain options with natural labels.
376: What changes. An information box of one or two natural-language sentences, including — where true — that nothing running now changes, and that it can be switched back.
377: Commit. A natural-language button.
378: 
379: Commit paths honour the versioning discipline: a committable rule writes a new versioned record server-side, recorded and reversible. A rule not yet committable through the surface states so honestly, in plain language — the surface is never a bypass around what the underlying system can actually do.
380: Recorded as your change, with today’s date.
381: 31  What I’ve Changed
382: Confirmation. A plain line for the latest change: what is now in effect, and from when.
383: Rows. Recent actions — a plain description of the change from one state to another, in words, who made it, and when. Counter-signed changes show both identities.
384: 
385: The full difference exists in the record and opens on demand behind a collapsed link. It is never the primary display — a person scans plain descriptions and drills in only where they need to.
386: Every row carries its full diff. This trail is itself append-only and readable by the compliance surface.
387: 32  Scope Split
388: This console owns the operational rule classes: pricing models and tier locks, fleet apportionment, and the classification taxonomy. Compliance rule classes render here read-only, carrying the marker "owned by Compliance." Two consoles, one rulebook, no ambiguity anywhere about who writes what.
389: 33  Roles and Rights
390: Define roles and per-console rights. Changes are plain-language, consequence-visible, and ledgered — the change-a-rule pattern applied identically to role grants.
391: 34  Counter-Sign Duties
392: The pending banner surfaces items awaiting this console’s counter-signature, with what changes, who initiated, and the consequence class.
393: Symmetry. An Administration-side operational change that loosens protection requires Compliance counter-signature; a Compliance-initiated loosening requires Administration counter-signature. The check binds in both directions — there is no hierarchy between the two consoles, and neither can loosen protection alone.
394: Signed by {initiator} · counter-signed by {checker} · recorded with both identities.
395: An honesty note carried into the record: while one person holds both roles — as happens in a small deployment — dual control is ceremony rather than substance. The seam is built now regardless, because it is cheap now and expensive to retrofit once an organisation has grown past needing it.
396: PART VII‑A
The Watch Console
397: 34‑A  What It Is
398: The Watch Console is the security authority's one surface: where the watch officer — and the compliance owner, read-only — sees the state of the watch, reads its record, manages what is under suspicion, and takes the few decisions the Watch reserves for people. It is a peer to the Trust Center, never a tab inside it: the two authorities' consoles share the record and share nothing else, and access to each runs under its own authority's identity per the matrix in Document 9.
399: Every rule in Part I binds here without exception — and one binds hardest: no build state on any surface. The Watch's internal register — its engine and arm names — never appears on this console. The screen speaks the organisation's language: the watch, the record, under watch, decisions.
400: 34‑B  The Four Panels
401: Panel
402: What it carries
403: State
404: The promise as two live figures — detection latency and response latency against their bounds — then the population by class and trust standing, the two spend gauges (autonomous-action budget and friction budget), the health of the watch itself with its last drill result, and anything currently held. This band is built never to render all-clear; on a real estate, all-clear is a rendering defect.
405: Record
406: The verdict stream in three lanes, sorted by what followed: noted with no action taken — the restraint record; noted and acted — each action carrying the policy row that fired and its live expiry countdown, with actions released clean kept visible as the honest false-positive record; and held — the certainty events. Drills appear in these same lanes as rows marked for what they are, filterable, never a separate book. Any row expands into its full evidence walk: signal, verdict with replay, policy row, action, outcome, witness — every hop a receipt reference, and a row that cannot complete its walk renders broken rather than dressed.
407: Under watch
408: Where suspicion is managed. The accumulation view — actors whose noted events are individually dismissible and collectively a shape — with each curve's signal mix and time at elevation. From here a person promotes a suspect into misdirection, observes live misdirection sessions as occupancy and findings — never the environment's construction — reviews the marked, and files a re-declaration request where the innocent explanation is honest change. De-marking is dual-control and routes to Decisions.
409: Decisions
410: Exactly what the Watch reserves for people, ranked by blast radius, each arriving with its walk pre-opened: containment-to-severance promotions, expiry extensions, de-mark requests with both signatures visible, the two authorities' disagreements shown side by side, and the ceremony watch — every rule change in countdown that touches the Watch, cancellable from here. An item aging past its class bound escalates itself; a class that repeatedly reaches this panel is a policy defect to redefine, never a queue to work faster.
411: 
412: 34‑C  What This Console Never Renders
413: A watch console is itself a target: whoever reads it learns the detection landscape. So the constitution applies to the screen. No thresholds, trip points, or jitter bands render anywhere, ever. No canary or mark placement detail renders — the record shows that a tripwire was touched, never where the others sit. No behavioural profile renders — trust standing and its movement, yes; the shape of a person's habits, never, to this or any surface. No misdirection construction renders. And the console is watched: every session on it is receipted, its viewers enveloped like any actor, its anomalies lanes in its own record.
414: Read-only for assurance, adversarial to comfort — the Trust Center's own posture, inherited whole. The watch officer's work is deciding what surfaced items mean; the surfacing is the machine's. A Watch Console that only shows green is marketing, not security.
415: PART VIII
The Consequence-Class Checker
416: 35  The Mechanism
417: Consequential rule changes get a second pair of eyes, and the check is attached to consequence, not to role — this is what preserves compliance independence, and what makes the check bind symmetrically rather than running downhill from whichever console happens to be senior.
418: Every rule class carries a consequence attribute with one of two values. Compliance-initiated loosening is counter-signed by Administration; Administration-initiated loosening is counter-signed by Compliance. The direction of the signature follows the direction of the loosening, never the org chart.
419: Pending items render on both consoles’ banners simultaneously, and the counter-signing console sees the full plain-language consequence statement before it signs — never a bare approval button with the substance hidden behind it.
420: While one person holds both constitutional roles — as happens in a small deployment — dual control is ceremony rather than substance in practice. The seam is built regardless, and built now, because it is cheap now and expensive to retrofit once an organisation has grown past needing the honesty of saying so.
421: PART IX
The Reference Application
422: 36  What It Is
423: The reference application is not a platform surface. It is an application, specified fully because it demonstrates the platform’s own contract for every future application to follow. It consumes the platform through an Integration-Console-issued key, on identical terms to any third party — including a third party built by Syni itself. Nothing about it is privileged.
424: 37  Ask
425: What do you need to know?
426: One plain question, centred, and an answer the reader can act on and defend. The output is preset: a composed conclusion, for a person, synthesized whole, at their floor. There is no output picker anywhere on this surface, because choosing an output form is a commissioning act, and this surface is not for commissioning — that capacity lives in the Extraction Console, reached deliberately, not stumbled into from a chat box.
427: Class is present wherever a claim is, in plain language, as the headline — never as a buried score a reader has to go looking for.
428: 37.1  The three lenses
429: Progressive disclosure over one object, not three different objects. An executive stops at the first lens. An analyst works in the second when a number looks surprising. An auditor lives in the third.
430: Lens
431: What it shows
432: Answer
433: The finding itself, with per-claim marking and the honesty strip — what this can and cannot say.
434: Reasoning
435: The evidence strip: which units the answer rests on, and how they were composed.
436: Raw trail
437: The full trace — the same record the compliance audit reaches, resolvable by anyone holding the trace identity.
438: 
439: All three lenses read one object. This is what makes the executive’s summary and the auditor’s trail structurally incapable of disagreeing with each other — they are never two different renderings assembled by two different processes.
440: 37.2  Refusal classes render distinctly
441: Not-extracted-yet, evidence-cannot-support, and something-broke are three visually distinct states, and the third shares nothing with the first two — not components, not colour, not layout. A reader must be able to tell, without reading a word, whether the platform declined or the platform failed.
442: 37.3  Export
443: Export is a rendering of the same artefact with its class markings intact. It is not a second product and not a re-shaping.
444: A different form or grain is a new objective. This is the rule that prevents analytics drift through export — a figure that quietly changes shape somewhere downstream of the record that produced it is exactly the failure this rule exists to close off.
445: 37.4  The machine form
446: Integrating applications receive the identical object as a structured envelope, including all three refusal shapes as first-class response types — not error codes an application has to interpret, but named shapes it is expected to render.
447: An application must handle a decline at build time. This is what prevents the most common downstream corruption of a governed system: a wrapper that swallows a refusal and substitutes a plausible generated answer of its own in its place.
448: 38  Commercial Applications
449: The commercial product is specified separately from this canon and does not appear on any platform surface. What binds here regardless: any commercial application reaches platform output only through the governed boundary, with a scoped external key, passing the full outer gate including the disclosure-budget debit — identical to any third-party caller in every respect.
450: A sample shown to a prospective buyer is an egress. It passes the full outer gate and debits the cumulative-disclosure budget, or it is exactly the assembly attack the disclosure ledger exists to catch: buy nothing, sample repeatedly, reconstruct the dataset for free. There is no disclosure-free sample path, under any commercial pressure.
451: PART X
The Environment
452: 39  What This Part Is
453: Everything specified in Parts IV through IX above is the platform: the four consoles and the reference application, real, and specified to the letter every builder needs. What follows is different in kind, and the difference is stated plainly rather than left for a reader to discover.
454: The environment is application layer, not platform layer. It carries the organisation’s own name, and every surface inside it — including the ones built by Syni — reaches the platform through the identical Integration-Console boundary any third party uses. No platform decision optimises this layer’s experience directly; the platform optimises the guarantees it issues to it.
455: This part organises the applications an organisation actually opens day to day into five pillars over one control band. The organisation of these pillars, and every surface named in them beyond what is explicitly marked sourced below, is original design — built on the real console and boundary mechanics specified above, but invented at the level of which applications exist and how they group. A builder must not mistake the confidence of this document’s prose for the confidence of a specification transcribed from a ratified source; where that distinction matters, it is marked, item by item, in Section 42.
456: 40  The Five Pillars and the Control Band
457: Pillar
458: Applications
459: Lead
460: ThinkLab, Monitor, Pulse, News — executive surfaces for structured thinking, watching the organisation’s own operations, the internal feed, and external information.
461: Work
462: Chat, Analyze, Documents — the daily surfaces for knowledge work on the organisation’s own material.
463: Build
464: Extract, Train, Studio — where data becomes qualified facts, trained models, and purpose-built agents.
465: 3rd Party
466: Applications the organisation builds itself, and vendor tools it integrates.
467: Learn
468: Programmes that build the organisation’s capability to use and govern what it has deployed.
469: 
470: Beneath the pillars, spanning all five without exception, sits the Control band: Connect, Estate Map, Rulebook, Access, Watch. It spans rather than sitting beside them because it governs every pillar including the third-party one — a vendor application integrated through 3rd Party is subject to the identical Rulebook, the identical Access surface, and the identical Watch as anything Syni built.
471: 41  The Control Band, Mapped to the Real Consoles
472: The Control band is not a fifth invention beside four others — it is the customer-facing presentation of the four real consoles specified in Parts IV through VII, wearing the organisation’s own vocabulary rather than the platform’s.
473: Control surface
474: Sourced from
475: Notes
476: Estate Map
477: The Extraction Console’s Registry Dashboard and Registry Administration.
478: Sourced. The screen, its fields, and its binding copy are as specified in Part IV.
479: Rulebook
480: The Compliance Console’s rulebook, plus the operational rule classes owned by the Administration Console.
481: Sourced. Both consoles already render through the identical plain-language rule pattern; a unified surface showing both, each row marked with its owning console, is a direct application of that pattern rather than a new one.
482: Connect
483: The Integration Console’s registration and administration screens.
484: Sourced for application registration. Model and compute connection management is new — marked in Section 42.
485: Access
486: The Administration Console’s roles, rights, and key management, plus counter-sign duties.
487: Sourced.
488: Watch
489: Document 8 and Part VII‑A below.
490: Designed under the Watch authority. Rendered in the organisation's own vocabulary; the Watch's internal engine names never appear on it, identically to every other surface under §2.1.
491: 42  What Is Sourced, and What Is Designed
492: Every application named in Section 40 is marked here without exception. A builder implementing this canon should treat a sourced item as a specification and a designed item as a brief — the second needs product judgement the first does not.
493: Application
494: Status
495: Basis
496: Extract
497: Sourced
498: The Extraction Console’s shaping wizard, Parts IV §14–16, specified to the field.
499: Chat
500: Sourced
501: The reference application, Part IX, specified to the lens.
502: 3rd Party (both surfaces)
503: Sourced
504: The Integration Console, Part VI, specified to the screen.
505: Train
506: Designed
507: Built on the real training and acceptance mechanics of Document 4 Part VIII, but the surface itself — its screens, its layout — has no source specification and is original design.
508: Studio
509: Designed
510: No precedent in any source document. A governed agent-builder is implied by the inheritance doctrine of Document 1 but was never itself specified; this is new design, built to honour that doctrine rather than transcribed from it.
511: Analyze
512: Designed
513: No source specification. Built to the design law of Part I and the visual system of Part II; its actual screens and states are original.
514: Documents
515: Designed
516: No source specification, as above.
517: ThinkLab
518: Designed
519: No source specification, as above.
520: Monitor
521: Designed
522: No source specification, as above.
523: Pulse
524: Designed
525: No source specification, as above.
526: News
527: Designed
528: No source specification, as above. The one binding rule that does carry from elsewhere: News is the single Lead surface whose content originates outside the perimeter, and every item it shows is labelled as external at the item, always — the provenance discipline of Document 3’s boundary governor, applied here.
529: Learn
530: Designed
531: No source specification. What populates it is a product decision, not an interface one, and is explicitly out of scope for this document.
532: 
533: A designed surface is still bound by every rule in Part I. The eight global rules, the four response classes, the visual system — none of it relaxes because a surface is new rather than sourced. What is absent for a designed surface is only the field-level and screen-level specification a sourced surface carries; the design law is never optional.
534: 43  Why the Split Is Drawn Here, and Not Elsewhere
535: The platform, the reference application, and the Extraction and Integration Consoles carry real, ratified specification because they are what the source canon actually documents. The remaining pillar applications do not exist in any source document — not because they were considered and rejected, but because the source canon specifies a platform and one demonstrating application, and everything else an organisation might build on that platform is, by the inheritance doctrine itself, exactly the kind of thing the platform is supposed to make buildable rather than the kind of thing it prescribes.
536: This document therefore does two different jobs at once, and keeps them visibly separate: it transcribes what is ratified, and it proposes what the ratified platform makes possible. A future ratification of any designed surface above supersedes this document’s proposal for it, at the item, without disturbing anything else here.

# SOURCE: assessment_workspace/canon/unpacked/Akki_Canon_6_User_Journeys.docx
Coordinate: document.xml paragraph in body order, tables included

1: AKKI CANON  ·  DOCUMENT 6 OF 9
2: Akki User Journeys
3: Every journey from founding an instance through the working rhythm an organisation settles into, and how they compound into one loop
4: PART I
Register and Scope
5: 1  How to Read This Document
6: This document walks every journey the platform serves, from founding an instance through the rhythm an organisation settles into once one has been running for months. Each journey states who performs it, what it produces, and how it unfolds — cross-referenced to the exact mechanics specified in the documents before this one, never restated from memory.
7: A journey is not a permission grant. What a person may actually do is specified in Documents 1, 3, and 7; what follows here is what doing it feels like and looks like. The two must never be read as contradicting each other — where this document says a business user asks a question, Document 3’s authority model is what actually admits or refuses that question underneath.
8: 2  The Role Register
9: The platform names its authorities formally where precision matters — in the doctrine, the access model, and the governance engines specified earlier in this canon — and addresses the same people in plain language wherever they are actually working. Both are correct; neither supersedes the other. This document uses the plain-language address throughout, because it describes lived experience rather than authority, and matches the register Document 5 already establishes for every screen a person actually sees.
10: Formal authority
11: Addressed on screen as
12: Specified in
13: Master Admin
14: the instance owner
15: Documents 1, 3
16: Data Protection Officer
17: the compliance owner
18: Documents 1, 3, 7
19: Operator
20: the operator — unchanged in both registers
21: Documents 1, 3, 4
22: Watch Officer
23: the watch officer
24: Documents 8, 9
25: 
26: Three further terms recur through the journeys below without carrying formal authority of their own: a business user or product owner is whoever inside the organisation has a question or a need, with no standing permission beyond what any employee holds; a commissioner is whoever’s objective a given piece of work runs under, a role that changes with every commission rather than a fixed seat; a technical lead and an integrating engineer are whoever builds and connects an application, roles held by employees or by a contracted third party alike.
27: These are motions, not a permissions taxonomy. A single person may hold several across a single week — the compliance owner asking an exploratory question is, in that moment, also a business user. What is fixed is that each motion has one home surface answering its question completely, never a console that tries to serve every motion at once.
28: PART II
Founding
29: 3  Setup
30: Who
31: What it produces
32: The instance owner and the compliance owner, together, once.
33: An instance running under the organisation’s own policy, with verified sources attached.
34: A guided sequence captures the organisation’s identity, the compliance owner’s contact, the six governed seam values — each explained in one plain sentence with a recommended default — and the source list with the rights held on each. The review step states plainly that these choices are permanently recorded, and that changing any of them later requires two approvals.
35: The same sequence captures the first declarations: each seat-holder's role and working interests, entered as the admission baseline Document 3 §6.1 requires of every actor thereafter. From this morning forward no actor — person or agent — enters the instance undeclared, and honest change is handled by re-declaring, not by drifting.
36: Then, source by source: connect, test, and — for structured sources — confirm the mapping sample. This is the Extraction Console’s Registry Administration screen, specified in Document 5 Part IV, walked once per source rather than all at once.
37: The whole journey is a working morning, and it ends with a signed setup record rather than a configuration file. On revisit, the screen is read-only, with a change request that routes to the rule-change ceremony specified in Document 3.
38: 4  Day Zero
39: Who
40: What it produces
41: The instance owner and the compliance owner, first week.
42: The estate map as a first deliverable in its own right, and a signed commissioning certificate.
43: The census runs, and the Registry Dashboard — Document 5 §12.1 — fills for the first time: holdings per source with proof links; composition by language, era, type, and condition, with real counts; territory not yet measured, drawn as such rather than left blank; and capability the estate does not need, shown unlit rather than hidden entirely. For most organisations this is the first complete measured picture of their own data, and it stands as a deliverable independently of anything mined afterward — exportable and citable on its own.
44: In parallel, the compliance owner opens the Verification Runner and executes plain-language test packs — the mechanism specified in Document 3 §31: personal data is masked before any model call; deletion requires two approvers; an unanswerable question is refused with a reason. Each pack shows the rail firing with its proof, and the compliance owner signs the commissioning record on that basis.
45: The Watch commissions the same way: its response rails fire in demonstration — a seeded hostile input refused at the boundary, a planted credential touched and severed, a containment expiring clean — and the watch officer signs on the drill receipts. A rail that cannot be demonstrated firing is not in force, for security exactly as for governance.
46: Day-zero mining is verification that the organisation’s own parameters work — never value production, and never a demonstration staged for the vendor’s benefit. Both dashboards live and populated, simultaneously, is what day zero actually means.
47: PART III
The Working Rhythm
48: 5  Exploration
49: Who
50: What it produces
51: Business users, continuously.
52: Defensible answers, and a shortlist of what is worth commissioning next.
53: A business user browses the registry: what has already been extracted and verified, what has not, and which gaps other people have already hit, and how often. Opportunity Briefs — Document 5 §19 — propose what the estate could support, each figure linked to its own measurement, refreshed as the census grows, and marked advisory throughout.
54: Then the user asks. The answer arrives as an answer card: the finding stated in prose, each individual claim tagged measured or modelled, an evidence strip naming its sources and strata and confirming the privacy floor held, an honesty strip naming plainly what the answer cannot say and why, and a set of actions — break it down, draft the memo, walk the proof. Where the answer meets a genuine gap, one action files the work as a candidate carrying its own demand evidence, entering the loop specified in Part VII below. Where the answer meets an entitlement rule instead, the user sees an entitlement refusal in place of the answer card — a different message entirely, since nothing here was missing from the estate, only withheld from this particular asker.
55: Exploration is deliberately pre-purchase. A user finds out what the estate would support before committing any budget to actually extracting it — this is the entire reason Sampling, specified in Document 5 §16, exists as a first-class capability rather than a shortcut.
56: 6  Commissioning and Buying
57: Who
58: What it produces
59: A business user or product owner, then the operator.
60: A commissioned objective with an accepted quote, where the work is priced.
61: The objective wizard — the Extraction Console’s Commission screen, Document 5 §14 — turns a need into governed work in five steps: the need stated in plain words; scope selected from what the registry says actually exists; standards and rights confirmed against explained defaults; a plan preview — extraction volume as a range, reusable stock already identified, expected coverage of the goal, and what cannot be covered, all shown before any commitment; and commissioning itself, with a confirmation stating precisely what becomes permanent at that moment.
62: Where the work is priced, a quote follows: line items, a validity window with an expiry, a delivery estimate as a range, and cancellation terms with itemised liability for whatever has already completed by that point. Acceptance is recorded and becomes the objective of record — this is the Freeze specified in Document 5 §15, and the freeze itself is the immutable event Document 3’s Admit stage performs underneath it.
63: The operator then approves the work to run through commit review, or returns it with a reason. Both are ledger events. The journey’s entire design intent is that no one is ever surprised — cost, coverage, and limits are all visible before any money actually moves.
64: 7  Mining and Delivery
65: Who
66: What it produces
67: The operator and the commissioner, continuously.
68: Finished products, with their paperwork attached.
69: Extraction runs under the frozen objective. Objective tracking shows coverage toward the goal with the basis of the figure stated alongside it, completed runs each carrying a proof link, and a batch board where a quarantined batch appears with its status and its resolution path — never simply disappearing from view, per Document 4 §31.
70: Deliverables land on the shelf as they complete: datasets, briefs, standing feeds, occurrence indexes — each carrying its contents, its licence label, its privacy attestation, its quality card, and its proof trail. Where the instance’s own rules require it, a person releases a deliverable through review before it reaches its recipient.
71: Mining is ongoing work, not a launch event. An organisation does not schedule a mining programme so much as develop a mining practice — which is precisely what Part VII below describes at the scale of the whole instance rather than one objective.
72: PART IV
Ownership
73: 8  Ownership and Integration
74: Who
75: What it produces
76: A technical lead and an integrating engineer.
77: Models the organisation owns, and applications running on governed intelligence.
78: As extraction accumulates labelled material, adapters train on it. Each accepted model appears with its base model, its full training lineage and inherited rights, its six-criterion acceptance scorecard with real measured numbers — the Model Output Acceptance Criteria specified in Document 4 §45 — and its complete version history. Before any model exists for a given class, the surface says so plainly rather than rendering an empty error in its place.
79: Integration is commissioned in one flow: the application’s standing objective is shaped, its memory plane is configured — retrieval scope, write-back on or off with a per-cycle volume ceiling, storage ceiling, retention and precompute parameters, per Document 7 §19–23 — and a scoped key is issued, all as a single recorded act rather than several separate ones.
80: The engineer registers a webhook, reads the live answer envelope including all three refusal shapes, makes a test call, and watches that call appear in the compliance record immediately. There is no warm-up period in which an integration runs unobserved — the first call is governed exactly like the thousandth.
81: PART V
Assurance
82: 9  Assurance
83: Who
84: What it produces
85: The compliance owner, continuously.
86: Assurance the compliance owner produces personally, rather than receives on trust from a vendor.
87: The Trust Center holds every rule with its setting, who set it and when, and the count of automated checks actually enforcing it — beside the full track record: refusals with their reasons, quarantines with their resolutions, deletions with their certificates, rule changes with their ceremony stage and countdown, destruction attestations per run, per-application memory activity, and the quality layer’s own scorecard, including — honestly — when its own calibration has gone stale.
88: One action proves any operation end to end; another exports the regulator pack. Both are generated entirely from the record specified in Document 3 Part VII, never assembled by hand for the occasion.
89: 9‑A  The Watch Day
90: Who
91: What it produces
92: The watch officer, continuously.
93: Threats detected, contained, and converted into the record's own intelligence — with legitimate work never interrupted.
94: 
95: The watch officer opens the Watch Console to its state band: the two latency figures against their bounds, the population and its trust standing, the spend gauges, the last drill. Most days the record's first lane — noted, no action — is the whole story, and reading it *is* the job: the restraint record is where the slow play first becomes a shape. In the accumulation view, one actor's curve has been climbing for a week — individually dismissible events, collectively a pattern. The officer promotes the actor into misdirection and watches the session as occupancy and findings. An innocent does ordinary work and releases on expiry, their period reconciled honestly; this one touches a planted credential, and the finding is structural: a mark is minted, severance executes on its own authority, and the decision panel receives the aftermath rather than the request.
96: What the officer never does is as designed as what they do: no threshold is visible to tune defensively, no profile is readable to browse, no action requires them before it executes within its bounds. Their decisions are exactly the reserved set — promote a containment, extend an expiry, sign a de-mark, resolve a disagreement between the authorities, cancel a ceremony in countdown. A class of item that keeps reaching them is redefined at the policy table, never worked faster. And the drill record answers the auditor's question before it is asked: the watch proves itself on schedule, and the proof is receipts, not attestation.
97: Everything in this journey runs under the Watch's identity, on the shared record, per the matrix in Document 9. The compliance owner reads the same record through the Trust Center under governance identity — same facts, two readings, and neither console renders the other's interior.
98: PART VI
The External Path
99: 10  The Buyer and the Customer
100: A buyer acquiring intelligence, and a customer who has already purchased it, follow a path specified fully in Document 7 Parts V–VI — the buyer path and the customer portal — and are not restated here. What is worth stating plainly at this level is the shape of the two journeys together: know what you are buying, acquire it lawfully, receive it, integrate against it, and see exactly what you have consumed, all without ever touching a console or the extraction machinery underneath.
101: Neither the buyer nor the customer ever holds a privileged path. Both reach the platform through the identical governed boundary any application does, specified once in Document 5 §28 and never varied for a commercial relationship, however large.
102: PART VII
The Loop
103: 11  Mining as a Practice
104: The rhythm an organisation settles into has four beats, and no journey above is complete without seeing how they connect into one another.
105: questions arrive from the business, and are asked of the estate
106:    ↓
107: most are answered  ── the rest produce filed gaps, carrying their own demand evidence
108:    ↓
109: gaps accumulate and rank themselves — no one maintains a priority list
110:    ↓
111: objectives are commissioned against the top of that list, priced with their coverage stated
112:    ↓
113: the resulting extraction changes what the next round of questions can be answered from
114: 
115: Two properties of this loop are unusual, and both are worth holding onto precisely.
116: Demand is discovered rather than forecast. The organisation learns what its estate is worth by observing what people actually try to ask of it — which is more reliable than any upfront value assessment could ever be, because it costs nothing to be wrong about and updates itself continuously.
117: The loop is self-limiting in a healthy way. When the gap list stops producing high-demand candidates, the estate has been mined to the depth its current questions actually require — mining further than that would be building inventory nobody asked for.
118: No role is required to be present for the loop to continue, which is what allows the practice to survive staff changes intact. The record carries the context that would otherwise live only in someone’s head — why a gap was filed, what was tried against it, what the material could not yet support — and the next person to touch it does not begin from nothing.
119: 12  What Every Journey Above Has in Common
120: Each journey names a different set of people and produces a different artefact, but every one of them rests on the identical five things specified earlier in this canon, and none of them would hold without all five.
121: One record. Every journey above writes to the same append-only ledger specified in Document 3, whichever console or application it passed through to get there.
122: One boundary. Every application any journey touches — first-party or third — crosses the identical governed boundary specified in Documents 5 and 7. No journey above ever finds a shorter path.
123: Three verdicts, never more. Every step in every journey above resolves to answered, held, or refused — never a fourth outcome invented to smooth over an awkward moment.
124: Provenance that survives the whole path. A figure a business user reads in Exploration traces, without exception, to the same census run a compliance owner would cite in Assurance.
125: A loop that compounds. What the organisation learns in one journey changes what every later journey can accomplish — this is the platform’s entire promise about time, made concrete across eight different kinds of working day.
126: And beneath all five, one presence the journeys above never had to mention because it never interrupted them: every actor in every journey was declared, enveloped, and watched, every gate they crossed evaluated the marks, and the Watch's whole ambition — stated in Document 8 and honoured across each of these days — is that the people doing legitimate work never noticed it was there.

# SOURCE: assessment_workspace/canon/unpacked/Akki_Canon_7_Integration_and_Quality.docx
Coordinate: document.xml paragraph in body order, tables included

1: AKKI CANON  ·  DOCUMENT 7 OF 9
2: Akki Integration Service and Quality Rulebook
3: The contract every application meets, entitlement enforcement, the memory layer, the Function & Promise Registry, the Critic Seam, and the discipline the build itself is held to
4: PART I
The Integration Chain
5: 1  Scope
6: This document specifies how governed intelligence reaches the people and systems that consume it, and the discipline the build itself is held to while producing it. It covers the answering service, the async delivery contract, the memory layer, the applications specified fully enough to demonstrate the platform’s contract, the Function & Promise Registry, the Critic Seam, and the defect classes and process rules that bind anyone — owner, builder, or system — working on the platform itself.
7: Integration is accountable for one thing: that intelligence reaches its consumers under the rights and masking in force, and that consumption returns value the organisation can account for. Failure looks like capability that exists but nothing consumes, consumption that escapes its rights envelope, or value that leaves unmetered.
8: 2  The Standard the Chain Holds
9: Governance travels inline, everywhere. No response shape separates a claim from its class — on the synchronous path, on the async path, and in every artefact handed over.
10: A refusal is a governed outcome, not an error. It is distinguished by a discriminator in the body, never by a status code, and an infrastructure fault is never rendered as a refusal.
11: Rules are derived from one place. Where a rule is enforced at two points — admission and shaping, for instance — both import the same module. A negative scan prevents reimplementation, because a rule implemented twice is a rule that will eventually disagree with itself.
12: Nothing partial egresses, including on cancellation. A cancelled run is still recorded.
13: PART II
The Answering Service
14: 3  What It Is
15: The answering service is where a question becomes an answer or a named refusal. It carries admission, composition, grounding, the async lifecycle, cancellation, and the refusal machinery. It is the surface every integrated application meets, and the surface the platform’s own reference application sits on.
16: 4  Admission and the Fork
17: A request is checked for completeness, admissibility, and entitlement before anything else happens. An external request missing any required field is refused with the validation envelope; a shaped work order arrives already complete, because the wizard could not have frozen it otherwise. Entitlement is the third check: whether the requester’s own attributes satisfy the rules governing the content the request would need to draw on, specified in Document 3 §22.1. It runs alongside completeness, not after it — an incomplete request that is also unentitled is refused for both reasons together, not one at a time.
18: Declaration is checked in the same breath. Every calling application, and every agent acting through one, carries the declaration Document 3 §6.1 requires — the standing objective, capabilities, and risks it was admitted under — and a request from an actor whose declaration is missing or stale refuses with its own named reason. The declaration is what the Watch reconciles conduct against, per Document 8; admission is where it is checked, because a baseline verified anywhere later is a baseline some path skips.
19: The warm/fresh fork happens here, once. An ask servable from qualified intelligence already held is answered synchronously. One requiring fresh extraction returns the async contract. The determination comes from the feasibility query against the Registry — a membership and convergence test, never an estimate — and everything downstream honours it rather than re-deriving it, because a second derivation could disagree with the first and the consumer would have been told one thing and given another.
20: 5  Admission Refusal
21: Refusal reasons are enumerated and versioned. The reason sets are files, versioned in sequence, with the highest version in force — a refusal issued under an earlier version stays interpretable after the set grows, because the version it was issued under is always recoverable.
22: The taxonomy is closed. Every refusal resolves to a named reason in the set. No ad-hoc refusal path exists, and no module composes a refusal string of its own.
23: The Watch's refusals join this taxonomy the way every family joins it: a versioned addition to the reason registry, never a parallel grammar. A hold at the input seat, a containment, a mark-gated denial — each resolves to a named reason, renders through the identical envelope, and offers only actions its reader can actually take. A Watch fault, like any fault, is never dressed as a refusal.
24: 5.1  Actor-appropriate paths forward
25: A refusal offers only what its reader can actually do. Where a conclusion falls below an objective’s floor, the three available actions are exactly: accept it as a recorded statement, narrow the objective, or lower the standard. Offering an approval route where none exists, or an action this actor cannot perform, converts a refusal into a dead end dressed as a door.
26: Every refusal cell carries a non-empty path forward, including cells unreachable from live dispatch today. An unreachable cell that is ever reached should still speak properly, and a standing test asserts that none is empty.
27: 5.2  Entitlement refusal
28: An entitlement refusal is a distinct named reason in the closed taxonomy, never folded into an evidence-floor refusal and never sharing its wording. The two mean entirely different things: evidence-floor says the material cannot support the claim; entitlement says this requester specifically may not receive it, regardless of how well the material supports it for someone else.
29: The three evidence-floor actions do not apply here and are never offered. Accepting, narrowing, or lowering the standard makes no sense against a rule about who is asking. An escalatable entitlement rule offers exactly one action — request access from the authority the rule names. An absolute entitlement rule offers none, identically to any other absolute refusal.
30: The refusal names the rule in the compliance owner’s own words, exactly as any other refusal does — never a generic "access denied," because a generic message teaches a requester nothing about whether asking a different way, or asking someone else, would help.
31: 6  The Shared-Derivation Pattern
32: Where a rule is enforced at more than one point, one module owns it and every caller imports that module — a structural pattern rather than a convention, with a negative scan preventing reimplementation elsewhere.
33: Shipping a shaping surface that can freeze an objective the transform layer must later refuse produces execution-time discovery — the objective is committed, priced, and run before anyone learns it cannot deliver what it promised. A single derivation shared by the shaping surface and the admission surface is what makes that impossible rather than merely unlikely.
34: 7  Grain and Form Compatibility
35: Not every grain is available for every output form, and the matrix is explicit rather than discovered by trial. Qualified data supports per-claim and aggregated grains, never synthesized-whole — that combination is a composed conclusion, a different form entirely. A composed conclusion is synthesized-whole only. A knowledge artifact supports per-claim and aggregated. A callable skill answers per-claim or synthesized-whole depending on the query it receives.
36: An incompatible combination is refused at the point it is chosen, with a path forward naming the form that does support the grain the requester actually wants.
37: 8  Provenance Preservation
38: Each output form declares the minimum standard its transform can preserve, and the rule table stating this is declarative — the shaping wizard evaluates it in conversation without running anything.
39: A below-floor combination refuses during shaping, never at execution. This is what allows a refusal to arrive while a user is still shaping their request, rather than after they have already committed to it.
40: 9  Licence Class
41: Licence classes are configuration, versioned rather than frozen — class names, commissioner mappings, and per-feed attributes live in versioned files, with the highest version in force winning. This is deliberate: a licence taxonomy must be able to grow as an organisation’s own agreements change, and freezing it would turn every commercial change into a contract event.
42: Selection is single-source. Class derivation, the selection filter, and every per-feed standing attribute are read from one place, consumed identically by the packaging path, the standing declaration table, and the outer gate’s own generalisation. Distributed copies of this logic were consolidated precisely because they had already begun to disagree.
43: 10  Composition
44: Two composition paths, matching two forms.
45: Qualified data is packaged. Selection by reach, a standard filter, and licence class, then packaging, then export through the outer gate. Per-claim provenance stays intact end to end, and below-floor units never enter the deliverable at all — the standard is an input filter, not a downstream check.
46: A composed conclusion is reasoned. Five-stage composition over selected units, the load-bearing set identified, and the conclusion’s class computed as the floor over that set. The trace is mandatory, and the class travels inline with the answer.
47: 
48: Every composition that reaches for a model carries a deterministic fallback beneath it. The mechanical composer is preserved byte-identical as that fallback, so a system whose highest rung is unavailable degrades to a knowable output rather than an unbounded one.
49: 11  Grounding
50: Grounding is proven, not asserted. A sentence that cannot be anchored to material is not a weaker sentence — it is a refusal.
51: Composed output carries a per-sentence anchor map, and a gate enforces it, protected by its own cell suite including a cell that asserts the failure path itself: that an ungrounded composition refuses rather than degrading. A gate whose failure path has never been tested is a gate that has never actually been shown to close. Class honesty is bounded structurally beneath this — a negative scan over the whole answering service prevents a composition from ever misstating the class it is answering at.
52: 12  Telemetry
53: Every model-reaching composition emits a sidecar record carrying the mode, the metering, and the outcome — separately from the answer itself, so telemetry can be retained and analysed on its own lifecycle without ever touching the answer’s own envelope.
54: PART III
Delivery
55: 13  The Async Contract
56: The fork made at admission determines the contract entirely. Warm returns a synchronous, full response. Fresh returns an accepted acknowledgement carrying the objective identity, the status, a delivery estimate, and a quote where one applies.
57: 13.1  States
58: Late refusal is a first-class outcome. Accepted, then refused, is a normal terminal state, never a failure. A run admitted and later found inadmissible — because the estate changed, because a rule changed, because reasoning could not reach the floor — has not failed; it has been governed, and integrating applications render it as exactly that: a governed refusal.
59: Sub-stages are deliberately not states. Exposing mining and transforming as distinct states would make every application’s own state machine depend on the platform’s internal pipeline — and a pipeline change would then be a breaking change for every consumer of it, which is a coupling this contract exists to prevent.
60: 14  Thin Webhook, Governed Fetch
61: The webhook payload carries the event, the objective identity, the trace identity, and the status. It never carries claim content. The result is fetched over the application’s own authenticated key, where scope is enforced server-side; polling the objective endpoint is the fallback wherever a webhook cannot be received.
62: Pushing claims to an application-configured URL would be an egress path the gates do not control. The webhook is thin for that reason and no other — a future convenience that put content in the payload would move an egress outside the perimeter, and the perimeter is the product. The webhook tells an application that something is ready; the gate decides whether that application may actually have it.
63: 15  Idempotency
64: An idempotency key is required on every external submission. A retried request must not double-commission or double-charge — the same key resolves to the same objective, and a duplicate submission returns the existing state rather than creating a second one.
65: Idempotency runs at the boundary, never in the worker. A worker-level guard would still admit two objectives and reconcile afterward — a reconciliation problem rather than a prevention, and reconciling after a charge has already been raised is a commercial problem wearing a technical one’s clothes.
66: 16  Cancellation
67: Cancellation requires no reason. It references the terms already agreed at commission, halts queued work, and retains whatever has already completed.
68: Nothing partial egresses on cancellation, and the cancelled run is still recorded. A cancelled run that left no record would be a run the system performed and cannot account for; partial egress on cancellation would make the perimeter probabilistic rather than absolute.
69: 17  Versioning and Sandbox
70: Envelopes are frozen and additive. A field is added; a shape is never mutated. A breaking change is a new path version, so an application built against the current contract keeps working indefinitely.
71: Sandbox is a key mode set at registration, served entirely from fixture estate. An engineer exercises the full contract — including every refusal shape and the whole async lifecycle — before any real material ever moves. A sandbox that behaved differently from production would teach the wrong contract, so the only difference between them is the estate behind it, and nothing else.
72: PART IV
The Memory Layer
73: 18  The Promise
74: The integration surface extends from query access to a full memory service. Every integrated application receives a durable, governed memory plane that grows in proportion to its own use.
75: To the integrating builder: the application arrives stateless and becomes knowledgeable. What it reads, contributes, and repeatedly needs persists for it, under the same governance as everything else on the platform, with zero memory infrastructure built on the application’s own side. To the estate holder: every application’s memory is visible, receipted, rights-bound, and revocable — integration deepens without governance ever thinning to accommodate it.
76: The platform knows the objective and does not know the application — not what it renders, not what it does with what it receives, not who its users are. This is what allows a thousand integrations to exist without any one of them shaping the platform’s own surface.
77: 19  The Plane
78: Every integration key is issued with exactly one memory plane: a durable, instance-scoped, key-scoped partition, created at commissioning and existing for the key’s entire lifetime.
79: 19.1  Isolation
80: Plane isolation is by construction. The persistence layer refuses any read or write not scoped to a key’s own plane — the identical scoped-accessor pattern that enforces instance isolation. A cross-plane read does not exist as an operation to be permitted or denied; it cannot be expressed at all.
81: Sharing happens only through the Registry, by rights-bound publication. There is no direct path from one plane to another, and no aggregate view across planes that any application can reach.
82: 19.2  Ledger-reconstructible
83: Every plane operation writes a ledger row — read, write, retention change, revocation. A plane can be reconstructed entirely from the ledger, which is what makes a question about what an application knew at a particular point in time answerable rather than merely asserted.
84: 19.3  Revocation and deletion
85: Key revocation freezes the plane: no reads, no writes. Freezing is immediate and does not require the deletion ceremony, because it removes access without destroying evidence. Plane deletion, when it happens, follows the instance’s own deletion ceremony — two-person approval, the single authorised path, a destruction attestation.
86: A revoked application’s contributed units survive in the Registry if and only if they were published. Unpublished contributions delete with the plane, because they were never the estate’s material — they were the application’s own working material, held under the estate’s governance in the meantime.
87: 20  Two Memories, Separated by Provenance
88: What may be reused across keys and what may not is decided by where material came from, and it is decided when the material is written rather than when it is later read. Deciding at read time makes the boundary a policy every reader must apply correctly, forever; deciding at write time makes it a property of the store itself.
89: Where provenance is mixed or unclear, the material stays in the plane. A derivation shaped partly by estate material and partly by a customer’s own framing is not split by judgement call — the estate may take the fact stripped of its framing, and the framing never travels. Failing closed toward the customer’s own thinking is the only defensible default while the law around this remains unsettled.
90: The consequence in practice: one key never learns that another asked, what it asked, or the shape of its inquiry — even where its own answers later improve because extraction the other key’s questions provoked has enriched the shared estate underneath.
91: 21  The Write-Back Contract
92: An application may contribute derived context, corrections, and conclusions back to its own plane. This is what turns a query surface into an actual memory service: the application’s own work accumulates rather than evaporating between calls.
93: 21.1  Shape
94: Every contribution lands as a qualified unit in the five-ring shape. No free-form blobs. Content, provenance — the application, its key, and the calls it derived from — defensibility class, context, and a re-derivation handle are all required at write.
