# SOURCE: assessment_workspace/canon/w11_new_docs/audio_intel_plane_spec.docx
Coordinate: document.xml paragraph in body order, tables included

1: SYNI.AI   ·   ENGINEERING SPECIFICATION
2: The Audio Intelligence Plane
3: Extraction · Learning · Training · Invention — end to end
4: Including the Commission View surface adjustment across all extraction types · v1.0
5: Status of this document: consolidated build specification. It supersedes the working drafts (Audio Capability Spec v1.0 and Addendum v1.1.2) and is the single reference for build. Behavioural clauses state what the system must and must not do, including on failure. Technical clauses state contracts and acceptance criteria. Items requiring verification against current code before build are marked [VERIFY] and collected in §16.
6: Contents
7: 
8: 
9: 
10: 1  Governing Doctrine
11: Five principles govern every clause in this specification. Where a later clause appears to conflict with one of these, the principle wins and the clause is defective.
12: 1.1  An audio file is a data estate, and the framing is recursive
13: The archive is an estate; a programme is an estate; a single file is an estate. Segments are rows; the extractable layers — content, language, condition, prosody, occurrence, code-switch, music, group-level character — are columns; no schema exists until one is declared. Census, admission, registry, and record apply at every scale.
14: 1.2  Modality extension, not parallel machinery
15: The audio plane introduces no sibling services. Mtafiti gains an audio modality; Northena gains audio data classes; the wizard gains an objective variant; Targeta gains a training object. Anything in this document that reads as a parallel to an existing service is rule proliferation and must be collapsed into the existing service before build.
16: 1.3  One record
17: Mtafiti and Northena collaborate to produce a single record, written once. Working state — loss curves, intermediate metrics, partial coverage counts — is scratch, not truth; it becomes record only when finalized and stamped. No local ledger exists. If a measured throughput ceiling ever demands relief, the relief is batched stamping (one row certifying N events with a digest), which remains a single record. That change is made only when a measurement demands it.
18: 1.4  Measure, do not assert
19: No data-volume requirement, accuracy expectation, or cost figure is quoted without a measurement behind it. The calibration stage exists to convert assertions into measurements before commitment.
20: 1.5  Unrepresentable, not policed
21: Safety boundaries are enforced by making the violating state impossible to express in the contract — the pattern established by the assertion floor — not by review after the fact. The Character Register write path (§6) and the voice identity distance gate (§7) both follow this pattern.
22: 2  Capability Statement and Plane Overview
23: Given governed access to an audio estate, the plane provides four functions in one loop:
24: Extraction — audio is converted into provenance-paired facts: transcripts, entities, occurrences, and character observations.
25: Learning — a Character Register accumulates group-level knowledge of how the estate’s languages and audio behave.
26: Training — model production is commissioned against a falsifiable Target Outcome, planned and priced before compute is spent, with per-example provenance.
27: Invention — synthesized voice identities are constructed from the register: authentically of the language, provably of no individual.
28: 
29: Each function feeds the next: extraction populates the register; the register defines the strata training plans against; trained models improve extraction; invention consumes the register’s learned layers. The loop is the capability.
30: Flow of a commission, end to end:
31: Objective Wizard session → compile {TargetOutcome, Collection Schema}
32: → Sampling & Reflection (calibration) → proposed Milestones + priced quote
33: → Owner agrees milestones → Commission opens
34: → Collection → Register update → Curriculum → Training runs → Certificates
35: → Commission View reports against milestones throughout → Commission sealed
36: 3  Tokenized Audio Representation
37: 3.1  Behaviour
38: All downstream audio work — extraction, character analysis, training — operates on discrete token sequences produced by a neural audio codec, not on waveforms.
39: Tokenization exposes two separable streams per segment: the content stream (what was said — input to ASR/NER) and the character stream (how it was said — input to the Character Register). The character stream is retained and routed, never discarded as noise.
40: Control markers (language, register, segment type) are splice-able tokens, enabling one model per estate rather than one per language, and native handling of code-switched speech.
41: Failure behaviour: audio in an unsupported condition fails closed with a stated reason. The codec never silently degrades quality.
42: 3.2  Technical contract
43: Item
44: Specification
45: Service
46: perception/audio_codec/ — registered like any other perception model; census-visible; runs in-perimeter on tenant compute.
47: Input
48: Audio segment (bounds per ingestion segmentation) + declared or detected condition profile.
49: Output
50: { content_tokens[], character_stream, codec_version }
51: Target token rate 50–100 tokens/second of audio.
52: Provenance
53: codec_version is a mandatory field of every downstream artifact’s provenance. A transcript states which codec produced its tokens.
54: Pretraining
55: The codec pretrains unsupervised on unlabelled estate audio, under the standard commissioned-job contract.
56: [VERIFY]
57: Perception router contract: where model registration occurs, and whether the router carries a second output stream per segment or the character stream requires its own artifact type.
58: 
59: 3.3  Acceptance criteria
60: Round-trip fidelity is measured and recorded per codec version before that version serves any commission.
61: A downstream artifact lacking codec_version in provenance is rejected at the registry boundary.
62: An unsupported-condition input produces a refusal with a stated reason and no output artifact.
63: 4  Extraction Layer
64: 4.1  Language identification
65: Behaviour: every segment carries a real language signal. The current plumbing value (language_hint: None) is retired.
66: A lightweight offline language identifier (CPU-viable, in-perimeter) runs at segment level during ingestion.
67: Recorded per segment: languages[], confidences, and code-switch points where multiple languages occur in one utterance.
68: The signal routes downstream model selection (ASR path, NER path, de-identification path) and is written into provenance.
69: [VERIFY] Segment boundaries in current ingestion — confirm the unit to which a language label attaches.
70: 4.2  Code-switch points as facts
71: Switch points (position, from-language, to-language, context class) are registered facts with provenance — not preprocessing metadata. They populate the register’s code-switch layer and stratify test sets.
72: 4.3  Condition profiling
73: Channel condition — studio / field / telephone band, transmission artefacts, background class — is derived per segment at first ingestion. It is cheap to compute, directly predictive of extraction error, and required for training stratification. It is captured at first ingestion because re-ingesting an estate to recover it is the unaffordable mistake.
74: 4.4  Synthesis-relevant attribute capture
75: During the same ingestion pass, group-level acoustic attributes required by any future synthesis capability (pitch statistics, energy contours, duration patterns) are captured, subject to the custody conditions of §6.4. This forecloses nothing and costs little; omitting it forecloses the invention function or forces re-ingestion.
76: 4.5  Deduplication as augmentation
77: The occurrence index already identifies repeated content. Its output contract is extended: for each deduplicated item, the instance condition map — the set of channel/time/condition variants under which identical content occurred — is retained. One canonical extraction is stored; the variant set enters training curricula as a designated robustness stratum at zero acquisition cost. No new detection work; this is a change to what dedup keeps.
78: 4.6  Acceptance criteria
79: No segment leaves ingestion without languages[], condition profile, and (where applicable) switch points in provenance.
80: A deduplicated item without its instance condition map fails the ingestion invariant test.
81: Baseline-tier capture (§9.2) runs for all admitted material regardless of any active objective.
82: 5  The Character Register — Learning
83: 5.1  Definition
84: A registry-modality store of learned, group-level audio characteristics, built from the character stream. Same doctrine as the fact registry: every entry carries provenance to source material and an occurrence count. It is Mtafiti’s qualification-and-index doctrine applied to acoustic observations — an extension, not a sibling (§1.2).
85: 5.2  Layers
86: Layer
87: Contents
88: Primary consumers
89: Phonetic
90: Per-lexeme pronunciation variants, frequency, regional distribution.
91: Curriculum; extraction lexicons; evaluation stratification
92: Prosodic
93: Intonation contours, stress, rate distributions, pause structure.
94: Training; programme-type classification
95: Condition
96: Channel and environment profiles.
97: Stratification; error prediction
98: Code-switch
99: Switch-point patterns, language pairs, context classes.
100: Training; test-set design
101: 
102: 5.3  Build process
103: Unsupervised clustering over the character stream yields candidate strata. A cluster asserts that a distinct variant exists — not what it is called. Naming and validation are human work applied to a sample, commissioned like any other qualified work with quoted cost.
104: 6  Register Custody Boundary
105: 6.1  Governing distinction: organic versus learned
106: Organic characteristics are anatomical — vocal tract length, formant structure, glottal source, fundamental frequency range. They cannot be acquired or shed; they are what speaker verification keys on; they are biometric. They are never registered.
107: Learned characteristics are acquired from a speech community — phonological inventory, pronunciation variants, prosody, code-switching habits. They are group properties by construction. Only learned characteristics may be registered.
108: 6.2  The four conditions — all must hold
109: Acquired, not anatomical. The attribute is learnable by a speaker from a different background.
110: Shared. Observed across at least N distinct speakers. N is a governed seam value; its default inherits the platform minimum-group-size parameter unless the tenant sets a register-specific value.
111: Non-reconstructive in combination. Tested against attribute combinations, not attributes in isolation: language + region + age band + one distinctive feature can reach a single person even when each attribute is group-level.
112: Stored as description, not exemplar. Centroids, distributions, frequencies. Never stored audio; never per-utterance speaker embeddings. Embeddings used during clustering are destroyed after cluster assignment. Provenance points to material, not to speaker identity.
113: 6.3  Enforcement shape
114: The register write path exposes no field through which an instance-level representation can be stored: the schema cannot represent a voiceprint. Unrepresentable, not policed (§1.5). An automated invariant test attempts each known leakage path (small stratum, idiolect marker, narrowing combination, exemplar storage) and must fail to store all of them on every change to the register code.
115: 6.4  Idiolect rule
116: Habitual fillers, characteristic phrasings, and idiosyncratically pronounced words are learned but individuating. They fail condition 2 or 3 and are excluded. “Learned” alone is never sufficient; the four conditions are conjunctive.
117: 7  Synthesized Voice Identity — Invention
118: 7.1  Mechanism: inherit the learned, synthesize the organic
119: Learned characteristics are inherited from the register — this is what makes the voice sound like a speaker of the language rather than a foreigner reading it.
120: Organic characteristics are constructed — vocal tract parameters, F0 range, formant structure, glottal parameters are chosen as a point in acoustic space that no real speaker occupies.
121: This is the inverse of a voice clone. A clone copies the organic and frequently gets the learned wrong; this gets the learned right and owns the organic outright.
122: 7.2  The distance guarantee (mandatory, fail-closed)
123: Every constructed identity is scored against every speaker representation derivable from the corpus using standard speaker-verification methods. A minimum distance from all of them is required. Below threshold, the identity is rejected and resampled. There is no override. The threshold value and the verification method are recorded with the identity.
124: 7.3  The certificate
125: A passing identity is issued a certificate stating that the voice is provably derived from no individual, naming the method, the threshold, and the corpus version scored against. The certificate is a first-class sellable artifact.
126: 7.4  Identity composition and versioning
127: Component
128: Source
129: Acoustic identity
130: Constructed organic parameters (§7.1).
131: Speech character
132: Inherited from register — phonetic and prosodic layers.
133: Interaction character
134: Turn-taking, formality, code-switch behaviour — inherited from register.
135: 
136: Each identity is a versioned artifact with a ledger entry. Changing one is a ceremony with the standard waiting period, because audience recognition accrues to the voice and recognition is the asset. Identities never drift.
137: 7.5  Scope note
138: Rendering requires a synthesis stack, which is a separate build from recognition. What this specification requires now is non-foreclosure: the identity specification (attribute schema, distance method, certificate format) is defined, and §4.4’s ingestion capture ensures the substrate exists when rendering is built.
139: 8  The Objective Wizard — Schema Compiler
140: 8.1  Role
141: No business user hand-writes a Target Outcome. The Objective Wizard — a new variant of the existing shaping wizard, reusing its agent interface, guards, session persistence, and ledger sidecar — elicits an objective in plain language and compiles two governed artifacts:
142: TargetOutcome (§10) — handed to the Training Planner.
143: Collection Schema (§9) — the data dictionary for this objective: which data points are extracted from the sound, at what granularity, at what quality bar.
144: 8.2  Elicitation sequence
145: The question the model must answer — operational and falsifiable.
146: The population — resolved against existing register strata; unresolved populations are flagged as unmeasured and generate census work.
147: The acceptance bar — per stratum, two-dimensional (§10), with the gate-or-document decision recorded explicitly.
148: The collection consequences — the wizard derives required columns, shows which are already collected (baseline tier), which exist but are uncollected, and the cost of collecting them. The owner sees the price of the schema before commissioning.
149: 8.3  Dynamism within scope: propose, qualify, graduate
150: Propose. The agent side may propose novel data points no prior objective collected. This is where innovation enters.
151: Qualify. A proposed column never enters collection directly. It is admitted as a candidate: collected on a sample only, its evidence of value measured against the objective — the same qualification path any fact travels.
152: Graduate. Qualified candidates graduate into the objective tier for that commission. Graduation into the baseline tier is ceremony-governed (proposal, countersignature, waiting period), because a baseline column is paid on every hour ingested for the life of the estate.
153: The compile stage is deterministic throughout: the agent proposes; only qualified columns compile. Mechanical guards prove against a stub agent before any LLM is plugged in, per the existing standing disposition.
154: 8.4  Compile-time rejections
155: The wizard cannot emit an artifact the downstream contracts would refuse. Rejected at compile, not warned:
156: An Outcome without an existing test_set_ref.
157: An acceptance bar missing the per-stratum dimension.
158: A Collection Schema requiring a column whose capture violates the custody conditions of §6.2.
159: 8.5  Record and handoff
160: Every session stamps to the ledger via the existing turn-ledger pattern under a distinct data class (objective_session), including options considered and rejected — which is what makes a later “why was the model built this way” answerable. Compiled artifacts hand off to Targeta through the existing admission-handoff pattern. Objective → schema → plan → run is one provenance chain.
161: [VERIFY] The B-2/B-3 landing state of the current wizard, before choosing between extending the existing state machine with an objective variant or standing up a sibling machine sharing the agent interface and ledger sidecar.
162: 9  The Collection Schema
163: 9.1  Definition
164: The declared data dictionary of a commission: what is extracted from the sound, for what purpose, at what quality bar. It is the admission standard of the audio estate, per objective (§1.1). It has two tiers.
165: 9.2  Baseline tier
166: Standing, objective-independent, collected at first ingestion for all admitted material. Membership criterion: cheap to collect now, unaffordable to collect later. Contents at v1.0: language identification, code-switch points, condition profile, dedup instance condition map, synthesis-relevant group-level acoustics (§4). Changes to the baseline are seam-governed — ceremony, countersignature, waiting period — because silently narrowing the baseline is how an estate quietly becomes unre-readable.
167: 9.3  Objective tier
168: Declared per commission by the Objective Wizard. Collected against material already in governed scope, priced before collection starts, recorded in the commission’s registry namespace. Candidate columns enter through propose–qualify–graduate (§8.3) only.
169: 10  The Target Outcome
170: 10.1  Schema
171: TargetOutcome {
172:   task          operational statement of what the model must do
173:   domain        context of use
174:   population    defined by reference to register strata, not labels
175:   acceptance    threshold per stratum; two-dimensional (accuracy, coverage)
176:   gate_policy   per Outcome: missed stratum gates release | ships documented
177:   test_set_ref  must exist before the Outcome is accepted
178:   constraints   latency, compute budget, deployment target
179: }
180: 
181: 10.2  Binding rules
182: Population is register-defined. “Language L, accent clusters 1–4, telephone band and studio, adult” — never “speakers of L.” This is what makes coverage computable.
183: Acceptance is per stratum. A single global threshold hides the failure that matters: 94% on the majority variant and 61% on the rest passes one test and fails the one that decides whether the work reaches the people it was built for.
184: The test set precedes the training. An Outcome without an existing, stratified test set is rejected at definition time.
185: The gate decision is recorded on the Outcome at definition — not decided ad hoc at ship time.
186: 11  The Training Planner
187: 11.1  Architecture
188: The existing planner pattern is reused unchanged: a deterministic core computes eligibility; a learned layer may only reorder an already-eligible set it receives stripped of the values that decided eligibility; a gate compares learned output against the deterministic baseline; every plan is reproducible from its recorded inputs.
189: 
190: Extraction planning (existing)
191: Training planning (new)
192: Object
193: Source locations
194: Register strata
195: Floor
196: Defensibility class
197: Acceptance threshold — accuracy × coverage
198: Output
199: Mining plan
200: Training plan + curriculum + milestones
201: 
202: 11.2  Sampling & Reflection (calibration) — mandatory first stage
203: Data requirements for low-resource fine-tuning are empirical; no analytical answer exists. The first commissioned stage is therefore a calibration: train at three to four data volumes, evaluate per stratum against the test set, fit the scaling curve, extrapolate to the acceptance threshold. Only then is the full run quoted, with a stated confidence interval — never a point estimate. A plan without a calibration stage is rejected. The first job prices the real job.
204: 11.3  Milestones — the accountability output
205: Sampling & Reflection has two customers. It prices the real job, and it authors the accountability structure: its output to the objective owner is not a curve but a proposed milestone list — the checklist of what must be done, in what order, for the commission to succeed. Each milestone carries a done-condition and an owner. The objective owner reviews and agrees the list at commission; from that point, all reporting is against it. Accountability is set before spend, not discovered during.
206: 11.4  Planner outputs
207: Coverage report — per target stratum: hours available, quality distribution, gaps, cost of closing each gap.
208: Curriculum — ordering and weighting across strata derived from the register, not from the corpus’s natural distribution, which is always skewed toward whatever occurred most. The dedup instance condition map enters as a designated robustness stratum.
209: Proposed milestone list (§11.3).
210: Cost quote with a stated confidence interval.
211: 11.5  Provenance through training
212: Every training example carries its provenance into the training manifest. Consequences: rights are enforceable per example; an example whose rights lapse is identifiable and the affected models enumerable; and “the trained model is the customer’s property” is a statement backed by a manifest, not an assertion.
213: 11.6  Run governance
214: Training runs are commissioned jobs under the existing contract: quoted before start, metered during, certificated on completion. The completion certificate records compute consumed, data touched, manifest hash, and per-stratum results against the Outcome. Failed strata are reported as plainly as passed ones.
215: 12  Record and Registry Integration
216: 12.1  Registry (Mtafiti audio modality)
217: Per commission, a scoped namespace within the registry holds: the Collection Schema (versioned), collected data points mapped against it — with declared-but-not-yet-collected as first-class state — the strata referenced by the Outcome, and coverage state per stratum. Reads compose with the global registry; writes are namespace-scoped. On close, the namespace is sealed, not deleted: it is the record of what was collected and why, and the next objective’s wizard session queries prior schemas and coverage so the second project starts from the first project’s map.
218: 12.2  Record (Northena data classes)
219: Training-workflow operations stamp into the one ledger under training-specific data classes: collection events, calibration runs, curriculum decisions, milestone status changes, run certificates. The workflow’s view of “its” record is a scoped lens filterable by commission ID — a view, not a store. Working state (loss curves, intermediate metrics, partial counts) is scratch until finalized and stamped once (§1.3).
220: 13  Surface Specification — the Commission View
221: 13.1  Scope
222: This surface adjustment applies to all commissioned work on the platform — extraction, census, and training commissions alike, across every extraction type. No modality receives its own UI, and no surface is a rendering of backend internals: rendering internals quietly commits the backend to building displayable versions of its own machinery.
223: 13.2  Behaviour
224: The surface is milestones. The artifacts are evidence behind them.
225: At Sampling & Reflection, the proposed milestone list is presented to the objective owner for agreement. Commission does not open until it is agreed.
226: The Commission View reports against the agreed checklist: each milestone with its done-condition and owner; status in plain terms — done, on track, behind, missed. Missed is shown as plainly as done.
227: Spend against quote is shown at the same plain level.
228: Technical material — calibration results, strata coverage, Collection Schema state — is drill-down evidence for whoever asks why a milestone reads as it does. It is never the front page.
229: 13.3  Modality leaf
230: Modality appears at exactly one leaf: evidence inspection. Where provenance resolves to a recording, the source plays at its timestamp rather than rendering as a page region — the existing trust-receipt pattern (“a disputed number is answered by playing the tape”), unchanged.
231: 13.4  Backend cost constraint
232: Milestones are records with done-conditions; the platform already stamps events. No new machinery is built for display. Any surface element in this section found to require new backend computation beyond reading existing artifacts is out of specification and must be removed or re-specified.
233: 14  Interface Summary
234: Surface
235: Contract
236: audio_codec
237: audio in → { content_tokens, character_stream, codec_version }; fail-closed on unsupported condition.
238: Language ID
239: segment → { languages[], confidences, switch_points }; written to provenance.
240: Occurrence index (ext.)
241: dedup item → + instance condition map.
242: Character Register
243: Write path: schema cannot represent instance-level identity (§6.3). Read path: strata queries for planner and evaluation.
244: Objective Wizard
245: session → { TargetOutcome, CollectionSchema }; deterministic compile; compile-time rejection of contract-violating artifacts; session stamped to ledger.
246: TargetOutcome
247: Rejected without existing test_set_ref; acceptance per stratum; gate_policy recorded at definition.
248: Training Planner
249: Outcome → { coverage report, curriculum, milestone list, quote ± interval }; reproducible plan_id; plan without calibration stage rejected.
250: Training run
251: Commissioned-job contract; completion certificate incl. manifest hash and per-stratum results.
252: Voice identity
253: register strata + constructed organic parameters → identity; distance gate mandatory, fail-closed; certificate issued on pass; versioned; change by ceremony.
254: Commission View
255: Reads milestones, statuses, spend, and existing artifacts only; introduces no new backend computation.
256: 15  Build Sequence
257: Ordered by dependency and cost-of-deferral, not by size.
258: #
259: Item

263: Everything downstream consumes these; only cheap at first ingestion. Deferral cost is a full re-pass over the estate.

# SOURCE: assessment_workspace/canon/w11_new_docs/canon_17_19.docx
Coordinate: document.xml paragraph in body order, tables included

1: AKKI · GOVERNED ARTIFACT · CANON SPECIFICATION
2: Documents 17–19
3: The Multidimensional Training Engine · Callable Skill Files · Quality Assurance & Evidence Integrity
4: Companion to Documents 1–16. Written to the same standard: every requirement is CANON (already ratified, cited to its source), RULED (an Owner decision on record, not yet executed), or OPEN (genuinely undecided). Nothing here is invented; where this document reuses existing code or a ratified spec, the source file is cited inline.
5: DOCUMENT 17   The Multidimensional Training Engine
6: The Multidimensional Training Engine
7: Extends and completes Promises #22, #23, #24 (Documents 13–14) with the technical requirements layer those documents named but did not land.
8: 17.1 · The promise, in plain language
9: The platform trains models across any modality the estate holds — not audio alone — on its own, against a target made falsifiable before training starts, at a price measured before commitment, producing models whose ingredients are provable per example and whose configuration is a versioned, evidence-gated object rather than code. This is Promise #22 and #23's own language, generalised past the audio-specific frame: “the platform trains models on its own … meeting every criterion on uncurated held-out material or not entering service” (#22); “before committing a training job, the platform works with the user to get the objective right … only then does the job commit” (#23).
10: 17.2 · The service that powers it
11: Targeta — the walled yield layer already named under #22 — extended by a modality-agnostic trainer runner (unbuilt; §17.5) and a training-data custody seam that routes every training read through the same custody discipline as any other read (Document 1).
12: 17.3 · Definition of the promise
13: Decomposed from the Training & Optimization Techniques Specification v1.0 (RMS-IQ-Core-2, docs/requirements/training_techniques_spec_v1.md — Owner-ratified 2026-07-17) and the training-planning specification (Aug-2026), reused here as the governing definition, not restated from memory.
14: Foundation method is fixed, not chosen per run
15: Every model the platform trains is a LoRA/PEFT adapter over a registered open base model — never a full fine-tune, never an unregistered model. This is FACT-class in the ratified spec, meaning it is not revisited per training job; it is a standing constraint on what “training” is allowed to mean on this platform. Training material is drawn exclusively from de-duplicated, VAD-cleaned, qualified units — the same units the estate's extraction pipeline already produces, never raw source reached around that pipeline. Acceptance runs exclusively through MOAC on uncurated held-out sets: a model is never accepted on the material it was tuned against.
16: Configuration is a governed object, not code
17: If the optimizer, the learning-rate schedule, the batch and epoch parameters, and the adapter's rank and target modules lived in code, every change to how a model trains would be a code change — reviewed on a different cadence, by different people, invisible to the ledger that governs every other consequential object on the platform. Instead, all of it lives under training_params@v0, a sidecar configuration class carrying the identical discipline already proven for extraction_params@v0: versioned, ledgered, kept outside contracts/, with no Parity contact. A recipe change and a rule change are now the same kind of act, auditable the same way.
18: The seat starts empty; evidence fills it, not judgement
19: No default recipe exists at commission. The first real training run does not consume a pre-set configuration — it is the mechanism that produces one, through the measured optimizer-selection protocol below (§17.3, Training Planner). This is a deliberate inversion of the usual order: most systems ship a default and revise it under pressure; this one ships nothing until something has actually been measured. Every trained model's registry entry cites the exact recipe_version that produced it, extending MOAC's lineage criterion (M-d) by this field — which base model, which optimizer, which schedule is never a matter of asking someone, only of reading the record.
20: Revision is cheap; unevidenced revision is a defect
21: Recipe revisions carry no approval ceremony — they are DEFAULT-class, expected to happen as evidence accumulates. But every revision must attach the measured comparison that justifies it and must write a ledger row. The absence of ceremony is not the absence of accountability: a revision with no attached evidence is not a lighter-weight change, it is a defect, indistinguishable in the record from an engineer overriding the platform's own evidentiary standard by hand.
22: The Target Outcome — training cannot be commissioned against an unfalsifiable goal
23: A training job is not admitted from a task description alone. It is admitted from a Target Outcome, a schema that forces the goal into a form that can actually fail:
24: TargetOutcome:
25:   task            operational statement of what the model must do
26:   domain          context of use
27:   population      defined by reference to register strata, not labels
28:   acceptance      threshold per stratum — two-dimensional (accuracy, coverage)
29:   test_set_ref    must exist before the plan is accepted
30:   constraints     latency, compute budget, deployment target
31: Two rules are binding, not advisory. Population is register-defined: “language L, accent clusters 1–4, telephone band and studio, adult”, never “speakers of L” — because only a register-defined population makes coverage a computable number rather than a felt impression. Acceptance is per stratum, not global: a single aggregate figure hides exactly the failure that matters — 94% on the majority variant and 61% on everything else passes one test and fails the one that decides whether the work reaches the people it was built for. Whether a missed stratum blocks release is a governed decision recorded on the Outcome at definition time, not an ad-hoc call made under ship-date pressure. And the ordering constraint is absolute: the test set precedes the training. An Outcome submitted without an existing, stratified test set is rejected at definition, before a single GPU-hour is spent.
32: The Training Planner — the same pattern as extraction, a different object and floor
33: The planner is not new architecture. It reuses, unchanged, the pattern already proven for extraction planning: a deterministic core computes eligibility; a learned layer may only reorder an already-eligible set, and it receives that set stripped of the values that decided eligibility in the first place, so it cannot learn to game the floor; a gate compares the learned layer's output against the deterministic baseline before anything ships; every plan is reproducible from its own recorded inputs. What changes between the two is only the object being planned over and the floor that governs it:
34: 
35: Extraction planning (existing)
36: Training planning (new)
37: Object
38: Source locations
39: Register strata
40: Floor
41: Defensibility class
42: Acceptance threshold — accuracy × coverage
43: Output
44: Mining plan
45: Training plan + curriculum + milestones
46: Planner outputs, per commissioned Outcome, are four things: a coverage report per target stratum — hours available, quality distribution, gaps, and the cost of closing each gap; a curriculum, ordered and weighted from the register itself, deliberately not from the corpus's natural distribution, which is always skewed toward whatever occurred most — the dedup instance-condition map enters here as a designated robustness stratum, at zero additional acquisition cost; the calibration commission (below); and a cost quote carrying a stated confidence interval, never a bare point estimate.
47: Calibration is the planner's mandatory first stage, not an optional safeguard. Data requirements for low-resource fine-tuning are empirical — no analytical formula predicts how much data a given stratum needs to cross its acceptance threshold. So the first commissioned job is never the real job: it trains at three or four data volumes, evaluates against the test set per stratum, fits the scaling curve, and only then extrapolates to what the full run would cost and how likely it is to clear the threshold. A plan without a calibration stage is rejected outright — the first job's entire purpose is to price the real one honestly.
48: Calibration has a second customer beyond pricing: it authors the accountability structure the objective owner will be held to. Its output is not only a curve, it is a proposed milestone list — the checklist of what must be done, in what order, for the commission to succeed, each milestone carrying a done-condition and an owner. The objective owner reviews and agrees this list at commission, before spend begins; every status report afterward is measured against it. Accountability is set before the money moves, not reconstructed afterward from whatever happened to get done.
49: Provenance survives the training, not just the extraction. Every training example carries its provenance into the training manifest, which has three consequences that matter beyond bookkeeping: rights are enforceable per example, so an example whose rights lapse is identifiable and every model it touched is enumerable, not merely suspected; “the trained model is the customer's property” becomes a defensible statement backed by a manifest rather than an assertion made because it sounds right; and the dedup instance-condition map enters the curriculum as a designated robustness stratum at zero acquisition cost, because it was already being computed for a different purpose.
50: 17.4 · Delivery experience expectations
51: What the organisation experiences (human-facing)
52: Defines a target outcome — task, domain, register-defined population, per-stratum acceptance — and the platform rejects it outright if the test set doesn't already exist.
53: Watches the mandatory first stage, calibration, as staged progress: three to four data volumes trained and evaluated per stratum, the scaling curve fit, the full run quoted only after — with a confidence interval, never a point estimate.
54: Receives the calibration run's second output alongside the price: a proposed milestone list, each with a done-condition and an owner, agreed before spend rather than discovered during it.
55: Sees an optimizer or recipe-component candidate proven or rejected by a measured two-arm comparison against the current baseline — both arms' numbers reported, parity mandatory for adoption, the verdict an Owner ruling on evidence rather than a preset threshold.
56: Gets a model that provably cleared all six MOAC criteria, or a recorded rejection with its numbers — never a manually waved-through model — with rejected candidates kept on the shelf permanently.
57: What a consuming system experiences (machine-facing)
58: Reads a model's registry entry citing its recipe_version, base model, and the rights lineage that trained it — lineage is enumerable, not asserted.
59: Reads a training run's completion certificate: compute consumed, data touched, manifest hash, and per-stratum results against the Outcome — failed strata reported as plainly as passed ones.
60: What is produced and retained
61: The training manifest — every example's provenance carried through to the trained artifact, so a lapsed-rights example is identifiable and every model it touched is enumerable.
62: The completion certificate and the recipe_version record, both permanent.
63: On rejection, the candidate and its measured numbers, retained — a negative result is still a result.
64: 17.5 · Technical and behavioural requirements
65: Governance layer — already ratified, reused verbatim from RMS-IQ-Core-2
66: A17.1  [CANON] Configuration lives outside code.
67: Optimizer and its parameters, learning-rate schedule, batch and epoch parameters, and adapter rank and target modules MUST live under training_params@v0, a sidecar configuration class with the same discipline as extraction_params@v0: versioned, ledgered, outside contracts/, no Parity contact. The effect is that a training configuration change is reviewable and auditable the same way a rule change is — not a deploy note buried in a pull request.
68: T-1.1, training_techniques_spec_v1.md
69: A17.2  [CANON] The seat ships empty.
70: No default recipe exists until the first training run fills it through the §3 optimizer-selection protocol (A17.5–A17.6). Nothing may pre-populate training_params@v0 by convention, template, or engineer judgement — the first value ever written to it must carry the measured comparison that produced it.
71: A17.3  [CANON] Lineage extends to configuration.
72: Every trained model's registry entry MUST cite the recipe_version that trained it. MOAC's lineage criterion (M-d) extends by this field, so “which configuration produced this model” is answered by reading the registry, never by asking whoever happened to run the job.
73: A17.4  [CANON] Revision is DEFAULT-class, but never unevidenced.
74: Recipe revisions carry no approval ceremony. Each revision MUST attach the measured comparison that justifies it and MUST write a ledger row. A revision without attached evidence is a defect — the absence of ceremony is a statement of trust in the evidentiary standard, not an exemption from it.
75: A17.5–A17.6  [CANON] The optimizer-selection protocol: two arms, identical conditions, parity mandatory.
76: The protocol executes at the first adapter training on real material, inside the P4-instrumented run. Its shape is one two-arm comparison — the current baseline optimizer versus a candidate, Muon named as the first — with identical training data, identical base model, identical evaluation sets, and an identical compute-budget cap, run on the smallest stratum that still yields a valid MOAC evaluation. Four measured outputs are reported for both arms without exception: target-stratum improvement (MOAC's M-a), non-target regression (M-b), wall-clock and GPU-hours to convergence, and calibration quality (an M-e input). Quality parity on M-a and M-b is mandatory for the candidate to remain eligible at all; compute-to-convergence is reported, never gating — a faster optimizer that regresses quality is not eligible regardless of its speed. The adopt/reject decision is then an Owner ruling made on the measured results, with no adoption threshold fixed in advance of the evidence, and verdict samples are uncurated per the platform's standing D-7 doctrine (evaluation inputs may be engineered; evaluation samples may not). On adoption, the winning arm writes training_params@v0 v1 with the comparison attached; on rejection, the candidate is recorded as tested, with its numbers, permanently. The identical protocol governs every future recipe-component candidate — this is not a one-time bootstrap, it is how the recipe seat is filled from now on.
77: A17.7  [CANON] Ensemble critics detect; they never decide.
78: Multiple reviewing instances are legitimate where a single critic's detection quality is insufficient, and prohibited from ever holding decision authority — the boundary follows from the platform's design (one walled learner, one reasoning faculty, the standing QA-1 rule that the layer detects and never decides) and is permanent, not a current-scope limitation. Deployment order is fixed: when seeded audits show a single critic's catch-rate below the standing bar on any fall class across two consecutive audits, rubric and context repair MUST execute first; an ensemble MAY deploy only if the repaired single critic still misses on a subsequent audit. Members MUST differ genuinely — a different base model or a materially different context shape — because same-base, same-context replicas are correlated reviewers that share failure modes and add cost without adding detection. All ensemble output is findings only; voting, override, and critic-of-critic structures are prohibited outright. Disagreement between critics is itself a finding class, routed to rulings like any other. Bounds: N ≤ 3 members without an explicit Owner ruling, with cost-per-review telemetry emitted per member, and the ensemble retires on its own kill metric — if its catch-rate gain over the single repaired critic falls under 10 percentage points after one full calibration cycle, it is rent not worth paying.
79: A17.8  [CANON] Cascade offload builds only against a measured shortfall, never speculatively.
80: A local-cascade — a local model drafts, an LLM handles only what the local model cannot — reduces metered spend where a cheaper model can filter most of a workload, but carries a documented failure mode: past a certain escalation rate, each escalated item pays twice, local and LLM both, and the cascade turns net-negative. The platform already minimizes LLM load by construction (the rung ladder, record-derived facts never re-asked of the LLM, the mechanical composition arm, the critic-succession seat), so a cascade is deliberately not pre-built. It MAY begin only when F3 telemetry, with cost columns active, shows LLM spend on a named seam exceeding a threshold the Owner sets at that time — no threshold exists in advance of metered evidence, and before the trigger fires, no cascade scaffolding, draft-model acquisition, or routing machinery may be built at all (the D7 fence). Its shape, once triggered, is local model drafts → deterministic acceptance check → LLM invoked only on rejects, where the acceptance check is rung-1 machinery, not a second model's judgement. It MUST emit its own kill metric — the double-pay rate, the share of items incurring both local and LLM cost — from its first run, and MUST retire if escalation makes it net-negative against the pre-cascade baseline.
81: A17.9  [CANON] Execution mode is explicit or the process refuses to start.
82: PERCEPTION_EXECUTION_MODE is read from the environment at import time and must be exactly “cpu” or “gpu”; an unset variable raises an import-time failure rather than defaulting silently, because a GPU deployment quietly running on CPU is the same silent-swap risk in the opposite direction from what governance normally worries about — it fails safe in the wrong direction, producing correct-looking but unrepresentative results rather than an obvious error. execution_mode is then carried in result telemetry, so attribution of GPU-hours and yield to a mode the record doesn't state is closed the same way fabricated model attribution is closed elsewhere in the canon.

Empty per data-blind misapplies the posture: data-blind governs assumptions about the estate's content, not tool provenance — a model registry entry is tooling attestation, and an empty registry plus a provenance gate is the CD-E3 deadlock again (nothing can pass).”

111: 17.6 · What must be true for the service to deliver as intended
112: No training run commits without an existing, stratified test set — a target outcome without one is rejected at definition, not at run time.
113: No model enters service without clearing all six MOAC criteria on uncurated held-out material, with no human in the acceptance path.
114: The recipe seat is never filled speculatively — only by measured evidence from a real run against real material.
115: Base model selection never precedes the census it depends on.
116: No ensemble critic holds decision authority; ensembles surface findings, never verdicts.
117: Cascade offload never builds ahead of a measured cost pressure that names its own trigger.
118: A GPU deployment never silently runs on CPU, and a CPU deployment never silently claims GPU throughput.

120: DOCUMENT 18   Callable Skill Files
121: Callable Skill Files
122: A new promise — Promise #33. Owner-confirmed architecture (July 2026, RMS-IQ-Core-2); complete donor code exists but is not in the current build.
123: 18.1 · The promise, in plain language
124: A skill is a stay-running, key-scoped query capability over a defined corpus slice — an application calls it and receives governed answers, repeatedly, on the platform's own infrastructure. It is not model weights, and it is not a file handed over: governance does not end at delivery, because there is no delivery. It travels into every call, for the life of the skill.
125: 18.2 · The service that powers it
126: The existing inner-gate crossing infrastructure (Document 1), extended by the callable-skill donor package — complete implementation, ~356 LOC, present in both RMS-IQ-Core-2 and Akki-OS-V1: a frozen provisioning contract, a per-call governance gate, and write-once persistence. Not in the current build; sized by the builder at a clean ~40% LIFT into the W11 envelope alongside Document 17's runner.
127: 18.3 · Definition of the promise
128: The reasoning below is reused close to verbatim from the July 2026 architecture ruling, because the reasoning is the part worth keeping intact — a conclusion without it invites re-litigating the same ground later.
129: Why this needed its own ruling, not an extension of the export model
130: Every output the platform can produce looks, at first, like a variation on “produce something, then define who can access it.” Treating all outputs that way is a trap: it architects the live ones as static deliverables, and the mistake surfaces only once a skill gets queried a thousand times and turns out to need per-call governance the export model was never built to carry. The real distinction is not output-then-access. It is whether the system finishes and hands over, or stays running and answers.
131: Two classes, one dividing line
132: Hand-over: qualified data, a knowledge artifact, a trained model file. The system produces, packages, and delivers a finished thing; governance is enforced once, at export. Stay-running: a callable skill, an API feed. The system stays up and a consumer queries it repeatedly; governance has to travel into every one of those calls, live. Skills are stay-running by definition — an application queries them, they are not model weights, and the “trained behaviour” reading of “skill” belongs to the model-output form (§17), not here. This is not new architecture: it is the identical governance-travels-inline requirement the platform's integration surface already carries for API responses, now extended to a standing service rather than a single call.
133: What this fixes about the delivery model, concretely
134: Hand-over outputs continue to fit the existing two-perimeter export model without change. Stay-running outputs need per-call inline governance, which is the reason this document exists as its own promise rather than a line item under an existing one — the liability model, the access architecture, and the governance surface for “a file the consumer runs themselves” and “a service they call on the platform's own infrastructure, forever” are genuinely different products, and conflating them is what produces the failure mode described above.
135: Grain is per_claim and synthesized_whole, per query — deliberately distinct from a knowledge artifact's per_claim/aggregated grain, because a skill composes a fresh answer to each specific question rather than exporting one fixed graph once.
136: 18.4 · Delivery experience expectations
137: What the organisation experiences (human-facing)
138: Provisions a skill over a frozen, named corpus slice and hands a consumer a scoped key and an endpoint — nothing else about the underlying data.
139: Revokes a skill and has every subsequent call refuse immediately — enforcement is server-side, not a client convention that can be ignored.
140: Reads the provisioning record for any skill: who was granted what scope, over which slice, from when to when.
141: What a consuming system experiences (machine-facing)
142: Calls the skill repeatedly and receives an answer with its class carried inline on every response — never a response the inner gate hasn't governed.
143: Queries below the skill's floor and receives the refusal envelope, not a degraded or partial answer.
144: Cannot reach a slice wider than the one bound at provisioning — a changed slice is a new skill, never a silent edit of the old one.
145: What is produced and retained
146: The provisioning record itself: skill_id, corpus_slice_ref, key_grant_id, floor, scope, endpoint_path, provisioned_at, and revoked_at once set.
147: Every call's governance class, carried on the response, per the inner gate's existing per-call record discipline.
148: 18.5 · Technical and behavioural requirements
149: A18.1  [CANON] The provisioning record, reused verbatim.
150: This is the frozen contract every skill is created against — not a draft to redesign, a specification already anchored to owner rulings TF-E2/TF-E4 and reused as-is:
151: Callable-skill provisioning record
152:   { skill_id, corpus_slice_ref: artifact-store key,
153:     key_grant_id, floor, scope, endpoint_path,
154:     provisioned_at, revoked_at?: str }
155: §3.7 annex, RMS Intelligence spec, 2026-07
156: A18.2  [CANON] The slice freezes; it never edits.
157: Corpus slice binds at freeze, an endpoint is provisioned against it, and a key is scoped to that endpoint. The slice persists via the artifact store, write-once. If the underlying material needs to change, the platform provisions a new skill against a new slice — it does not mutate the old one, because a mutating slice would mean the governance decision made at provisioning (“this key may see this material”) silently stops describing what the key can actually reach.
158: A18.3  [CANON] Governance rides every response, not just the first one.
159: Every response carries its class inline through the inner gate's per-call governance — the platform's existing live-response contract, applied here to a standing service instead of a single crossing. Nothing about the mechanism is new; what changes is that it now runs once per query for the life of the skill, rather than once per delivery.
160: A18.4  [CANON] Below the floor is a refusal, never a degraded answer.
161: The standard is enforced per call. A query that falls below the skill's floor returns the refusal envelope — the same governed refusal shape used everywhere else on the platform — rather than a thinner or hedged version of an answer.
162: A18.5  [CANON] Scope is enforced server-side, not by client discipline.
163: Access rides the engineer key-grant records. A consuming application's own good behaviour is never the control — scope is checked at the gate on every call, so a compromised or careless client can narrow what it asks for but cannot widen what it's able to get.
164: A18.6  [PROPOSED] Async delivery, if fresh extraction ever backs a skill's answer.
165: Not yet confirmed as part of skill files specifically, but already a ratified contract shape elsewhere in the same source, and the natural fit if a skill's query ever requires extraction rather than a warm read: fork at admission — warm returns a synchronous full response; fresh returns 202 with { objective_id, status: accepted, delivery_estimate, quote? }. States move accepted → running → delivered | refused, with a late refusal a normal terminal state carrying the same refusal envelope, never rendered as a failure. Delivery is a thin webhook plus a governed fetch: the webhook payload is { event, objective_id, trace_id, status } — never claim content — and the actual result is pulled over the caller's authenticated key, scope enforced there, not pushed to an app-configured URL, because pushing claims to arbitrary endpoints would be an egress path the gates don't control. No partial egress, including on cancellation — a cancelled run is still ledgered. An idempotency key is required on submission so a retried call cannot double-commission or double-charge.
166: §7, RMS Intelligence spec, 2026-07 — proposed here for skill files by extension, not yet owner-confirmed for this specific case
167: A18.7  [RULED] The concept is owner-confirmed; its adoption into this canon is not inherited.
168: “Skill files” as a named artifact appear nowhere in the 16-document canon. The architecture above is owner-confirmed [STAKED] in the July specification — that ruling is real and reused here verbatim — but formally landing it as Promise #33, with its own number in this codebase's canon, is this document's own act. It should be read as adoption, not as a restatement of a decision already made at this level.
169: A18.8  [OPEN] Complete donor code exists; it is not in this build.
170: Roughly 356 lines across RMS-IQ-Core-2 and Akki-OS-V1 implement the frozen provisioning contract, the per-call governance gate, and write-once persistence — a clean ~40% of it liftable directly. Build scope: the remaining contracts, the corpus-slice custody seam (shared with Document 17's execution layer), and a skill-files registry surface on the frontend, delivered inside the same W11 envelope as the trainer runner.
171: 18.6 · What must be true for the service to deliver as intended
172: A corpus slice is bound and frozen before an endpoint is ever provisioned — no skill is provisioned against a moving target.
173: No response leaves the inner gate without its governance class carried inline.
174: Revocation is enforced at the gate, not at the client — a revoked key produces a refusal even if a consumer never checks its own state.
175: A widened or changed slice is never expressed as an edit to a live skill — only as a new one, with its own provisioning record.

177: DOCUMENT 19   Quality Assurance & Evidence Integrity
178: Quality Assurance & Evidence Integrity
179: Two parts. Part A, the Critic Seam, is CANON — Owner-ratified 2026-07-15, reused here in full. Part B, the Evidence Protocol, is PROPOSED — my own prior synthesis from an August chat, explicitly offered there for ratification and never confirmed adopted; checked directly against both repositories, with no trace of a build or a ruling. It is written here to the same standard as everything ratified, with its status stated plainly rather than smoothed over.
180: 19A.1 · The promise, in plain language
181: Every intelligent worker in this build — the builder agent executing phases, any LLM worker the platform harnesses at runtime, and the ruling authority's own drafts and rulings — has its output checked against the on-disk record before it can mislead, not corrected by hand after it already has. The layer mechanizes exactly the half of quality assurance that is mechanizable: verification against canon. It deliberately does not attempt the other half — reframing the problem, changing the product's direction — which remains the Owner's seat, permanently.
182: 19A.2 · The service that powers it
183: No single named engine; a layer integrated into the standing build loop itself — the Registry (every function's mandate, promise, service trace, enforcement, cost, owner), the Registry Doctrine's binding rules, and the existing ruling loop (dispatch → Stage A proposal → escalation → ruling → execution → close report). It extends two precedents already standing in the build rather than introducing new machinery: the standing queries' findings-not-actions pattern, and Targeta's wall — the constitutional precedent that a subordinate intelligence detects and optimizes but never decides, which the critic inherits verbatim.
184: 19A.3 · Definition of the promise
185: Origin: every check mechanizes a catch the Owner actually made, by hand
186: This is not a speculative layer designed against a hypothetical failure mode. Five documented fall classes from this build's own correction history fix its boundary: memory-ruling (asserting something false against the on-disk record — the origin of doctrine rule D-11); re-derivation (proposing something as fresh advice that the Owner's own specification already states, caught once at the cost of a full audit cycle); invented scope or schedule (work categories or sequencing authored without instruction, against an explicit fence); false status (a register claiming a close was never returned while it sat on disk, a day old); and unclassed assertion (values and claims stated without their evidence class). The line that fixes the layer's boundary: every catch above is a verification — the truth existed on disk and the worker diverged from it. The Owner's other interventions in this build's history were frame changes — rewriting canon rather than diverging from it — and no layer that verifies against canon can catch a correction to canon. Frame authority is permanently outside this layer's reach.
187: Five design principles, each tied to a standing precedent
188: Detect, never decide — the layer emits findings; every consequence is a ruling. A QA layer with veto power would be a governor nobody mandated.
189: Canon is the oracle — all deterministic verification resolves against the on-disk record, never a summary, a context window, or another model's recollection.
190: Zero loop drag — the layer adds no turns to the dispatch loop; deterministic checks run as cells at submission boundaries, the critic runs asynchronously between turns, findings arrive with the artifacts they review, never before them.
191: Halving, not zeroing, stated honestly — a critic sharing a worker's blind spot misses what both cannot see; the claim is a measurable shrinkage of the residual, not its elimination, which is why the layer measures itself rather than trusting itself.
192: The layer pays rent — its own catch and false-alarm ledger is standing; if it stops catching and starts noising, it shrinks or retires by ruling, the same discipline every other function on the platform is held to.
193: 19A.4 · Delivery experience expectations
194: What the organisation experiences (human-facing)
195: The Owner's reviewing role compresses; it does not disappear. Instead of reading every artifact, a measured fraction of critic findings and all-clears is sampled for review — the sampling rate itself shrinks as the critic's measured reliability accumulates.
196: Sees findings, never a blocked workflow — the one exception is a hard format gate on missing required sections, form only, never substance.
197: Reads a standing calibration ledger: the critic's catch-rate and false-alarm rate per worker class, versioned like model calibration, so “how much can I trust this layer” is a citable number rather than a felt impression.
198: What a consuming system experiences (machine-facing)
199: A Stage A proposal or close report submitted without its required sections — including the self-audit table — is rejected at the format gate before it enters the loop at all.
200: Every other check returns a finding row, never a block: citation mismatches, untraceable scope, unclassed assertions, schema gaps, status contradicted by the repository, and lexical collisions with existing Registry entries all surface as findings, not failures.
201: What is produced and retained
202: Findings reports, evidence-classed and cited like every other producer's output on this platform — an unclassed finding is itself a finding.
203: The calibration ledger, carrying a staleness field; a critic whose calibration falls outside its window renders its findings UNCALIBRATED rather than silently stale.
204: The checks themselves register in the Registry with their own rows — they are functions, and functions pay rent like every other function on the platform.
205: 19A.5 · Technical and behavioural requirements
206: Tier 1 — deterministic record-verification (rung 1)
207: Six check families, all mechanical, all resolving against the repository, running on Stage A proposals and close reports at submission:
208: Check
209: Definition
210: Mechanizes
211: RV-1 citation-existence
212: Every SHA, file path, ruling id, registry row id, and contract name cited resolves to an existing on-disk object; cited SHAs match the object's actual hash.
213: Memory-ruling
214: RV-2 scope-trace
215: Every work item traces to an authorizing instrument — a dispatch, a register row, a ruling. Untraceable items are scope-invention candidates.
216: Invented scope
217: RV-3 evidence-class presence
218: Classed assertions (status, values, verdicts) carry FACT/NORM/DEFAULT or fact/recalled/inferred, matching their class's required form.
219: Unclassed assertion
220: RV-4 schema-completeness
221: Required sections present — band, escalations, registry rows, self-audit table for proposals; gate roster, artifact SHAs, self-audit table for closes. The one hard gate (QA-2).
222: Submission discipline
223: RV-5 status-truth
224: Every status claim about an on-disk artifact is cross-checked against actual repository state at submission time.
225: False status (the LT-1 class)
226: RV-6 novelty collision
227: Proposed function ids, promise ids, and concept labels are matched against the Registry and mandate documents; collisions flag for semantic confirmation.
228: Re-derivation, first line of defense
229: Tier 1's conceded limit, stated by the source rather than discovered later: it verifies form and existence, not pertinence — an artifact can cite real SHAs for irrelevant objects and pass. Pertinence is exactly what Tier 2 is for; the two tiers are designed as a pair, and adopting Tier 1 alone buys the cheap half while advertising the whole.
230: Tier 2 — the critic pass (rung 3/4), independent by construction
231: An independent model instance reviews each Stage A and close asynchronously, after landing, against a fixed six-item rubric drawn directly from the Owner's own catch history: anti-re-derivation (does this already exist in the record under any name), anti-fabrication (is any claim stronger than its evidence class permits), the conflation test (does every proposed function trace to a real named service), scope semantics (does the work's substance stay inside the dispatch's intent, beyond what the mechanical trace alone catches), enforcement honesty (is any rule proposed whose only enforcement is prose), and self-audit audit (does the artifact's own self-audit table's reasoning hold, or is it reflexive pass-stamping). The critic never shares the worker's conversation — its context is exactly the artifact under review, the canon set, and the rubric, never the worker's reasoning or drafts, because a critic reading the worker's own justification inherits the worker's frame, which is precisely the blind-spot-sharing failure the design exists to avoid. No worker ever critics its own output; where critic and worker share a base model, independence is by context isolation alone, and Tier 3's seeded audits exist specifically to measure whether that isolation is sufficient rather than assume it. The critic runs at the cheapest sufficient rung, and its findings carry the same evidence-classing and citation discipline as every other producer on the platform.
232: Tier 3 — human calibration sampling: the Owner's role compresses, it does not vanish
233: Verdict sampling: a fraction of critic findings and all-clears (default 20% of findings, 10% of all-clears, decaying as measured reliability accumulates) is human-scored as a true catch, a false alarm, or a miss.
234: Seeded-defect audits: on a standing cadence, a known defect from a documented fall class is deliberately planted in a review copy — never a landing artifact — and the critic's catch or miss is recorded. This is the only honest measurement of a reviewer that mostly reports clean: detection proven on known positives, drawn across fall classes, never curated toward the critic's own strengths.
235: The calibration ledger: catch-rate and false-alarm rate per worker class and rubric item, versioned like model calibration, with a staleness field — a critic whose calibration is stale past its window renders its findings UNCALIBRATED at the point of use, the same honesty rule the platform applies to model confidence generally.
236: Behavioural rules, binding on adoption
237: QA-1  [CANON] Detect, never decide. No finding blocks execution, edits an artifact, or gates a phase — every consequence is a ruling. One scoped exception: QA-2.
238: QA-2  [CANON] The format gate. Schema-completeness (RV-4) is the single hard gate — a submission missing its required sections is returned for completion before it enters the loop. Form, never substance.
239: QA-3  [CANON] No self-review. No worker critics its own output; independence is by context isolation, itself measured by seeded audits.
240: QA-4  [CANON] Findings carry the honesty grammar — every finding is evidence-classed and cited; an unclassed finding is itself a finding.
241: QA-5  [CANON] The layer pays rent. The catch/false-alarm ledger is standing; a layer that stops catching shrinks by ruling. A second QA layer above this one is a meta-spiral defect on sight.
242: QA-6  [CANON] Frame authority is untouchable. No check, rubric item, or finding may dispute an Owner ruling, a service sentence, or a frame decision — the layer verifies divergence from canon; it has no standing on changes to canon.
243: 19A.6 · What must be true for the service to deliver as intended
244: It is not a governor — it holds no mandate, asserts nothing about the estate, and gates nothing but submission format.
245: It is not the Owner's replacement — the build's largest course-corrections were frame changes, which this layer would catch none of, by design; claiming otherwise is exactly the overclaim its own anti-fabrication rubric item exists to flag.
246: It is not inline — nothing here adds a synchronous step to any serving path or a turn to the dispatch loop.
247: It makes no zero-residual claim — it halves the residual, measurably and repeatedly, and its own dashboard is built to show its misses, not hide them.
