249: PART B — STATUS: PROPOSED, NOT RATIFIED
250: 19B.1 · The promise, in plain language
251: No number earns the right to be quoted outside the platform until it resolves to a register row — its method, its judges, their measured agreement, the rubric version, and the source rows behind it. A judgement call becomes a published figure only through this door, never around it. This is my own synthesis, proposed for ratification in an August 2026 chat and never confirmed adopted; the source specification it responded to (sections A-1 through A-4) was not found as a standalone document in either repository, and neither the evidence register nor the dual-judge protocol appears anywhere in the current build. It is written here at full weight because the reasoning holds regardless of its ratification status — not to imply that status is settled.
252: 19B.2 · The service that powers it
253: No existing named engine. Proposed as one capability with two parts: an evidence register (a ledger-backed record, structurally similar to the Registry's own pattern) and the dual-judge protocol (A-2) as its scoring mechanism, applied wherever a judgement call is about to become a published number.
254: 19B.3 · Definition of the promise
255: The register's proposed schema: one row per figure, carrying the figure itself, the method that produced it, the judges and their versions, the rubric version applied, the inter-annotator agreement (kappa), the date, and the source rows it derives from. The standing rule proposed alongside it: no figure is quoted externally without resolving to a register row — mechanizing a discipline the platform already practises informally (the source chat cites an existing re-measurement practice, 1,523 revised to 1,559, as evidence the norm already exists in spirit; the register would make it structural rather than a matter of remembering to do it).
256: 19B.4 · Delivery experience expectations
257: Named application sites — proposed, not built
258: The terminal test itself: the platform's human-qualified benchmark slice, scored dual-judge with a published kappa — named as the highest-priority site, since the single verdict everything else rests on is currently single-judge.
259: Per-language custody recall: the claim most exposed under diligence, currently single-scored by design.
260: Model Acceptance (Document 17, MOAC): the canon already mandates human quality judgement over the six checks — that judgement is exactly the artifact dual-judging exists to make defensible.
261: Refusal correctness (Document 8): the refusal-health surface counts refusals today but scores whether the named rule actually justified each one; a sampled dual-judge audit would give the refusal grammar a measured integrity figure.
262: The existing verification loop: builder verification versus independent tester is already de facto dual-judge; recording their disagreement rate per cycle turns an existing process into a measured instrument at close to zero additional cost.
263: What is produced and retained, if adopted
264: The evidence register itself — the single place any externally-quoted figure must resolve to.
265: A-4, proposed as a companion mechanism, never a build gate: claims validation functioning as the re-entry path for previously killed backlog (a parked idea returns only with a three-arm result behind it) and as the bake-off court for competing implementation choices.
266: 19B.5 · Technical and behavioural requirements
267: Evidence register row (proposed)
268:   { figure, method, judges: [..], judge_versions: [..],
269:     rubric_version, kappa, date, source_rows: [..] }
270:   Standing rule: no figure quoted externally without
271:   resolving to a register row.
272: EP-1  [PROPOSED] Build the register first — cheapest piece, and it immediately hardens the custody-recall and Model Acceptance sites above.
273: EP-2  [PROPOSED] Dual-judge scoring (A-2) applies at every named site in §19B.4, plus any future site where a judgement call becomes a published number.
274: EP-3  [PROPOSED] A-4 (claims validation) rides inside this capability, scoped explicitly as validation, never a build gate — its real experiments require real material and naturally sequence after the terminal test.
275: EP-4  [OPEN] Hard ordering constraint, stated by the original proposal: the evidence register and dual-judge protocol must exist before the terminal test runs, or that test's verdict is single-judge permanently — there is no retroactive fix once the terminal test has already run single-judge.
276: EP-5  [PROPOSED] Explicitly not adopted, per the same proposal: the source spec's “insurance telemetry” aside (serves a goal never named) and its internal reduction-skill mandate (process tooling the Quality Rule Book already covers in doctrine — building enforcement machinery for it fails the platform's own reduction test).
277: 19B.6 · What must be true for the service to deliver as intended
278: No figure reaches an external document without a resolvable register row — stated as absolute in the proposal, not aspirational.
279: The register and protocol exist before the terminal test runs — the one constraint the proposal calls genuinely ordering rather than merely preferred.
280: A-4 never becomes a gate by drift — its scope is validation and re-entry, and staying there is a condition of adoption, not a detail.
281: This entire part remains PROPOSED, not CANON, until an explicit Owner ruling says otherwise — nothing above should be cited elsewhere as settled.

# SOURCE: assessment_workspace/canon/w11_new_docs/training_capacity.docx
Coordinate: document.xml paragraph in body order, tables included

1: SYNI.AI   ·   MODULE BRIEFING
2: Incremental Training & Capacity
3: A module for objective-driven model training, designed on the Theory of Constructive Operators
4: This document defines the module: the problem it solves, the theory it draws on, the concepts it introduces, the components that implement it, the surfaces it touches, and how it is built and validated. It is a platform module — modality-independent. Audio is its first consumer, not its container.
5: Contents
6: 1   The problem this module solves	2
7: 2   The theory, and the discipline around it	2
8: 3   Concepts and definitions	3
9: 4   Components	4
10: 5   Design rationale — why this shape	6
11: 6   Surfaces and handoffs	7
12: 7   Build order	8
13: 8   Validation gate	8
14: 9   Open decisions	9
15: 
16: 1  The problem this module solves
17: The platform trains models against specific customer objectives, on customer estates, as commissioned work. Four problems arise in that setting, and they compound.
18: 1.1  Every objective starts from nothing
19: A commission trains a model for an objective. A later commission on the same estate trains for a related objective and begins again — no record exists of what the first model demonstrably learned, at what level, on which material. Capability is produced and then lost as an asset. The second commission costs what the first cost, indefinitely.
20: 1.2  Nobody knows what an objective actually demands
21: An objective arrives as a description of a desired outcome. Nothing converts it into a statement of what the model must be able to do — how many distinct capabilities must be correct at the same moment for a single output to be right. Without that, planning is guesswork: the work is scoped by intuition, priced by analogy, and the first real evidence of difficulty arrives after the compute is spent.
22: 1.3  Gaps are discovered, not predicted
23: Trained models fail unevenly. They perform on the material the corpus is rich in and fail on the variants it is thin in — minority dialects, degraded channels, code-switched speech, unusual document conditions. Today those gaps surface at evaluation, after training. Nothing in the process identifies, before training begins, which strata are at risk and why.
24: 1.4  The corpus’s own skew steers the model
25: Left to its natural distribution, training follows whatever the estate holds most of. That is not neutral: it actively pulls the model toward the dominant variant and away from the ones that most need deliberate attention. The skew is invisible in the training configuration and visible only in the results.
26: 
27: The module addresses all four with one mechanism: state what an objective demands, measure what the trainer already holds, plan from the difference, and record what each commission adds.
28: 2  The theory, and the discipline around it
29: 2.1  What the Theory of Constructive Operators says
30: Juan Pascual-Leone’s Theory of Constructive Operators explains why children move between cognitive stages. Piaget described the stages; TCO supplies the mechanism. A child can perform a task when their mental attentional capacity — how many mental schemes they can hold and coordinate at once — meets the number of schemes the task requires coordinated simultaneously. Capacity grows with development; when it crosses a task’s demand, the task becomes solvable.
31: The theory also describes forces acting on that capacity: a field pull toward whatever is perceptually dominant, and silent operators that boost relevant schemes and suppress interfering ones. It distinguishes facilitating situations, where the obvious response is the correct one, from misleading situations, where capacity must be spent inhibiting a wrong but dominant response.
32: 2.2  What transfers to model training
33: The structural correspondence is close enough to be useful without being forced:
34: TCO
35: Module equivalent
36: Schemes
37: Trained capabilities — what a model demonstrably does, held as reusable units.
38: Capacity (M-power)
39: What a model line demonstrably holds, measured on the estate.
40: Task demand (M-demand)
41: What an objective requires held at once, computed at compile.
42: Baseline plus growth
43: A frozen base model plus incrementally trained capability.
44: Stage transition on capacity meeting demand
45: A training stage is admissible only when its demand is within reach of measured capacity.
46: Field pull
47: The corpus’s natural distribution — the majority variant’s gravity.
48: Silent operators (boost / suppress)
49: Curriculum weighting, and no-regression gates against interference with prior capability.
50: Facilitating vs misleading situations
51: Strata the data supports, versus strata where surface statistics work against the required behaviour.
52: 2.3  The discipline: shape, not numbers
53: What the module borrows is the shape — measure capacity, compute demand, stage transitions by the gap, reuse what is held, guard against interference. What it does not borrow is any quantity. TCO’s growth rates and capacity units are empirical claims about children; they say nothing about transformers on a broadcast archive.
54: Every rate, step and threshold in this module is measured per commission. Nothing is assumed from the theory, and the module’s central claim — that demand-staged training produces fewer gaps than flat training — is held unpublished until it is measured (§8).
55: 3  Concepts and definitions
56: Seven terms carry the module. They are used with these meanings throughout the platform.
57: 3.1  Scheme
58: A discrete, named, reusable capability a model either holds or does not — for example, entity recognition in a given language, transcription under telephone-band conditions, table extraction from degraded scans, clause identification in commercial contracts. Schemes are modality-independent and drawn from a shared taxonomy so that a scheme name means the same thing across commissions.
59: 3.2  Stratum
60: A defined slice of material with distinct characteristics — a language variant, a channel condition, a document class, an accent cluster. Strata come from the platform’s registry work: they are what the estate is actually made of, measured rather than assumed. Demand, capacity and acceptance are all expressed per stratum, because that is where performance genuinely differs.
61: 3.3  Coordination breadth (B)
62: For a required output, the number of schemes that must be simultaneously correct for that output to be correct. B is the maximum co-activation across the objective’s outputs — not a total inventory of everything the objective touches somewhere.
63: Worked example. For the output “brand X was mentioned by presenter Y at time T”, three schemes must all be right at once: transcription in the segment’s language, brand entity recognition, and speaker attribution. B = 3. On code-switched segments, switch handling must also be right at the same moment: B = 4. The same objective therefore makes different demands of different strata, which is precisely what the table is for.
64: 3.4  Interference (I)
65: A per-stratum flag marking strata where the corpus’s natural pull opposes the required behaviour — majority-variant gravity over a minority variant, cross-language model pull on non-English text, frequency pull from heavily repeated material. In TCO terms these are misleading situations: capacity must be spent suppressing a dominant wrong response, so interference adds to demand rather than sitting beside it.
66: I is binary at introduction. It is re-weighted only if calibration data shows misleading strata cost more than one unit of capacity — measured, never assumed.
67: 3.5  Effective demand (E)
68: E = B + I, per stratum. Effective demand is a fact about the objective: model-independent, portable across model lines, computed once at compile and never revised downstream.
69: 3.6  Capacity (C)
70: What a model line demonstrably holds, per scheme, at a measured level — established by probing during calibration, not inferred from training history. Capacity is a fact about the trainer on a particular estate, and it changes as commissions complete.
71: 3.7  Gap, step, and saturation
72: Gap = E − C per stratum. It is what the plan must close, and the planner’s first computation.
73: Step = how much new coordination the model absorbs in one stage while retaining what it already holds. Measured at calibration on this estate; never a constant.
74: Saturation = the state of a capability whose measured level stops moving as data is added. Derived from marginal-gain records, never declared.
75: 4  Components
76: Four components implement the module. Each attaches to a surface that already exists; none is a new service.
77: 4.1  The Demand Table
78: Compiled by the Objective Wizard alongside the TargetOutcome and Collection Schema, for every objective. It states what the objective requires, per stratum.
79: DemandTable {
80:   schemes[]      each: { id, named_failure }
81:   per_stratum {
82:     B            coordination breadth — max simultaneous co-activation
83:     I            interference flag — corpus pull opposes required behaviour
84:     E = B + I    effective demand
85:   }
86: }
87: 
88: The admissibility rule
89: A scheme enters the table only with its named failure — the concrete thing that breaks without it. “Code-switch handling, because entity boundaries break at switch points” is admissible. “Robustness” is not. The compile stage rejects unnamed-failure schemes as it rejects an objective with no test set.
90: This rule exists for one reason: it keeps the table a surgical map of what the objective actually needs, rather than an inventory that grows to look thorough. A demand count that cannot be audited to named failures is a busyness score, and would corrupt every plan built on it.
91: 4.2  The Capacity Ledger
92: A modality within the existing registry service — not a new store. It records what has been built, so the next commission does not begin from nothing.
93: CapacityEntry {
94:   scheme_id
95:   stratum        per-stratum where flagged; ‘global’ otherwise
96:   level          measured, from calibration
97:   provenance[]   which commission(s) built it
98:   marginal_gain  what the last data increment moved
99:   state          building | held | saturated   (derived)
100: }
101: 
102: Resolution rule
103: Per-stratum entries for schemes touched by strata flagged I = 1, plus any stratum the objective’s acceptance gates on. Global entries elsewhere. Precision where risk lives, economy everywhere else: the ledger can afford completeness, but the calibration probe suite must stay selective or it becomes the expensive part of every commission.
104: 4.3  The capacity probe
105: An addition to Sampling & Reflection — the calibration stage that already precedes every commissioned training run. It gains one function and changes nothing else:
106: Read the ledger for the schemes named in the Demand Table.
107: Probe only what the resolution rule requires: which schemes are held, at what level, per flagged stratum.
108: Measure the step — how much new coordination the model absorbs while retaining prior capability.
109: Write marginal-gain rows back to the ledger.
110: Calibration continues to do what it already did: price the job and author the proposed milestone list. It now also answers what the trainer already knows.
111: 4.4  Gap-shaped staged plans
112: The Training Planner’s first computation becomes the gap, and the plan takes its shape from it:
113: Small gap — compose the schemes already held; train only the residual.
114: Large gap — a staged curriculum: stages ordered by ascending effective demand, facilitating strata before misleading ones, each stage introducing no more new coordination than the measured step.
115: Stage gate — each stage must retain prior capability, checked against earlier stage test sets, before the next opens. This is the suppression half of the mechanism: growth that destroys what came before is not growth.
116: Near-saturated schemes — shift the quote from training spend to composition work, before the quote is issued.
117: 5  Design rationale — why this shape
118: 5.1  Demand travels with the objective; capacity stays with the trainer
119: Demand is analytic and model-independent: the same objective makes the same demand of any model that attempts it, so it is computed once at compile and travels with the objective. Capacity and growth rate are empirical and specific: they belong to a model line on an estate, and are measured at calibration.
120: Mixing them would make objectives non-portable and put invented constants into the compile stage — the exact failure the analogy discipline (§2.3) exists to prevent.
121: 5.2  Per-stratum resolution, selectively probed
122: Global capability figures hide the failures that matter: a model at a high average can be failing the minority stratum entirely. Per-stratum resolution is where the module earns its value. But probing every scheme on every stratum would make calibration the dominant cost of a commission, so resolution is full in the ledger and selective in the probe.
123: 5.3  Provenance ships on day one
124: Every capacity write records which commission built it. Nothing in the module requires this today. It is included now because a ledger without provenance cannot later answer whose data built a capability — and that question must be answerable before any capability is ever shared across commissions or tenants, given that trained models are the customer’s property.
125: It is the one field that cannot be retrofitted: adding it later means rebuilding the ledger from source.
126: 5.4  Saturation is a discount, not a checkpoint
127: As incremental modelling matures, later commissions increasingly find their demand already met and additional data stops moving measured capability. The module makes that visible without making it a burden:
128: Derived, never declared. Computed from marginal-gain rows calibration already writes. No one enters it; no one maintains it.
129: Informational, never gating. Nothing blocks on saturation. No ceremony to enter or exit the state. No user action is ever required by it.
130: Acts only in the customer’s favour. Its single effect is the quote shift in §4.4 — cheaper composition instead of futile training.
131: Shared-learning policy — cross-commission transfer, common substrates, tenant boundaries — is deliberately deferred until marginal-gain data exists to inform it. The schema above is sufficient preparation; deciding the policy now would be assertion where measurement is pending.
132: 6  Surfaces and handoffs
133: The module touches six surfaces and introduces no new one. It adds no human approval anywhere: the only decisions in the journey remain the two that already exist — the objective owner agrees milestones at commission, and decides on a budget-ceiling breach.
134: Surface
135: What the module adds
136: Objective Wizard
137: Compiles the Demand Table alongside its existing outputs; enforces the named-failure admissibility rule at compile.
138: Capability taxonomy
139: A shared scheme vocabulary, governed by the existing propose–qualify–graduate mechanism — no new governance body.
140: Registry (Mtafiti)
141: A capacity modality holding the ledger. Not a new service.
142: Sampling & Reflection
143: The capacity probe; marginal-gain writes; the measured step.
144: Training Planner
145: Gap as first computation; staged curricula; composition-versus-training split.
146: Commission View
147: Stages appear as milestones with no-regression as done-conditions — the existing surface, no new display machinery.
148: Record (Northena)
149: Stage gates, regression results and capacity writes stamp under training data classes on the one record.
150: 
151: 6.1  Handoff chain
152: Each step produces a typed artifact with a single owner. The consumer is prohibited from redoing what the producer guaranteed — redoing upstream work is a specification violation, not diligence.
153: Step → owner
154: Produces
155: Consumer must not
156: Compile → Objective Wizard
157: Demand Table (with TargetOutcome and Collection Schema)
158: Re-validate schemes; recompute demand
159: Probe → Sampling & Reflection
160: Capacity Report; marginal-gain rows; measured step
161: Re-probe held schemes; assume unreported capacity
162: Plan → Training Planner
163: Stage Plan; quote ± interval; proposed milestones
164: Re-measure capacity; re-derive demand
165: Commission → objective owner
166: Agreed milestones (the stage gates verbatim)
167: Add approval layers
168: Train → commissioned jobs
169: Stage results; regression results; capacity writes with provenance
170: Advance past a failed gate; write capacity without provenance
171: Close → registry and record
172: Sealed namespace; completion certificate
173: Duplicate records
174: 
175: Ownership check: demand is computed only at compile; capacity only at probe; the plan only at plan; approval only at commission; capability writes only during training. No surface owns the same value twice.
176: 7  Build order
177: Six items. Order is by dependency, and by what becomes expensive if deferred.
178: #
179: Item
180: Depends on
181: Complete when
182: 1
183: Capability taxonomy
184: —
185: Scheme identity is stable across commissions; graduation runs on the existing propose–qualify–graduate path.
186: 2
187: Capacity Ledger schema
188: 1
189: Writes without provenance are unrepresentable; the resolution rule is implemented; saturation is a legal state with no logic attached.
190: 3
191: Demand Table in wizard compile
192: 1
193: The compile stage rejects unnamed-failure schemes; B, I and E are emitted per stratum; the table is stamped to the record with the session.
194: 4
195: Capacity probe in Sampling & Reflection
196: 2, 3
197: Calibration reads the ledger, probes selectively, measures the step, and writes marginal gain.
198: 5
199: Gap-shaped staged planning
200: 3, 4
201: The planner computes the gap first; stages respect the measured step; near-saturated schemes are quoted as composition.
202: 6
203: Staged runs with no-regression gates
204: 5
205: A staged plan executes end to end; a failed gate halts advance and reports plainly; gates surface as milestone done-conditions.
206: 
207: Items 1 and 2 carry the deferral cost. Taxonomy instability makes every later scheme name ambiguous, and a ledger without provenance must be rebuilt from source rather than amended.
208: 8  Validation gate
209: The module makes one mechanism claim: that demand-staged training produces better coverage — particularly on misleading strata — than training on the corpus’s natural distribution or on a flat curriculum. That claim is held until it is measured.
210: 8.1  The experiment
211: Three arms, equal budget, scored per stratum under the platform’s blind dual-judge protocol:
212: Baseline: training on the corpus’s natural distribution.
213: Naive control: a flat curriculum — deliberate ordering, but without demand computation or staging.
214: Full mechanism: demand-staged curriculum with no-regression gates.
215: The naive control is the arm that matters: it isolates whether the structure does the work, or whether deliberate ordering alone would have produced the same result.
216: 8.2  What follows from the result
217: If staging beats the flat curriculum on misleading-strata acceptance, the claim is published with its measurement. If it does not, the claim is not published — internally or externally — and the Demand Table remains in force regardless, because task analysis and the capacity ledger earn their place independent of whether staging outperforms.
218: The result is recorded either way. A negative result retires the claim, not the record.
219: 9  Open decisions
220: Decision
221: Note
222: Taxonomy graduation sign-off
223: Which product role owns admitting a new scheme to the shared taxonomy.
224: Probe-selectivity threshold
225: Proposed default: per-stratum resolution for strata flagged I = 1, plus strata the objective’s acceptance gates on. Confirm or adjust.
226: Validation gating
227: Whether §8 must complete before staged plans are used on customer commissions, or runs in parallel with the first. Gating is more honest; parallel is faster.
228: Interference weighting
229: I is binary at introduction. Decide the trigger for moving to a weighted I — proposed: calibration data showing misleading strata consistently cost more than one unit.
230: 
231: End of briefing. This module is platform-wide and modality-independent; the audio intelligence plane is its first consumer. Component-level contracts are carried in the Incremental Training & Capacity Specification.

# SOURCE: assessment_workspace/canon/w11_new_docs/training_techniques.docx
Coordinate: document.xml paragraph in body order, tables included

1: AKKI · GOVERNED ARTIFACT · REQUIREMENTS SPECIFICATION
2: Training & Optimization Techniques Specification v1.0
3: The training-recipe seat · optimizer selection · ensemble critics · cascade offload · Owner-ratified · 2026-07-17
4: Scope and reading guide: this specification governs four technique areas in Akki's model-producing and quality-assurance paths. It is written for a reader with no prior context: §1 supplies the systems each requirement references. Adoption principle, Owner-ratified: a technique enters the platform only where proven use cases match the platform's targeted results, and every adoption decision is made on measured evidence from the platform's own material. Normative language: MUST / MUST NOT / MAY. Evidence classes on values: FACT (established, verifiable) · NORM (anchored in a defensible range) · DEFAULT (operating constant, revisable on evidence without reopening this document).
5: §1 — Referenced systems
6: Model training path: Akki trains adapters (LoRA/PEFT) on registered open base models, using qualified, de-duplicated units from the customer estate. Trained models are accepted through MOAC — six criteria including improvement over base (M-a), no collateral regression (M-b), lineage completeness (M-d), and calibration (M-e) — defined in the Transformation Quality Specification v1.0 §6.
7: P4 baseline harness: the first real-material run of any extraction or training pipeline is instrumented by design — utilization, throughput, and quality deltas emitted from run one (EAB Tier-1 Adoption Spec v1.1, Part X).
8: The Critic Seam: the three-tier QA layer for worker output — deterministic checks, an independent critic model, human calibration with seeded-defect audits (Critic Seam Specification v1.0). QA-1: the layer detects and never decides.
9: F3 run telemetry: every run emits throughput telemetry; cost columns activate only when compute is metered.
10: ES-4: efficiency machinery builds only against a measured shortfall; a measured shortfall makes it mandatory.
11: D-7: verdicts are never curated — evaluation inputs may be engineered, evaluation samples may not.
12: §2 — T-1 · The training-recipe seat
13: Purpose
14: Every trained model must be reproducible and attributable to the exact configuration that produced it, and configuration must improve only on evidence. The recipe seat makes training configuration a governed, versioned object rather than code.
15: Requirements
16: T-1.1 · All training configuration — optimizer and its parameters, learning-rate schedule, batch and epoch parameters, adapter rank and target modules — MUST live under training_params@v0, a sidecar configuration class with the same discipline as extraction_params@v0: versioned, ledgered, outside contracts/, no Parity contact.
17: T-1.2 · The seat ships EMPTY. No default recipe exists until the first training run fills it through the §3 protocol.
18: T-1.3 · Every trained model's registry entry MUST cite the recipe_version that trained it. MOAC M-d (lineage) extends by this field.
19: T-1.4 · Recipe revisions are DEFAULT-class: no approval ceremony. Each revision MUST attach the measured comparison that justifies it and MUST write a ledger row. A revision without attached evidence is a defect.
20: T-1.5 · Foundation methods (FACT, standing from Operating Values §1–§2): LoRA/PEFT adapters on registered open bases; training material drawn exclusively from de-duplicated, VAD-cleaned, qualified units; acceptance exclusively through MOAC on uncurated held-out sets.
21: §3 — T-2 · Optimizer selection protocol
22: Purpose
23: The optimizer is a recipe component with material effect on compute cost and model quality. Candidate optimizers — Muon is the first named candidate — are selected by measured comparison on the platform's own workload, because published optimizer results concentrate at transformer pretraining scale and the platform's workload is adapter fine-tuning.
24: Requirements
25: T-2.1 Trigger: the protocol executes at the first adapter training on real material, inside the P4-instrumented run.
26: T-2.2 Shape: one two-arm comparison — the baseline optimizer versus the candidate — with identical training data, identical base model, identical evaluation sets, and an identical compute budget cap, executed on the smallest stratum that yields a valid MOAC evaluation. The comparison's cost MUST be disclosed in the carrying phase's LoC/compute band.
27: T-2.3 Measured outputs: target-stratum improvement (the MOAC M-a metric) · non-target regression (M-b) · wall-clock and GPU-hours to convergence · calibration quality (M-e input). All four MUST be reported for both arms.
28: T-2.4 Verdict rule: quality parity on M-a and M-b is MANDATORY for a candidate to remain eligible. Compute-to-convergence is REPORTED. The adopt/reject decision is an Owner ruling made on the measured results; no adoption threshold exists in advance of the evidence. Verdict samples are uncurated per D-7.
29: T-2.5 Outcome recording: on adoption, the winning arm writes training_params@v0 v1 with the comparison attached (satisfying T-1.4). On rejection, the candidate is recorded as tested with its numbers. Either way the result is permanent record.
30: T-2.6 Recurrence: the same protocol governs every future optimizer or recipe-component candidate: two arms, identical conditions, parity mandatory, Owner-ruled on evidence.
31: §4 — T-3 · Ensemble critics
32: Purpose
33: Detection quality in the Critic Seam may require more than one reviewing instance. Ensembles are legitimate for detection and prohibited for decision: multiple reviewers may surface findings; no collection of models may hold decision authority on any platform surface. This boundary is permanent and follows from the platform's design (one walled learner; one reasoning faculty; QA-1).
34: Requirements
35: T-3.1 Deployment order: when Tier-3 seeded audits show single-critic catch-rate below the standing bar on any fall class across two consecutive audits, rubric and context repair MUST execute first. An ensemble MAY deploy only if the repaired critic still misses on a subsequent audit.
36: T-3.2 Independence: ensemble members MUST differ genuinely — a different base model, or a materially different context shape. Same-base, same-context replicas are prohibited: correlated reviewers share failure modes and add cost without detection gain (FACT, established ensemble-diversity results).
37: T-3.3 Findings-only: all ensemble output is findings, per QA-1. Voting, override, and critic-of-critic structures are prohibited.
38: T-3.4 Disagreement: disagreement between critics is itself a finding class (CRITIC-DISAGREE), routed to rulings like every finding class.
39: T-3.5 Bounds: N ≤ 3 members without an Owner ruling. Cost-per-review telemetry MUST be emitted per member.
40: T-3.6 Rent: the ensemble retires if its catch-rate gain over the single repaired critic is under 10pp (DEFAULT) after one full calibration cycle.
41: §5 — T-4 · Local-cascade LLM offload
42: Purpose
43: Where a metered LLM carries workload that cheaper local models could filter, a cascade — local model drafts, LLM handles only what the local model cannot — reduces spend. Cascades carry a documented failure mode: when too many items escalate, each escalated item pays twice and the cascade is net-negative. The platform already minimizes LLM load by construction (the rung ladder; record-derived facts are never re-asked of the LLM; the mechanical composition arm; the critic-succession seat), so a cascade builds only against demonstrated cost pressure.
44: Requirements
45: T-4.1 Trigger: cascade work MAY begin only when F3 telemetry, with cost columns active, shows LLM spend on a named seam exceeding a threshold the Owner sets at that time. No threshold is defined in advance of metered evidence.
46: T-4.2 Pre-work: before the trigger, no cascade scaffolding, draft-model acquisition, or routing machinery may be built (D7 fence). ES-4 governs: a measured shortfall makes the build mandatory; absent one, it never builds.
47: T-4.3 Shape: local model drafts → deterministic acceptance check → LLM invoked only on rejects. The acceptance check is rung-1 machinery, not a second model judgment.
48: T-4.4 Kill metric: the double-pay rate — the share of items incurring both local and LLM cost. The cascade MUST emit it from first run and MUST retire if escalation makes the cascade net-negative against the pre-cascade baseline.
49: §6 — Registry and execution
50: R4 registry rows for these requirements land only with their carrying phases: T-1 and T-2 with the first training phase; T-3 with a Critic Seam calibration phase; T-4 only if its trigger fires. Nothing lands from this specification alone.
51: This document is the drafting source for those phases' Stage As. It lands on-disk as requirements canon with the first carrying phase, or earlier on Owner word, via the standard doc-landing pattern (verbatim conversion, SHA reply, governance pointer).
52: Syni.ai · Training & Optimization Techniques Specification v1.0 · 2026-07-17 · Companion to: Operating Values v1.0 · Transformation Quality Specification v1.0 · Critic Seam Specification v1.0 · EAB Tier-1 Adoption Specification v1.1
